Aggregate 35 problems

▼

A single table of granular records → one summary row per group with aggregated values.

Signal words: "for each," "per," "how many," "total," "average," "count of," "at least N"

Technique: GROUP BY, HAVING, COUNT DISTINCT, CASE WHEN inside aggregates, self-join + GROUP BY

Reference Techniques used in Aggregate Per Group

▼

5 SQL techniques relevant to this recipe, with what they do, when to reach for them, and a generic code example.

Technique What It Does When to Reach for It Example Code
GROUP BY Collapses rows into one row per group so aggregates can be computed The output needs one summary row per group (per department, per month, per user) 
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM Emp
GROUP BY dept;
HAVING Filters groups after GROUP BY, using aggregate results The condition depends on a count, sum, or other aggregate (e.g., "groups with more than 1 row") 
SELECT dept, COUNT(*)
FROM Emp
GROUP BY dept
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;
SUM / COUNT / AVG / MAX / MIN Computes a single summary value from multiple rows With GROUP BY: one value per group. Without GROUP BY: one value for the whole table 
SELECT MAX(salary) AS top_pay,
       AVG(salary) AS mean_pay,
       COUNT(*)    AS headcount
FROM Emp;
CASE WHEN Returns different values based on conditional logic, like an if/else per row You need to classify, label, or remap values based on conditions 
SELECT name,
       CASE WHEN age >= 18 THEN 'Adult'
            ELSE 'Minor' END AS group
FROM Users;
DISTINCT Removes duplicate rows from the output You want unique values but do not need a count or other aggregate 
SELECT DISTINCT country
FROM Customers;

Easy #2356 Number of Unique Subjects Taught by Each Teacher

▼

For each teacher, count distinct subjects taught (across all departments).

Schema: Teacher(teacher_id, subject_id, dept_id)

Goal: For each teacher, count distinct subjects taught (across all departments).

Why this matters
Universities need to understand teacher versatility and curriculum coverage.
▶ Rank 1: Simple GROUP BY + COUNT(DISTINCT)
SELECT teacher_id, COUNT(DISTINCT subject_id) AS cnt FROM Teacher GROUP BY teacher_id ORDER BY teacher_id;

Why rank 1: Straightforward, efficient. COUNT(DISTINCT col) handles duplicates automatically. Single scan of the table with in-database deduplication.

Performance: O(n) with early aggregation. No subqueries or joins.

Easy #1729 Find Followers Count

▼

For each user, count how many followers they have. Ordered by user_id ascending.

Schema: Followers(user_id, follower_id)

Goal: For each user, count how many followers they have. Ordered by user_id ascending.

Why this matters
Social media platforms need to track influence and user engagement metrics at scale.
▶ Rank 1: GROUP BY user_id + COUNT + ORDER BY
SELECT user_id, COUNT(follower_id) AS followers_count FROM Followers GROUP BY user_id ORDER BY user_id ASC;

Why rank 1: Direct aggregation with sorting. Each user_id groups all their followers; COUNT(follower_id) tallies each group.

Performance: Single pass with sort at the end (linear for small result sets). No risk of NULL issues since we count a NOT-NULL column.

Easy #596 Classes With at Least 5 Students

▼

Find all classes with 5 or more students (filter after grouping).

Schema: Courses(student, class)

Goal: Find all classes with 5 or more students (filter after grouping).

Why this matters
Schools use enrollment thresholds to determine whether classes run or merge; HR departments filter teams by minimum size for resource allocation.
▶ Rank 1: GROUP BY class + HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5
SELECT class FROM Courses GROUP BY class HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5;

Why rank 1: HAVING is the correct clause for filtering groups after aggregation. WHERE runs before GROUP BY, so it can't see aggregate results.

Performance: O(n log n) due to grouping, but scales well. HAVING condition is evaluated after aggregation, avoiding unnecessary work.

⚠️
Common Trap
Using WHERE instead of HAVING: WHERE COUNT(*) >= 5 will error because WHERE runs before GROUP BY. Always use HAVING for aggregate conditions.

Medium #1211 Queries Quality and Percentage

▼

For each query_name, calculate quality (avg of rating/position) and poor_query_percentage (% with rating < 3), both rounded to 2 decimals.

Schema: Queries(query_name, result, position, rating)

Goal: For each query_name, calculate quality (avg of rating/position) and poor_query_percentage (% with rating < 3), both rounded to 2 decimals.

Why this matters
Search engine and database optimization: ranking quality by position and user satisfaction (rating), identifying low-quality queries for improvement.
▶ Rank 1: GROUP BY + AVG(rating/position) + Conditional Aggregation
SELECT query_name, ROUND(AVG(rating::numeric / position), 2) AS quality, ROUND(100 * SUM(CASE WHEN rating < 3 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS poor_query_percentage FROM Queries GROUP BY query_name ORDER BY quality DESC, query_name;

Why rank 1: Demonstrates conditional aggregation with CASE WHEN inside SUM/COUNT. The casting to numeric avoids integer division. Single pass through data.

Performance: O(n) scan with in-database aggregation. CASE WHEN is evaluated row-by-row within each group.

⚠️
Integer Division Trap
In PostgreSQL, integer / integer = integer (truncates). Cast to numeric: rating::numeric / position, or use CAST. Otherwise 1 / 200 = 0 instead of 0.005.

Easy #1141 User Activity for the Past 30 Days I

▼

Count daily active users (DAU) for a 30-day period ending 2019-07-27. A user is active if they had ≥1 activity on that day.

Tables: Activity (user_id, session_id, activity_date, activity_type)

View on LeetCode →

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern A: Row-Level Filtering + Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation

Real-World Example

Product analytics generates Daily Active Users (DAU) metrics for management dashboards. A 30-day rolling metric shows user engagement trends; users with multiple activities in one day count as 1 DAU.

▶ 1 WHERE with Date Range + GROUP BY + COUNT DISTINCT
SELECT activity_date AS day, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS active_users FROM Activity WHERE activity_date BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27' GROUP BY activity_date ORDER BY activity_date;

Why this is best: BETWEEN filters to exact 30-day window (inclusive both ends). COUNT DISTINCT user_id deduplicates multiple activities per user per day. Simple and efficient.

Performance: O(n) for WHERE, then aggregation. Index on activity_date helps filter. COUNT DISTINCT adds minimal cost (hash or sort).

▶ 2 WHERE with Date Arithmetic
SELECT activity_date AS day, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS active_users FROM Activity WHERE activity_date >= '2019-07-27' - INTERVAL '29 days' AND activity_date <= '2019-07-27' GROUP BY activity_date ORDER BY activity_date;

Why this works: Dynamically calculates date range from end date. "29 days" (not 30) because we include both endpoints. Useful for parameterized queries (pass @end_date dynamically).

Performance: Identical to approach #1. INTERVAL syntax varies (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLServer differ). Slightly more flexible.

▶ 3 Subquery with DISTINCT (Less Efficient)
SELECT activity_date AS day, COUNT(*) AS active_users FROM ( SELECT DISTINCT user_id, activity_date FROM Activity WHERE activity_date BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27' ) unique_activities GROUP BY activity_date ORDER BY activity_date;

Why this works: Subquery deduplicates (user_id, activity_date) pairs first, then GROUP BY counts. COUNT(*) instead of COUNT DISTINCT on pre-deduplicated data.

Performance: Subquery adds overhead: extra scan for DISTINCT, then outer GROUP BY. Slower than approach #1 (two aggregation passes). Use only if readability strongly preferred.

Medium #1193 Monthly Transactions I

▼

For each month and country, count total transactions and sum amount, plus count and sum of approved transactions only.

Schema: Transactions(id, country, state, amount, trans_date) where state is 'approved' or 'declined'

Goal: For each month and country, count total transactions and sum amount, plus count and sum of approved transactions only.

Why this matters
Financial reporting and compliance: tracking transaction volumes and values by geography and time, separately for approved vs. all transactions to measure approval rates and fraud risk.
▶ Rank 1: GROUP BY month + country + Conditional SUM for approved
SELECT TO_CHAR(trans_date, 'YYYY-MM') AS month, country, COUNT(*) AS trans_count, SUM(amount) AS trans_total_amount, SUM(CASE WHEN state = 'approved' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS approved_count, SUM(CASE WHEN state = 'approved' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS approved_total_amount FROM Transactions GROUP BY TO_CHAR(trans_date, 'YYYY-MM'), country ORDER BY month, country;

Why rank 1: Single pass with all metrics calculated in one GROUP BY. CASE WHEN inside SUM filters by state for conditional aggregation. TO_CHAR formats dates to YYYY-MM.

Performance: O(n) scan. All aggregations happen in one group-by phase—very efficient.

💡
Date Formatting
PostgreSQL uses TO_CHAR for date formatting. MySQL uses DATE_FORMAT. Always adjust for your database system. Some systems also support DATE_TRUNC for month boundaries.

Medium #1612 Monthly Transactions II

▼

Extend #1193 with chargebacks: for each month and country, report approved count/amount and chargeback count/amount, excluding all zero rows.

Schema: Transactions(id, country, state, amount, trans_date), Chargebacks(trans_id, trans_date)

Goal: For each month and country, report approved_count, approved_amount, chargeback_count, chargeback_amount. Chargebacks use the chargeback date (not the original transaction date). Exclude rows where all four values are zero.

View on LeetCode →

Why this matters
Chargeback monitoring is critical for payment fraud detection and merchant risk scoring. Combining approved transactions with chargebacks by month and country reveals dispute hotspots and helps compliance teams flag anomalies.

Composite (3 moves): Move 1: pre-filter (WHERE state = 'approved' so declined rows never enter the pipeline). Move 2: enrich + union-stack (JOIN chargebacks to transactions for country/amount, then UNION ALL both streams with a type label). Move 3: pivot-aggregate (conditional SUM/COUNT by type).

▶ Rank 1: Pre-filter + UNION ALL + Conditional Aggregation
WITH approved AS ( SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', trans_date)::date AS month, country, amount FROM Transactions WHERE state = 'approved' ), chargebacks AS ( SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', c.trans_date)::date AS month, t.country, t.amount FROM Chargebacks AS c JOIN Transactions AS t ON c.trans_id = t.id ), stacked AS ( SELECT month, country, amount, 'approved' AS type FROM approved UNION ALL SELECT month, country, amount, 'chargeback' AS type FROM chargebacks ) SELECT TO_CHAR(month, 'YYYY-MM') AS month, country, SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'approved' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS approved_count, SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'approved' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS approved_amount, SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'chargeback' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS chargeback_count, SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'chargeback' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS chargeback_amount FROM stacked GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1;

Why this works: Three CTEs, each with one job. approved pre-filters to only approved transactions, so declined rows never enter the pipeline. chargebacks joins to the original transaction for country and amount, using the chargeback date for the month. stacked combines both streams with a clean type label. The final SELECT pivots with conditional aggregation.

Performance: Two scans (Transactions + Chargebacks), one join, one UNION ALL, one GROUP BY pass.

Key details:

  • Pre-filter eliminates HAVING: by excluding declined transactions upfront, every row in stacked contributes to at least one output column, so no all zero rows can form
  • Chargeback date vs transaction date: the problem counts chargebacks by when they were filed (c.trans_date), not when the original transaction occurred
  • Type label instead of flag: a readable 'approved' / 'chargeback' string makes the CASE WHEN expressions self documenting
  • No DISTINCT needed: source tables have unique rows, so DISTINCT adds overhead without changing results
💡
Builds on #1193
#1193 Monthly Transactions I uses the same conditional aggregation pattern but on a single table. This sequel adds a second table (Chargebacks) requiring a UNION ALL stack. The key insight: pre-filtering to approved transactions avoids the all zero row problem entirely, eliminating the need for a HAVING clause.

Easy #1731 The Number of Employees Which Report to Each Employee

▼

For each manager (employee with at least 1 direct report), show their id, name, count of direct reports, and average age of reports (rounded).

Schema: Employees(employee_id, name, reports_to, age)

Goal: For each manager (employee with at least 1 direct report), show their id, name, count of direct reports, and average age of reports (rounded).

Why this matters
Organizational hierarchies and team management: understanding span of control and team composition (age diversity, team size).
▶ Rank 1: Self-JOIN + GROUP BY + HAVING COUNT >= 1
SELECT e1.employee_id, e1.name, COUNT(e2.employee_id) AS reports_count, ROUND(AVG(e2.age)) AS average_age FROM Employees e1 JOIN Employees e2 ON e1.employee_id = e2.reports_to GROUP BY e1.employee_id, e1.name HAVING COUNT(e2.employee_id) >= 1 ORDER BY e1.employee_id;

Why rank 1: Self-join connects each employee to their direct reports. GROUP BY manager, aggregate report counts and ages. HAVING filters to managers only.

Performance: O(n log n). The inner join naturally excludes employees with no reports (no matching rows), so HAVING >= 1 is implicit and safe.

Note on ROUND
PostgreSQL's ROUND(numeric) rounds to nearest integer. For 38.5, it rounds to 39 (banker's rounding in some versions, but standard rounding in others—test with your database).

Medium #570 Managers with at Least 5 Direct Reports

▼

Find managers (employees who have ≥5 direct reports). Return manager names.

Tables: Employee (id, name, department, managerId)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Self-Join & Relational Queries → Pattern E: Self-Joins

Real-World Example

Organizational analysis identifies managers with large span of control. HR uses this to assess management workload and plan succession for high-span-of-control roles.

▶ 1 Self-Join with GROUP BY and HAVING
SELECT m.name FROM Employee e JOIN Employee m ON e.managerId = m.id GROUP BY m.id, m.name HAVING COUNT(e.id) >= 5;

Why this is best: Self-join pairs each employee (e) with their manager (m). GROUP BY m aggregates reports per manager. HAVING filters to ≥5. Clear intent.

Performance: O(n log n) for self-join. Hash join optimal. Index on (managerId) speeds up join. One pass for GROUP BY/HAVING.

▶ 2 Subquery with IN
SELECT name FROM Employee WHERE id IN ( SELECT managerId FROM Employee WHERE managerId IS NOT NULL GROUP BY managerId HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5 );

Why this works: Subquery finds manager IDs with ≥5 reports, then outer query retrieves their names. Two-stage: aggregate first, then fetch.

Performance: Two scans. IN with subquery has been optimized in modern DBs to equivalent of join. Slightly slower if subquery returns many managers, but often comparable to approach #1.

▶ 3 Window Function (PostgreSQL)
WITH report_counts AS ( SELECT managerId, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY managerId) AS report_count FROM Employee WHERE managerId IS NOT NULL ) SELECT DISTINCT m.name FROM report_counts rc JOIN Employee m ON rc.managerId = m.id WHERE rc.report_count >= 5;

Why this works: Window COUNT tallies reports per managerId in one scan. Then JOIN to get names, filter to ≥5.

Performance: One pass for window function, one join. Comparable to approach #1, but more complex code. Use if reporting on multiple aggregates per manager.

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation

Medium #1098 Unpopular Books

▼

Return books available before last month that sold fewer than 10 copies in the past year.

Tables: Books (book_id, name, available_from), Orders (order_id, book_id, quantity, dispatch_date)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation

Real-World Example

A bookseller trims catalog bloat. Older titles that sold fewer than 10 copies in the last year are flagged for delisting.

▶ 1 LEFT JOIN with Date Filter + HAVING
-- Keep books old enough to have had a fair shot, then sum trailing-year sales SELECT b.book_id, b.name FROM Books b LEFT JOIN Orders o ON o.book_id = b.book_id AND o.dispatch_date BETWEEN '2018-06-23' AND '2019-06-23' WHERE b.available_from < '2019-05-23' GROUP BY b.book_id, b.name HAVING COALESCE(SUM(o.quantity), 0) < 10;

Why this is best: LEFT JOIN preserves books with no sales. COALESCE treats missing sums as zero so never-sold books are correctly flagged.

Why this is best: First-per-user-then-group-by-day is the standard new-user-by-day pattern.

Medium #1205 Monthly Transactions II

▼

For each (month, country), report approved and chargeback counts and amounts.

Tables: Transactions (id, country, state, amount, trans_date), Chargebacks (trans_id, trans_date)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation

Real-World Example

A payments team reviews approved vs chargeback volume by country each month to track fraud exposure and cost of risk.

▶ 1 UNION ALL Then Group
-- Combine approved and chargeback rows, then aggregate per month/country SELECT month, country, SUM(approved_count) AS approved_count, SUM(approved_amount) AS approved_amount, SUM(chargeback_count) AS chargeback_count, SUM(chargeback_amount) AS chargeback_amount FROM ( SELECT DATE_FORMAT(trans_date, '%Y-%m') AS month, country, CASE WHEN state = 'approved' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS approved_count, CASE WHEN state = 'approved' THEN amount ELSE 0 END AS approved_amount, 0 AS chargeback_count, 0 AS chargeback_amount FROM Transactions UNION ALL SELECT DATE_FORMAT(c.trans_date, '%Y-%m'), t.country, 0, 0, 1, t.amount FROM Chargebacks c JOIN Transactions t ON t.id = c.trans_id ) u GROUP BY month, country HAVING approved_count + chargeback_count > 0;

Why this is best: Stacking two queries into a common schema, then grouping once, is clean for mixed-source metrics.

Easy #1322 Ads Performance

▼

→

Why this is best: NULLIF guards against divide-by-zero when an ad has no eligible rows. IFNULL returns 0 CTR in that case.

Performance: One aggregate pass.

Medium #1841 League Statistics

Decision Tree Path

A league feed computes a running standings table updated after every match. Points = 3 for a win, 1 for a draw, 0 for a loss.

▶ 1 UNION ALL Home/Away + GROUP BY

Scalar 12 problems

▼

A single table (possibly grouped first) → one row, one column: a scalar result.

Signal words: "the single," "the highest," "second highest," "the one," "overall percentage"

Technique: MAX of filtered set, OFFSET for Nth value, MIN subquery + percentage

Reference Techniques used in Extract Single Value

▼

3 SQL techniques relevant to this recipe, with what they do, when to reach for them, and a generic code example.

Technique What It Does When to Reach for It Example Code
SUM / COUNT / AVG / MAX / MIN Computes a single summary value from multiple rows With GROUP BY: one value per group. Without GROUP BY: one value for the whole table 
SELECT MAX(salary) AS top_pay,
       AVG(salary) AS mean_pay,
       COUNT(*)    AS headcount
FROM Emp;
LIMIT / OFFSET Restricts how many rows are returned or skips a number of rows from the top You need the top 1, the Nth value, or need to skip incomplete window rows 
SELECT name
FROM Emp
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;  -- 2nd highest
CASE WHEN Returns different values based on conditional logic, like an if/else per row You need to classify, label, or remap values based on conditions 
SELECT name,
       CASE WHEN age >= 18 THEN 'Adult'
            ELSE 'Minor' END AS group
FROM Users;

Common Trap: WHERE Returns 0 Rows Instead of NULL

Many scalar-extract problems expect NULL when nothing qualifies (e.g., "second highest salary" when there is only one salary, or the table is empty). If you use WHERE rank = 2 and no row has rank 2, your query returns 0 rows — not a row containing NULL. That fails the test case.

Why it breaks: WHERE can only remove rows. If every row gets removed, the result set is empty. There is no row left to hold a NULL value.

The fix: Move the filter into a subquery inside SELECT. The outer SELECT has no FROM clause, so it always produces exactly 1 row. The subquery fills in the value — if nothing matches, it returns NULL.

-- BREAKS: returns 0 rows when nothing qualifies
SELECT salary FROM rankings WHERE rank = 2;

-- WORKS: always returns 1 row, NULL if nothing qualifies
SELECT (SELECT salary FROM rankings WHERE rank = 2) AS result;

How to spot this: If the problem says "return NULL if no result exists" or the expected output includes a NULL row, you need the subquery-in-SELECT pattern. Look for phrases like "if there is no second highest," "if no such value exists," or an empty table test case.

Easy #619 Biggest Single Number

▼

Find the largest number that appears exactly once. Return NULL if no such number exists.

Schema: MyNumbers(num)

Goal: Find the largest number that appears exactly once. Return NULL if no such number exists.

Why this matters
Data quality and outlier detection: finding records that occur exactly once (duplicates removed) vs. those appearing multiple times.
▶ Rank 1: Subquery with GROUP BY + HAVING + MAX
SELECT MAX(num) AS num FROM ( SELECT num FROM MyNumbers GROUP BY num HAVING COUNT(*) = 1 ) AS singles;

Why rank 1: Clear intent: first isolate single numbers with HAVING, then find the max. Handles NULL correctly (no single numbers → NULL result).

Performance: Two passes (subquery aggregation + outer MAX), but still O(n). Simpler to read than CTE version.

Medium #176 Second Highest Salary

▼

HR teams use second-highest salary to find runner-up compensation levels for benchmarking and market analysis.

Schema: Employee(id, salary)

Find the second highest distinct salary. Return NULL if fewer than 2 distinct values exist.

Business Context: Compensation Benchmarking

HR teams use second-highest salary to find runner-up compensation levels for benchmarking and market analysis.

▶ Rank 1: Subquery in LIMIT OFFSET Uncorrelated, NULL-safe with IFNULL
SELECT IFNULL( (SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM Employee ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1), NULL ) AS SecondHighestSalary;

Why this ranks first: Uses OFFSET to skip the highest and grab the next. Wrapping in IFNULL handles empty result sets (returns NULL when only 1 distinct salary exists). Uncorrelated subquery executes once.

▶ Rank 2: DENSE_RANK Window Function Window function alternative (PostgreSQL 12+)
SELECT COALESCE( (SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM ( SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk FROM Employee ) ranked WHERE rnk = 2), NULL ) AS SecondHighestSalary;

Tradeoff: More explicit (DENSE_RANK = 2 clearly means "second value"), but requires wrapping in subquery to extract the single result. Works in modern PostgreSQL.

▶ Rank 3: MAX WHERE salary < MAX Nested aggregates (avoid—often slower)
SELECT IFNULL( MAX(salary), NULL ) AS SecondHighestSalary FROM Employee WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employee);

Tradeoff: Reads Employee twice (once for MAX, once for WHERE filter). Clear intent but less efficient than LIMIT OFFSET on larger datasets.

Performance Note: LIMIT vs. Window vs. Nested

LIMIT OFFSET is typically fastest on indexed salary (single scan with sort). Window functions (DENSE_RANK) require a scan and rank computation. Nested MAX requires two full table scans. For small Employee tables, differences are negligible; for 1M+ rows, LIMIT OFFSET wins.

Medium #1174 Immediate Food Delivery II

▼

Food delivery platforms track the percentage of customers whose first order was fulfilled immediately (same day) to measure onboarding success.

Schema: Delivery(delivery_id, customer_id, order_date, customer_pref_delivery_date)

For each customer's first order (MIN order_date), count how many have order_date = customer_pref_delivery_date (immediate). Return as a percentage, rounded to 2 decimals.

Business Context: First-Order Experience Quality

Food delivery platforms track the percentage of customers whose first order was fulfilled immediately (same day) to measure onboarding success.

▶ Rank 1: CTE with Conditional Aggregation Readability + performance
WITH FirstOrders AS ( SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_date) AS first_order_date FROM Delivery GROUP BY customer_id ) SELECT ROUND( 100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN d.order_date = d.customer_pref_delivery_date THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2 ) AS immediate_percentage FROM Delivery d INNER JOIN FirstOrders f ON d.customer_id = f.customer_id WHERE d.order_date = f.first_order_date;

Why this ranks first: CTE makes the "first order per customer" logic explicit. CASE WHEN counts immediate orders (order_date = pref_date). JOIN isolates first orders only. Single pass through Delivery.

▶ Rank 2: Subquery in WHERE (Uncorrelated) Inline, no CTE
SELECT ROUND( 100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN order_date = customer_pref_delivery_date THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2 ) AS immediate_percentage FROM Delivery WHERE (customer_id, order_date) IN ( SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_date) FROM Delivery GROUP BY customer_id );

Tradeoff: Subquery in WHERE finds (customer_id, first_order_date) pairs. Avoids CTE syntax but slightly less readable. Same efficiency.

▶ Rank 3: Correlated Subquery (Slow) For small datasets only
SELECT ROUND( 100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN d.order_date = d.customer_pref_delivery_date THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2 ) AS immediate_percentage FROM Delivery d WHERE d.order_date = ( SELECT MIN(order_date) FROM Delivery WHERE customer_id = d.customer_id );

Tradeoff: Correlated subquery runs for each row in Delivery. O(n²) complexity. Avoid for 100k+ rows. Readable but inefficient.

Uncorrelated vs. Correlated Trade-off

The CTE (Rank 1) and IN subquery (Rank 2) compute "first order per customer" once. The correlated subquery (Rank 3) computes it per row. For 10k customers, correlated runs the MIN() 10k times. Use uncorrelated unless table is under 1k rows.

Medium #177 Nth Highest Salary

▼

Return the N-th highest distinct salary, or NULL if there are fewer than N.

Tables: Employee (id, salary)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation

Real-World Example

HR asks analytics for the "rank N" compensation benchmark to align new hire offers to the distribution.

▶ 1 DENSE_RANK on Distinct Salaries
SELECT ( SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM ( SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk FROM Employee ) t WHERE rnk = N ) AS getNthHighestSalary;

Why this is best: DENSE_RANK handles ties correctly. Returning one row (or NULL) is the scalar output.

Performance: One window scan.

▶ 2 LIMIT/OFFSET with DISTINCT
SELECT IFNULL( (SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM Employee ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET N-1), NULL ) AS getNthHighestSalary;

Why this works: OFFSET skips N-1 salaries; LIMIT 1 returns the N-th. Simpler but less expressive on ties.

Performance: One sort. Equivalent cost.

Easy #586 Customer Placing the Largest Number of Orders

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation

Real-World Example

Account management asks for the top buyer to flag for personal concierge service.

▶ 1 GROUP BY + ORDER BY + LIMIT
SELECT customer_number FROM Orders GROUP BY customer_number ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC LIMIT 1;

Why this is best: When the problem guarantees a single top, LIMIT is the cleanest scalar pattern.

Performance: One aggregate + one sort.

Easy #597 Friend Requests I: Overall Acceptance Rate

▼

Compute overall accepted/requested rate, rounded to two decimals.

Tables: FriendRequest (sender_id, send_to_id, request_date), RequestAccepted (requester_id, accepter_id, accept_date)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation

Real-World Example

A social-graph analyst reports platform health as the share of friend requests that are accepted.

▶ 1 Ratio of Distinct Pairs
SELECT ROUND( IFNULL( (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT requester_id, accepter_id) FROM RequestAccepted) / NULLIF((SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT sender_id, send_to_id) FROM FriendRequest), 0), 0 ), 2) AS accept_rate;

Why this is best: Distinct pairs prevent duplicate rows from inflating numerator or denominator.

Easy #1142 User Activity for the Past 30 Days II

▶ 1 Two DISTINCT Counts Ratio
SELECT IFNULL( ROUND(COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) / NULLIF(COUNT(DISTINCT user_id), 0), 2), 0 ) AS average_sessions_per_user FROM Activity WHERE activity_date BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27';

Easy #1173 Immediate Food Delivery I

▼

Return the percent of orders whose order_date equals preferred delivery date.

▶ 1 Boolean Mean
SELECT ROUND(AVG(order_date = customer_pref_delivery_date) * 100, 2) AS immediate_percentage FROM Delivery;

Medium #1715 Count Apples and Oranges

▼

Return total apples and total oranges across boxes and their chests.

Tables: Boxes (box_id, chest_id, apple_count, orange_count), Chests (chest_id, apple_count, orange_count)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation

Real-World Example

A warehouse audit reconciles containers and nested containers to produce a single-row corporate inventory count.

▶ 1 SUM with LEFT JOIN and COALESCE
SELECT SUM(b.apple_count + COALESCE(c.apple_count, 0)) AS apple_count, SUM(b.orange_count + COALESCE(c.orange_count, 0)) AS orange_count FROM Boxes b LEFT JOIN Chests c ON c.chest_id = b.chest_id;

Easy #2072 The Winner University

▼

Return the university (New York / California) with more students scoring 90+.

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation

Real-World Example

An admissions report compares two programs on a single-number scoring benchmark.

▶ 1 Compare Two Scalar Subqueries

Rank & Percentile 20 problems

▼

A single table with a group key → score each row's position in the group, then either annotate every row with a rank or percentile, or filter to the top-N rows per group.

Signal words: "top N per," "Nth highest," "highest in each," "most recent per," "median," "P50 / P90," "percentile," "quartile," "decile," "top X%"

Technique: ROW_NUMBER / RANK / DENSE_RANK / NTILE / PERCENT_RANK / PERCENTILE_CONT / PERCENTILE_DISC OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric) — then either keep every row (annotate) or filter on the score (top N, top X%).

Cross-link: The multi-table version (top customer per region, etc.) lives at Rank Within Groups (Multi-Table). LAG / LEAD neighbour comparison lives at Compare. Rolling and running aggregates live at Window.

Reference Techniques used in Rank & Percentile (7 window functions)

▼

The 7 window functions this recipe uses, what each returns, and when to reach for it. ROW_NUMBER / RANK / DENSE_RANK are position-based; NTILE / PERCENT_RANK / PERCENTILE_CONT / PERCENTILE_DISC are distribution-based.

Function What it returns When to reach for it Example
ROW_NUMBER() A unique 1, 2, 3 ... per partition; ties broken deterministically by ORDER BY "Top N per group" with exact row count; "most recent per entity"; deduping to one row per key ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts DESC)
RANK() Ties tied (same value → same rank); the next rank SKIPS (1, 2, 2, 4) "Nth highest" where ties should share the rank RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC)
DENSE_RANK() Ties tied; the next rank does NOT skip (1, 2, 2, 3) "Nth distinct value" (3rd highest distinct salary) DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC)
NTILE(n) An integer bucket 1..n per partition, splitting rows as evenly as possible "Quartile (n=4) or decile (n=10) each row falls in"; bucket-based segmentation NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC) — bucket 1 = highest
PERCENT_RANK() A fraction from 0 to 1 of rows ranked below this one: (rank - 1) / (rows - 1) "Top X% of rows per group" — X is a fraction of ROW COUNT, not a value band PERCENT_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY rate DESC) <= 0.10
PERCENTILE_CONT(p) ONE interpolated value at percentile p (continuous); aggregate, not per-row "The median (p=0.5) of latency per region"; "P90 session length" PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency)
PERCENTILE_DISC(p) ONE real value FROM the data at or just past percentile p (discrete) "Top X% by value band" — threshold catches every row tied at the boundary PERCENTILE_DISC(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY rate)

How to pick: decision tree

▼

What your output needs to show routes you to the method, then to the leaf below.

Q1. Do you need ONE value per group, or PER-ROW info?

  • One value (the median, the P90 cutoff, the median latency per region) → ✓ use PERCENTILE_CONT / DISC.
  • Per-row info → Q2.

Q2. What does the per-row label encode?

  • "Top N rows per group" (exact count: top 3, latest 1) → ✓ use ROW_NUMBER + filter rn ≤ N.
  • "Top X% of rows per group" (fraction of rows) → ✓ use PERCENT_RANK ≤ X / 100.
  • "Quartile / decile each row falls in" → ✓ use NTILE(n).
  • "Nth highest, ties share the rank" (ranks skip after a tie) → ✓ use RANK.
  • "Nth distinct value" (ranks do not skip after a tie) → ✓ use DENSE_RANK.
  • "The median" as a single output value → ✓ use PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) or, for MySQL without it, the expand-then-rank fallback.

Trap to watch: "top 10%" is ambiguous.

  • "Top 10% of rows" (fraction of ROW COUNT) → PERCENT_RANK <= 0.10.
  • "Top 10% by value" (rate ≥ P90) → PERCENTILE_DISC(0.9) + >= — this catches every row tied at the boundary value.
  • When in doubt, count the rows in the example output relative to the input. A row count that does not match X% of input is the value-band reading.

Generic templates per method

▼

Copy-paste skeleton for each method the decision tree routes to. Swap the placeholder names; the shape stays the same.

ROW_NUMBER + filter rn ≤ N (back to tree)

▼

Use when: keep the highest, latest, or first N rows per group, with deterministic tiebreaking.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Apply ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric DESC) inside a CTE so every row in each group is numbered 1, 2, 3 ...
  2. Add a tiebreaker column to the ORDER BY so numbering is deterministic when two rows tie on the main metric.
  3. Outer SELECT filters rn ≤ N to keep exactly N rows per group.
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT t.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group_col
                            ORDER BY rank_col DESC, tiebreak_col) AS rn
  FROM t
)
SELECT group_col, rank_col, ...
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= N;

RANK (ties tied, ranks skip)

▼

Use when: "Nth highest" where rows with the same value should share that rank.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Apply RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric DESC) — ties share the same rank, the next rank skips.
  2. Filter rk = N in the outer query to keep the Nth-highest tier; multiple rows can come back when there are ties at that rank.
SELECT
  metric_col,
  RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY group_col ORDER BY metric_col DESC) AS rk
FROM t;
-- Then filter on rk = N. Multiple rows can share rk = N.

DENSE_RANK (Nth distinct)

▼

Use when: "the 3rd highest distinct salary" — ties share the rank, but ranks do NOT skip.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Apply DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY metric DESC) — ties share the rank but ranks do NOT skip.
  2. Wrap in a subquery, then SELECT DISTINCT on the metric column to drop the duplicate "Nth-distinct" rows.
  3. Filter dr = N in the outer query to return the Nth distinct value.
SELECT DISTINCT metric_col
FROM (
  SELECT metric_col,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY metric_col DESC) AS dr
  FROM t
) x
WHERE dr = N;

NTILE(n) (quartile / decile buckets)

▼

Use when: "which bucket each row falls in" with even-ish bucket sizes. ORDER BY metric DESC puts the best in bucket 1; ASC puts the worst in bucket 1.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Apply NTILE(n) OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric) — bucketizes rows into n even-ish groups.
  2. Use DESC for "bucket 1 = best", ASC for "bucket 1 = worst".
  3. Each row carries its bucket number directly; no further filter unless you only want a specific bucket.
SELECT
  entity_col, metric_col,
  NTILE(4) OVER (PARTITION BY group_col ORDER BY metric_col DESC) AS quartile
FROM t;

PERCENT_RANK ≤ X / 100 (top X% of rows)

▼

Use when: "top X% per group" measured as a fraction of ROW COUNT. Order DESC so the best row sits at pr = 0; filter pr <= X/100.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Apply PERCENT_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric DESC) inside a CTE — returns 0..1 where 0 = best.
  2. Order DESC so the best row sits at pr = 0.
  3. Filter pr ≤ X / 100 in the outer query to keep the top X% of rows per group.
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT t.*,
         PERCENT_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY group_col ORDER BY metric_col DESC) AS pr
  FROM t
)
SELECT group_col, entity_col, metric_col
FROM ranked
WHERE pr <= 0.10;   -- top 10% of rows per group

PERCENTILE_CONT / PERCENTILE_DISC (one value per group)

▼

Use when: you need a single value — the median, P90, top X% by value band. CONT interpolates; DISC returns a real data value (use DISC with >= to catch ties at the boundary).

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Use PERCENTILE_CONT(p) (interpolated) or PERCENTILE_DISC(p) (real data value) as an aggregate.
  2. WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY metric) sets the sort axis for the percentile.
  3. GROUP BY the entity column to get ONE percentile value per group.
-- One median per region (aggregate)
SELECT region,
       PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency) AS median_latency
FROM t
GROUP BY region;

-- Top 10% by value band: every row at or above the P90 cutoff
WITH cutoff AS (
  SELECT PERCENTILE_DISC(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY rate) AS p90
  FROM t
)
SELECT t.* FROM t, cutoff WHERE t.rate >= cutoff.p90;

ROW_NUMBER for top-N per group 1 problem

▼

nb01 qtype: window_top_n_per_group — ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY rank_col) wrapped in a CTE and filtered to rn ≤ N. The canonical way to pick the latest, highest, or first N rows per group. Pick ROW_NUMBER (not RANK / DENSE_RANK) when you want EXACTLY N rows per group with deterministic tiebreaking.

Medium #1164 Product Price at a Given Date

▼

When a customer reports a historical transaction, e-commerce needs to show what price they were charged. Product had 3 price changes but customer bought on 2019-08-15 when it was $30, not current $50.

📌
Pattern: ROW_NUMBER with Date Filter

Use ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY change_date DESC) to get most recent price before target date. COALESCE to default price. Business: E-commerce price history lookup.

Business Context
When a customer reports a historical transaction, e-commerce needs to show what price they were charged. Product had 3 price changes but customer bought on 2019-08-15 when it was $30, not current $50.
▶ Rank 1: ROW_NUMBER DESC + COALESCE Handles missing products elegantly
SELECT DISTINCT product_id, COALESCE( (SELECT new_price FROM Products p2 WHERE p2.product_id = p1.product_id AND p2.change_date <= '2019-08-16' ORDER BY change_date DESC LIMIT 1), 10 ) AS price FROM ( SELECT DISTINCT product_id FROM Products ) p1 ORDER BY product_id;

Performance Analysis: Correlated subquery for each distinct product. Outer DISTINCT: O(n). Inner subquery: must find all changes <= target date per product = O(n/products) on average. With index on (product_id, change_date), becomes O(log n) seek + O(1) fetch. Total: O(products * log n). Alternative with window function avoids subquery overhead.

Why Rank 1: Correlated subquery is readable. COALESCE(10) handles products never changing price (default 10).

▶ Rank 2: Window Function + LEFT JOIN Most efficient for full product catalog
WITH latest_prices AS ( SELECT product_id, new_price, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY change_date DESC) AS rn FROM Products WHERE change_date <= '2019-08-16' ) SELECT p.product_id, COALESCE(lp.new_price, 10) AS price FROM (SELECT DISTINCT product_id FROM Products) p LEFT JOIN latest_prices lp ON p.product_id = lp.product_id AND lp.rn = 1 ORDER BY p.product_id;

Performance Analysis: Window function: O(n log n) to sort all products by (product_id, change_date). ROW_NUMBER(): O(n) once sorted. Filter change_date <= target: O(n). LEFT JOIN: O(products) seek + O(n) on Products side. Total: O(n log n) dominated by window sort. Much faster than correlated subquery when many products have many price changes.

Why Rank 2: Window function avoids subquery overhead but more code. Better for large product catalogs.

RANK for Nth highest, ties tied no problems yet

▼

nb01 qtype: percentile_metrics (rank flavor coming) — RANK() OVER (...) returns the same rank to tied rows and SKIPS the next rank. Use this when the prompt says "Nth highest" and ties should share the position; if the prompt says "Nth distinct value," use DENSE_RANK instead. Worked example to be added.

No worked card in this leaf yet. See the generic template above and the DENSE_RANK leaf for the contrast on ties.

DENSE_RANK for Nth distinct value no problems yet

▼

nb01 qtype: percentile_metrics (dense_rank flavor coming) — DENSE_RANK() OVER (...) returns the same rank to tied rows but does NOT skip after a tie. Use this when the prompt says "Nth distinct" (the 3rd highest distinct salary). Worked example to be added.

No worked card in this leaf yet. See the generic template above.

NTILE(n) for quartile / decile buckets 2 problems

▼

nb01 qtype: percentile_metrics (ntile_buckets flavor) — NTILE(n) OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric DESC) bucketizes rows into n even-ish groups. DESC puts the best in bucket 1; ASC puts the worst in bucket 1. NTILE only accepts a LITERAL integer.

Medium Tutor Quartile Ranking by Completion Rate

▼

Assign each tutor to a quartile (1-4) based on completion_rate (completed / total), where bucket 1 holds the highest rates. Output one row per tutor with completion_rate and quartile. Exclude tutors with total_sessions = 0.

Tables: tutors (tutor_id, tutor_name, completed_sessions, total_sessions)

→

Decision Tree Path

Rank & Percentile decision tree: per-row bucket label, even-ish sizes → NTILE template.

Real-World Example

A tutoring marketplace segments tutors into 4 performance buckets by completion rate, so the matching service can route demand to bucket-1 tutors and trigger coaching for bucket-4.

Trace — sort DESC, then NTILE(4) splits 8 rows into 2 + 2 + 2 + 2:

tutor_name completed / total completion_rate position (sorted DESC) NTILE(4)
Alice Chen95 / 1000.9511
David Park45 / 500.9021
Bob Martinez78 / 900.8732
Carol Kim60 / 800.7542
Emma Wilson30 / 600.5053
Grace Taylor15 / 300.5063
Frank Lee18 / 400.4574
Henry Zhang5 / 250.2084

8 rows divided into 4 buckets land exactly 2 per bucket. Emma and Grace tie at 0.50 but both fall inside positions 5-6, so they share bucket 3 — ties only split across buckets when they straddle a boundary (see watch-outs).

▶ 1 NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY rate DESC)
WITH base AS ( SELECT tutor_name, completed_sessions, total_sessions, COALESCE(ROUND(completed_sessions::numeric / total_sessions, 2), 0.00) AS completion_rate FROM tutors WHERE total_sessions > 0 ) SELECT tutor_name, completion_rate, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY completion_rate DESC) AS quartile FROM base ORDER BY quartile, completion_rate DESC;

Why this is best: NTILE(4) is the right tool when the prompt asks "which bucket each row falls in" with even-ish sizes. Sorting DESC puts the best rates in bucket 1 (lowest bucket number = best), which matches the prompt. The CTE computes completion_rate once so both the NTILE expression and the final ORDER BY use the same rounded value.

Watch out:

  • Integer division. completed_sessions / total_sessions with two INT columns returns 0 for every fractional rate. Cast the numerator to NUMERIC (or use ::numeric) so the division stays decimal.
  • NTILE only accepts a LITERAL integer. You cannot pass a column or a parameter. NTILE(p_n) from a DO block argument will not compile.
  • Direction trick. ORDER BY rate DESC → bucket 1 = best. ORDER BY rate ASC → bucket 1 = worst. Read the prompt for which the user means.
  • Uneven row counts. 8 rows / 4 buckets = exactly 2 each. With 9 rows the extra row goes to the LOWER bucket numbers (bucket 1 gets 3, the rest get 2). With 10 rows buckets 1-2 get 3 each and 3-4 get 2.
  • Ties at a bucket boundary split. If two tied rows straddle the 4→5 position boundary, one goes to bucket 2 and the other to bucket 3 even though their values are equal. NTILE does not tie-extend — if that matters, use PERCENT_RANK or a value-band cutoff instead.
  • The COALESCE here is technically redundant because WHERE total_sessions > 0 already excludes the divide-by-zero case. It is harmless as a safety belt; some style guides drop it.

Performance: One window pass plus the final sort.

Medium Quartile Segmentation of Customer Basket Spend (NULL handling with NULLS LAST)

▼

Online grocery: bucket customers into quartiles by avg_basket_value with quartile 1 = highest spend. Include customers with NULL averages, but place them at the BOTTOM (quartile 4), not the top. The whole lesson is one keyword: NULLS LAST on the NTILE's ORDER BY.

Tables: customer_metrics (customer_id, customer_name, avg_basket_value, total_orders, last_order_date)

Real-World Example

A grocery growth team segments customers into spend tiers for personalized promotions; brand-new or churned customers without any orders (NULL basket value) get assigned to the lowest tier rather than the highest, so they don't dominate the "VIP" cohort by accident.

The NULL-ordering trap: DESC puts NULLs FIRST by default in Postgres

In Postgres (and ANSI SQL), ORDER BY col DESC defaults to NULLS FIRST; ORDER BY col ASC defaults to NULLS LAST. So ORDER BY avg_basket_value DESC ranks NULL above the highest real value — and NTILE then places the NULL customer in bucket 1 instead of bucket 4.

Fix: append NULLS LAST to the NTILE's ORDER BY. Now NULL sorts below every real value, and the NULL customer lands in bucket 4 (or wherever the bucket boundary falls), matching the prompt's "NULL values should be sorted last."

What this query does, step by step:

  1. Read each customer's pre-computed avg_basket_value directly from the metrics table — no JOIN, no per-row aggregation needed.
  2. NTILE(4) across the population with ORDER BY avg_basket_value DESC NULLS LAST — ranks real values from highest to lowest, with NULLs at the bottom.
  3. Final ORDER BY matches the prompt: by quartile ASC, then by basket value DESC. With 8 rows / 4 buckets, NTILE assigns exactly 2 per bucket.

Trace — what happens without and with NULLS LAST:

customer avg_basket_value position with DESC (default NULLS FIRST) bucket (wrong) position with DESC NULLS LAST bucket (right)
107 GraceNULL11 (wrong)84 (right)
103 Carol215.802111
105 Emma198.403221
101 Alice142.504232
108 Henry125.605342
102 Bob87.306353
104 David63.207463
106 Frank45.908474

Without NULLS LAST, Grace sits at position 1 and grabs the top quartile spot, shifting EVERY real customer down one bucket boundary. The example data was small enough that this bug was visually obvious (Grace at quartile 1 with NULL spend); on hidden data with many NULLs the wrong quartile boundaries are easy to miss.

▶ 1 NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY ... DESC NULLS LAST)
SELECT customer_id, avg_basket_value, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY avg_basket_value DESC NULLS LAST) AS spend_quartile FROM customer_metrics ORDER BY spend_quartile, avg_basket_value DESC;

Why this is best: One pass, one window function, no CTE needed. The fix is a single keyword on the NTILE's ORDER BY clause. The outer ORDER BY then sorts the result for display: by quartile ASC (so 1 comes first), then by basket value DESC within each quartile.

Watch out:

  • The default depends on DESC vs ASC. ORDER BY col DESC → NULLs FIRST. ORDER BY col ASC → NULLs LAST. So the same NULL-handling bug shows up on DESC-sorted ranks but NOT on ASC-sorted ones. Read the direction before deciding whether to add NULLS LAST or NULLS FIRST.
  • NULLS LAST/FIRST goes inside the OVER, not in the outer ORDER BY. The OVER's ORDER BY drives the bucket assignment; the outer ORDER BY just sorts the display. Adding NULLS LAST to the outer ORDER BY does nothing to fix the bucket.
  • This trap exists for RANK, DENSE_RANK, PERCENT_RANK, ROW_NUMBER too — any window function whose OVER uses ORDER BY col DESC places NULLs at the top by default. Same fix everywhere.
  • MySQL syntax differs. Older MySQL versions do not accept NULLS LAST directly — use ORDER BY avg_basket_value IS NULL, avg_basket_value DESC instead. Postgres, DuckDB, and modern MySQL 8+ accept the standard syntax.
  • NTILE only takes a literal integer. NTILE(p_n) where p_n is a parameter or column will not compile — the bucket count must be a constant.
  • Ties at a bucket boundary still split. NTILE does not tie-extend; if two customers tie at the cutoff between bucket 2 and 3, one goes to 2 and one to 3 by row order. Add a tiebreaker (customer_id ASC) to make it deterministic.

Performance: One window pass + one final sort. Linear in the number of customers.

PERCENT_RANK for top X% of rows migrate next

▼

nb01 qtype: percentile_metrics (top_n_percent flavor) — PERCENT_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric DESC) returns a fraction from 0 to 1 measuring row position. Order so the best row sits at pr = 0 and filter pr ≤ X / 100. Beware "top 10%" by VALUE band — that is PERCENTILE_DISC, not PERCENT_RANK.

The Top 10% Trial Sites anchor and the row-fraction vs value-band contrast (#2346) currently live in the Transform recipe. They will move here in the next pass. See the generic template above for the shape.

PERCENTILE_CONT / DISC for one value per group migrate next

▼

nb01 qtype: percentile_metrics (percentile_aggregate flavor) — PERCENTILE_CONT(p) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY metric) returns ONE interpolated value at percentile p; PERCENTILE_DISC(p) returns a real data value. Aggregate, not per-row. Use CONT for medians and reported percentiles; DISC + >= for "top X% by value band" where boundary ties must be kept.

The gig-workers PERCENT_RANK vs PERCENTILE_DISC contrast currently lives in the Transform recipe. It will move here in the next pass. See the generic template above for the shape.

Median fallback (frequency-based, expand-then-rank) no problems yet

▼

For dialects without PERCENTILE_CONT (e.g. MySQL), or for #571-style frequency-table prompts, EXPAND the frequency table into one row per occurrence, ROW_NUMBER over the expanded set, and pick the middle one (or two for even N, then AVG). Skip if PERCENTILE_CONT is available.

Worked example to be added. Use this leaf for problems where PERCENTILE_CONT is unavailable or the input is a frequency table that needs expansion first.

Top 1 by metric per group (single-table) 8 problems

▼

nb01 qtype: window_top_n_per_group — ROW_NUMBER PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric DESC, rn = 1. When the prompt says "highest in each " and everything you need is in one table.

Medium #1112 Highest Grade For Each Student

▼

For each student, pick the course with the highest grade (ties broken by smallest course_id).

Tables: Enrollments (student_id, course_id, grade)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

An academic record extracts each student's best course for a transcript highlight.

▶ 1 ROW_NUMBER per Student
SELECT student_id, course_id, grade FROM ( SELECT student_id, course_id, grade, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY student_id ORDER BY grade DESC, course_id) AS rn FROM Enrollments ) t WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY student_id;

Why this is best: ROW_NUMBER with the specified tie-breaker returns exactly one row per student.

Performance: One window.

Medium #1831 Maximum Transaction Each Day

▼

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

A fraud ops team reviews each day's largest transaction for anomalies.

▶ 1 RANK per Day
SELECT transaction_id FROM ( SELECT transaction_id, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY DATE(day) ORDER BY amount DESC) AS rk FROM Transactions ) t WHERE rk = 1 ORDER BY transaction_id;

Why this is best: Standard top-1-per-partition. RANK keeps ties.

Performance: One window pass.

Medium #2112 The Airport With the Most Traffic

▼

Airports with the highest total traffic (either direction).

Tables: Flights (departure_airport, arrival_airport, flights_count)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

A network planner identifies traffic hubs to prioritize capacity investments.

▶ 1 Normalize Direction + Aggregate + RANK
WITH n AS ( SELECT departure_airport AS airport_id, flights_count FROM Flights UNION ALL SELECT arrival_airport, flights_count FROM Flights ), totals AS (SELECT airport_id, SUM(flights_count) AS total FROM n GROUP BY airport_id) SELECT airport_id FROM ( SELECT airport_id, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total DESC) AS rk FROM totals ) t WHERE rk = 1;

Why this is best: Sum traffic regardless of direction; RANK handles ties.

Performance: Two passes + window.

Medium #2820 Election Results

▼

Candidates with the most total votes, splitting each voter's share across their chosen candidates.

Tables: Votes (voter, candidate)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

A rank-choice election vote-share system apportions fractional votes when voters pick multiple candidates.

▶ 1 Share Per Voter + Aggregate
WITH w AS ( SELECT candidate, 1.0 / COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY voter) AS share FROM Votes WHERE candidate IS NOT NULL ), totals AS (SELECT candidate, SUM(share) AS s FROM w GROUP BY candidate) SELECT candidate FROM ( SELECT candidate, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY s DESC) AS rk FROM totals ) t WHERE rk = 1 ORDER BY candidate;

Why this is best: Compute share per voter, aggregate, rank.

Performance: One window + one aggregate + one rank.

Medium #2984 Find Peak Calling Hours for Each City

▼

For each city, find the hour(s) with maximum call count.

Tables: Calls (caller_id, recipient_id, call_time, city)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

A telco capacity planner identifies peak call hours per city to align staffing and networks.

▶ 1 Per-City-Hour Count + RANK
WITH counts AS ( SELECT city, HOUR(call_time) AS h, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM Calls GROUP BY city, HOUR(call_time) ) SELECT city, h AS peak_calling_hour, cnt AS number_of_calls FROM ( SELECT *, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY cnt DESC) AS rk FROM counts ) t WHERE rk = 1 ORDER BY city DESC, peak_calling_hour DESC;

Why this is best: Classic top-per-group on derived hourly counts.

Performance: Aggregate + window.

Medium #2988 Manager of the Largest Department

▼

Return the manager(s) of the department with the most employees.

Tables: Employees (emp_id, emp_name, dept_id, position)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

An HR dashboard highlights the leader of the biggest team as a candidate for cross-org collaboration duties.

▶ 1 Dept Size + RANK
WITH sizes AS ( SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS c FROM Employees GROUP BY dept_id ) SELECT e.emp_name AS manager_name, e.dept_id FROM Employees e JOIN sizes s ON s.dept_id = e.dept_id JOIN ( SELECT dept_id, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY c DESC) AS rk FROM sizes ) r ON r.dept_id = e.dept_id WHERE e.position = 'Manager' AND r.rk = 1;

Why this is best: Rank departments by size, then pull the manager.

Performance: Aggregate + window + join.

Medium #1951 All the Pairs With the Maximum Number of Common Followers

▼

Return user pairs whose common-follower count matches the maximum across all pairs.

Tables: Relations (user_id, follower_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

A social-graph ops team finds most-overlapping audience pairs for cross-promotion suggestions.

▶ 1 Pair Counts + RANK 1
WITH pairs AS ( SELECT a.user_id AS user1_id, b.user_id AS user2_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM Relations a JOIN Relations b ON a.follower_id = b.follower_id AND a.user_id < b.user_id GROUP BY a.user_id, b.user_id ) SELECT user1_id, user2_id FROM ( SELECT *, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY cnt DESC) AS rk FROM pairs ) r WHERE rk = 1;

Why this is best: Self-join on shared follower, count overlap per pair, rank.

Performance: O(followers^2) worst case.

A survey platform ranks questions by completion to improve form flows.

SELECT question_id AS survey_log FROM SurveyLog GROUP BY question_id ORDER BY SUM(action='answer') / SUM(action='show') DESC, question_id LIMIT 1;

Why this is best: Group-level ratio expression sorted directly.

For each employee, return the highest (most recent) salary record.

Payroll exports use the latest salary per employee for the current check run.

▼

Most recent end time per bike.

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

A bike fleet manager spots bikes dormant longest to prioritize relocation or maintenance.

▶ 1 Max per Bike
SELECT bike_number, MAX(end_time) AS last_used FROM Bikes GROUP BY bike_number ORDER BY last_used DESC;

Hard #2752 Customers with Maximum Number of Transactions on Consecutive Days

▼

Return customers whose longest daily-streak transaction run equals the overall max across customers.

Tables: Transactions (transaction_id, customer_id, transaction_date)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

A loyalty program rewards customers with the longest daily purchase streak.

▶ 1 Islands + Compare Max
WITH d AS ( SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, transaction_date FROM Transactions ), g AS ( SELECT customer_id, transaction_date, DATE_SUB(transaction_date, INTERVAL ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY transaction_date) DAY) AS grp FROM d ), runs AS (SELECT customer_id, grp, COUNT(*) AS run_len FROM g GROUP BY customer_id, grp), max_run AS (SELECT customer_id, MAX(run_len) AS maxlen FROM runs GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT customer_id FROM max_run WHERE maxlen = (SELECT MAX(maxlen) FROM max_run) ORDER BY customer_id;

Why this is best: Islands give streak lengths; compare each customer's max to the global max.

Performance: Two aggregates + one window.

Top N (N > 1) per group (single-table) 1 problem

▼

nb01 qtype: window_top_n_per_group — ROW_NUMBER PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric DESC, rn ≤ N. Use ROW_NUMBER for exactly N per group; switch to RANK / DENSE_RANK if the prompt says ties share the rank.

Hard #2991 Top Three Wineries

▼

For each country, return the top three wineries by total points (with fallback labels).

Tables: Wineries (id, country, points, winery)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

A sommelier tool publishes each country's top 3 wineries with placeholder text for countries with fewer entries.

▶ 1 RANK per Country + Labels
WITH totals AS ( SELECT country, winery, SUM(points) AS pts FROM Wineries GROUP BY country, winery ), ranked AS ( SELECT country, winery, pts, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY pts DESC, winery) AS rn FROM totals ) SELECT country, MAX(CASE WHEN rn = 1 THEN CONCAT(winery,' (',pts,')') END) AS top_winery, COALESCE(MAX(CASE WHEN rn = 2 THEN CONCAT(winery,' (',pts,')') END), 'No second winery') AS second_winery, COALESCE(MAX(CASE WHEN rn = 3 THEN CONCAT(winery,' (',pts,')') END), 'No third winery') AS third_winery FROM ranked GROUP BY country ORDER BY country;

Why this is best: Pivot the top-3 rows into one row per country with labeled fallbacks.

Performance: Aggregate + window + pivot.

▼

nb01 qtype: window_top_n_per_group — ROW_NUMBER PARTITION BY group ORDER BY sort_key, rn = N exactly. The 2nd most recent, 3rd transaction shape. Often paired with a fallback for groups that have fewer than N rows.

Hard #1369 Get the Second Most Recent Activity

▼

Second most recent activity per user; if only one, return it.

Tables: UserActivity (username, activity, startDate, endDate)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

A profile page shows the previous activity behind the most recent one; falls back to the only activity for new users.

▶ 1 ROW_NUMBER Descending + Count Guard
WITH ranked AS ( SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY username ORDER BY startDate DESC) AS rn, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY username) AS cnt FROM UserActivity ) SELECT username, activity, startDate, endDate FROM ranked WHERE (cnt > 1 AND rn = 2) OR (cnt = 1 AND rn = 1);

Why this is best: Row number identifies the second-latest; count guards the single-activity case.

Performance: Two window passes.

Medium #2986 Find Third Transaction

▼

For each user, return the 3rd transaction if its spend beats both previous ones.

Tables: Transactions (user_id, spend, transaction_date)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

A product analyst finds users whose third purchase escalates spend relative to the first two — a strong retention signal.

▶ 1 ROW_NUMBER + LAG Compare
WITH ranked AS ( SELECT user_id, spend, transaction_date, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY transaction_date) AS rn, LAG(spend, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY transaction_date) AS p1, LAG(spend, 2) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY transaction_date) AS p2 FROM Transactions ) SELECT user_id, spend AS third_transaction_spend, transaction_date AS third_transaction_date FROM ranked WHERE rn = 3 AND spend > p1 AND spend > p2;

Why this is best: Row number isolates the 3rd; two LAG values enable the comparison.

Performance: One window pass.

Hard #569 Median Employee Salary

▼

For each company, return the median salary row(s).

Tables: Employee (id, company, salary)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

Finance compares median salary benchmarks per company subsidiary.

▶ 1 Row Numbers from Both Ends
SELECT id, company, salary FROM ( SELECT id, company, salary, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY company ORDER BY salary, id) AS asc_n, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY company ORDER BY salary DESC, id) AS desc_n FROM Employee ) t WHERE ABS(asc_n - desc_n) <= 1;

Why this is best: Median rows always have |ascending_rn - descending_rn| <= 1, covering both odd and even group sizes.

Performance: Two window passes.

Medium #1867 Orders With Maximum Quantity Above Average

▼

Return orders whose max quantity exceeds the average overall max.

Tables: OrdersDetails (order_id, product_id, quantity)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Rank within Partition

Real-World Example

An inventory audit spotlights orders with unusually large line items compared to typical order ceilings.

▶ 1 Per-Order Max + Compare to Overall Avg
WITH per_order AS ( SELECT order_id, MAX(quantity) AS max_q FROM OrdersDetails GROUP BY order_id ) SELECT order_id FROM per_order WHERE max_q > (SELECT AVG(max_q) FROM per_order);

Why this is best: Two-step aggregate: per-order max, then per-order comparison to its own average.
