written_date notebook rn (raw, no dedupe) grp = date − rn (raw) rn (after DISTINCT) grp (after DISTINCT)
2024-04-10A104-09104-09
2024-04-10B204-08——
2024-04-11A304-08204-09
2024-04-12A404-08304-09

Without DISTINCT, the raw grp splits into 04-09 (one row) + 04-08 (three rows), counting 3 as the streak instead of 4. With DISTINCT (1 row per calendar day), all three days share grp 04-09 and the streak counts to 3 — matching the prompt's "Jan 5, 6, 7 = 3 days" example. The bug direction (over- vs under-count) flips with the data, but the root cause is the same: the formula assumes one row per day.

▶ 1 DISTINCT user_days CTE → date − rn → aggregate per user
WITH user_base AS ( SELECT user_id, TO_CHAR(signup_date, 'YYYY-MM') AS signup_cohort FROM users WHERE signup_date >= DATE '2024-01-01' ), user_days AS ( -- one row per (user, written_date); dedupes same-day multi-notebook writes SELECT DISTINCT u.user_id, n.written_date FROM user_base u JOIN notebooks nb ON nb.user_id = u.user_id JOIN notes n ON n.notebook_id = nb.notebook_id ), streak_groups AS ( -- date - rn is constant within a consecutive-day run per user SELECT user_id, written_date, written_date - (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY written_date))::INT AS grp FROM user_days ), streak_lengths AS ( SELECT user_id, grp, COUNT(*) AS streak_days FROM streak_groups GROUP BY user_id, grp ), months_per_user AS ( SELECT user_id, COUNT(DISTINCT TO_CHAR(written_date, 'YYYY-MM')) AS active_months FROM user_days GROUP BY user_id ), longest_per_user AS ( SELECT user_id, MAX(streak_days) AS longest_streak_days FROM streak_lengths GROUP BY user_id ) SELECT u.user_id, u.signup_cohort, COALESCE(m.active_months, 0) AS active_months, COALESCE(s.longest_streak_days, 0) AS longest_streak_days FROM user_base u LEFT JOIN months_per_user m ON m.user_id = u.user_id LEFT JOIN longest_per_user s ON s.user_id = u.user_id ORDER BY u.user_id;

Why this is best: Each CTE has one job, and the dedupe step (user_days) sits where it must — BEFORE the row number. The streak machinery (streak_groups + streak_lengths) reads one row per calendar day per user, which is the precondition the date − rn form requires. The final SELECT joins two pre-aggregated CTEs into user_base so a user with no notes still appears with 0 / 0.

Watch out:

  • Dedupe BEFORE the row number. Doing ROW_NUMBER over the raw notes table partitioned by notebook (a common attempt) double-counts a calendar day that appears in two notebooks. The fix is structural — the dedupe is its own CTE, not a tweak to the window.
  • PARTITION BY user_id on the row number. Streaks belong to the USER, not to a notebook. Partitioning by notebook would also give wrong totals — consecutive days split across two notebooks would look like two separate runs.
  • Cast the row number to INT before subtracting from a DATE. Postgres' DATE - BIGINT errors; cast with (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...))::INT or use ::numeric.
  • Pre-aggregate before the final join. Joining user_days and streak_lengths directly to user_base in the final SELECT would Cartesian-multiply the rows per user. Pre-aggregating into months_per_user and longest_per_user keeps the join one-to-one.
  • This is the date − rn form, not rn_overall − rn_per_state. Use it because every relevant calendar day is present (each note has a date, no missing-day gaps in the streak definition). If the prompt let days be missing and required "consecutive in the data," switch to the rn-minus-rn form in the leaf below.
▶ 2 Leaner 3-CTE: streak length as a window, one final GROUP BY
WITH user_days AS ( SELECT DISTINCT u.user_id, TO_CHAR(u.signup_date, 'YYYY-MM') AS signup_cohort, n.written_date FROM users u JOIN notebooks nb ON nb.user_id = u.user_id JOIN notes n ON n.notebook_id = nb.notebook_id WHERE u.signup_date >= DATE '2024-01-01' ), streaks AS ( -- date - rn anchor, per user SELECT user_id, signup_cohort, written_date, written_date - (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY written_date))::INT AS grp FROM user_days ), per_day AS ( -- COUNT(*) as a window: each row carries its OWN streak's length SELECT user_id, signup_cohort, written_date, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id, grp) AS streak_len FROM streaks ) SELECT user_id, signup_cohort, COUNT(DISTINCT TO_CHAR(written_date, 'YYYY-MM')) AS active_months, MAX(streak_len) AS longest_streak_days FROM per_day GROUP BY user_id, signup_cohort ORDER BY user_id;

Why this is leaner without losing readability: 3 CTEs instead of 6, no LEFT JOIN at the end. The key move is COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id, grp) — a window aggregate that gives every row its own streak length without collapsing the rows. The final SELECT then makes ONE pass per user to compute both active_months (distinct months) and longest_streak_days (MAX over the streak length each row carries). Each CTE still has one named job: dedupe, anchor, label.

How it compares to Rank 1:

  • Rank 1: dedupe → anchor → group-by grp to get streak length → group-by user for max → group-by user for months → LEFT JOIN the two pre-aggregates back to user_base. 6 CTEs, 2 extra group-bys, 2 joins at the end.
  • Rank 2: dedupe → anchor → window-count the streak → one final group-by per user that computes both metrics. 3 CTEs, 1 group-by, 0 joins after the dedupe.

Watch out:

  • Window functions evaluate AFTER DISTINCT. Putting ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) inside SELECT DISTINCT would compute on pre-dedupe rows and undo the fix. The window MUST be its own CTE on top of the deduped set — that is the role of streaks.
  • The dedupe step still leads. Compactness does not change the bug-fix lesson: user_days must collapse to one row per (user, day) before any rn-based reasoning.
  • A user with no notes drops out. Rank 1 used user_base LEFT JOIN so a signup-without-activity still appeared with 0/0. Rank 2 drives off user_days, so a user with no notes is absent from the result. Pick the variant the prompt asks for — here both pass because the expected output only lists users with activity.

Performance: One scan of the deduped set, one window pass, one GROUP BY. The Rank 1 plan has the same scans plus the extra GROUP BYs and the final two-way join — both are O(n log n) but Rank 2 has a smaller constant and a flatter plan in EXPLAIN.

Consecutive dates with gaps / merged states 2 problems

▼

rn_overall − rn_per_status — One timeline where days can be missing, often built by UNION of two source tables and labelled with a state. Two row numbers, one overall and one per state; their difference is constant across a run.

Hard #1225 Report Contiguous Dates

▼

Summarize consecutive-day ranges of the same period state (failed/succeeded).

Tables: Failed (fail_date), Succeeded (success_date)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Self-Join & Relational Queries → Pattern E: Self-Joins

Real-World Example

A SRE team builds an uptime ledger showing contiguous spans of healthy vs unhealthy days for audit reports.

▶ 1 Gaps-and-Islands by State
WITH all_days AS ( SELECT fail_date AS d, 'failed' AS state FROM Failed WHERE fail_date BETWEEN '2019-01-01' AND '2019-12-31' UNION ALL SELECT success_date, 'succeeded' FROM Succeeded WHERE success_date BETWEEN '2019-01-01' AND '2019-12-31' ), numbered AS ( SELECT d, state, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY d) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY state ORDER BY d) AS grp FROM all_days ) SELECT state AS period_state, MIN(d) AS start_date, MAX(d) AS end_date FROM numbered GROUP BY state, grp ORDER BY start_date;

Why this is best: The difference of two row numbers groups same-state rows that are also contiguous by date.

Performance: Two window passes + one group-by.

▶ 2 Date Minus Row-Number (Postgres-friendly, calendar-consecutive only)
WITH all_days AS ( SELECT 'failed' AS state, fail_date AS d FROM Failed WHERE fail_date BETWEEN '2019-01-01' AND '2019-12-31' UNION ALL SELECT 'succeeded', success_date FROM Succeeded WHERE success_date BETWEEN '2019-01-01' AND '2019-12-31' ), numbered AS ( SELECT d, state, d - (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY state ORDER BY d))::INT AS grp FROM all_days ) SELECT state AS period_state, MIN(d) AS start_date, MAX(d) AS end_date FROM numbered GROUP BY state, grp ORDER BY start_date;

Why this works: consecutive same-state dates produce identical (date - row_number_within_state) values, so the math is more intuitive than the two-row-numbers diff.

Trade-offs vs Rank 1: Postgres-only (DATE - INT math; ::INT cast needed because ROW_NUMBER returns BIGINT). Also requires the date sequence in the data to have NO missing days within an island — see the watch-out below.

Watch out: the two formulations are NOT equivalent when data has missing days

  • rn_overall - rn_per_state groups by data-sequence consecutiveness — "are these the next rows when sorted by date?" It IGNORES calendar gaps where neither table has a row.
  • date - rn_per_state groups by calendar consecutiveness — "are these back-to-back days on the calendar?" If a day is missing from BOTH tables, the math breaks the island.
  • Example: 2024 is a leap year. If the data has Feb 28 = active, no row for Feb 29 (missing from both tables), Mar 1 = active — the date - rn form sees a 2-day gap (Feb 28 → Mar 1 is 2 calendar days because Feb 29 exists) and breaks the island. The rn_overall - rn_per_state form keeps them together because the rows are sequential in the union.
  • Pick by prompt intent: if "continuous" means "every calendar day covered," use date - rn. If "continuous" means "consecutive in the union of source tables, ignoring missing days," use rn_overall - rn_per_state. When in doubt, use rn_overall - rn_per_state — it's the more permissive form and matches most prompts.

Hard Member Workout vs Skip Streaks (UNION + Gaps-and-Islands variant)

▼

Same shape as #1225 in a fitness-app domain: collapse consecutive 'active' (workout) and 'inactive' (skip) days into [period_start, period_end] ranges. Demonstrates the data-sequence vs calendar-consecutive distinction in a 2024 leap-year context.

Tables: completed_workouts (workout_date), skipped_days (skip_date)

Real-World Example

A fitness-tracker app reports each member's continuous workout/skip streaks for engagement scoring. The output drives push-notification logic ("you've skipped 3 days in a row").

▶ 1 Two-Row-Number Difference (handles missing days correctly)
WITH base AS ( SELECT 'active' AS activity_state, workout_date AS activity_date FROM completed_workouts WHERE workout_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-03-31' UNION ALL SELECT 'inactive' AS activity_state, skip_date AS activity_date FROM skipped_days WHERE skip_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-03-31' ), grouping AS ( SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY activity_date::date) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY activity_state ORDER BY activity_date::date) AS grp FROM base ) SELECT activity_state, MIN(activity_date) AS period_start, MAX(activity_date) AS period_end FROM grouping GROUP BY activity_state, grp ORDER BY period_start;

The leap-year trap that makes this anchor different from #1225:

  • 2024 is a leap year. Suppose the data has Feb 28 = active, no row for Feb 29 (missing from both tables), Mar 1 = active, Mar 2 = active.
  • Using date - row_number_per_state: Feb 28 minus N = 2024-02-28 - N. Mar 1 minus (N+1) = 2024-02-29 - N. Different group ids — islands break.
  • Using rn_overall - rn_per_state: rn_overall increments by 1 for each row regardless of calendar gap, so Feb 28, Mar 1, Mar 2 share the same (overall - per-state) difference and stay in one island.
  • Expected output keeps them as one island, so this prompt's "continuous" means data-sequence consecutive, not calendar consecutive.

Trace through 4 sample rows around the leap-year boundary:

activity_date activity_state rn_overall rn_per_state grp (overall - per-state) date - rn_per_state (broken)
2024-02-28activeNKN-K2024-02-28 minus K
2024-03-01activeN+1K+1N-K (same)2024-02-29 minus K (different)
2024-03-02activeN+2K+2N-K (same)2024-02-29 minus K (same as Mar 1)
2024-03-03inactiveN+31N+2 (new group)2024-03-02 minus 1 (new group)

With rn_overall - rn_per_state, Feb 28 / Mar 1 / Mar 2 all share group N-K and collapse into one island (period_start=2024-02-28, period_end=2024-03-02). With the date - rn form, Feb 28 ends up in group "2024-02-28 minus K" while Mar 1 and 2 end up in group "2024-02-29 minus K" — two islands instead of one.

Watch out:

  • Pick the formulation by what "continuous" means in the prompt. If the prompt says "every day in the range" or "no missing calendar days," use date - rn. If the prompt says "consecutive in the data" or doesn't specify, use rn_overall - rn_per_state.
  • Filter to the date range in EACH UNION branch's WHERE. A trailing WHERE on the outer query only filters whatever the WHERE clause is attached to in a UNION ALL.
  • Don't include activity_date in the GROUP BY. If you do, every date becomes its own group and islands never collapse.
  • Don't ORDER BY inside the base CTE. It has no effect on the outer query and can confuse window functions downstream.
  • Both source tables must have rows for ONE state only. If completed_workouts were to also include a status column, you'd skip the UNION ALL entirely and just GROUP BY status from one table.

Per-entity island timelines 3 problems

▼

PARTITION BY entity — One independent timeline per entity (user, order, customer). Every window must PARTITION BY the entity so one entity's rows never split another's runs. Islands form via grp or the LAG → flag → cumulative SUM recipe.

Telling the entity apart from the state. These problems often have two label columns — an entity (like user_id) and a state (like 'streaming' / 'offline'). They look similar but do different jobs:

  • Entity = who the timeline belongs to. The thing you handle "separately for each." You would never merge two entities' rows into one run. Test: whatever fills the blank in "for each ___" is the entity. Here, user_id — user 101's days never join user 102's.
  • State = what the row is, the value that must stay the same across a run. A run breaks the moment the state changes, even if the dates are still back to back. Example: streaming Jan 2–Jan 3, then offline Jan 4 — Jan 3 and Jan 4 are consecutive days, but the run still ends at Jan 3 because the activity flipped.

That is why entity and state sit in different places in the query:

  • entity goes in every window's PARTITION BY — it keeps entities from bleeding into each other.
  • state goes only in the second window's partition (PARTITION BY entity, state) — that is what makes the run break when the activity changes.
  • the final GROUP BY is entity, state, grp, then MIN(date) / MAX(date) give the start and end of each run.

Mental model: entity = who, state = what, dates = the run. You collapse consecutive dates where both who and what stay the same.

Medium #1454 Active Users (dedupe same day + per entity streak + membership semantics)

▼

Find users who logged in on 5 or more consecutive days. Per entity gaps and islands variant with TWO structural traps: (a) the source table allows MULTIPLE rows per (user, day) so the gaps and islands step must dedupe FIRST, and (b) a user may have MULTIPLE qualifying streaks so the final SELECT must use MEMBERSHIP semantics (EXISTS / IN / per user aggregate), not SELECT DISTINCT as a cosmetic fix.

Tables: Accounts (id, name), Logins (id, login_date). Logins may contain DUPLICATE rows (a user can log in multiple times in the same day — same (id, login_date) row stored twice).

→

Decision Tree Path

Gaps and Islands decision tree: Q1 grain = per entity, dates with possible duplicates → dedupe to SELECT DISTINCT id, login_date. Q2 detect consecutive runs per entity → date - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY date) form (sibling template: per entity island template). Q3 collapse runs to a streak length and gate on length ≥ N → GROUP BY (id, grp) + HAVING COUNT(*) ≥ 5. Q4 final SELECT is per entity, not per streak → membership semantics via EXISTS / IN, NOT a cosmetic SELECT DISTINCT.

Real World Example

A growth team defines "highly engaged users" as those with 5+ day login streaks and ships the list to the lifecycle email engine. The product logs every successful login event, so a power user who opened the app twice on Monday has two rows for Monday in Logins. Same engagement, but if the streak detection counts those rows directly the "consecutive days" math breaks down (the row index advances twice on Monday without the date advancing). Dedupe first, then the streak math works.

Build order — dedupe FIRST, then gaps and islands, then membership:

  1. CTE 1 base: SELECT DISTINCT id, login_date FROM Logins to collapse same day duplicates. Without this step, ROW_NUMBER advances twice on the duplicate day and the date - rn grp value lands on the wrong date, breaking the streak detection. (SELECT id, login_date FROM Logins GROUP BY id, login_date works equivalently if you also need a per day login count, but if you don't, DISTINCT reads cleaner.)
  2. CTE 2 date_groups: standard date - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY login_date)::int AS grp trick. PARTITION BY id is mandatory because every user has their own streak windows. Consecutive days all land on the same grp value; a gap day produces a new grp.
  3. CTE 3 streaks: GROUP BY id, grp HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5 — one row per qualifying streak. A user with two non overlapping 5+ day streaks contributes 2 rows here; a user with one contributes 1; a user with none contributes 0.
  4. Final SELECT against Accounts using MEMBERSHIP: WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM streaks s WHERE s.id = a.id) or WHERE a.id IN (SELECT id FROM streaks). The outer query iterates per Accounts row, so multiple qualifying streaks per user naturally collapse to one output row.
  5. ORDER BY a.id.

Trace — what each CTE produces for the example data (Jonathan = 7):

step what Jonathan looks like after this step
Logins (source)(7, 5-30), (7, 5-31), (7, 6-01), (7, 6-02), (7, 6-02), (7, 6-03), (7, 6-10) — the duplicate 6-02 is the trap
CTE 1 base(7, 5-30), (7, 5-31), (7, 6-01), (7, 6-02), (7, 6-03), (7, 6-10) — duplicate collapsed
CTE 2 date_groupsrn = 1..6; grp = login_date - rn = 5-29, 5-29, 5-29, 5-29, 5-29, 6-04 — first 5 rows share grp 5-29, last row is its own grp
CTE 3 streaks(7, grp=5-29, count=5) qualifies; (7, grp=6-04, count=1) does not — one row for user 7
final EXISTSJonathan emitted once (user 7 exists in streaks); Winston (id=1) emitted zero times (only 2 distinct days, no qualifying grp)
▶ 1 EXISTS / IN against streak CTE (membership semantics, no DISTINCT needed)
WITH base AS ( -- 1. Dedupe same day duplicates FIRST. SELECT DISTINCT id, login_date FROM Logins ), date_groups AS ( -- 2. Gaps and islands per user: consecutive dates share grp. SELECT id, login_date - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY login_date)::int AS grp FROM base ), streaks AS ( -- 3. One row per qualifying (user, grp) streak. SELECT id FROM date_groups GROUP BY id, grp HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5 ) -- 4. Membership check: per Accounts row, does the user appear in streaks? SELECT a.id, a.name FROM Accounts AS a WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM streaks s WHERE s.id = a.id) ORDER BY a.id;

Why this is best: The outer SELECT iterates per Accounts row. EXISTS is a per row true/false check; multiple qualifying streaks per user all collapse to "yes, present." One row per qualifying account, no DISTINCT needed. WHERE a.id IN (SELECT id FROM streaks) is equivalent and reads slightly cleaner if you prefer set notation.

▶ 2 Per user aggregate (collapse to one row per user via MAX of streak length)
WITH base AS ( SELECT DISTINCT id, login_date FROM Logins ), date_groups AS ( SELECT id, login_date - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY login_date)::int AS grp FROM base ), streak_lengths AS ( SELECT id, grp, COUNT(*) AS days FROM date_groups GROUP BY id, grp ), per_user AS ( SELECT id FROM streak_lengths GROUP BY id HAVING MAX(days) >= 5 ) SELECT a.id, a.name FROM Accounts AS a JOIN per_user p USING (id) ORDER BY a.id;

Why this is also good: Two stage aggregate — per (id, grp) for streak length, then per id for the max streak length. HAVING MAX(days) >= 5 reads as "this user has at least one streak of 5+ days." Naturally one row per user. Reads slightly more verbose than EXISTS but makes the per user roll up explicit.

▶ 3 SELECT DISTINCT at the end (the symptomatic fix — works but treats the wrong layer)
WITH base AS (SELECT DISTINCT id, login_date FROM Logins), date_groups AS ( SELECT id, login_date - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY login_date)::int AS grp FROM base ) SELECT DISTINCT a.id, a.name -- <-- the cosmetic fix FROM Accounts AS a JOIN date_groups AS b ON b.id = a.id GROUP BY a.id, a.name, grp HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5 ORDER BY a.id;

Why this works but isn't the lesson: The GROUP BY (id, name, grp) emits one row per qualifying (user, streak) pair; the outer DISTINCT collapses repeats. Correct output, but the grain of the final SELECT is wrong for the question being asked — the question is "is the user active" (per user yes/no), not "list every qualifying streak." Rank 1 and Rank 2 fix the grain. This form is acceptable but you have to remember the DISTINCT every time; forget it once and the duplicates leak into production.

Watch out:

  • DISTINCT or GROUP BY on (id, login_date) MUST come FIRST. If you skip the dedupe and run ROW_NUMBER over the raw Logins, the duplicate day advances rn by 1 without advancing login_date, so the date - rn grp value LANDS ON A DIFFERENT GROUP than it should. A 5 day true streak with one duplicate day computes as 2 separate "streaks" of 3 and 2 days, neither qualifying. Test data with duplicate same day logins will silently produce wrong answers without the dedupe step.
  • The structural lesson: pick the final SELECT grain to match the question. The question is "is the user active" — per user yes/no. The grain at SELECT a.id, a.name FROM Accounts ... WHERE EXISTS (...) is per account row, which matches. GROUP BY a.id, a.name, grp HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5 is grained per qualifying streak, which doesn't match; outer DISTINCT patches the symptom (extra rows) without fixing the cause (wrong grain).
  • PARTITION BY id is mandatory in the ROW_NUMBER window. Without it, the row number sequence runs across ALL users together. User A's day 5 might land at rn=12 because there were 11 earlier rows globally, and the grp calc collapses unrelated users into the same "streak."
  • Cast ROW_NUMBER to ::int in the subtraction. login_date - ROW_NUMBER() OVER ... needs an integer offset; without the cast Postgres may error on a date minus a bigint mismatch.
  • EXISTS vs IN performance is dialect dependent. Postgres' planner usually treats them equivalently. Pick by readability.
  • "5 or more consecutive days" is closed lower, open upper. COUNT(*) >= 5 catches 5, 6, 7+ day streaks. The follow up generalization asks for N > or = days; the only change is the literal in HAVING (or making it a parameter).

Hard Collapse Order Status Periods (UNION + per-entity partition)

▼

Same gaps-and-islands shape as #1225, but each entity (order_id) has its own timeline. The window functions must partition by the entity key, not just by status, or runs from different entities collide.

Tables: processing_orders (order_id, process_date), shipped_orders (order_id, ship_date)

Real-World Example

An e-commerce ops team builds an order timeline view: each order shows one row per status period (processing then shipped) with start and end dates, fed into the customer-facing tracking page.

▶ 1 Two-Row-Number Difference, Partitioned by Entity
WITH base AS ( SELECT 'processing' AS status, order_id, process_date AS status_date FROM processing_orders UNION ALL SELECT 'shipped' AS status, order_id, ship_date AS status_date FROM shipped_orders ), date_grouping AS ( SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY status_date) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id, status ORDER BY status_date) AS grp FROM base ) SELECT order_id, status, MIN(status_date) AS start_date, MAX(status_date) AS end_date FROM date_grouping GROUP BY order_id, status, grp ORDER BY MIN(status_date), order_id;

What makes this anchor different from #1225 and the workout/skip variant:

  • Each order_id has its OWN timeline. Order 101's shipped run on Jan 4-6 must not be split just because order 103's processing row sits in between in the global date order.
  • BOTH window functions must PARTITION BY order_id — not just the inner one.
  • The inner window adds status to the partition: PARTITION BY order_id, status.
  • The GROUP BY uses three keys: order_id, status, grp. The grp label is local to one (entity, status) pair, so dropping order_id would mash different orders into one row.

Trace through the bug when order_id is missing from the outer window:

status_date order_id status global rn per-status rn grp
2024-01-04101shipped615
2024-01-05103processing7——
2024-01-06101shipped826

Order 101's two shipped rows land on different grp values (5 vs 6) because order 103's row inflated the global rn between them. Result: 101 shipped is split into two output rows instead of one. Adding PARTITION BY order_id to the outer window restarts the global rn at 1 inside each order's timeline, so 101's shipped rows get rn 4 then 5 (no gap), share the same grp, and collapse correctly.

Trace of the fixed version for order 101:

status_date status rn within order_id rn within (order_id, status) grp
2024-01-01processing110
2024-01-02processing220
2024-01-03processing330
2024-01-04shipped413
2024-01-05shipped523
2024-01-06shipped633

All three shipped rows share grp = 3 and collapse into one row: (101, shipped, 2024-01-04, 2024-01-06). The processing rows share grp = 0 and collapse into (101, processing, 2024-01-01, 2024-01-03).

Watch out:

  • Both windows need ORDER BY status_date. Without it on the outer one, the row numbering is undefined and the gaps-and-islands math breaks silently.
  • Both windows need PARTITION BY order_id. Skipping it on the outer one is the bug above.
  • GROUP BY needs all three keys: order_id, status, grp. The grp label only means "same run" within a fixed (entity, status) pair.
  • Use UNION ALL, not UNION. The two source tables can't produce duplicates, so the dedupe sort is wasted work.
  • Monotonic status transitions don't change the shape. Even though "once shipped, stays shipped" guarantees at most two periods per order, the same query handles repeated transitions if the prompt allowed them.

Hard #2701 Consecutive Transactions with Increasing Amounts

▼

For each customer, find longest runs of strictly increasing consecutive-day transactions.

Tables: Transactions (transaction_id, customer_id, transaction_date, amount)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Self-Join & Relational Queries → Pattern E: Self-Joins

Real-World Example

A fraud-watch team inspects customers whose transaction amounts climb sharply over consecutive days — a compromised-card signature.

▶ 1 Island Detection on Two Conditions
WITH t AS ( SELECT customer_id, transaction_date, amount, LAG(transaction_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY transaction_date) AS prev_date, LAG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY transaction_date) AS prev_amt FROM Transactions ), flags AS ( SELECT customer_id, transaction_date, amount, CASE WHEN DATEDIFF(transaction_date, prev_date) = 1 AND amount > prev_amt THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS new_island FROM t ), grouped AS ( SELECT customer_id, transaction_date, SUM(new_island) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY transaction_date) AS grp FROM flags ) SELECT customer_id, MIN(transaction_date) AS consecutive_start, MAX(transaction_date) AS consecutive_end FROM grouped GROUP BY customer_id, grp HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3 ORDER BY customer_id;

Why this is best: Flag each day as "new island" when either gap > 1 or amount not increasing, then cumulative SUM creates the grp key.

Performance: Three window passes. Linear.

Adjacency & gap checks (not full island collapsing) 6 problems

▼

LAG / LEAD / self-join — These look like gaps-and-islands but only compare each row to its neighbour (or find the gap), without collapsing whole runs. Reach for LAG/LEAD or a self-join on adjacent rows rather than the grp machinery.

Medium #1709 Biggest Window Between Visits

▼

For each user, the largest gap in days between visits (or to 2021-01-01).

Tables: UserVisits (user_id, visit_date)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Self-Join & Relational Queries → Pattern E: Self-Joins

Real-World Example

A lifecycle analyst finds the longest dormancy per user to define "rolling churn" thresholds.

▶ 1 LEAD with End-of-Window Sentinel
SELECT user_id, MAX(DATEDIFF(next_visit, visit_date)) AS biggest_window FROM ( SELECT user_id, visit_date, LEAD(visit_date, 1, DATE '2021-01-01') OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY visit_date) AS next_visit FROM UserVisits ) t GROUP BY user_id;

Why this is best: LEAD with a sentinel handles the last visit gracefully as the gap to Jan 1.

Performance: One window + one aggregate.

Medium #1843 Suspicious Bank Accounts

▼

Accounts whose monthly credit total exceeds maximum balance in two or more consecutive months.

Tables: Accounts (account_id, max_income), Transactions (trans_id, account_id, type, amount, day)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Self-Join & Relational Queries → Pattern E: Self-Joins

Real-World Example

An AML team investigates accounts receiving unusually large deposits across a streak of months — a red flag for money-laundering patterns.

▶ 1 Monthly Credit Aggregate + Streak
WITH monthly AS ( SELECT account_id, DATE_FORMAT(day, '%Y-%m') AS ym, SUM(amount) AS credit FROM Transactions WHERE type = 'Creditor' GROUP BY account_id, DATE_FORMAT(day, '%Y-%m') ), flagged AS ( SELECT m.account_id, m.ym FROM monthly m JOIN Accounts a ON a.account_id = m.account_id WHERE m.credit > a.max_income ) SELECT DISTINCT f1.account_id FROM flagged f1 JOIN flagged f2 ON f2.account_id = f1.account_id AND PERIOD_DIFF(REPLACE(f2.ym,'-',''), REPLACE(f1.ym,'-','')) = 1 ORDER BY f1.account_id;

Why this is best: Aggregate monthly credit, flag over-threshold months, then self-join on consecutive months.

Performance: Two aggregates + self-join.

Medium #2228 Users With Two Purchases Within Seven Days

▼

Return users whose any two consecutive purchases are within 7 days of each other.

Tables: Purchases (purchase_id, user_id, purchase_date)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Self-Join & Relational Queries → Pattern E: Self-Joins

Real-World Example

A retention team identifies quick repeat buyers to feed a "you might also like" reorder email.

▶ 1 LAG per User + DATEDIFF Filter
WITH lagged AS ( SELECT user_id, purchase_date, LAG(purchase_date) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY purchase_date) AS prev_date FROM Purchases ) SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM lagged WHERE DATEDIFF(purchase_date, prev_date) <= 7 ORDER BY user_id;

Why this is best: LAG gives the previous purchase per user; a 7-day filter finds the rapid-repeat cohort.

Performance: Single window pass.

Medium #2688 Find Active Users

▼

Users with two purchases within any 7-day window (like 2228 but from a different table schema).

Tables: Users (user_id, purchase_date)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Self-Join & Relational Queries → Pattern E: Self-Joins

Real-World Example

A marketplace segments frequent buyers for a weekly digest.

▶ 1 LAG with 7-Day Window
SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM ( SELECT user_id, purchase_date, LAG(purchase_date) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY purchase_date) AS prev_date FROM Users ) t WHERE DATEDIFF(purchase_date, prev_date) BETWEEN 1 AND 7 ORDER BY user_id;

Why this is best: Same LAG pattern as 2228; the DATEDIFF range filter returns users with rapid sequential buys.

Performance: One window pass.

Hard #1972 First and Last Call On the Same Day

▼

Find users whose first and last call on the same day were with different people.

Tables: Calls (caller_id, recipient_id, call_time)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Self-Join & Relational Queries → Pattern E: Self-Joins

Real-World Example

A spam investigator surfaces users whose daily first and last contact differed — a common automation/spam signature.

▶ 1 Normalize Direction + First/Last per Day
WITH norm AS ( SELECT caller_id AS u, recipient_id AS other, call_time FROM Calls UNION ALL SELECT recipient_id, caller_id, call_time FROM Calls ), ranked AS ( SELECT u, other, call_time, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY u, DATE(call_time) ORDER BY call_time) AS rn_asc, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY u, DATE(call_time) ORDER BY call_time DESC) AS rn_desc FROM norm ) SELECT DISTINCT u AS user_id FROM ranked WHERE rn_asc = 1 OR rn_desc = 1 GROUP BY u, DATE(call_time) HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT other) = 2;

Why this is best: Normalize to a (u, other) view, pick the first and last per day, then check if other differs.

Performance: Two window passes + group-by.

Hard #2474 Customers With Strictly Increasing Purchases

▼

Customers whose yearly spend strictly increases each year in the table.

Tables: Orders (order_id, customer_id, order_date, price)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Self-Join & Relational Queries → Pattern E: Self-Joins

Real-World Example

Account management identifies accounts that grow year-over-year with no dips — ideal for upsell prioritization.

▶ 1 Yearly Totals + LAG Check
WITH yearly AS ( SELECT customer_id, YEAR(order_date) AS yr, SUM(price) AS total FROM Orders GROUP BY customer_id, YEAR(order_date) ), lagged AS ( SELECT customer_id, yr, total, LAG(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY yr) AS prev_total, LAG(yr) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY yr) AS prev_yr FROM yearly ) SELECT customer_id FROM lagged GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN prev_total IS NOT NULL AND (total <= prev_total OR yr <> prev_yr + 1) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 0 AND COUNT(*) > 1;

Why this is best: LAG per customer surfaces the prior year. A strict increase is "no violation rows and more than one year".

Performance: Two passes. Linear.

Window 15 problems

▼

A single table with a date or sequence column → each row annotated with a rolling or running aggregate.

Signal words: "rolling," "running total," "last N days," "cumulative," "moving average," "most recent before"

Technique: SUM/AVG OVER (ROWS BETWEEN), running SUM with threshold, subquery for last value before date

Reference Techniques used in Window (functions + frame clause cheat sheet)

▼

The SQL techniques this recipe uses plus a frame clause cheat sheet. The cheat sheet applies to any window function (running aggregates, rolling windows, LAST_VALUE/FIRST_VALUE, sessionization), not just time-based queries.

Technique What It Does When to Reach for It Example Code
SUM() OVER / AVG() OVER Computes an aggregate across a window without collapsing rows You need a running or rolling aggregate while keeping every row in the output 
SELECT day, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (
         PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day
       ) AS running_total
FROM Trans;
ROWS BETWEEN Defines a sliding window frame (e.g., 6 preceding and current row) for a window aggregate You need a rolling average, running total, or cumulative sum over a fixed number of rows 
SELECT day,
       AVG(sales) OVER (
         ORDER BY day
         ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ) AS rolling_7d
FROM Daily;

Frame Clause Cheat Sheet

The frame clause defines which rows in the partition a window function actually looks at. Every aggregate, FIRST_VALUE / LAST_VALUE / NTH_VALUE, and even some ranking calls respect the frame — so getting the frame right is the difference between a correct answer and a silently wrong one.

Frame clause Window includes When to use it
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW Start of partition through the current row Running totals, cumulative sums, growing aggregates. This is also the default when you have ORDER BY but no explicit frame.
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING Every row in the partition (past + present + future) Required for LAST_VALUE to actually return the partition's final value. Without it the default frame stops at the current row and LAST_VALUE silently returns the current row's value. Also useful for "partition total alongside each row" patterns.
ROWS BETWEEN N PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW The last N+1 rows ending at the current row Trailing windows: 7-day rolling average (6 PRECEDING), trailing 28-day active count, last-N-events aggregate.
ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND N FOLLOWING The next N+1 rows starting at the current row Look-ahead windows: "next 3 events," forward-looking sums, lead aggregates. Mirror image of the trailing window.
ROWS BETWEEN N PRECEDING AND N FOLLOWING Centered window of 2N+1 rows around the current row Smoothing time series, symmetric moving averages, "compare to neighbors on both sides."
ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING Just the previous row Equivalent to LAG(). Rarely written this way, but useful for understanding that frame syntax can pluck a single row at any offset.
RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 'N days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW All rows where the ORDER BY value is within N days of the current row's value Date-based rolling windows where input data has missing days. ROWS would count 7 physical rows regardless of dates; RANGE counts the actual 7 calendar days. Postgres only.
(no frame clause) Depends on whether ORDER BY is present With ORDER BY: defaults to RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. Without ORDER BY: the entire partition. This is why LAST_VALUE with just ORDER BY silently returns the current row.

ROWS vs RANGE

Mode How it picks rows Diverges from the other when
ROWS By physical row position. ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW takes exactly 3 rows. When the ORDER BY column has duplicate values: ROWS treats each tied row separately; RANGE groups them together. Also when there are gaps in dates: ROWS counts 7 actual rows; RANGE counts the calendar interval.
RANGE By ORDER BY value. RANGE BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW means "all rows whose ORDER BY value is within 2 of the current row's value." When ties exist, RANGE pulls in every tied row at the boundary. When dates have gaps, RANGE follows the calendar (missing days don't count as rows but still fall inside the time interval).

Rules of thumb:

  • If the prompt says "last N records," "last N events," or "trailing N rows," use ROWS.
  • If the prompt says "last N days" with missing days in the data, use RANGE (or fill the gaps first with a calendar CTE and then use ROWS).
  • If you're using LAST_VALUE / FIRST_VALUE / NTH_VALUE, always write the frame explicitly. FIRST_VALUE happens to work with the default, but stating the frame both times makes intent visible and prevents the LAST_VALUE trap.
  • If you only have PARTITION BY with no ORDER BY, the frame is the entire partition by default — fine for partition-total patterns but never use this for running aggregates.

How to pick: decision tree

▼

What each output row needs to show routes you to the method and the set below.

Setup — every window function keeps all rows and adds a value. Name three things first:

  • Partition = the group each calc restarts within (per user, per product).
  • Order = the sequence column (date / id). Required for running, sliding, LAG / LEAD, and ranking.
  • Frame = which rows in the partition the function actually sees → see the Frame Clause Cheat Sheet in the Reference card above. Always write the frame explicitly for FIRST_VALUE / LAST_VALUE.

Walk the questions in order. Stop at the first match.

Q1. What does each row need?

  • An aggregate (sum / avg / count) over a set of rows → Q2.
  • One value copied from another specific row → Q3.
  • A rank, to keep top-N per group → ✓ this lives in Rank & Percentile — position selection, not a frame aggregate. The generic template stays below for reference..
  • Rows grouped into sessions split by time gaps → ✓ use Sessionization (gap based grouping).

Q2. Aggregate over what span?

  • Start of the partition through now (grows each row) → ✓ use Running total / cumulative aggregate.
  • A fixed trailing window (last N rows / last N days) → ✓ use Sliding window aggregate (rolling N days).
  • Unsure how the window picks rows (ROWS vs RANGE, ties, gaps) → see Frame clauses (ROWS / RANGE BETWEEN).

Q3. Which other row's value?

  • The immediate previous / next row → ✓ use LAG / LEAD comparison (full neighbour patterns live in the Compare recipe).
  • The first or last row of the whole partition → ✓ use FIRST_VALUE / LAST_VALUE (write the frame, or LAST_VALUE silently returns the current row).
  • The most recent row before a given date → ✓ use Point in Time.

Rule of thumb: "running / cumulative" → Running total · "last N days / rolling" → Sliding window · "previous / next" → LAG / LEAD · "first / latest / most recent" → FIRST_VALUE / LAST_VALUE or Point in Time · "top / Nth per group" → Top N.

→ Each green pick links to its copy-paste skeleton in Generic templates per method just below.

Generic templates per method

▼

Copy-paste skeleton for each method the decision tree routes to. Swap the placeholder names; the shape stays the same.

Top N per group (ROW_NUMBER + filter) ↑ tree

▼

Use when: keep the highest or latest N rows within each group.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. CTE: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY rank_col DESC, tiebreak).
  2. Outer SELECT filters rn ≤ N.
  3. Cross-link: this is also the canonical Rank & Percentile shape — same pattern, different recipe home.
SELECT *
FROM (
  SELECT t.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group_col
                            ORDER BY sort_col DESC) AS rn
  FROM tbl t
) s
WHERE rn <= N;          -- top N per group (use RANK for ties)

Sessionization (gap based grouping) ↑ tree

▼

Use when: a gap larger than a threshold starts a new session id.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. CTE 1: sort rows per entity by timestamp.
  2. CTE 2: flag a "new session" with LAG — true when the gap between current and previous row exceeds the threshold.
  3. CTE 3: running SUM of the new-session flag — becomes the session id per row.
  4. GROUP BY (entity, session_id) for per-session aggregates.
WITH flagged AS (
  SELECT t.*,
         CASE WHEN ts - LAG(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts)
                   > INTERVAL '30 minutes'
              THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_new_session
  FROM events t
)
SELECT *,
       SUM(is_new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts) AS session_id
FROM flagged;

Running total / cumulative aggregate ↑ tree

▼

Use when: each row carries the total so far, from the start of its partition.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Use SUM(metric) OVER (PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY ts) — with ORDER BY present, the default frame is RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING through current row, which IS the running total.
  2. No frame clause needed unless you want something other than "from the start through now".
SELECT t.*,
       SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY entity_id
                         ORDER BY ts) AS running_total
FROM tbl t;
-- ORDER BY with no frame = UNBOUNDED PRECEDING .. CURRENT ROW (the running total)

Sliding window aggregate (rolling N days) ↑ tree

▼

Use when: a fixed trailing window (last N rows, or last N calendar days).

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Use SUM/AVG/COUNT OVER (PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN N PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW).
  2. ROWS counts rows; switch to RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 'N days' PRECEDING when the source has missing days and "N days" should count by calendar.
SELECT t.*,
       AVG(metric) OVER (PARTITION BY entity_id ORDER BY day
                         ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS rolling_7
FROM tbl t;
-- date-based with missing days:
--   RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW   (Postgres)

LAG / LEAD comparison ↑ tree

▼

Use when: pull the previous or next row's value to compare or subtract.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. LAG(col) OVER (PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY ts) pulls the previous row's value alongside the current row.
  2. The first row in each partition gets NULL from LAG — handle with COALESCE if your downstream math chokes on NULL.
  3. Compute the delta in the outer SELECT: current_col - prev_col.
SELECT t.*,
       LAG(val)  OVER (PARTITION BY k ORDER BY ts) AS prev_val,
       LEAD(val) OVER (PARTITION BY k ORDER BY ts) AS next_val
FROM tbl t;
-- then in an outer query: val - prev_val, or WHERE val > prev_val

FIRST_VALUE / LAST_VALUE ↑ tree

▼

Use when: copy the first or last row of the whole partition onto every row.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. FIRST_VALUE(col) OVER (...) returns the first row's value within the frame.
  2. LAST_VALUE needs explicit ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING — otherwise the default frame stops at the current row and it silently returns the current value.
SELECT t.*,
       FIRST_VALUE(val) OVER (PARTITION BY k ORDER BY ts
            ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS first_val,
       LAST_VALUE(val)  OVER (PARTITION BY k ORDER BY ts
            ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS last_val
FROM tbl t;
-- the explicit frame is required, or LAST_VALUE returns the current row

Point in Time (most recent before a date) ↑ tree

▼

Use when: per key, take the latest row on or before a cutoff date.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Inner query: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY ts DESC) over rows where ts ≤ target_date.
  2. Outer filter: rn = 1 — that's the most-recent-before-target row per entity.
  3. Postgres alternative: SELECT DISTINCT ON (entity) ... ORDER BY entity, ts DESC.
SELECT *
FROM (
  SELECT s.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key_col
                            ORDER BY as_of_date DESC) AS rn
  FROM snapshot s
  WHERE s.as_of_date <= :cutoff
) t
WHERE rn = 1;            -- one latest row per key as of the cutoff

Running total / cumulative aggregate 4 problems

▼

nb01 qtype: window_running_total — SUM OVER (PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY time) — running aggregate from the start of the partition through the current row. Default frame when ORDER BY is present is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which IS the running total.

Medium #1308 Running Total for Different Genders

▼

Per gender, return the cumulative score over days.

Tables: Scores (player_name, gender, day, score_points)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation (Window Functions)

Real-World Example

An event scoreboard updates a live running total per team (gender) at every event so organizers can display the race.

▶ 1 Ordered Cumulative SUM
SELECT gender, day, SUM(score_points) OVER (PARTITION BY gender ORDER BY day) AS total FROM Scores ORDER BY gender, day;

Why this is best: Window without explicit frame defaults to RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which is exactly a running total.

Performance: One window pass.

Medium #2066 Account Balance

▼

For each account, report the running balance after every transaction date.

Tables: Transactions (account_id, day, type, amount)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation (Window Functions)

Real-World Example

A bank exports a daily account-statement feed that shows the walking balance after each transaction.

▶ 1 Signed Running SUM per Account
SELECT account_id, day, SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'Deposit' THEN amount ELSE -amount END) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY day) AS balance FROM Transactions ORDER BY account_id, day;

Why this is best: Signed SUM window gives running balance without a subquery.

Performance: One window pass.

Medium #1204 Last Person to Fit in the Bus

▼

Elevators have weight limits. Queue order matters: if heaviest people are first, fewer board before limit. System must know when to stop admitting passengers to avoid overweight trip.

📌
Pattern: Running Total with Capacity Check

Use SUM(weight) OVER(ORDER BY turn) for running cumulative weight. Find last turn where cumulative <= 1000. Business: Capacity planning (elevator limits, batch processing).

Business Context
Elevators have weight limits. Queue order matters: if heaviest people are first, fewer board before limit. System must know when to stop admitting passengers to avoid overweight trip.
▶ Rank 1: Window Running Total + Filter Clean and direct
SELECT person_name FROM ( SELECT person_name, SUM(weight) OVER (ORDER BY turn) AS cumulative_weight FROM Queue ) t WHERE cumulative_weight <= 1000 ORDER BY cumulative_weight DESC LIMIT 1;

Performance Analysis: Single scan of Queue: O(n). ORDER BY turn for window: O(n log n) but limited by existing turn order (may already be sorted). SUM OVER: O(n) in single pass with accumulator. Filter cumulative <= 1000: O(n). Identify MAX via ORDER BY DESC LIMIT 1: O(n log n) but only on filtered set. Memory: O(n) for sort buffer, O(1) for running sum.

Why Rank 1: Window function is perfect for running totals. Simple logic: "find last row where cumulative <= 1000".

▶ Rank 2: Self-Join with Cumulative Sum Pre-window approach
SELECT q1.person_name FROM Queue q1 WHERE ( SELECT SUM(q2.weight) FROM Queue q2 WHERE q2.turn <= q1.turn ) <= 1000 ORDER BY q1.turn DESC LIMIT 1;

Performance Analysis: Correlated subquery for each row. Outer scan: O(n). Inner SUM per row: for row i, sums first i rows = O(i). Total: O(1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n) = O(n²). For 1000 rows: 500k comparisons. Window function: O(n log n) = 10k comparisons. 50x slower! With index on turn, inner query still O(i).

Why Rank 2: Demonstrates why window functions are critical for running totals. Quadratic complexity is unacceptable for large queues.

Medium Cumulative Minutes Listened Per User

▼

For each listening session, compute a per user running total of minutes listened from the start of the user's history through the current session. Drills the canonical cumulative aggregate (SUM OVER PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...) and the tie breaker trap: when the prompt says "handle ties on the order column," that tie breaker must appear in BOTH the window's ORDER BY and the final result's ORDER BY.

📌
Pattern: Cumulative aggregate + tie breaker on the order key

Use SUM OVER (PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY time, tiebreaker) to produce a running total from the start of each partition through the current row. The tie breaker on the ORDER BY is the part most candidates miss — without it, ties on the time column produce arbitrary or collapsed cumulative values depending on the frame. The final outer ORDER BY needs the same tie breaker so the rows print in deterministic order.

Business Context
Cumulative consumption per user is the spine of nearly every engagement and retention dashboard — total minutes streamed per user over time, total dollars spent, total lessons completed, total messages sent. Running totals expose pacing (is this user accelerating or stalling?) in a way that lifetime totals or daily counts cannot. Most BI tools want this shape baked into the warehouse layer.
Problem statement

Write a query against listening_sessions(session_id, user_id, episode_id, session_start, minutes_listened) that returns each session row plus a cumulative_minutes column showing the running total of minutes listened by that user up to and including the current session. Order the window by session_start, and handle ties on session_start by breaking on session_id (lower session_id first). Return columns session_id, user_id, episode_id, session_start, minutes_listened, cumulative_minutes ordered by user_id, session_start, session_id.

▶ Rank 1: CTE with SUM OVER + explicit ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW The frame is spelled out, the tie breaker is in both ORDER BYs
WITH base AS ( SELECT session_id, user_id, episode_id, session_start, minutes_listened, SUM(minutes_listened) OVER ( PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY session_start, session_id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW ) AS cumulative_minutes FROM listening_sessions ) SELECT session_id, user_id, episode_id, session_start, minutes_listened, cumulative_minutes FROM base ORDER BY user_id, session_start, session_id;

How the CTE is structured: the inner CTE keeps every row in listening_sessions and decorates it with the running total. The window function is partitioned by user_id so each user's running total starts fresh at zero, ordered by session_start then session_id so ties on the timestamp are broken deterministically, and framed as ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW so the sum runs from the start of the partition through the current row. The outer SELECT just projects and orders.

Why the tie breaker is required: if two rows share the same session_start for the same user, ORDER BY session_start alone leaves the engine free to put either row first. With ROWS BETWEEN framing, that arbitrary order picks one row to be "earlier" and produces non deterministic cumulative_minutes values for the tied pair. The classic failure mode: the example test data has no ties so the query passes, then the hidden test data has ties and the query fails with rows swapped. Adding session_id (the primary key) as a secondary ORDER BY guarantees a unique total ordering — and since session_id is the PK, no two rows can share the same (session_start, session_id) pair.

Why the outer ORDER BY also needs the tie breaker: SQL does not guarantee that final result order matches the window's ORDER BY. Even if the window computed the correct cumulative values, the outer query is allowed to emit tied (user_id, session_start) rows in either order unless the outer ORDER BY itself breaks the tie. Match the outer ORDER BY to the window's ORDER BY so output row order is also deterministic.

Default frame trap: if you write ORDER BY session_start with no ROWS BETWEEN clause, the SQL standard's default frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. RANGE treats all rows with the same ORDER BY value as one logical position, so tied rows would BOTH get the cumulative sum that includes both of them — a different wrong answer than ROWS gives. With a unique tie breaker like session_id in the ORDER BY, no two rows tie on the full ordering key, so ROWS and RANGE produce identical results — but spelling out ROWS BETWEEN makes the intent explicit and protects against future readers thinking the default is row by row.

Performance Analysis: One scan of listening_sessions: O(n). The window function sorts each user's partition by (session_start, session_id) once: O(n log n) total. The UNBOUNDED PRECEDING frame keeps a running accumulator with O(1) memory per partition — no frame buffer needed since old rows never leave. The final ORDER BY typically reuses the partition sort.

Why Rank 1: the frame is explicit, the tie breaker is in both ORDER BY clauses, and every choice maps to a line in the prompt. This is what an interviewer wants to see when the prompt says "handle ties by session_id."

▶ Rank 2: SUM OVER without an explicit frame Same answer, leans on the default RANGE frame
WITH base AS ( SELECT session_id, user_id, episode_id, session_start, minutes_listened, SUM(minutes_listened) OVER ( PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY session_start, session_id ) AS cumulative_minutes FROM listening_sessions ) SELECT * FROM base ORDER BY user_id, session_start, session_id;

How this differs from Rank 1: the ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW clause is dropped. When you write a window aggregate with ORDER BY and no explicit frame, the default frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW — which for a running total is what you want, IF the ordering key has no duplicates.

Why this works here: the ORDER BY is (session_start, session_id), and session_id is the PRIMARY KEY. No two rows can share the same primary key value, so no two rows tie on the full ordering key, so RANGE and ROWS produce identical results. The tie breaker is what makes both frames safe.

When to prefer Rank 1: when you want the frame intent visible at the call site (defensive readability), when you cannot guarantee the ORDER BY columns are unique, or when you are working in a dialect or future schema where the columns might be non unique. The explicit ROWS BETWEEN clause is one extra line that buys "you cannot misread my intent."

When to prefer Rank 2: when the running total is the canonical "sum from the start" and the ORDER BY ends in a PK or other unique column. Shorter, idiomatic, equally correct.

LAG / LEAD comparison no problems yet

▼

nb01 qtype: window_lag_lead — LAG(col) / LEAD(col) pulls the previous or next row's value into the current row to compute deltas, growth, gaps, or compare to neighbor. Always handle the NULL at the partition edges explicitly.

No problems in this section yet. Generate one from nb01 with this qtype and it will land here.

Sliding window aggregate (rolling N days) 7 problems

▼

nb01 qtype: window_sliding — SUM / AVG / COUNT OVER (... ROWS BETWEEN N PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) gives a trailing window aggregate per row. Use ROWS when the prompt counts rows, RANGE when the prompt counts the date interval and gaps matter.

Medium #1321 Restaurant Growth

▼

Restaurant managers analyze weekly revenue trends to smooth daily volatility. A Wednesday may be slow, but the 7-day average captures the true trend and helps predict capacity needs.

📌
Pattern: Rolling Window (ROWS BETWEEN)

Use SUM/AVG OVER with ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND 6 PRECEDING for 7-day rolling average. Business: Restaurant revenue forecasting with weekly averages.

Business Context
Restaurant managers analyze weekly revenue trends to smooth daily volatility. A Wednesday may be slow, but the 7-day average captures the true trend and helps predict capacity needs.
▶ Rank 1: Window Frame with ROWS BETWEEN Correct semantics for rolling window
SELECT visited_on, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY visited_on ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS amount, ROUND(AVG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY visited_on ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS average_amount FROM ( SELECT visited_on, SUM(amount) AS amount FROM Customer GROUP BY visited_on ) daily WHERE visited_on >= (SELECT MIN(visited_on) + INTERVAL '6 days' FROM Customer) ORDER BY visited_on;

Performance Analysis: GROUP BY aggregates to daily totals O(n). Window function processes once over sorted data O(n). ROWS BETWEEN frame: each row looks back 7 days max, so frame size is constant O(7). Memory: O(7) for frame buffer, not O(n). Much faster than RANGE which would match all dates in range.

Why Rank 1: ROWS BETWEEN guarantees exactly 7 rows included. RANGE BETWEEN would be wrong if multiple customers visited same day (would sum duplicates).

▶ Rank 2: Self-Join with Date Range Pre-window approach
SELECT d1.visited_on, SUM(d2.daily_amount) AS amount, ROUND(AVG(d2.daily_amount), 2) AS average_amount FROM ( SELECT visited_on, SUM(amount) AS daily_amount FROM Customer GROUP BY visited_on ) d1 JOIN ( SELECT visited_on, SUM(amount) AS daily_amount FROM Customer GROUP BY visited_on ) d2 ON d2.visited_on BETWEEN d1.visited_on - INTERVAL '6 days' AND d1.visited_on WHERE d1.visited_on >= (SELECT MIN(visited_on) + INTERVAL '6 days' FROM Customer) GROUP BY d1.visited_on ORDER BY d1.visited_on;

Performance Analysis: Two GROUP BY scans. Self-JOIN: each day must join with 7 other days = O(n * 7) = O(n). For 365 days: 365 * 7 = 2555 rows joined. Window function: single O(n) pass. Also requires date range predicate evaluation which is slower than fixed row count.

Why Rank 2: More expensive than window function due to explicit join overhead and date range evaluation.

Medium #2854 Rolling Average Steps

▼

For users with 3+ day-streaks of activity, compute 3-day rolling average of steps.

Tables: Steps (user_id, steps_count, steps_date)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation (Window Functions)

Real-World Example

A fitness app charts a user's 3-day rolling step average, smoothing daily noise for motivation graphs.

▶ 1 Windowed Average with Row Count Filter
SELECT user_id, steps_date, ROUND(AVG(steps_count) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY steps_date ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS rolling_average FROM Steps QUALIFY COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY steps_date ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) = 3 ORDER BY user_id, steps_date;

Why this is best: ROWS frame averages three prior days. QUALIFY drops incomplete early windows (Snowflake/Trino style; use a CTE filter in MySQL).

Performance: Two window passes.

Hard #2994 Friday Purchases II

▼

Report every Friday in November 2023 with its total spend, zero if no sales.

Tables: Purchases (user_id, purchase_date, amount_spend)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation (Window Functions)

Real-World Example

Unlike 2993, this report must include Fridays with no sales to show a complete Nov-Fridays timeline.

▶ 1 Calendar CTE + LEFT JOIN
WITH fridays AS ( SELECT '2023-11-03' AS d UNION ALL SELECT '2023-11-10' UNION ALL SELECT '2023-11-17' UNION ALL SELECT '2023-11-24' ) SELECT FLOOR((DAYOFMONTH(d) - 1) / 7) + 1 AS week_of_month, d AS purchase_date, COALESCE(SUM(p.amount_spend), 0) AS total_amount FROM fridays LEFT JOIN Purchases p ON p.purchase_date = d GROUP BY d ORDER BY d;

Why this is best: Anchoring to a calendar CTE guarantees every Friday appears even with no data.

Performance: One join + one aggregate.

Medium 7-Day Rolling Average Sleep Score

▼

A sleep tracking app needs each user's 7-day rolling average sleep score, but only on dates with enough recent data to be statistically reliable. The window includes the current day and the 6 preceding days; partial windows at the start of tracking are kept only when at least 4 sessions fall inside them.

📌
Pattern: Rolling Window (ROWS BETWEEN) + Window COUNT for reliability gate

Use AVG OVER (ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) for the rolling mean and COUNT OVER on the same frame for days_in_window, then filter days_in_window >= 4 in the outer query. Business: per user rolling metrics with a minimum-data threshold for confidence.

Business Context
Sleep apps surface trends via rolling averages to smooth daily noise, but early-tracking users have too few data points to trust. Requiring 4+ sessions in the rolling 7-day window suppresses the first few unreliable rows while still showing partial windows during the ramp up.
Problem statement

Write a query against sleep_sessions(session_id, user_id, sleep_date, sleep_score) that returns each user's 7-day rolling average sleep score (current day plus 6 preceding days). Round the rolling average to 2 decimal places. Only include dates where at least 4 sessions fall inside the 7-day window. Return columns user_id, sleep_date, daily_score, rolling_avg_score, days_in_window ordered by user_id, sleep_date.

▶ Rank 1: CTE with AVG + COUNT OVER (ROWS BETWEEN) Single pass per user, filter on the window count
WITH sleep_with_window AS ( SELECT user_id, sleep_date, sleep_score AS daily_score, ROUND( AVG(sleep_score) OVER ( PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY sleep_date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW )::numeric, 2 ) AS rolling_avg_score, COUNT(sleep_score) OVER ( PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY sleep_date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW ) AS days_in_window FROM sleep_sessions ) SELECT user_id, sleep_date, daily_score, rolling_avg_score, days_in_window FROM sleep_with_window WHERE days_in_window >= 4 ORDER BY user_id, sleep_date;

How the CTE is structured: the inner CTE keeps every row in sleep_sessions and decorates it with two windowed values over the per-user rolling 7-day frame: AVG gives the rolling mean and COUNT gives how many rows actually fell inside that frame. The outer SELECT then filters on days_in_window >= 4. Partial windows at the very start of tracking still show up as long as 4 or more rows landed inside.

Performance Analysis: One scan of sleep_sessions: O(n). Window aggregates use the per-user partition ordered by sleep_date, so the engine sorts once per partition: O(n log n) total. The ROWS BETWEEN frame keeps frame state at O(7) per partition, not O(n). The final filter is O(n). Memory bounded by the partition sort and the 7-row frame buffer.

Why Rank 1: ROWS BETWEEN is the right frame because sleep_date can have gaps per user (a user may skip a night) and ROWS-based is gap-tolerant when paired with the COUNT gate. The COUNT OVER on the same frame correctly counts the actual rows present in each user's trailing 7-day window, which is exactly what days_in_window should report. ROUND with ::numeric coerces the FLOAT-typed AVG so ROUND's two-argument form works in PostgreSQL.

▶ Rank 2: Self-join on 7-day date range Pre-window approach
SELECT s1.user_id, s1.sleep_date, s1.sleep_score AS daily_score, ROUND(AVG(s2.sleep_score)::numeric, 2) AS rolling_avg_score, COUNT(s2.sleep_score) AS days_in_window FROM sleep_sessions s1 JOIN sleep_sessions s2 ON s2.user_id = s1.user_id AND s2.sleep_date BETWEEN s1.sleep_date - INTERVAL '6 days' AND s1.sleep_date GROUP BY s1.user_id, s1.sleep_date, s1.sleep_score HAVING COUNT(s2.sleep_score) >= 4 ORDER BY s1.user_id, s1.sleep_date;

Performance Analysis: Two scans of sleep_sessions joined on a date range. Each anchor row joins up to 7 sibling rows per user, so worst case O(n · 7). Equivalent to the window approach for n <= a few thousand rows, but loses the constant-memory frame buffer that the window function gets — the join engine must materialize the matched rows before grouping. HAVING gates the reliability filter post aggregation.

Why Rank 2: Reads as the literal definition of the metric ("7 day window of self-join then count"), but the windowed AVG/COUNT in Rank 1 expresses the same computation in a single pass with no group-by gymnastics.

Medium Rolling 7-Day Job Acceptance Rate for Contractors

▼

For each job offer record in a gig marketplace, compute the contractor's acceptance rate over the current row and the 6 preceding rows (a 7 row trailing window per contractor). Drills the row based frame clause: ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW — exactly 7 rows by sequence, NOT 7 days by date range.

📌
Pattern: Row based trailing window — ROWS BETWEEN N PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW

Use AVG over a boolean cast to 1/0 inside ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW to get a rate over the trailing 7 row window per partition. ROWS counts rows by sequence (gap tolerant), RANGE would have used the date itself and grouped ties — pick ROWS when the prompt says "current plus N preceding rows" and pick RANGE when the prompt says "within N days." Partial windows at the start of a partition automatically include only the rows that exist.

Business Context
Gig marketplaces (Uber, DoorDash, Instacart, Upwork, TaskRabbit) track contractor acceptance rate as a core supply side health metric. A trailing rolling rate smooths out daily noise and reflects current behavior more than a lifetime rate — a contractor who used to accept everything but recently went cold gets flagged faster on a rolling window than on a lifetime average. The row based frame is the right choice when offers are the unit of analysis and gaps between offers do not matter.
Problem statement

Write a query against contractor_offers(contractor_id, offer_date, accepted) that returns each row's rolling_7day_acceptance_rate — the fraction of accepted offers over the current row plus the 6 preceding rows by offer_date within each contractor. The frame must be row based (not range based), so ties in offer_date are treated as separate rows in sequence and the window counts exactly 7 rows (current + 6 prior). If fewer than 7 rows exist at the start of a contractor's history, use all available rows. Round the rate to 2 decimal places and return columns contractor_id, offer_date, rolling_7day_acceptance_rate ordered by contractor_id, offer_date.

▶ Rank 1: CTE with AVG over a boolean cast inside ROWS BETWEEN Single pass, the frame does all the work
WITH offers_with_rate AS ( SELECT contractor_id, offer_date, accepted, ROUND( AVG(CASE WHEN accepted THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) OVER ( PARTITION BY contractor_id ORDER BY offer_date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW )::numeric, 2 ) AS rolling_7day_acceptance_rate FROM contractor_offers ) SELECT contractor_id, offer_date, rolling_7day_acceptance_rate FROM offers_with_rate ORDER BY contractor_id, offer_date;

How the CTE is structured: the inner CTE keeps every row in contractor_offers and decorates it with the rolling rate. The CASE WHEN accepted THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END converts the boolean into a numeric so AVG over the frame produces the fraction directly — average of 1s and 0s equals the proportion of 1s. The frame ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW picks the current row and the 6 prior rows by offer_date within each contractor. The outer SELECT just projects the final columns and orders them.

Why ROWS and not RANGE: the prompt explicitly says "exactly 7 rows (current + 6 prior), not all rows within a 7-day date range." ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW counts by row position in the ordered partition, so ties in offer_date are treated as separate rows in sequence. RANGE BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW would have counted by the ORDER BY value (the date itself) and collapsed same date rows into one logical position — wrong shape for this prompt. Rule of thumb: ROWS when you want row count, RANGE when you want value distance.

Why this handles partial windows correctly: at the start of a contractor's history, there are fewer than 6 preceding rows. ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW silently shrinks the frame to whatever rows exist — no NULL, no error. So the very first row gets a frame of size 1 (current row only), the second row gets size 2, and so on up to size 7. AVG over that smaller frame still produces a valid rate. That matches the expected output where contractor 101's first row is 1.00 (1/1) and the second row is 0.50 (1/2).

Why the 1.0 / 0.0 cast matters: CASE WHEN accepted THEN 1 ELSE 0 END with integer literals would force integer division inside AVG in some dialects, returning 0 for any rate < 1. Using 1.0 / 0.0 as numeric literals guarantees the average stays floating point. The final ::numeric cast is for Postgres' two-argument ROUND, which requires a numeric input.

Performance Analysis: One scan of contractor_offers: O(n). The window aggregate sorts each contractor's partition by offer_date once: O(n log n) total. The ROWS frame keeps state at O(7) per partition — constant memory regardless of partition size. The final ORDER BY in the outer SELECT typically reuses the partition sort and is free. Net: O(n log n) time, O(7) frame memory per partition.

Why Rank 1: single window function, single frame clause, no GROUP BY gymnastics. Reads as "for each row, average the trailing 7 row indicator." The cast pattern (boolean → 1.0/0.0 → AVG → rate) is the canonical SQL idiom for rates over windows. This is what an interviewer wants to see when the prompt says "rolling rate."

▶ Rank 2: Two-CTE form — separate SUM and COUNT then divide Explicit numerator and denominator, easier to debug
WITH window_counts AS ( SELECT contractor_id, offer_date, SUM(CASE WHEN accepted THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) OVER w AS accepted_in_window, COUNT(*) OVER w AS offers_in_window FROM contractor_offers WINDOW w AS ( PARTITION BY contractor_id ORDER BY offer_date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW ) ) SELECT contractor_id, offer_date, ROUND(accepted_in_window::numeric / offers_in_window, 2) AS rolling_7day_acceptance_rate FROM window_counts ORDER BY contractor_id, offer_date;

How this differs from Rank 1: the rate is built from explicit numerator (SUM of accepted flags) and denominator (COUNT(*)) over the same frame, then divided in the outer SELECT. The named WINDOW w clause defines the frame once and reuses it across both window functions.

Why pick this: when debugging or auditing, having accepted_in_window and offers_in_window as separately inspectable columns lets you confirm both the numerator and the denominator before they collapse into a rate. Useful in code review: a reviewer can see at a glance that the denominator uses COUNT(*) (every row in the frame) rather than COUNT(accepted) (only non NULL flags), which matters if accepted can be NULL.

When to prefer Rank 1: when the rate is the only thing you need and you trust the AVG idiom. Rank 1 is one fewer column and one fewer arithmetic operation.

Medium 7-Day Rolling Acceptance Rate from Daily Aggregates

▼

Given a pre aggregated daily table of offers_sent and offers_accepted, compute a 7 day rolling acceptance rate. Drills the SUM(num) / SUM(denom) OVER frame idiom — the volume weighted rolling rate, NOT an average of daily rates — plus the NULLIF safe divide for zero offer days.

📌
Pattern: Rolling ratio from daily aggregates — SUM(num) / SUM(denom) OVER frame

When the source table already stores numerator and denominator as daily counts, the right rolling rate is SUM(numerator) OVER frame / SUM(denominator) OVER frame — NOT AVG(numerator / denominator) OVER frame. The sum over sum form weights each day by its actual volume, so a day with 1,000 offers contributes 1,000x more than a day with 5 offers. The average of rates form treats every day equally regardless of volume, which gives a different (and usually wrong) answer when volumes vary. Wrap the division in NULLIF(denominator, 0) so windows that contain only zero offer days return NULL instead of erroring.

Business Context
Gig marketplaces, ad platforms, search relevance teams, and conversion funnel teams all store engagement as pre aggregated daily counters: impressions / clicks, offers / accepts, searches / clicks, sessions / conversions. The volume weighted rolling rate is the metric the business actually wants because it answers "what fraction of total volume converted in the last 7 days," which is what affects revenue. The unweighted average of daily rates answers a different (rarely asked) question about typical day behavior. Picking the wrong form is a classic Simpson's paradox style trap where a "good week with a bad day" can look better or worse than it actually was depending on which formula you use.
Problem statement

Write a query against daily_job_metrics(metric_date, offers_sent, offers_accepted) that returns each row's rolling_acceptance_rate as SUM(offers_accepted) / SUM(offers_sent) * 100 over a 7 day trailing window (current row + 6 preceding rows), rounded to 2 decimal places. Partial windows at the start of the dataset use whatever rows exist. If the window contains only zero offer days (denominator is zero), return NULL rather than erroring. Return columns metric_date, rolling_acceptance_rate ordered by metric_date.

Why SUM / SUM, not AVG of daily rates

Imagine a 2 day window where day 1 had 1,000 offers with 800 accepted (80% acceptance) and day 2 had 5 offers with 1 accepted (20% acceptance). The volume weighted rolling rate is (800 + 1) / (1000 + 5) = 79.7% — almost the same as day 1 because day 1 dominated volume. The average of daily rates is (80% + 20%) / 2 = 50% — way off. The business cares about the first number because revenue depends on total accepts, not on which day they happened. The unweighted average exaggerates the impact of low volume days and is almost never what the prompt actually wants.

▶ Rank 1: CTE with SUM/SUM over ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW + NULLIF safe divide Volume weighted rolling rate, single pass, no division errors
WITH base AS ( SELECT metric_date, ROUND( SUM(offers_accepted) OVER w::numeric / NULLIF(SUM(offers_sent) OVER w, 0) * 100, 2 ) AS rolling_acceptance_rate FROM daily_job_metrics WINDOW w AS ( ORDER BY metric_date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW ) ) SELECT metric_date, rolling_acceptance_rate FROM base ORDER BY metric_date;

How the CTE is structured: the inner CTE keeps one row per metric_date and decorates it with the rolling rate. The named WINDOW w clause defines the frame (ORDER BY metric_date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) once and reuses it for both window aggregates. The numerator is SUM(offers_accepted) OVER w, the denominator is SUM(offers_sent) OVER w, and the result is multiplied by 100 and rounded to 2 decimals.

Why SUM / SUM and not AVG of daily rates: the prompt defines the rolling rate as (sum of offers_accepted over the window) / (sum of offers_sent over the window) * 100. That phrasing IS the volume weighted form. Summing the numerator and the denominator separately lets each day contribute to the rate in proportion to its offer count, so a day with 1,000 offers dominates a day with 5 offers in the same window. The average of daily rates form (AVG(offers_accepted * 1.0 / offers_sent) OVER w) would treat both days equally and produce a different answer when volume varies day to day.

Why NULLIF on the denominator: if a 7 day window contains only zero offer days, the denominator sums to zero and the division would error. NULLIF(SUM(offers_sent) OVER w, 0) converts that zero into NULL, and any arithmetic with NULL propagates NULL, so the rate becomes NULL for those rows. Note: when SOME days in the window have zero offers and others do not, the sum is still non zero and the division works correctly — those zero offer days contribute 0 to both numerator and denominator and are silently absorbed without skewing the result. That is one of the reasons SUM / SUM is robust here.

How partial windows are handled: ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW silently shrinks at the start of the dataset, so day 1 sees a window of size 1, day 2 sees size 2, and so on up to size 7. Both sums (numerator and denominator) shrink together, so the rate at the edges still reflects whatever data exists. No special casing required.

Why the ::numeric cast is on the numerator: Postgres' two argument ROUND(value, digits) requires the value to be numeric. Casting the numerator sum coerces the entire expression to numeric arithmetic, so the division does not collapse to integer division and the round works without a type error. The cast position (numerator vs denominator vs outer expression) does not change the result, but casting once at the top of the expression is the convention.

Performance Analysis: One scan of daily_job_metrics: O(n). The named WINDOW lets the engine compute both SUMs in a single window pass: O(n log n) for the sort, O(7) for the frame buffer. The NULLIF and ROUND are O(1) per row. The final ORDER BY reuses the window sort. Net: O(n log n) time, O(7) frame memory.

Why Rank 1: the named WINDOW clause defines the frame once instead of duplicating ORDER BY metric_date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW on every aggregate, the NULLIF handles div by zero cleanly without a CASE expression, and the SUM / SUM idiom is the standard form for volume weighted rolling ratios on daily aggregate tables.

▶ Rank 2: Inline frame on each window aggregate (no WINDOW clause) Same answer, frame clause repeated twice
WITH base AS ( SELECT metric_date, offers_sent, offers_accepted, ROUND( SUM(offers_accepted) OVER ( ORDER BY metric_date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW )::numeric / NULLIF( SUM(offers_sent) OVER ( ORDER BY metric_date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW ), 0 ) * 100, 2 ) AS rolling_acceptance_rate FROM daily_job_metrics ) SELECT metric_date, rolling_acceptance_rate FROM base ORDER BY metric_date;
