How this differs from Rank 1: instead of defining the frame once via the WINDOW w clause, each window aggregate spells out its own OVER (ORDER BY metric_date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW). Functionally identical to Rank 1 — most engines still recognize the duplicate frame definitions and compute both aggregates in one pass.

When to prefer this: when you target a SQL dialect that does not support the named WINDOW clause (older MySQL, some legacy engines), or when the duplication is more readable than the indirection for a short query. The named WINDOW clause is supported in Postgres, MySQL 8+, SQL Server, Oracle, and BigQuery; if you target any of those, Rank 1 is cleaner.

When to prefer Rank 1: when the frame is non trivial or you want to add a third or fourth aggregate later, naming the window once prevents drift between the frame clauses (a classic bug: the numerator frame and the denominator frame accidentally differ because one was updated and the other was not).

Hard #579 Find Cumulative Salary of an Employee

▼

For each employee, sum the salary in the current month plus the two prior months (treating missing months as 0), then drop the row for each employee’s most recent working month.

Tables: Employee (id, month, salary)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation (Window Functions)

Real-World Example

Finance reports trailing 3-month salary totals for a pro-rata bonus calculation, excluding the latest unfinished month. The trick is handling employees who skipped months: a gap in month numbers must count as $0, not as silently pulling older rows into the window.

Gotcha — ROWS vs RANGE on missing months: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING counts the two previous rows in the sort, which silently skips over missing months (month 7 after a gap at 5 and 6 would pull in months 4 and 3 instead of treating 5 and 6 as 0). Use RANGE BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING or pad the table with zero-rows first.

▶ 1 Minimal: RANGE Window Handles Missing Months Automatically
WITH rolled AS ( SELECT id, month, salary, SUM(salary) OVER ( PARTITION BY id ORDER BY month RANGE BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW ) AS cum_salary, MAX(month) OVER (PARTITION BY id) AS max_month FROM Employee ) SELECT id, month, cum_salary AS Salary FROM rolled WHERE month <> max_month ORDER BY id ASC, month DESC;

Why this is best: RANGE BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING treats month as a numeric value range, so missing months contribute 0 to the sum automatically — no padding, no cross join. One CTE handles both the rolling sum and the max-month computation.

Performance: Two window passes over Employee directly, no extra rows generated.

▶ 2 Staircase CTE: Build a Full Grid, Zero-Fill, Then Roll
WITH distinct_months AS ( SELECT generate_series(1, MAX(month))::int AS month FROM Employee ), distinct_employee AS ( SELECT DISTINCT id FROM Employee ), employee_months AS ( SELECT id, month, MAX(month) OVER (PARTITION BY id) AS max_month FROM Employee ), id_month AS ( SELECT e.id, m.month FROM distinct_employee e CROSS JOIN distinct_months m ), base_table AS ( SELECT i.id, i.month, COALESCE(e.salary, 0) AS salary FROM id_month i LEFT JOIN Employee e ON i.id = e.id AND i.month = e.month ), sum_window AS ( SELECT id, month, salary, SUM(salary) OVER ( PARTITION BY id ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW ) AS cum_salary FROM base_table ) SELECT sw.id, sw.month, sw.cum_salary AS Salary FROM sum_window sw JOIN employee_months em ON sw.id = em.id AND sw.month = em.month AND sw.month <> em.max_month ORDER BY id ASC, month DESC;

Why this works: Explicitly builds a full (id, month) grid via CROSS JOIN + generate_series, zero-fills missing months with COALESCE, then a ROWS window works correctly because every month is now a real row. The final JOIN to employee_months keeps only the months each employee actually worked, minus the latest.

Why pick this: Longer but every step is independently verifiable — you can inspect each CTE’s output while debugging. Good when you don’t trust RANGE semantics or the engine you’re on doesn’t fully support them.

Performance: 6 CTE passes plus two joins. Noticeably more work than Rank 1 but linear in output size.

FIRST_VALUE / LAST_VALUE 2 problems

▼

nb01 qtype: window_first_last — FIRST_VALUE / LAST_VALUE pull a specific value from the window's frame. LAST_VALUE silently returns the current row unless you spell out ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING — the classic frame trap.

Medium #2388 Change Null Values in a Table to the Previous Value

▼

Fill NULL coffee values forward with the most recent non-NULL value, preserving order.

Tables: CoffeeShop (id, drink)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation (Window Functions)

Real-World Example

A product catalog pipeline cleans sparsely-recorded fields by carrying the last known good value forward — a common ETL fill-forward.

▶ 1 Fill Forward via Windowed Grouping
WITH grp AS ( SELECT id, drink, COUNT(drink) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS grp_id FROM CoffeeShop ) SELECT id, FIRST_VALUE(drink) OVER (PARTITION BY grp_id ORDER BY id) AS drink FROM grp ORDER BY id;

Why this is best: Counting non-NULLs as a running counter creates a group id that increments every time a new non-NULL appears. FIRST_VALUE within the group fills forward.

Performance: Two window passes.

Medium Installment Plan Payment Spread Analysis

▼

For each installment plan in a buy-now-pay-later service, return the earliest scheduled payment amount and the latest scheduled payment amount. Drills the canonical FIRST_VALUE / LAST_VALUE frame gotcha — and an equivalent ROW_NUMBER recipe that sidesteps the gotcha entirely.

📌
Pattern: First and last per partition (with the LAST_VALUE frame gotcha)

Decorate every row with the partition's first and last value using window functions, then collapse to one row per partition with DISTINCT or GROUP BY. The trap: LAST_VALUE's default frame stops at the current row, so you must explicitly extend the frame to ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING. The ROW_NUMBER recipe avoids the frame trap by ranking from both directions and plucking the rn=1 row from each side.

Business Context
Buy-now-pay-later services need to know how each plan's payment schedule shapes up — does the first payment match the last (uniform installments) or does the schedule taper / spike? Comparing first-amount vs last-amount per plan surfaces structural changes (downpayment-heavy plans, balloon-final plans, hardship plan re-renegotiations).
Problem statement

Write a query against installment_payments(payment_id, plan_id, due_date, amount, payment_status) that returns plan_id, first_payment_amount, last_payment_amount. The first amount is from the earliest due_date per plan; the last is from the latest. Some plans may have only one payment scheduled — those return the same value in both columns. Order by plan_id ascending.

▶ Rank 1: FIRST_VALUE + LAST_VALUE with explicit frame Reads closest to the prompt's wording
WITH base AS ( SELECT plan_id, FIRST_VALUE(amount) OVER ( PARTITION BY plan_id ORDER BY due_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING ) AS first_payment_amount, LAST_VALUE(amount) OVER ( PARTITION BY plan_id ORDER BY due_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING ) AS last_payment_amount FROM installment_payments ) SELECT DISTINCT plan_id, first_payment_amount, last_payment_amount FROM base ORDER BY plan_id;

How the recipe works: the CTE decorates every row in installment_payments with two windowed values over the partition (plan_id) ordered by due_date. Because every row inside the same plan gets the SAME first and last value, the outer SELECT DISTINCT collapses the duplicates to one row per plan.

The LAST_VALUE frame trap: without an explicit frame, LAST_VALUE uses the default RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. That means at each row, SQL only "sees" the rows from the start of the partition up to the current row — never the future. As a result last_payment_amount would equal the CURRENT row's amount, not the partition's final amount. Adding ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING extends the frame to cover the entire partition so the function can actually reach the last row. FIRST_VALUE works with the default frame (the first row is always behind you), but you should add the same frame to both for symmetry and to make intent obvious.

Performance Analysis: Single scan of installment_payments: O(n). Window aggregates sort once per partition: O(n log n). Constant memory per partition for the frame state. The DISTINCT pass at the end is O(n).

Why Rank 1: Reads closest to the prompt's wording ("first payment by due_date, last payment by due_date"). The frame clause is the gotcha that interviewers like to probe — knowing it cold is the point of the drill.

▶ Rank 2: ROW_NUMBER from both directions + MAX(CASE WHEN) Avoids the frame trap entirely
WITH ranked AS ( SELECT plan_id, amount, due_date, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY plan_id ORDER BY due_date ASC) AS rn_first, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY plan_id ORDER BY due_date DESC) AS rn_last FROM installment_payments ) SELECT plan_id, MAX(CASE WHEN rn_first = 1 THEN amount END) AS first_payment_amount, MAX(CASE WHEN rn_last = 1 THEN amount END) AS last_payment_amount FROM ranked GROUP BY plan_id ORDER BY plan_id;

How the recipe works: rank each row twice — once by due_date ASC and once by due_date DESC. The earliest row gets rn_first = 1; the latest row gets rn_last = 1. Then in the outer query, use a conditional aggregate (MAX(CASE WHEN rn_first = 1 THEN amount END)) to pluck out the amount from each side. This is the "label rows, then pivot to columns" idiom — broadly useful any time you need "the X-th row's value per group" as a column.

Why pick this over Rank 1: no frame clause to remember and no LAST_VALUE gotcha to debug. The mental model is concrete ("rank from each side, pick rn=1") and the same pattern extends to "second-to-last" (rn=2) or "Nth from the end" without any new SQL. Works in any dialect that supports window functions, including older MySQL.

Performance Analysis: Single scan of installment_payments with two window orderings: the engine sorts the partition once per ROW_NUMBER pass, so O(n log n) total. The MAX with CASE in the outer query is a single grouped aggregate: O(n). Constant memory per partition. Performance is roughly equivalent to Rank 1.

When to prefer Rank 1: when the prompt literally says "first value" or "last value" — the FIRST_VALUE / LAST_VALUE names read closer to the spec. Just don't forget the frame.

Sessionization (gap based grouping) 3 problems

▼

nb01 qtype: window_sessionization — Three step recipe: LAG to find the gap to the previous event, CASE flag of 1 when the gap exceeds a threshold (or row starts a new group), then cumulative SUM of the flag produces a session_id. The same shape powers gaps and islands streaks.

Medium Group Article Views into Reading Sessions (Sessionization)

▼

Group each user's event stream into sessions where a new session starts whenever the gap to the previous event exceeds a threshold. Drills the canonical LAG → flag → cumulative SUM sessionization recipe — the same three-step shape works for any "group consecutive events by inactivity gap" problem.

📌
Pattern: Sessionization in three steps — LAG, flag, cumulative SUM

Step 1: LAG the timestamp to find the gap to the previous event per user. Step 2: flag each row with 1 when it starts a new session (no previous row OR gap exceeds the threshold), 0 otherwise. Step 3: cumulative SUM of the flag over the partition produces a monotonically increasing session_id that resets per user. Then GROUP BY (user_id, session_id) to roll up per-session metrics.

Business Context
Sessionization is the foundation of almost every engagement analytics dashboard — DAU/MAU stickiness, time-on-app, sessions-per-day-per-user, conversion funnels measured in sessions rather than raw events. Every event log eventually needs sessionizing because raw events lie: 1,000 article views from one user in one hour is one engaged reader, not 1,000 distinct sessions. The 30-minute idle threshold is the industry default (Google Analytics, Adobe, Mixpanel all use it).
Problem statement

Write a query against article_views(view_id, user_id, article_id, viewed_at) that groups each user's views into reading sessions where a new session starts whenever the gap to the previous view exceeds 30 minutes. Return user_id, session_id, articles_viewed, session_start. session_id is sequential per user starting at 1; articles_viewed is the count of views in the session; session_start is the earliest viewed_at in the session. Order by user_id, session_id.

▶ Rank 1: 3-CTE recipe — LAG, flag, cumulative SUM The canonical sessionization shape, step by step
WITH with_prev AS ( SELECT user_id, viewed_at, LAG(viewed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY viewed_at) AS prev_viewed_at FROM article_views ), flagged AS ( SELECT user_id, viewed_at, CASE WHEN prev_viewed_at IS NULL OR viewed_at - prev_viewed_at > INTERVAL '30 minutes' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_session_flag FROM with_prev ), sessions AS ( SELECT user_id, viewed_at, SUM(new_session_flag) OVER ( PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY viewed_at ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW ) AS session_id FROM flagged ) SELECT user_id, session_id, COUNT(*) AS articles_viewed, MIN(viewed_at) AS session_start FROM sessions GROUP BY user_id, session_id ORDER BY user_id, session_id;

How the recipe works:

  1. with_prev (LAG): for each row, attach the previous row's timestamp from the same user. The first row per user has prev_viewed_at = NULL.
  2. flagged (CASE): compare the current timestamp to the previous one. If there is no previous row (NULL) OR the gap exceeds 30 minutes, this row starts a new session — flag = 1. Otherwise flag = 0.
  3. sessions (cumulative SUM): running sum the flag over each user's timeline. The flag value either stays the same (continuing session) or ticks up by 1 (new session starts), which IS the session_id.
  4. Outer SELECT (GROUP BY): roll up per (user_id, session_id) with COUNT(*) and MIN(viewed_at).

Why the threshold check uses OR with NULL: SQL's three-valued logic makes NULL > anything evaluate to UNKNOWN, not TRUE. Without the explicit prev_viewed_at IS NULL branch, the first row per user would get flag = 0 instead of 1, and the very first session_id would be 0 instead of 1 (or missing entirely). Always handle the LAG-returns-NULL case explicitly.

Dialect note on interval syntax: Postgres uses viewed_at - prev_viewed_at > INTERVAL '30 minutes'. MySQL uses TIMESTAMPDIFF(MINUTE, prev_viewed_at, viewed_at) > 30. SQL Server uses DATEDIFF(MINUTE, prev_viewed_at, viewed_at) > 30. The recipe shape is identical — only the gap expression changes.

Performance Analysis: Single scan of article_views: O(n). LAG sorts each partition once: O(n log n). The cumulative SUM in the third CTE reuses the same partition + order, so most engines fuse the two windows into one pass — effectively O(n log n) total with constant memory per partition. The final GROUP BY is O(n).

Why Rank 1: reads as three named steps that map 1:1 to the conceptual algorithm. When you debug a sessionization query (off-by-one session IDs, wrong gap, NULL not handled), having LAG / flag / cumsum as separately inspectable CTEs makes the bug obvious. This is what most interviewers want to see.

▶ Rank 2: Single-CTE compact version Same recipe, fewer CTEs, denser
WITH labeled AS ( SELECT user_id, viewed_at, SUM(CASE WHEN LAG(viewed_at) OVER w IS NULL OR viewed_at - LAG(viewed_at) OVER w > INTERVAL '30 minutes' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) OVER ( PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY viewed_at ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW ) AS session_id FROM article_views WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY viewed_at) ) SELECT user_id, session_id, COUNT(*) AS articles_viewed, MIN(viewed_at) AS session_start FROM labeled GROUP BY user_id, session_id ORDER BY user_id, session_id;

How this differs from Rank 1: the three CTEs are collapsed into one. The CASE expression embeds the LAG call directly inside the SUM OVER. The PostgreSQL WINDOW w AS (...) clause names the LAG's window once so the CASE can reuse it without repeating the partition / order syntax twice.

Why pick this over Rank 1: shorter, fewer CTEs to name. Useful when the recipe is muscle memory and you trust yourself to land the conditional without breaking it apart. Reads tightly when paired with the named WINDOW clause.

When to prefer Rank 1: when you're learning the recipe, debugging a sessionization bug, or writing for code review. The 3-CTE version makes each step independently inspectable — you can SELECT * FROM with_prev to see the LAG values, SELECT * FROM flagged to see which rows got flag = 1, and SELECT * FROM sessions to verify the session_id sequence before the final aggregation. The compact version hides those intermediate results.

MySQL portability: MySQL 8+ supports the WINDOW clause, but older MySQL does not. If you target older MySQL, repeat the LAG window inline twice (verbose but portable), or fall back to the 3-CTE form which is universally supported.

Hard #2173 Longest Winning Streak

▼

For each player, return the longest consecutive run of wins.

Tables: Matches (player_id, match_day, result)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern B: Grouping & Aggregation (Window Functions)

Real-World Example

A sports analytics newsroom reports player "hot streaks" — the longest win run ever for each athlete.

▶ 1 Gaps-and-Islands on Result
WITH runs AS ( SELECT player_id, match_day, result, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY match_day) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY player_id, result ORDER BY match_day) AS grp FROM Matches ) SELECT m.player_id, COALESCE(MAX(CASE WHEN r.result = 'Win' THEN cnt END), 0) AS longest_streak FROM (SELECT DISTINCT player_id FROM Matches) m LEFT JOIN ( SELECT player_id, result, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM runs GROUP BY player_id, result, grp ) r USING (player_id) GROUP BY m.player_id;

Why this is best: Difference of two row numbers groups consecutive equal-result matches; the max count per Win group is the streak.

Performance: Two window passes + one aggregate.

Medium Workout Session Detection with 20-Minute Gaps

▼

Group each user's exercise events into workout sessions, where a gap of 20 or more minutes since the previous exercise starts a new session, then report one row per user per session with its start, end, and exercise count.

Tables: exercise_completions (exercise_id, user_id, exercise_name, exercise_completed_at)

📌
Pattern: Sessionization in three steps, then roll up

Step 1: LAG the timestamp per user to measure the gap to the previous exercise. Step 2: flag a row with 1 when that gap reaches the 20 minute threshold (the first row's gap is NULL, so its flag is 0). Step 3: a cumulative SUM of the flag over the same window turns the flags into a running session_id; add 1 so the first session per user is 1 instead of 0. Then GROUP BY (user_id, session_id) and aggregate.

Business Context
A fitness app wants engagement measured in workout sessions, not raw exercise events. Three exercises ten minutes apart are one session; a 45 minute break starts a new one. The same gap based session id powers time on app, sessions per day, and conversion funnels measured in sessions across almost every product analytics stack.
▶ Rank 1: LAG → flag → cumulative SUM, roll up with MIN/MAX Cleanest, two window passes
-- 1) gap flag, 2) cumulative SUM = session_id, 3) GROUP BY to roll up WITH flagged AS ( SELECT user_id, exercise_completed_at, CASE WHEN exercise_completed_at - LAG(exercise_completed_at) OVER ( PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY exercise_completed_at) >= INTERVAL '20 minutes' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_new_session FROM exercise_completions ), sessions AS ( SELECT user_id, exercise_completed_at, SUM(is_new_session) OVER ( PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY exercise_completed_at) + 1 AS session_id FROM flagged ) SELECT user_id, session_id, MIN(exercise_completed_at) AS session_start, MAX(exercise_completed_at) AS session_end, COUNT(*) AS exercises_completed FROM sessions GROUP BY user_id, session_id ORDER BY user_id, session_id;

Why this is best: The flag's first row is NULL from LAG and resolves to 0, so the running SUM starts at 0; the + 1 shifts every session number up so each user's first session is 1, satisfying "the very first exercise always starts session 1." Once each row carries a stable session_id, the start, end, and count are a plain GROUP BY with MIN / MAX / COUNT — no extra window functions needed.

Performance: Two window passes (one LAG, one running SUM) over a sort on (user_id, exercise_completed_at), then one aggregation: O(n log n). An index on (user_id, exercise_completed_at) lets the planner skip the sort.

▶ Rank 2: Same session_id, edges via FIRST_VALUE / LAST_VALUE Works, more machinery
-- session_id identical to Rank 1; start/end pulled with framed window functions WITH base AS ( SELECT user_id, exercise_name, exercise_completed_at, CASE WHEN exercise_completed_at - LAG(exercise_completed_at) OVER ( PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY exercise_completed_at) >= INTERVAL '20 minutes' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_new_session FROM exercise_completions ), sessions AS ( SELECT *, SUM(is_new_session) OVER ( PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY exercise_completed_at) + 1 AS session_id FROM base ), session_states AS ( SELECT *, FIRST_VALUE(exercise_completed_at) OVER ( PARTITION BY user_id, session_id ORDER BY exercise_completed_at ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS session_start, LAST_VALUE(exercise_completed_at) OVER ( PARTITION BY user_id, session_id ORDER BY exercise_completed_at ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS session_end FROM sessions ) SELECT user_id, session_id, session_start, session_end, COUNT(exercise_name) AS exercises_completed FROM session_states GROUP BY user_id, session_id, session_start, session_end ORDER BY user_id, session_id;

Why this works: Identical to Rank 1 through session_id. It then computes the edges with FIRST_VALUE / LAST_VALUE partitioned by (user_id, session_id). The explicit ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING frame is required, or LAST_VALUE would stop at the current row and return the wrong end time.

Performance: Adds two more framed window passes and forces session_start / session_end into the GROUP BY. Same answer as Rank 1 but more work; prefer MIN / MAX in the final aggregate since you are grouping anyway.

Frame clauses (ROWS / RANGE BETWEEN) no problems yet

▼

nb01 qtype: window_frames — Drills the frame clause itself — ROWS vs RANGE, UNBOUNDED PRECEDING vs N PRECEDING, the LAST_VALUE default trap. See the Frame Clause Cheat Sheet inside the Reference container above for the full reference.
