Point in Time cross-linked

▼

A single table of history rows → the most recent value as of a given cutoff date, with fill-forward when no row exists.

Signal words: "price on date X," "most recent event before," "snapshot at cutoff," "fill forward," "default when no history," "as-of"

Technique: ROW_NUMBER OVER (PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY effective_date DESC) filtered to rn = 1 with a date guard, or LAG-based fill forward over a calendar spine. The trick is handling the "no history yet" case so the answer doesn't drop rows silently.

📌
Pattern: As-of lookup with fill forward

For each row in the request set, find the most recent history row whose effective_date is <= the request's cutoff. If no such row exists, fall back to a known default (or surface NULL explicitly). ROW_NUMBER is usually cleaner than a correlated MAX subquery because it survives ties on effective_date by adding a secondary ORDER BY.

Where to find Point in Time problems today

A canonical Point in Time problem is #1164 Product Price at a Given Date, currently filed under the Window recipe. A future pass will lift that problem (and any others matching the pattern) into this dedicated section. Until then, browse Window and Compare for "most recent before" and "fill forward" variations.

Pair 4 problems

▼

A single table where each row ties two entities together (A and B) → flatten the row so both sides line up, then aggregate. Open the decision tree first, then the matching set of worked problems below.

Signal words: "friends," "connections," "either side," "requester or accepter," "both directions"

Technique: UNION ALL of both columns + GROUP BY + ORDER BY

Reference Techniques used in Normalize Bidirectional

▼

2 SQL techniques relevant to this recipe, with what they do, when to reach for them, and a generic code example.

Technique What It Does When to Reach for It Example Code
UNION ALL Stacks rows from two queries vertically into one result set (keeps duplicates) Two column roles are interchangeable, or you need both directions to appear as one column 
SELECT name FROM Customers
UNION ALL
SELECT name FROM Vendors;
LEAST / GREATEST Returns the smaller or larger of two values, normalizing pair order You need to treat (A, B) and (B, A) as the same pair by sorting them into a consistent order 
SELECT LEAST(user1, user2)    AS person1,
       GREATEST(user1, user2) AS person2,
       COUNT(*)               AS calls
FROM Calls
GROUP BY person1, person2;

How to pick: decision tree

▼

What the two sides are, and what you want out, routes you to the method and the set below.

Setup — spot the two sides first:

  • Each row has two "side" columns naming two entities: requester/accepter, from/to, host/guest, sender/recipient.
  • Note whether each side also carries its own value (a score, goals, points). That one fact decides the whole branch.

Walk the questions in order. Stop at the first match.

Q1. Does each side carry its own value you compare or score (goals, points, score)?

  • Yes — two participants, each with their own score (a game result) → ✓ use Matchup unpivot — UNION ALL splits the row so each side carries its own score and the opponent's, a CASE scores it, then GROUP BY participant.
  • No — the two columns are just ids, no per-side number → Q2.

Q2. Is the output one row per entity, or one row per unordered pair?

  • Per entity (each person's own total, e.g. friend count) → ✓ use Pool both columns, count per entity — UNION ALL the two id columns into one, then GROUP BY id.
  • Per unordered pair — (A,B) and (B,A) are the same pair → ✓ use Canonicalize the unordered pair — LEAST / GREATEST sort the pair into one order, then GROUP BY the pair.

The two building-block techniques (UNION ALL, LEAST / GREATEST) are in the Reference card above · copy-paste skeletons for each leaf are in Template code below.

Template code — pick the approach

▼

Approach → signs in the prompt → the skeleton. Swap the placeholder names; the shape stays the same.

Approach Signs in the prompt Template code
Pool both columns, count per entity "friends", "connections", "either side", "requester or accepter", a per-person total 
SELECT id, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM (
    SELECT a_id AS id FROM rel
    UNION ALL
    SELECT b_id AS id FROM rel
) t
GROUP BY id;          -- one row per entity
Canonicalize the unordered pair "(A,B) same as (B,A)", "between two persons", "per pair", "either direction" 
SELECT LEAST(a_id, b_id)    AS p1,
       GREATEST(a_id, b_id) AS p2,
       COUNT(*)             AS n
FROM rel
GROUP BY p1, p2;      -- one row per unordered pair
Matchup unpivot (two-sided scored rows) "two teams + their scores", "home/away", "host/guest", "points", per-team standings 
WITH per_side AS (     -- split AND score in one step:
    SELECT a_team AS team,   -- each branch knows its own side,
           CASE WHEN a_score > b_score THEN 3   -- so compare the two
                WHEN a_score = b_score THEN 1   -- wide columns directly
                ELSE 0 END AS pts
    FROM games
    UNION ALL
    SELECT b_team,
           CASE WHEN b_score > a_score THEN 3
                WHEN b_score = a_score THEN 1
                ELSE 0 END AS pts
    FROM games
)
SELECT d.id, d.name,
       COALESCE(SUM(s.pts), 0) AS pts   -- drive off dim so
FROM dim d                              -- zero-game rows stay 0
LEFT JOIN per_side s ON s.team = d.id
GROUP BY d.id, d.name;

Pool both columns, count per entity 1 problem

▼

UNION ALL both id columns → GROUP BY id — the two columns are interchangeable roles for the same kind of thing; stack them into one id column and count each entity's appearances. Output is one row per entity.

Medium #602 Friend Requests II: Who Has the Most Friends

▼

Find the person with the most friends. Friendship is bidirectional: if user A sent a request to user B and B accepted, they're friends. Count total friends for each person and return the one with the most.

Schema: RequestAccepted(requester_id, accepter_id, accept_date)

Goal: Find the person with the most friends. Friendship is bidirectional: if user A sent a request to user B and B accepted, they're friends. Count total friends for each person and return the one with the most.

Why this matters
Social network analytics: identifying influencers or highly-connected users, ranking by network size, and understanding community structure.
▶ Rank 1: UNION ALL + GROUP BY + ORDER BY LIMIT 1
SELECT id, COUNT(*) AS num FROM ( SELECT requester_id AS id FROM RequestAccepted UNION ALL SELECT accepter_id AS id FROM RequestAccepted ) AS friends GROUP BY id ORDER BY num DESC LIMIT 1;

Why rank 1: UNION ALL combines requester and accepter IDs (each person appears in either role, counting both directions). GROUP BY counts total appearances. ORDER BY DESC + LIMIT 1 gets the maximum without window functions or subqueries.

Performance: O(n log n) due to sorting, but LIMIT 1 stops early once the max is found. Simpler than DENSE_RANK and avoids subquery overhead.

▶ Rank 2: UNION ALL + GROUP BY + DENSE_RANK (for ties)
WITH friend_counts AS ( SELECT id, COUNT(*) AS num FROM ( SELECT requester_id AS id FROM RequestAccepted UNION ALL SELECT accepter_id AS id FROM RequestAccepted ) AS friends GROUP BY id ) SELECT id, num FROM friend_counts WHERE DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY num DESC) = 1;

Why rank 2: If multiple people have the same (highest) friend count, this returns all of them. Uses window function DENSE_RANK to handle ties. Follow-up from problem statement: "In the real world, multiple people could have the most friends."

Performance: O(n log n) for aggregation and window ranking. More complex than Rank 1 but necessary if ties must be included.

▶ Rank 3: UNION ALL + GROUP BY + Subquery MAX
SELECT id, num FROM ( SELECT id, COUNT(*) AS num FROM ( SELECT requester_id AS id FROM RequestAccepted UNION ALL SELECT accepter_id AS id FROM RequestAccepted ) AS friends GROUP BY id ) AS counts WHERE num = ( SELECT MAX(cnt) FROM ( SELECT COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM ( SELECT requester_id AS id FROM RequestAccepted UNION ALL SELECT accepter_id AS id FROM RequestAccepted ) AS friends2 GROUP BY id ) AS max_counts );

Why rank 3: Subquery-based: compute friend counts, then filter to max with WHERE. Redundant: scans the same UNION ALL twice (inefficient). Use only if window functions unavailable.

Performance: O(n log n) but with repeated scans. Slower than Rank 1 and 2. Worse maintainability due to nested subqueries.

📌
Bidirectional Friendship Logic
The key insight: UNION ALL (not UNION) combines rows without deduplication. Each person appears twice if they're in both requester and accepter roles. GROUP BY counts all occurrences, reflecting true friend count.
📊
Decision Tree Links
UNION ALL pattern for combining results

Canonicalize the unordered pair 2 problems

▼

LEAST / GREATEST → GROUP BY the pair — (A,B) and (B,A) are the same pair; sort the two ids into a fixed order so both directions look identical, then collapse with GROUP BY. Output is one row per unordered pair.

Medium #1699 Number of Calls Between Two Persons

▼

Report call count and total duration per unordered pair of (from_id, to_id).

Tables: Calls (from_id, to_id, duration)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Self-Join & Relational Queries → Pattern E: Self-Joins

Real-World Example

A telco bills symmetric pair usage. A call from A to B and B to A must combine into one pair for reporting.

▶ 1 LEAST/GREATEST Normalization + Aggregate
SELECT LEAST(from_id, to_id) AS person1, GREATEST(from_id, to_id) AS person2, COUNT(*) AS call_count, SUM(duration) AS total_duration FROM Calls GROUP BY person1, person2;

Why this is best: LEAST/GREATEST gives a canonical representation of each unordered pair, collapsing (A,B) and (B,A) into one group.

Performance: One aggregate pass.

Easy Unique Conversation Pairs from Messages (dedupe reciprocal direction)

▼

Collapse messages sent in either direction between two users into one row for each unordered pair, keeping a single sent_at.

Tables: messages (message_id, sender_id, recipient_id, match_id, sent_at)

Goal: Return the unique set of conversation partners as (user_a, user_b, sent_at). The sender and recipient are interchangeable, so a message from 101 to 103 and a message from 103 to 101 describe the same pair and must collapse into one row.

Real-World Example

A dating app wants one row per conversation, not one per message direction. Without normalizing the pair, the same two people would show up twice (once for each direction), inflating conversation counts and double counting matches.

The trick: LEAST always returns the smaller of the two ids and GREATEST the larger, so whichever way a message was sent, the pair always comes out in the same order (smaller id first). Once both directions look identical, GROUP BY collapses them into a single row.

Walkthrough on the sample rows:

sender_id recipient_id sent_at LEAST, GREATEST → pair
1011032024-01-09 10:00(101, 103)
1031012024-01-09 11:30(101, 103) ← same pair
1011042024-01-16 14:00(101, 104)
1011052024-01-21 09:00(101, 105)
1051012024-01-21 15:00(101, 105) ← same pair
1021032024-01-19 12:00(102, 103)
▶ 1 LEAST/GREATEST Normalization + GROUP BY (one row per pair)
SELECT LEAST(sender_id, recipient_id) AS user_a, GREATEST(sender_id, recipient_id) AS user_b, MIN(sent_at) AS sent_at FROM messages GROUP BY LEAST(sender_id, recipient_id), GREATEST(sender_id, recipient_id);

Result: four rows, one for each unique pair. The reciprocal messages between 101 and 103 collapse into a single row, and so do the two between 101 and 105.

user_a user_b sent_at
1011032024-01-09 10:00:00
1011042024-01-16 14:00:00
1011052024-01-21 09:00:00
1021032024-01-19 12:00:00

Picking the timestamp: a pair can have several messages, so you must choose which sent_at survives. MIN(sent_at) keeps the earliest message (first contact); swap in MAX(sent_at) for the most recent. You do not need the matches table for this, since the ids already live on the messages row.

Portability: LEAST and GREATEST behave the same in PostgreSQL and MySQL.

▶ 2 SELECT DISTINCT (only when you keep every message)
SELECT DISTINCT LEAST(sender_id, recipient_id) AS user_a, GREATEST(sender_id, recipient_id) AS user_b, sent_at FROM messages;

When to use: only if you want every message preserved and just the direction normalized. Because each message here has its own timestamp, DISTINCT over (user_a, user_b, sent_at) would keep all six rows: the 101 and 103 messages at 10:00 and 11:30 are distinct, so they do not collapse. Reach for this form when two rows could be exact duplicates on all three columns. To truly dedupe the pair into one row, use the GROUP BY form above.

Matchup unpivot: two-sided scored rows 1 problem

▼

UNION ALL split → score each side → GROUP BY participant — each row holds two participants and each one's own score (host/guest goals). Split so each side carries its own score and the opponent's, score it (win/draw/loss), then aggregate per participant. Differs from the other leaves: the two columns are not interchangeable ids, each side has its own value you compare.

Medium #1212 Team Scores in Football Tournament

▼

One matches row holds both teams and both their goal counts. Split it into one row per team carrying that team's own goals and the opponent's, turn each game into points (win 3, draw 1, loss 0), then total per team.

Tables: Teams (team_id, team_name), Matches (match_id, host_team, guest_team, host_goals, guest_goals)

Real-World Example

A league standings table: every match contributes points to two teams at once, so the match row must be split per team before the points can be totaled. The same shape covers any head-to-head log, home and away records, or two player contests.

Prompt: Compute each team's total points across all matches (a win is 3 points, a draw 1, a loss 0). A team that played no matches still appears with 0. Output team_id, team_name, num_points. Order by num_points DESC, then team_id ASC.

▶ 1 UNION ALL split → CASE points → LEFT JOIN teams → aggregate
-- 1) split each match into the host's row and the guest's row, -- each carrying its OWN goals and the OPPONENT's WITH scored AS ( SELECT host_team AS team_id, CASE WHEN host_goals > guest_goals THEN 3 WHEN host_goals = guest_goals THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS pts FROM Matches UNION ALL SELECT guest_team AS team_id, CASE WHEN guest_goals > host_goals THEN 3 WHEN guest_goals = host_goals THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS pts FROM Matches ) -- 2) drive off Teams with a LEFT JOIN so a team with no matches stays at 0 SELECT t.team_id, t.team_name, COALESCE(SUM(s.pts), 0) AS num_points FROM Teams t LEFT JOIN scored s ON s.team_id = t.team_id GROUP BY t.team_id, t.team_name ORDER BY num_points DESC, t.team_id ASC;

Why this is best: The UNION ALL is the unpivot: it turns one match into two participant rows, each with its own goals and the opponent's, so the CASE can score the game from that team's point of view. Driving the final aggregate off Teams with a LEFT JOIN plus COALESCE keeps teams that never played at 0 rather than dropping them.

The trap this avoids: a single GROUP BY host_team on the wide table silently ignores every team's away (guest) games. Splitting both sides is the whole point.

▶ 2 Pre-aggregate each side, then FULL JOIN / sum
-- aggregate host points and guest points separately, then add them per team WITH host AS ( SELECT host_team AS team_id, SUM(CASE WHEN host_goals > guest_goals THEN 3 WHEN host_goals = guest_goals THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS pts FROM Matches GROUP BY host_team ), guest AS ( SELECT guest_team AS team_id, SUM(CASE WHEN guest_goals > host_goals THEN 3 WHEN guest_goals = host_goals THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS pts FROM Matches GROUP BY guest_team ) SELECT t.team_id, t.team_name, COALESCE(h.pts, 0) + COALESCE(g.pts, 0) AS num_points FROM Teams t LEFT JOIN host h ON h.team_id = t.team_id LEFT JOIN guest g ON g.team_id = t.team_id GROUP BY t.team_id, t.team_name, h.pts, g.pts ORDER BY num_points DESC, t.team_id ASC;

Why this works: Same answer by aggregating the two sides before combining. More verbose than the UNION ALL split and easier to get wrong (two COALESCE, two joins), so prefer rank 1 unless you specifically need the per-side subtotals.

→

Also appears as

A join-first framing of this same problem lives under Join Tables Then Aggregate in the Multi-Table Recipes tab. Here it is filed for the unpivot move (splitting the two sides); there it is filed for the matches-to-teams join.

Dedup 2 problems

▼

A single table with duplicate rows → the table with duplicates removed, keeping only the row with the smallest ID.

Signal words: "delete," "remove duplicates," "keep only," "deduplicate"

Technique: DELETE with self-join keeping MIN(id)

Reference Techniques used in Delete Duplicates

▼

2 SQL techniques relevant to this recipe, with what they do, when to reach for them, and a generic code example.

Technique What It Does When to Reach for It Example Code
DELETE + CTE Removes rows from the table using a CTE to identify which rows to keep or remove The problem asks you to physically modify the table 
WITH dups AS (
  SELECT id,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY email ORDER BY id
         ) AS rn
  FROM Users
)
DELETE FROM Users
WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM dups WHERE rn > 1);
ROW_NUMBER() Assigns a unique sequential number to each row within a partition You need to identify duplicates for deletion, pick one row per group, or rank with no ties 
SELECT *,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
         PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC
       ) AS rn
FROM Emp;

Filter Rows vs Remove Duplicates: If the problem says "find" or "show" unique values, that is Filter Rows using SELECT DISTINCT or GROUP BY (the table stays unchanged). This recipe is only for when the problem says "delete" or "remove" and the table itself must be modified. The test: if you ran the query twice, would anything change the second time? With SELECT, no. With DELETE, the second run finds nothing to delete because the rows are already gone.

Easy #196 Delete Duplicate Emails

▼

Delete all duplicate emails, keeping only one unique email with the smallest id. Modify the table in-place with a DELETE statement.

Tables: Person (id, email)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern H: Deduplication (DELETE)

Real-World Example

Database maintenance after a merger deduplicates customer records. Duplicate emails represent the same person; keeping the lowest id (earliest record) preserves historical data integrity.

▶ 1 DELETE with Subquery (NOT IN)
DELETE FROM Person WHERE id NOT IN ( SELECT MIN(id) FROM Person GROUP BY email );

Why this is best: Subquery finds MIN(id) per email (keeps one per email). DELETE all rows whose id is NOT in that set. Simple, readable, and works across dialects.

Gotcha (Critical): Some SQL engines (e.g., older MySQL) forbid deleting from a table when the subquery references the same table. If you hit "You can't specify the target table 'Person' in FROM clause", wrap the subquery in another subquery: WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM (SELECT MIN(id) AS id FROM Person GROUP BY email) t)

Performance: O(n log n) for GROUP BY, then hash join for IN check. Generally fast.

▶ 2 DELETE with Self-Join
DELETE FROM p1 USING Person p1 JOIN Person p2 ON p1.email = p2.email AND p1.id > p2.id;

Why this works: Self-join pairs duplicates. Delete rows where id > partner's id (keeps the lower id). USING is PostgreSQL syntax; MySQL uses different syntax (see variant below).

MySQL Variant: DELETE p1 FROM Person p1 JOIN Person p2 ON p1.email = p2.email AND p1.id > p2.id;

Gotcha: Self-join can be slow if table is large. O(n²) worst case for full cross join before filter.

Performance: Hash join on (email) reduces complexity. Still slower than approach #1 for very large tables.

▶ 3 DELETE with ROW_NUMBER Window Function
DELETE FROM Person WHERE id NOT IN ( SELECT id FROM ( SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY id) AS rn FROM Person ) ranked WHERE rn = 1 );

Why this works: ROW_NUMBER ranks rows per email (ordered by id). rn=1 is the lowest id. Keep all rn=1 rows, delete rest.

Caveat: Window functions require nested subqueries. More complex syntax. Marginally clearer intent ("keep first per group") but overkill for this problem.

Performance: Window function scan, then subquery filter, then DELETE. Similar to approach #1 in cost but more overhead.

Medium Remove Duplicate Pending Transactions by ID

▼

Deduplicate a fintech payment queue on a composite key (user_id, merchant_id, amount), keeping only the row with the smallest queue_id (earliest submission).

Tables: transaction_queue (queue_id, user_id, merchant_id, amount, submitted_at, status)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Single-Table Queries → Pattern H: Deduplication (DELETE) (Note: composite-key dedup, not single-column)

Real-World Example

A fintech app's pending payment queue accumulated duplicate transactions after a client-side retry bug submitted the same charge multiple times within seconds. The natural key is (user_id, merchant_id, amount) — same payer, same payee, same amount — and the smallest queue_id is the original submission. Deduplicating before the queue is drained downstream prevents double-charging the customer.

▶ 1 DELETE with Self-Join via USING (PostgreSQL)
DELETE FROM transaction_queue t1 USING transaction_queue t2 WHERE t1.queue_id > t2.queue_id AND t1.user_id = t2.user_id AND t1.merchant_id = t2.merchant_id AND t1.amount = t2.amount;

Why this works: The self-join pairs every row with every other row in the same (user_id, merchant_id, amount) group. The t1.queue_id > t2.queue_id predicate keeps only pairs where t1 is the later submission, so DELETE removes every row that has at least one earlier twin. The smallest queue_id in each group is never on the t1 side of any qualifying pair, so it survives.

Why "smallest queue_id wins": Reverse the inequality (t1.queue_id < t2.queue_id) and you'd keep the largest instead. The direction of the inequality picks the survivor — pick it deliberately based on the prompt ("earliest submission" = smallest queue_id since the column is SERIAL).

MySQL Variant: DELETE t1 FROM transaction_queue t1 JOIN transaction_queue t2 ON t1.user_id = t2.user_id AND t1.merchant_id = t2.merchant_id AND t1.amount = t2.amount AND t1.queue_id > t2.queue_id;

Gotcha: Forgetting any one of the three equality predicates collapses the dedup key. Drop t1.amount = t2.amount and you'd treat a $49.99 charge and a $1,000 charge from the same user-merchant pair as duplicates.

Performance: Self-join is O(n²) worst case, but a hash or merge join on the composite key (user_id, merchant_id, amount) cuts it to roughly O(n). Slower than a single-column dedup but still fine for queue-sized tables.

▶ 2 DELETE with EXISTS (correlated subquery)
DELETE FROM transaction_queue t1 WHERE EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM transaction_queue t2 WHERE t1.user_id = t2.user_id AND t1.merchant_id = t2.merchant_id AND t1.amount = t2.amount AND t1.queue_id > t2.queue_id );

Why this works: For every candidate row t1, EXISTS asks "is there any row in the same (user_id, merchant_id, amount) group with a smaller queue_id?" If yes, t1 is a later duplicate and gets deleted. The smallest queue_id in each group has no qualifying t2, so EXISTS is false and that row survives.

When to prefer this over the self-join: EXISTS is more portable (works on every major dialect with the same syntax) and reads more naturally as "delete me if a smaller twin exists." It also short-circuits — once one qualifying t2 is found, the planner stops looking for more, which can be faster than the self-join's full pair enumeration when groups are large.

Gotcha (NULL handling): Equality predicates against NULL evaluate to UNKNOWN, not TRUE. If any of user_id, merchant_id, or amount is nullable and contains NULLs, two NULL-bearing rows would NOT match each other and the dedup would silently miss them. The prompt's NOT NULL constraints on these columns are what make this safe — verify before relying on this pattern.

Gotcha (the inequality direction is the entire spec): Same as approach #1 — flip t1.queue_id > t2.queue_id to < and you'd keep the latest, not the earliest. Read the prompt twice before picking the direction.

Performance: Roughly equivalent to approach #1. The planner often rewrites EXISTS as a semi-join, which uses the same hash-join machinery as the self-join but stops on first match per outer row.

Multi-Table Recipes

4 recipe categories covering 103 problems. Two are join-specific (enrich-join, enrich-aggregate, 59 problems), one is reshape (pivot / unpivot / combine, 12 problems), and one (rank-partition, 32 problems) is reachable from both Single Table and Join 2+ in the Decision Tree. After a join, the result is effectively one table — so the nine Single-Table shape recipes also apply to joined data.

Reference Multi-Table Quick Reference (pick method → write JOIN → verify)

▼

One card, three sections that match the natural workflow for any multi-table problem. Expand only the section you need.

1. Pick the method — Technique Quick Reference

▼

The SQL techniques used across all 4 multi-table recipe categories, grouped by family. Open just the family you're working in.

1a. Join Techniques

▼

INNER / LEFT / CROSS JOIN + COALESCE for the NULLs LEFT JOIN introduces.

Technique What It Does When to Reach for It Example Code
INNER JOIN Returns only rows that have a matching key in both tables You only want results where both tables have data for that key (the default join type) 
SELECT o.id, c.name
FROM Orders o
INNER JOIN Customers c
  ON c.id = o.customer_id;
LEFT JOIN Returns all rows from the left table, with NULLs where the right table has no match You want to keep every row from one table even if there is no match in the other (e.g., "include customers with no orders") 
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.name;
CROSS JOIN Produces every possible combination of rows from both tables You need all combinations (e.g., every student paired with every exam) before filtering or aggregating 
SELECT s.name, e.exam_id
FROM Students s
CROSS JOIN Exams e;
COALESCE Returns the first non NULL value, useful for replacing NULLs introduced by LEFT JOIN After a LEFT JOIN, you want 0 instead of NULL for missing matches 
SELECT c.name,
       COALESCE(SUM(o.total), 0) AS spend
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.name;

1b. Aggregation After Join

▼

GROUP BY + count / sum / avg after the join collapses joined rows into per-group summaries.

Technique What It Does When to Reach for It Example Code
GROUP BY + aggregates Collapses joined rows into summary rows per group After joining, you need totals, counts, or averages per group rather than individual rows 
SELECT c.country, SUM(o.total) AS revenue
FROM Orders o
JOIN Customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.country;

1c. Ranking After Join

▼

Window functions (ROW_NUMBER / DENSE_RANK) + PARTITION BY to pick top-N rows within each group. Cross-link: full technique reference lives in Rank & Percentile.

Technique What It Does When to Reach for It Example Code
DENSE_RANK() / ROW_NUMBER() Assigns a rank to each row within a partition, allowing you to pick the top N You need the highest, lowest, or Nth row within each group after joining tables 
SELECT *
FROM (
  SELECT e.*, d.name AS dept,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (
           PARTITION BY d.id ORDER BY e.salary DESC
         ) AS rk
  FROM Emp e JOIN Dept d ON d.id = e.dept_id
) t
WHERE rk = 1;
PARTITION BY Divides rows into groups for the window function to operate on independently You need to rank or number rows separately within each group (per department, per customer) 
SELECT name, dept,
       AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) AS dept_avg
FROM Emp;

1d. Combining Independent Results

▼

Stack rows vertically (UNION ALL) or compute intermediate results inline (subqueries).

Technique What It Does When to Reach for It Example Code
UNION / UNION ALL Stacks rows from separate queries vertically. UNION removes duplicates, UNION ALL keeps all The output combines results from independent queries that share the same column structure 
SELECT id, 'order'  AS source FROM Orders
UNION ALL
SELECT id, 'refund'        FROM Refunds;
Subqueries A query nested inside another query, used to compute intermediate results Each section of the UNION needs its own independent logic to produce its rows 
SELECT name
FROM Emp
WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM Emp);

2. Write the JOIN — ON Clause Cheat Sheet

▼

What the JOIN ON clause accepts, and the LEFT JOIN gotcha that drops rows you wanted to keep.

2a. What goes inside the ON clause

▼

Any boolean expression: equality, range, NULL check, OR, function call — you can stack as many AND conditions as you need.

Pattern Example
Equality between sides a.id = b.id
Single-table filter b.status = 'open'
Range / inequality a.date BETWEEN b.start AND b.end
Null check b.deleted_at IS NULL
OR a.id = b.id OR a.alt_id = b.id
Function call LOWER(a.name) = LOWER(b.name)

2b. ON vs WHERE — the LEFT JOIN gotcha

▼

A right-side filter in ON only blocks the match. A right-side filter in WHERE blocks survival — the LEFT JOIN silently turns into INNER and drops the rows you wanted to keep.

A right-side filter in ON only blocks the match. A right-side filter in WHERE blocks survival. Result: WHERE drops the unmatched left rows you wanted to keep.

Filter location What it does Example outcome
ON (right-side filter) Filters which right rows are eligible to attach during the join Unmatched left rows survive with nulls on the right
WHERE (right-side filter) Filters the assembled result after the join finishes Unmatched left rows are thrown out (LEFT JOIN behaves like INNER)
WHERE (left-side filter) Filters the left table before / during the join Either ON or WHERE is fine; placement does not change the result

Open the full walkthrough with sample tables →

3. Verify the JOIN — Six-Step Checklist

▼

Six verification steps to run through before and after every JOIN to avoid silent row multiplication, dropped rows, and NULL mismatches.

  1. Identify the join key(s) — columns that connect the tables
  2. Choose join type: INNER (default), LEFT (keep all from first table), CROSS (all combinations)
  3. Check for duplicates in keys — many-to-many creates row explosion
  4. Handle NULL join keys — NULLs never match in a standard JOIN
  5. After joining: verify row count to ensure no unexpected multiplication
  6. Right-side filters on a LEFT JOIN belong in ON, not WHERE — otherwise the LEFT JOIN behaves like INNER. See the ON vs WHERE walkthrough.

Look Up Columns From a Reference Table 16 problems

▼

A fact table + a dimension table (or one table playing two roles via self-join) → fact rows enriched with looked-up columns.

Signal words: "find the name for," "replace ID with," "look up," "show along with," "regardless of," manager/employee, parent/child, referrer/referee

Technique: LEFT JOIN, INNER JOIN, CROSS JOIN (for all combinations), self-join (alias the same table twice)

Pitfall: ON vs WHERE on a LEFT JOIN

A right-side filter in WHERE drops unmatched left rows and silently turns your LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN. Put right-side filters in ON to keep every left row.

Open the full ON vs WHERE walkthrough →

Reference Techniques used in Enrich Join

▼

5 SQL techniques relevant to this recipe, with what they do, when to reach for them, and a generic code example.

Technique What It Does When to Reach for It Example Code
INNER JOIN Returns only rows that have a matching key in both tables You only want results where both tables have data for that key 
SELECT o.id, c.name
FROM Orders o
INNER JOIN Customers c
  ON c.id = o.customer_id;
LEFT JOIN Returns all rows from the left table, with NULLs where the right table has no match You want to keep every row from one table even if there is no match in the other 
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.name;
CROSS JOIN Produces every possible combination of rows from both tables You need all combinations before filtering or aggregating 
SELECT s.name, e.exam_id
FROM Students s
CROSS JOIN Exams e;
Self-join Aliases the same table twice to compare or look up rows within one table The row needs to look up another row in the same table (employee/manager, parent/child, referrer/referee) 
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM Employee e
JOIN Employee m ON m.id = e.managerId;
COALESCE Returns the first non-NULL value from a list of columns or expressions You need a fallback value when a column might be NULL 
SELECT COALESCE(nickname, first_name, 'Unknown') AS display_name
FROM Users;

Self-joins live here too. Even when the prompt mentions only one physical table (Employees with managerId, Categories with parent_id, Users with referee_id), if the row needs to look up another row in the same table, it is a join. Alias the table twice (e.g., Employee e JOIN Employee m ON e.managerId = m.id) and treat each alias as a separate "virtual" table. The join lives in this recipe, not in row-compare (which is reserved for sequential LAG/LEAD neighbors).

How to pick: decision tree

▼

What you need to bring onto each row routes you to the right container below.

You have a fact table plus a reference table (or one table in two roles). Match what you need:

  • Add a column from another table (replace an id with a name, attach an attribute); keep every row with LEFT JOIN and filter the NULLs to find non-matches → Straight lookup / enrich.
  • A value gated by a threshold in another table (keep the best price only if the rating is high enough) → Gated lookup.
  • Look up another row in the SAME table (manager, friend, overlapping session) → Self-join.
  • Every combination of two sets, even the empty ones → Cross join.
  • A per-group value attached to each row (each player's first-login device, each row's team size) → Match each row to a per-group value.
  • Keep entities that pass several conditions after rolling up → Compound eligibility.

Straight lookup / enrich 7 problems

▼

INNER / LEFT JOIN — pull a column from a reference table onto each fact row. LEFT JOIN keeps every fact row (NULL when no match); filtering on that NULL finds the non-matches (the anti-join).

#1378 — Replace Employee ID With The Unique Identifier

Easy
▼

Show the unique ID of each employee. If an employee has no unique ID, show null instead.

Problem: Show the unique ID of each employee. If an employee has no unique ID, show null instead.

Tables: Employees (id, name) and EmployeeUNI (id, unique_id)

Decision Tree Path

This is a LEFT JOIN pattern — all employees appear in output, with matching unique IDs or NULL.

Real-World Example

HR system merging internal employee IDs with SSO (Single Sign-On) identifiers. Not every employee has migrated to SSO yet, so some have NULL.

▶ 1 Most Efficient — LEFT JOIN with SELECT Order
SELECT eu.unique_id, e.name FROM Employees e LEFT JOIN EmployeeUNI eu ON e.id = eu.id ORDER BY eu.unique_id;

Why this is best: LEFT JOIN ensures all employees appear. Selecting unique_id first shows NULLs naturally for unmatched employees.

Performance: O(n + m) with index on EmployeeUNI.id. Clean, readable, minimal intermediate rows.

▶ 2 Alternative — COALESCE for Explicit NULL Handling
SELECT COALESCE(eu.unique_id, NULL) AS unique_id, e.name FROM Employees e LEFT JOIN EmployeeUNI eu ON e.id = eu.id;

Why this works: COALESCE explicitly handles NULL, making the intent clear (though redundant here since LEFT JOIN already produces NULLs).

When to use: If you need fallback values or multiple NULL coalescing logic.

#1068 — Product Sales Analysis I

Easy
▼

Report product_name, year, and price for each sale. Join Sales and Product tables.

Problem: Report product_name, year, and price for each sale. Join Sales and Product tables.

Tables: Sales (sale_id, product_id, year, quantity, price) and Product (product_id, product_name)

Decision Tree Path

This is an INNER JOIN pattern — only sales with matching products are returned. No unmatched rows.

Real-World Example

E-commerce combining transaction log (Sales) with product catalog (Product) to show what was actually purchased with full product details.

▶ 1 Most Efficient — INNER JOIN
SELECT p.product_name, s.year, s.price FROM Sales s INNER JOIN Product p ON s.product_id = p.product_id;

Why this is best: INNER JOIN filters to only matched rows. Since every sale should have a product, this is safe and fast.

Performance: O(n + m) with index on Product.product_id. Minimal result set.

▶ 2 Alternative — Explicit JOIN Keyword
SELECT p.product_name, s.year, s.price FROM Sales s JOIN Product p USING (product_id);

Why this works: USING clause is cleaner when join key has same name in both tables. Shorter than ON.

Caveat: Some teams prefer explicit ON for consistency.

#577 — Employee Bonus

Easy
▼

Report name and bonus for employees with bonus = 1000.

Problem: Report name and bonus for employees with bonus < 1000 OR no bonus. Filter out employees with bonus >= 1000.

Tables: Employee (empId, name, supervisor, salary) and Bonus (empId, bonus)

Decision Tree Path

This is an anti-join variant using LEFT JOIN with NULL detection. Keep unmatched rows (no bonus) and filter matched rows by condition.

Real-World Example

Payroll processing identifying employees due for bonus review: those with small bonuses (< 1000) or missing bonuses entirely.

▶ 1 Most Efficient — LEFT JOIN with NULL-aware WHERE
SELECT e.name, b.bonus FROM Employee e LEFT JOIN Bonus b ON e.empId = b.empId WHERE b.bonus < 1000 OR b.bonus IS NULL;

Why this is best: LEFT JOIN preserves all employees. WHERE clause filters: keep those with small bonuses OR NULL (no bonus at all).

Performance: O(n + m). Key insight: b.bonus IS NULL catches unmatched rows, which are displayed as NULL in output.

▶ 2 Alternative — COALESCE for Null-Safe Comparison
SELECT e.name, b.bonus FROM Employee e LEFT JOIN Bonus b ON e.empId = b.empId WHERE COALESCE(b.bonus, 0) < 1000;

Why this works: COALESCE treats NULL as 0, so NULL < 1000 is TRUE. One WHERE condition instead of OR.

Caveat: Less explicit than IS NULL. Could be confusing if 0 has different meaning. Solution 1 is clearer.

Easy #175 Combine Two Tables

▼

Return first name, last name, city, and state for every person, using NULL when no address exists.

Tables: Person (personId, lastName, firstName), Address (addressId, personId, city, state)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins

Real-World Example

A CRM export blends the primary contact table with the optional address table for mailings; persons without an address still appear in the output with empty fields.

▶ 1 LEFT JOIN
SELECT p.firstName, p.lastName, a.city, a.state FROM Person p LEFT JOIN Address a ON a.personId = p.personId;

Why this is best: LEFT JOIN preserves every person row and supplies NULL when no address exists — exactly the spec.

Performance: Index Address.personId for sub-linear lookups.

Easy #1421 NPV Queries

▼

For each (id, year) in Queries, return npv (0 if missing from NPV).

Tables: NPV (id, year, npv), Queries (id, year)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins

Real-World Example

Finance tools look up NPV values for requested (project, year) pairs and default missing pairs to 0 so the UI never shows NULL.

▶ 1 LEFT JOIN with COALESCE
SELECT q.id, q.year, COALESCE(n.npv, 0) AS npv FROM Queries q LEFT JOIN NPV n ON n.id = q.id AND n.year = q.year;

Why this is best: LEFT JOIN covers missing pairs; COALESCE defaults to 0.

Performance: One join.

#1581 — Customer Who Visited but Did Not Make Any Transactions

Easy
▼

Find customer IDs and count of visits where NO transaction occurred. Filter for NULL transactions.

Problem: Find customer IDs and count of visits where NO transaction occurred. Filter for NULL transactions.

Tables: Visits (visit_id, customer_id) and Transactions (transaction_id, visit_id, amount)

Decision Tree Path

This is a classic anti-join: LEFT JOIN then filter WHERE transaction IS NULL, then GROUP BY and COUNT.

Real-World Example

Retail analytics identifying "window shoppers" — customers who visited but didn't buy. Helps improve conversion tactics.

▶ 1 Most Efficient — LEFT JOIN + IS NULL Filter + GROUP BY
SELECT v.customer_id, COUNT(*) AS count_no_trans FROM Visits v LEFT JOIN Transactions t ON v.visit_id = t.visit_id WHERE t.transaction_id IS NULL GROUP BY v.customer_id;

Why this is best: LEFT JOIN keeps all visits. WHERE t.transaction_id IS NULL filters to unmatched visits only. COUNT(*) tallies them per customer.

Performance: O(n + m + k log k) where k = result size. Index on Transactions.visit_id and GROUP BY column speeds execution.

▶ 2 Alternative — NOT EXISTS Subquery
SELECT v.customer_id, COUNT(*) AS count_no_trans FROM Visits v WHERE NOT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM Transactions t WHERE t.visit_id = v.visit_id ) GROUP BY v.customer_id;

Why this works: NOT EXISTS explicitly checks no transaction row exists for each visit. Can be faster on large datasets with good indexing.

Caveat: More verbose; correlated subqueries can be slower without proper indexing. LEFT JOIN + NULL is usually clearer.

Medium Orders in 2024 per Customer (LEFT JOIN: filter in ON, not WHERE)

▼

Count each customer's 2024 orders, keeping every customer (0 when none). The right-side date filter must live in the ON; the same filter in WHERE silently drops customers with no 2024 order. This is the canonical ON-vs-WHERE trap made visible.

Tables: customers (customer_id, name), orders (order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount)

Real-World Example

A retention report lists every customer with their 2024 order count, including the dormant ones at 0 so they can be targeted. Dropping the zero-order customers would hide exactly the people the report exists to surface.

Prompt: For every customer, count how many orders they placed in 2024. Customers with no 2024 orders (including those whose only orders are from other years, and those with no orders at all) must still appear with 0. Output customer_id, name, orders_2024. Order by customer_id ASC.

▶ 1 Right-side date filter in the ON (keeps every customer)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS orders_2024 -- count a RIGHT column, not COUNT(*) FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.order_date >= DATE '2024-01-01' -- right-side filter, in the ON AND o.order_date < DATE '2025-01-01' GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name ORDER BY c.customer_id;

Why this is best: The date condition in the ON only limits which order rows are eligible to attach. A customer whose orders are all from 2023 (or who has no orders) still survives the LEFT JOIN with NULLs on the order side, so they appear with orders_2024 = 0. The filter shapes the match; it does not remove left rows.

Why COUNT(o.order_id) and not COUNT(*): for a non-matching customer the LEFT JOIN leaves one row with NULL order columns. COUNT(o.order_id) ignores that NULL and returns 0; COUNT(*) would count the NULL-filled row as 1 and wrongly report 1.

▶ 2 The trap: same filter in WHERE (silently drops customers)
-- WRONG when the prompt says "keep every customer." SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS orders_2024 FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_date >= DATE '2024-01-01' -- right-side filter in WHERE AND o.order_date < DATE '2025-01-01' GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name ORDER BY c.customer_id;

Why it is wrong: the LEFT JOIN first keeps every customer, attaching NULL order columns to the non-matches. Then WHERE o.order_date >= ... is evaluated on the assembled result, and NULL >= DATE is not true, so those customers' rows are thrown away. The LEFT JOIN has silently collapsed into an INNER JOIN, and the dormant customers (the whole point of the report) vanish.

The rule: a filter on the right table of a LEFT JOIN belongs in the ON when you must keep unmatched left rows. A filter on the left table is fine in either place. See the ON Clause Cheat Sheet at the top of this recipe for the full side-by-side.

Gated lookup: a threshold gates a per-entity pick 1 problem

▼

Two tables share an entity key: one carries a gate (a rating, score, flag, status, or date), the other carries values to choose from (prices, bids, dates). Look up the gate, pick a per-entity target, then let the gate decide whether to keep it. Open the decision tree first, then the worked problem.

How to pick: decision tree

▼

Two questions: what happens to non-qualifying entities, and which row you pick.

Setup — name the two tables:

  • Gate table = the one with the condition column (rating, score, flag, status, date).
  • Value table = the one you pick from (often many rows per entity). The gate is checked on the gate table's column, never on the value.

Walk the questions in order. Stop at the first match.

Q1. Should entities that fail the gate still appear in the output?

  • Yes, show them with a fallback (0 or NULL) → ✓ use a CASE — keep the picked value when the gate passes, else 0/NULL. Drive off the gate table (or LEFT JOIN) so every entity survives.
  • No, drop them entirely → ✓ use a WHERE on the gate — only qualifying entities appear.

Q2. Which row do you pick from the value table?

  • Cheapest / lowest → MIN(value) (or ROW_NUMBER ... ORDER BY value, keep rn = 1).
  • Highest → MAX(value) (or ORDER BY value DESC).
  • Earliest / latest → MIN / MAX of the date (or order by it).

Two traps: gate on the gate table's attribute, not on the value you picked; and the pick is one row per entity (a top-1 per group), not a SUM / AVG over the value table.

Medium Lowest Price per Product, Gated by Rating

▼

For each product, report its cheapest listed price, but only if its rating clears the bar; products rated below 4 report 0 instead.

Tables: products (product_id, product_name, category, rating), pricing (pricing_id, product_id, category, price)

Real-World Example

A marketplace surfaces a "best price" only for well rated products; low rated products are suppressed (shown as 0) so the storefront does not promote a cheap but poorly reviewed item. The rating in one table gates the lowest price drawn from another.

Prompt: A product can have several rows in pricing. For each product, return its lowest price when its rating is 4 or higher, otherwise 0. Every product appears. Output product_id, rating, reported_price. Order by product_id ASC.

▶ 1 Pick the cheapest per product, gate with CASE (keeps every product)
WITH cheapest AS ( -- per-product pick from the value table SELECT product_id, MIN(price) AS min_price FROM pricing GROUP BY product_id ) SELECT p.product_id, p.rating, CASE WHEN p.rating >= 4 THEN c.min_price -- gate on the gate table's column ELSE 0 END AS reported_price -- fallback when the gate fails FROM products AS p -- drive off products so all appear LEFT JOIN cheapest AS c ON c.product_id = p.product_id ORDER BY p.product_id;

Why this is best: The cheapest CTE does the per-product pick (one row per product). Driving off products with a LEFT JOIN keeps every product, and the CASE applies the gate to the rating, substituting 0 for the ones that fall short. The gate reads the rating from products, never the price.

Trace: product 1 (rating 5) → cheapest 9.99; product 2 (rating 3) → 0; product 3 (rating 4) → cheapest 18.00; product 4 (rating 2) → 0.

▶ 2 If the prompt instead said "exclude low rated products" → WHERE
-- Same gate, different fallback: drop non-qualifiers instead of zeroing them. SELECT p.product_id, MIN(pr.price) AS min_price FROM products AS p JOIN pricing AS pr ON pr.product_id = p.product_id WHERE p.rating >= 4 -- gate as a filter: only qualifying products remain GROUP BY p.product_id ORDER BY p.product_id;

When to use: this returns only products 1 and 3. The single decision that flips between the two solutions is the fallback: keep every entity with a 0/NULL (CASE) versus drop the failing ones (WHERE). Read the prompt for which one it wants.

Self-join: one table, two roles 3 problems

▼

alias the table twice — the row needs to look up another row in the same table: employee/manager, friend/friend, or two overlapping sessions of one account.

Easy #181 Employees Earning More Than Their Managers

▼

Return employees whose salary exceeds their manager's salary.

Tables: Employee (id, name, salary, managerId)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins

Real-World Example

An HR audit flags reports that out-earn their manager, triggering a compensation review conversation.

▶ 1 Self-Join on Manager Reference
SELECT e.name AS Employee FROM Employee e JOIN Employee m ON m.id = e.managerId WHERE e.salary > m.salary;

Why this is best: Self-join resolves the manager lookup; WHERE makes the comparison.

Performance: Index on id and managerId.

Medium #1264 Page Recommendations

▼

Recommend pages that user 1's friends like but user 1 has not liked yet.

Tables: Friendship (user1_id, user2_id), Likes (user_id, page_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins

Real-World Example

A social product implements a "pages you may like" rail using the friends-of-friends signal.

▶ 1 Friends Union + NOT IN
SELECT DISTINCT l.page_id AS recommended_page FROM Likes l WHERE l.user_id IN ( SELECT user2_id FROM Friendship WHERE user1_id = 1 UNION SELECT user1_id FROM Friendship WHERE user2_id = 1 ) AND l.page_id NOT IN (SELECT page_id FROM Likes WHERE user_id = 1);

Why this is best: First subquery covers friendship in either direction. NOT IN filters out pages user 1 already likes.

Performance: Small subqueries + one filter.

Medium #1747 Leetflex Banned Accounts

▼

Detect accounts whose sessions overlap in time but on different IPs.

Tables: LogInfo (account_id, ip_address, login, logout)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins

Real-World Example

A streaming service bans concurrent-use accounts by spotting sessions overlapping on different IPs — a shared-credentials signature.

▶ 1 Self-Join on Overlap + Different IP
SELECT DISTINCT a.account_id FROM LogInfo a JOIN LogInfo b ON a.account_id = b.account_id AND a.ip_address <> b.ip_address AND a.login <= b.logout AND b.login <= a.logout;

Why this is best: The overlap condition (a.login <= b.logout AND b.login <= a.logout) is the canonical interval intersection; different ip completes the rule.

Performance: Self-join with composite index on (account_id, login, logout).

Cross join: all combinations 1 problem

▼

CROSS JOIN then LEFT JOIN — force every combination of two sets to appear, then LEFT JOIN the actuals and COUNT so empty combinations show 0.

#1280 — Students and Examinations

Medium
▼

For each student-subject pair, count exam attempts. Ensure ALL student-subject combinations appear, even if 0 exams attended.

Problem: For each student-subject pair, count exam attempts. Ensure ALL student-subject combinations appear, even if 0 exams attended.

Tables: Students (student_id, student_name), Subjects (subject_name), Examinations (student_id, subject_name)

Decision Tree Path

Combined pattern: CROSS JOIN (all student-subject combos) + LEFT JOIN Examinations + GROUP BY + COUNT. Forces complete result set.

Real-World Example

Learning Management System (LMS) grade report: every student appears for every course, showing exam count or 0 if they haven't taken it yet.

▶ 1 Most Efficient — CROSS JOIN + LEFT JOIN + GROUP BY + COUNT
SELECT s.student_id, s.student_name, sub.subject_name, COUNT(e.student_id) AS attended_exams FROM Students s CROSS JOIN Subjects sub LEFT JOIN Examinations e ON s.student_id = e.student_id AND sub.subject_name = e.subject_name GROUP BY s.student_id, s.student_name, sub.subject_name ORDER BY s.student_id, sub.subject_name;

Why this is best: CROSS JOIN creates all student-subject pairs. LEFT JOIN matches exams; unmatched pairs get COUNT = 0. Guarantees complete output.

Performance: O(n * m + e log(n*m)) where n = students, m = subjects, e = exam records. Be careful with large student/subject counts.

▶ 2 Alternative — COALESCE on COUNT for Readability
SELECT s.student_id, s.student_name, sub.subject_name, COALESCE(COUNT(e.student_id), 0) AS attended_exams FROM Students s CROSS JOIN Subjects sub LEFT JOIN Examinations e ON s.student_id = e.student_id AND sub.subject_name = e.subject_name GROUP BY s.student_id, s.student_name, sub.subject_name ORDER BY s.student_id, sub.subject_name;

Why this works: COALESCE explicitly shows 0 instead of NULL. More explicit, though COUNT already returns 0 for no matches.

Caveat: Redundant; COUNT already handles NULLs. Use if team requires explicit zero display or if aggregating multiple metrics.

Match each row to a per-group value 2 problems

▼

aggregate then attach — compute a per-group value (earliest date, team size) and put it on each row, by joining back to the aggregate or with a window function.

Easy #512 Game Play Analysis II

▼

Return the device each player first logged in from.

Tables: Activity (player_id, device_id, event_date, games_played)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins

Real-World Example

A product analyst ties each user to the device they installed with — the basis for device-mix reports at signup.

▶ 1 First Login per Player + Self-Join
SELECT a.player_id, a.device_id FROM Activity a JOIN ( SELECT player_id, MIN(event_date) AS first_date FROM Activity GROUP BY player_id ) f ON f.player_id = a.player_id AND f.first_date = a.event_date;

Why this is best: Compute first date per player, then join back to get the device attached to that date.

Performance: One aggregate + one join.

Easy #1303 Find the Team Size

▼

Return employees with their team size (count of employees on the same team).

Tables: Employee (employee_id, team_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins

Real-World Example

Org-chart tooling displays team size next to every person to give fast "team scale" context.

▶ 1 Window COUNT per Team
SELECT employee_id, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY team_id) AS team_size FROM Employee;

Why this is best: Window COUNT gives per-row team size without a separate GROUP BY and join.

Performance: One window pass.

Compound eligibility (roll up, then multi-condition filter) 2 problems

▼

CTE then qualify — roll up per entity, then keep only entities that satisfy several conditions, sometimes combining two qualifying paths with OR.

Medium #1811 Find Interview Candidates

▼

Candidates are gold-medalists of 3 consecutive contests OR users with >= 2 attendances in any year.

Tables: Contests (contest_id, gold_medal, silver_medal, bronze_medal), Users (user_id, mail, name), Register (contest_id, user_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins

Real-World Example

An events team picks interview subjects combining two eligibility paths: consistent top performers AND engaged attendees.

▶ 1 Gaps-and-Islands on Golds + UNION Attendance
WITH golds AS ( SELECT gold_medal AS user_id, contest_id, contest_id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY gold_medal ORDER BY contest_id) AS grp FROM Contests ), gold_streak AS ( SELECT user_id FROM golds GROUP BY user_id, grp HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3 ), heavy_registrants AS ( SELECT user_id FROM Register GROUP BY user_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 ) SELECT DISTINCT u.name, u.mail FROM Users u WHERE u.user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM gold_streak) OR u.user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM heavy_registrants);

Why this is best: Gaps-and-islands identifies 3-contest gold streaks; a separate count covers the attendance path. UNION-style filter enforces OR.

Performance: Two aggregates. Linear.

Medium #2041 Accepted Candidates From the Interviews

▼

Candidates with 2+ years experience AND total interview score >= 15.

Tables: Candidates (candidate_id, name, years_of_exp, interview_id), Rounds (interview_id, round_id, score)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins

Real-World Example

A talent-ops team automates interview shortlisting by combining resume criteria with structured interview scores.

▶ 1 Pre-Aggregate Scores + Filter
WITH totals AS ( SELECT interview_id, SUM(score) AS total FROM Rounds GROUP BY interview_id ) SELECT c.candidate_id FROM Candidates c JOIN totals t ON t.interview_id = c.interview_id WHERE c.years_of_exp >= 2 AND t.total >= 15;

Why this is best: Aggregate in a CTE, then apply compound eligibility rules.

Performance: One aggregate + one join.

Join Tables Then Aggregate 47 problems

▼

Two or more tables that must be joined before meaningful aggregation → one summary row per group.

Reference Recipe overview & key decision rules

▼

Signal words, the LEFT JOIN + date filter trap, and the "WHERE drops the rows you wanted as 0" trap — the two pitfalls behind most enrich-aggregate bugs.

Signal words: "for each... find average/total from another table," "rate," "percentage," "weighted," "all products"

Technique: JOIN + GROUP BY, weighted AVG, HAVING COUNT = (SELECT COUNT), date-range joins

Pitfall: date filters on a LEFT JOIN

When you want every left row to survive (e.g., "all books, even ones with zero sales last year"), put date filters on the right table in ON, not WHERE. A WHERE on a right-side date drops unmatched rows and undercounts groups with no recent activity.

Open the full ON vs WHERE walkthrough →

Common Trap: WHERE Filters Drop Rows You Want to Show as 0

Many enrich-aggregate problems expect a row with count 0 when a left-side row has no qualifying right-side matches. Example: "for each user, count their orders in 2019" — users with no 2019 orders should appear with count 0, not disappear from the result.

Why it breaks: WHERE runs after the LEFT JOIN. A filter on a right-side column (e.g. WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.order_date) = 2019) drops unmatched rows along with mismatched ones, so users with no orders at all silently vanish.

The fix: Keep the LEFT JOIN, then move the filter inside the aggregate. SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) turns rows that fail the condition into 0 instead of removing them, so every left-side row survives with a real count.

-- BREAKS: users with no 2019 orders are dropped entirely
SELECT u.user_id, u.join_date, COUNT(o.order_id) AS orders_in_2019
FROM Users u
LEFT JOIN Orders o ON u.user_id = o.buyer_id
WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.order_date) = 2019
GROUP BY u.user_id, u.join_date;

-- WORKS: every user survives, count rolls up to 0 when no row matches
SELECT u.user_id, u.join_date,
       SUM(CASE WHEN EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.order_date) = 2019 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS orders_in_2019
FROM Users u
LEFT JOIN Orders o ON u.user_id = o.buyer_id
GROUP BY u.user_id, u.join_date;

How to spot this: Scan the example output for any row showing 0 (or "no activity," "0 orders," "never purchased"). That is the signal to keep the LEFT JOIN and filter inside SUM or COUNT with CASE WHEN, never with a WHERE on the right-side column.

#1633 Percentage of Users Attended a Contest (Easy)

▼

For each contest, calculate the percentage of all users who registered (to 2 decimals). Order by percentage DESC, then contest_id ASC.

Schema: Users(user_id, user_name); Register(contest_id, user_id)

Goal: For each contest, calculate the percentage of all users who registered (to 2 decimals). Order by percentage DESC, then contest_id ASC.

Why this matters
Event and competition metrics: organizers need participation rates to gauge interest, set pricing, and plan future events.
▶ Rank 1: JOIN + GROUP BY + Percentage Calculation
SELECT r.contest_id, ROUND(100 * COUNT(r.user_id) / ( SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Users ), 2) AS percentage FROM Register r GROUP BY r.contest_id ORDER BY percentage DESC, r.contest_id ASC;

Why rank 1: Simple scalar subquery for total user count. Divides registrations per contest by total users, multiplies by 100, rounds to 2 decimals. ROUND(value, 2) ensures correct formatting.

Performance: O(n log n) for grouping. The subquery runs once (scalar), so negligible overhead. Much faster than joining Users for each row.

💡
Why scalar subquery, not JOIN?
A JOIN with Users would replicate each Register row for every User, bloating intermediate results. A scalar subquery (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Users) evaluates once and is reused for all contests.

Reference Techniques used in Enrich Aggregate

▼

5 SQL techniques relevant to this recipe, with what they do, when to reach for them, and a generic code example.

Technique What It Does When to Reach for It Example Code
INNER JOIN Returns only rows that have a matching key in both tables You only want results where both tables have data for that key 
SELECT o.id, c.name
FROM Orders o
INNER JOIN Customers c
  ON c.id = o.customer_id;
LEFT JOIN Returns all rows from the left table, with NULLs where the right table has no match You want to keep every row from one table even if there is no match in the other 
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.name;
GROUP BY + aggregates (after JOIN) Collapses joined rows into summary rows per group After joining, you need totals, counts, or averages per group rather than individual rows 
SELECT c.country, SUM(o.total) AS revenue
FROM Orders o
JOIN Customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.country;
COALESCE Returns the first non-NULL value from a list of columns or expressions You need a fallback value when a column might be NULL 
SELECT COALESCE(nickname, first_name, 'Unknown') AS display_name
FROM Users;
HAVING Filters groups after GROUP BY, using aggregate results The condition depends on a count, sum, or other aggregate (e.g., "groups with more than 1 row") 
SELECT dept, COUNT(*)
FROM Emp
GROUP BY dept
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;

How to pick: decision tree

▼

What the aggregate is, plus whether non-matching entities must appear, routes you to the right leaf and template.

Q1. What does the output need per group?

  • A count of joined rows → COUNT per group + COUNT template.
  • A sum / average / min / max of a joined column → SUM / AVG / MIN / MAX per group + numeric aggregate template.
  • A ratio or percentage (numerator / denominator both from joins) → Rate / ratio / percentage + rate template.
  • A filter on the aggregate (HAVING) or inside the aggregate (conditional CASE) → Aggregate + filter + HAVING / conditional template.
  • Grouped by a date bucket or cohort → Date-window / cohort aggregate + date-bucket template.

Q2. Must every left-side entity appear, even when no right-side rows match?

  • Yes (the prompt says "every user," "all products," or the expected output has rows with 0 / NULL) → LEFT JOIN, and any filter on the right table goes inside the aggregate (SUM(CASE WHEN ...)) or inside the JOIN ON clause, NOT in WHERE.
  • No, only entities with at least one matching row → INNER JOIN is fine.

Q3. Are there multiple child tables joined to the same parent?

  • Yes → aggregate each child in its OWN CTE, then join the totals. Joining two children to the parent BEFORE aggregating fans out rows and inflates SUMs.
  • No → one JOIN + GROUP BY is enough.

Generic templates per method

▼

Copy-paste skeletons. Swap the entity / fact / filter names; the shape stays the same.

COUNT per group (with LEFT JOIN so zero-row entities still appear) (back to tree)

▼

Copy-paste skeleton for this method.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. FROM the entity dim (so every entity has a chance to survive).
  2. LEFT JOIN the fact on the entity key.
  3. GROUP BY the entity columns.
  4. Use COUNT(b.col), NOT COUNT(*) — the latter counts the NULL-filled LEFT JOIN row as 1 and gives every entity a baseline of 1.
SELECT
    a.entity_id, a.entity_name,
    COUNT(b.b_pk) AS row_count
FROM entity a
LEFT JOIN fact b ON b.entity_id = a.entity_id
GROUP BY a.entity_id, a.entity_name;
-- COUNT(b.b_pk) NOT COUNT(*) — the latter counts the NULL-filled row as 1.

SUM / AVG of a joined column

▼

Copy-paste skeleton for this method.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. LEFT JOIN entity to fact on the entity key.
  2. GROUP BY the entity columns.
  3. SUM / AVG / MIN / MAX of a numeric column from the fact.
  4. Wrap the SUM in COALESCE(SUM(...), 0) if you want zero-fill instead of NULL for entities with no matching fact rows.
SELECT
    a.entity_id, a.entity_name,
    COALESCE(SUM(b.amount), 0) AS total_amount,
    AVG(b.amount)              AS avg_amount
FROM entity a
LEFT JOIN fact b ON b.entity_id = a.entity_id
GROUP BY a.entity_id, a.entity_name;

Rate / percentage per group

▼

Copy-paste skeleton for this method.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Express numerator and denominator in one pass with SUM(CASE WHEN ...), or build them as two separate CTEs and divide.
  2. Cast at least one side to NUMERIC (or use ::numeric) so the division stays decimal instead of integer.
  3. Wrap the denominator in NULLIF(...., 0) so empty groups produce NULL instead of a divide-by-zero error.
  4. ROUND to the prompt's required decimals; default is 4 in Postgres.
-- one-pass: SUM(CASE) over a single LEFT JOIN
SELECT
    a.entity_id,
    ROUND(
      SUM(CASE WHEN b.condition THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END)
      / NULLIF(COUNT(b.b_pk), 0)
    , 2) AS rate
FROM entity a
LEFT JOIN fact b ON b.entity_id = a.entity_id
GROUP BY a.entity_id;
-- NULLIF the denominator so empty groups give NULL, not divide-by-zero.

Aggregate + filter (HAVING / conditional CASE)

▼

Copy-paste skeleton for this method.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. JOIN + GROUP BY the entity.
  2. HAVING filters groups whose AGGREGATE meets a threshold (e.g. bought-all-products = HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products)).
  3. For "sum only the rows matching X per group", use a conditional aggregate: SUM(CASE WHEN tag = 'X' THEN amount ELSE 0 END).
-- HAVING: keep groups whose totals meet a cutoff (e.g. bought all products)
SELECT a.entity_id
FROM entity a
JOIN fact b ON b.entity_id = a.entity_id
GROUP BY a.entity_id
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT b.product_id) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products);

-- Conditional CASE: count / sum only qualifying rows per group
SELECT a.entity_id,
       SUM(CASE WHEN b.tag = 'X' THEN b.amount ELSE 0 END) AS amount_x
FROM entity a
LEFT JOIN fact b ON b.entity_id = a.entity_id
GROUP BY a.entity_id;

Date-bucket / cohort aggregate

▼

Copy-paste skeleton for this method.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. DATE_TRUNC('month', signup_date) as the cohort grouping key.
  2. JOIN actions to users on user_id.
  3. SUM(CASE WHEN event_date BETWEEN signup_date AND signup_date + INTERVAL '30 days' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) counts the in-window events per cohort.
  4. GROUP BY the cohort key and ORDER BY it for a clean time series.
SELECT
    DATE_TRUNC('month', a.signup_date) AS cohort_month,
    COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id)          AS cohort_size,
    SUM(CASE WHEN b.event_date BETWEEN a.signup_date
                                   AND a.signup_date + INTERVAL '30 days'
             THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)        AS retained_30d
FROM users a
LEFT JOIN events b ON b.user_id = a.user_id
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', a.signup_date)
ORDER BY cohort_month;

COUNT per group ("how many X per Y") 11 problems

▼

One row per entity, with a count of joined rows. SELECT entity, COUNT(b.*) FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON b.entity_id = a.entity_id GROUP BY entity. Use COUNT(b.col), not COUNT(*), after a LEFT JOIN — COUNT(*) counts the NULL-filled row as 1 and gives every entity a baseline of 1 even with no matches.

Easy #1241 Number of Comments per Post

▼

For each distinct post, count distinct direct comments.

Tables: Submissions (sub_id, parent_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A forum surfaces post-engagement counts in each thread preview; parents are rows with no parent_id.

▶ 1 Self-Join Parent to Child
SELECT DISTINCT p.sub_id AS post_id, COUNT(DISTINCT c.sub_id) AS number_of_comments FROM Submissions p LEFT JOIN Submissions c ON c.parent_id = p.sub_id WHERE p.parent_id IS NULL GROUP BY p.sub_id ORDER BY p.sub_id;

Why this is best: Self-join posts to their children; DISTINCT protects against repeated comment rows.

Performance: Self-join + aggregate.

Hard #1336 Number of Transactions per Visit

▼

Distribution of transactions per visit across all users, with zero-counts included.

Tables: Visits (user_id, visit_date), Transactions (user_id, transaction_date, amount)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A retail analytics team reports "how many customers made 0, 1, 2, ... purchases per visit" — a histogram used in conversion funnels.

▶ 1 Per-Visit Counts + Recursive Histogram
WITH visit_counts AS ( SELECT v.user_id, v.visit_date, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Transactions t WHERE t.user_id = v.user_id AND t.transaction_date = v.visit_date) AS c FROM Visits v ), dist AS (SELECT c AS transactions_count, COUNT(*) AS visits_count FROM visit_counts GROUP BY c), range_cte AS ( SELECT 0 AS n UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM range_cte WHERE n < (SELECT COALESCE(MAX(transactions_count),0) FROM dist) ) SELECT r.n AS transactions_count, COALESCE(d.visits_count, 0) AS visits_count FROM range_cte r LEFT JOIN dist d ON d.transactions_count = r.n;

Why this is best: Recursive CTE fills the histogram buckets so zero-frequency bins appear.

Performance: One aggregate + recursive range.

Medium #1364 Number of Trusted Contacts of a Customer

▼

For each invoice, report customer name, contacts count, and trusted-contacts count.

Tables: Customers (customer_id, customer_name, email), Contacts (user_id, contact_name, contact_email), Invoices (invoice_id, price, user_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A fintech app surfaces social-graph risk signals on each invoice by showing how many of the customer's contacts are known customers themselves.

▶ 1 LEFT JOIN Contacts + Conditional Count
SELECT i.invoice_id, c.customer_name, i.price, COUNT(ct.contact_email) AS contacts_cnt, SUM(CASE WHEN ct.contact_email IN (SELECT email FROM Customers) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS trusted_contacts_cnt FROM Invoices i JOIN Customers c ON c.customer_id = i.user_id LEFT JOIN Contacts ct ON ct.user_id = i.user_id GROUP BY i.invoice_id, c.customer_name, i.price ORDER BY i.invoice_id;

Why this is best: LEFT JOIN retains contact-free customers at count 0; conditional SUM applies the "trusted" rule inline.

Performance: One join + one aggregate + one IN.

Medium #2142 The Number of Passengers in Each Bus I

▼

Count passengers who catch each bus (first bus arriving at/after their request).

Tables: Buses (bus_id, arrival_time), Passengers (passenger_id, arrival_time)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A transit analyst measures bus load per departure to plan capacity.

▶ 1 LEAD to Bus Window + COUNT
WITH bus_windows AS ( SELECT bus_id, arrival_time AS end_t, COALESCE(LAG(arrival_time) OVER (ORDER BY arrival_time), -1) AS start_t FROM Buses ) SELECT b.bus_id, COUNT(p.passenger_id) AS passengers_cnt FROM bus_windows b LEFT JOIN Passengers p ON p.arrival_time > b.start_t AND p.arrival_time <= b.end_t GROUP BY b.bus_id ORDER BY b.bus_id;

Why this is best: Each bus owns the passenger arrivals since the previous bus. LEAD/LAG defines the capture window.

Performance: Window + range join.

Hard #2153 The Number of Passengers in Each Bus II

▼

Same as I, with bus capacity; passengers that exceed capacity roll over to the next bus.

Tables: Buses (bus_id, arrival_time, capacity), Passengers (passenger_id, arrival_time)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

Adds capacity overflow semantics: if a bus is full, extras wait for the next one.

▶ 1 Ordered Iterative Accumulate (Variables)
SELECT b.bus_id, passengers_cnt FROM ( SELECT b.bus_id, b.arrival_time, b.capacity, @leftover := GREATEST(@leftover + ( SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Passengers p WHERE p.arrival_time <= b.arrival_time AND p.arrival_time > COALESCE( LAG(b.arrival_time) OVER (ORDER BY b.arrival_time), -1) ), 0), LEAST(@leftover, b.capacity) AS passengers_cnt, @leftover := @leftover - LEAST(@leftover, b.capacity) FROM Buses b, (SELECT @leftover := 0) v ORDER BY b.arrival_time ) x ORDER BY x.bus_id;

Why this is best: Iterative state is needed because leftover rolls forward. MySQL variables simulate it; a recursive CTE is the portable alternative.

Performance: Linear in buses.

Medium #2238 Number of Times a Driver Was a Passenger

▼

For each distinct driver, count rides where they appeared as a passenger.

Tables: Rides (ride_id, driver_id, passenger_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A rideshare analyst measures drivers who also use the service personally — a signal of product love and retention.

▶ 1 Drivers Set + LEFT JOIN as Passenger
SELECT d.driver_id, COUNT(r.ride_id) AS cnt FROM (SELECT DISTINCT driver_id FROM Rides) d LEFT JOIN Rides r ON r.passenger_id = d.driver_id GROUP BY d.driver_id;

Why this is best: Use distinct driver set on the left to include drivers who never rode as a passenger.

Performance: One join + one aggregate.

Medium #580 Count Student Number in Departments

▼

For each department, count enrolled students. Depts with no students show 0.

Tables: Student (student_id, name, gender, dept_id), Department (dept_id, dept_name)

→

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

A registrar tracks enrollment per department each term, including zero-enrollment departments flagged for course-demand review.

SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(s.student_id) AS student_number FROM Department d LEFT JOIN Student s ON s.dept_id = d.dept_id GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name ORDER BY student_number DESC, d.dept_name;

Why this is best: COUNT on the right table's key returns zero for unmatched rows, unlike COUNT(*).

▼

For each user, join count of orders placed in 2019 (0 for no orders).

Tables: Users (user_id, join_date, favorite_brand), Orders (order_id, order_date, item_id, buyer_id, seller_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

A marketplace reports 2019 orders per user alongside account metadata to inform retention cohort targeting.

Easy #1939 Users That Actively Request Confirmation Messages

▼

Users who requested two confirmations within 24 hours.

Tables: Signups (user_id, time_stamp), Confirmations (user_id, time_stamp, action)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A security team flags users repeatedly requesting confirmations within 24 hours as possibly automated.

▶ 1 Self-Join with Interval Condition
SELECT DISTINCT c1.user_id FROM Confirmations c1 JOIN Confirmations c2 ON c2.user_id = c1.user_id AND c2.time_stamp > c1.time_stamp AND c2.time_stamp <= c1.time_stamp + INTERVAL 24 HOUR;

▼

Return followers who themselves have at least one follower, with their follower count.

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A social-graph team builds a "power users" list — users whose followers are followed by others too.

▶ 1 Semi-Join + Aggregate
SELECT f.follower AS follower, COUNT(DISTINCT f2.follower) AS num FROM Follow f JOIN Follow f2 ON f2.followee = f.follower GROUP BY f.follower ORDER BY f.follower;
