Medium #2783 Flight Occupancy and Waitlist Analysis

▼

For each flight, return booked count and waitlist count based on capacity.

Tables: Flights (flight_id, capacity), Passengers (passenger_id, flight_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

An airline ops team monitors waitlist overflow per flight to trigger capacity-upgrade or rebooking workflows.

▶ 1 Per-Flight COUNT + LEAST / Minus
SELECT f.flight_id, LEAST(COUNT(p.passenger_id), f.capacity) AS booked_cnt, GREATEST(COUNT(p.passenger_id) - f.capacity, 0) AS waitlist_cnt FROM Flights f LEFT JOIN Passengers p ON p.flight_id = f.flight_id GROUP BY f.flight_id, f.capacity;

Why this is best: LEAST and GREATEST express the capacity clip in one aggregate pass.

Performance: One join + one aggregate.

SUM / AVG / MIN / MAX per group 13 problems

▼

Standard numeric aggregations of a joined column. The trap is multi-join double-counting: if you JOIN two child tables to a parent before aggregating, the SUMs balloon by a factor. Aggregate each child separately in a CTE, then join the totals.

#1075 — Project Employees I

Easy
▼

Report average experience years for employees on each project, rounded to 2 decimals.

Problem: Report average experience years for employees on each project, rounded to 2 decimals.

Tables: Project (project_id, employee_id) and Employee (employee_id, name, experience_years)

Decision Tree Path

JOIN + GROUP BY aggregation. INNER JOIN connects projects to employees, then aggregate experience per project.

Real-World Example

Resource management calculating average team seniority per project to assess project complexity or team strength.

▶ 1 Most Efficient — INNER JOIN + GROUP BY + ROUND
SELECT p.project_id, ROUND(AVG(e.experience_years), 2) AS average_years FROM Project p INNER JOIN Employee e ON p.employee_id = e.employee_id GROUP BY p.project_id;

Why this is best: INNER JOIN merges projects and employees. GROUP BY aggregates by project. ROUND ensures 2 decimal precision.

Performance: O(n log n) due to GROUP BY. Index on Employee.employee_id and Project.project_id speeds join.

▶ 2 Alternative — CAST for Decimal Precision
SELECT p.project_id, CAST(AVG(e.experience_years) AS DECIMAL(10, 2)) AS average_years FROM Project p INNER JOIN Employee e ON p.employee_id = e.employee_id GROUP BY p.project_id;

Why this works: CAST to DECIMAL(10, 2) guarantees output type. Useful if you need exact decimal type downstream.

Difference: ROUND is simpler for display; CAST is stricter for storage or type requirements.

#1251 Average Selling Price (Easy)

▼

E-commerce teams compute average realized price to track how time-varying price tiers impact revenue. Differs from list price due to volume discounts and promotions.

Schema: Prices(product_id, start_date, end_date, price), UnitsSold(product_id, purchase_date, units)

Join purchases to prices (using BETWEEN start_date and end_date). Calculate weighted average: SUM(price * units) / SUM(units) per product. Round to 2 decimals.

Business Context: Pricing Analytics

E-commerce teams compute average realized price to track how time-varying price tiers impact revenue. Differs from list price due to volume discounts and promotions.

▶ Rank 1: JOIN with BETWEEN Explicit range matching
SELECT u.product_id, ROUND( SUM(p.price * u.units) * 1.0 / SUM(u.units), 2 ) AS average_price FROM UnitsSold u INNER JOIN Prices p ON u.product_id = p.product_id AND u.purchase_date BETWEEN p.start_date AND p.end_date GROUP BY u.product_id;

Why this ranks first: BETWEEN is clear and efficient if start_date/end_date are indexed. INNER JOIN excludes products with no sales. Weighted average formula is standard. Clean one-pass aggregation.

▶ Rank 2: Subquery for Price Lookup Isolates price logic
SELECT u.product_id, ROUND( SUM(u.units * ( SELECT price FROM Prices p WHERE p.product_id = u.product_id AND u.purchase_date BETWEEN p.start_date AND p.end_date LIMIT 1 )) * 1.0 / SUM(u.units), 2 ) AS average_price FROM UnitsSold u GROUP BY u.product_id;

Tradeoff: Correlated subquery in SELECT per row. Assumes one price per product-date (guaranteed by problem statement). Less efficient for large UnitsSold but more compact.

▶ Rank 3: LEFT JOIN (All Products) For products with zero sales
SELECT COALESCE(u.product_id, p.product_id) AS product_id, ROUND( COALESCE(SUM(p.price * u.units), 0) * 1.0 / NULLIF(SUM(u.units), 0), 2 ) AS average_price FROM Prices p LEFT JOIN UnitsSold u ON p.product_id = u.product_id AND u.purchase_date BETWEEN p.start_date AND p.end_date GROUP BY COALESCE(u.product_id, p.product_id);

Tradeoff: LEFT JOIN includes products with no sales (returns 0 or NULL). Problem says "assume 0" for no sales, but INNER JOIN (Rank 1) is simpler. Use if you need all products listed.

JOIN with BETWEEN vs. Correlated Subquery

BETWEEN JOIN (Rank 1) is O(n log m) with indexes on (product_id, start_date, end_date). Correlated subquery (Rank 2) is O(n * m) if subquery can't use index. For millions of unit sales, JOIN wins. BETWEEN is also more database-optimizer-friendly.

Hard #615 Average Salary: Departments VS Company

▼

For each (month, department), report whether its average salary is higher, lower, or equal to the company average.

Tables: Salary (id, employee_id, amount, pay_date), Employee (employee_id, department_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

Comp benchmarks per dept are a monthly executive review input. This query delivers the directional label for dashboard annotations.

▶ 1 Dual Aggregates Joined for Comparison
WITH comp AS ( SELECT DATE_FORMAT(pay_date, '%Y-%m') AS ym, AVG(amount) AS company_avg FROM Salary GROUP BY ym ), dept AS ( SELECT DATE_FORMAT(s.pay_date, '%Y-%m') AS ym, e.department_id, AVG(s.amount) AS dept_avg FROM Salary s JOIN Employee e ON e.employee_id = s.employee_id GROUP BY ym, e.department_id ) SELECT d.ym AS pay_month, d.department_id, CASE WHEN d.dept_avg > c.company_avg THEN 'higher' WHEN d.dept_avg < c.company_avg THEN 'lower' ELSE 'same' END AS comparison FROM dept d JOIN comp c ON c.ym = d.ym;

Why this is best: Two independent aggregates joined on month give a clean comparison row per (month, department).

Performance: Two aggregates + one join.

Medium #1132 Reported Posts II

▼

Average daily removal rate for spam reports over distinct report days.

Tables: Actions (user_id, post_id, action_date, action, extra), Removals (post_id, remove_date)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A content mod team evaluates how effective their spam-handling pipeline is by reporting daily removal rate averaged across operating days.

▶ 1 Per-Day Rate Then AVG
WITH daily AS ( SELECT a.action_date, COUNT(DISTINCT a.post_id) AS reported, COUNT(DISTINCT r.post_id) AS removed FROM Actions a LEFT JOIN Removals r ON r.post_id = a.post_id WHERE a.extra = 'spam' AND a.action = 'report' GROUP BY a.action_date ) SELECT ROUND(AVG(removed / reported) * 100, 2) AS average_daily_percent FROM daily WHERE reported > 0;

Why this is best: Daily rate first, then average-of-averages gives the correct KPI definition.

Performance: Two aggregates.

Easy #1677 Product’s Worth Over Invoices

▼

For each product, return total rest, paid, canceled, and refunded amounts.

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Finance reconciliation shows per-product status totals for billing dashboards.

Why this is best: One GROUP BY produces all four totals per product.

Hard #1635 Hopper Company Queries I

▼

For each month in 2020, count active drivers and completed accepted rides.

Tables: Drivers (driver_id, join_date), Rides (ride_id, user_id, requested_at), AcceptedRides (ride_id, driver_id, ride_distance, ride_duration)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A rideshare ops report publishes monthly supply-side KPIs to the executive team.

▶ 1 Calendar CTE + Aggregate Joins
WITH months AS ( SELECT 1 AS m UNION ALL SELECT 2 UNION ALL SELECT 3 UNION ALL SELECT 4 UNION ALL SELECT 5 UNION ALL SELECT 6 UNION ALL SELECT 7 UNION ALL SELECT 8 UNION ALL SELECT 9 UNION ALL SELECT 10 UNION ALL SELECT 11 UNION ALL SELECT 12 ) SELECT m.m AS month, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Drivers d WHERE d.join_date <= DATE_ADD('2020-01-01', INTERVAL m.m MONTH) - INTERVAL 1 DAY) AS active_drivers, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM AcceptedRides ar JOIN Rides r ON r.ride_id = ar.ride_id WHERE YEAR(r.requested_at) = 2020 AND MONTH(r.requested_at) = m.m) AS accepted_rides FROM months m;

Why this is best: Anchor to a month calendar so every month appears, even zero-activity ones.

Performance: 12 iterations * aggregate per month. Small and fast.

Hard #1645 Hopper Company Queries II

▼

For each 2020 month, report percent of drivers working at least once (2 decimals).

Tables: Drivers (driver_id, join_date), Rides (ride_id, user_id, requested_at), AcceptedRides (ride_id, driver_id, ...)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A driver retention PM measures working-active-driver share per month to size the driver engagement strategy.

▶ 1 Active Drivers + Working Drivers Ratio
WITH months AS ( SELECT 1 AS m UNION ALL SELECT 2 UNION ALL SELECT 3 UNION ALL SELECT 4 UNION ALL SELECT 5 UNION ALL SELECT 6 UNION ALL SELECT 7 UNION ALL SELECT 8 UNION ALL SELECT 9 UNION ALL SELECT 10 UNION ALL SELECT 11 UNION ALL SELECT 12 ) SELECT m.m AS month, IFNULL(ROUND( 100.0 * ( SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT ar.driver_id) FROM AcceptedRides ar JOIN Rides r ON r.ride_id = ar.ride_id WHERE YEAR(r.requested_at) = 2020 AND MONTH(r.requested_at) = m.m ) / NULLIF(( SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Drivers WHERE join_date <= DATE_ADD('2020-01-01', INTERVAL m.m MONTH) - INTERVAL 1 DAY ), 0), 2), 0.00) AS working_percentage FROM months m;

Why this is best: Divide distinct working drivers in month by cumulative joined drivers by that month.

Performance: 12 * two aggregates.

Hard #1651 Hopper Company Queries III

▼

For each month m=1..12 in 2020, report the average ride_distance and ride_duration over the next 3 months.

Tables: Rides (ride_id, user_id, requested_at), AcceptedRides (ride_id, driver_id, ride_distance, ride_duration)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

Leadership reviews a rolling 3-month operational forecast to stabilize capacity planning.

▶ 1 Calendar + Range Filter per Bucket
WITH months AS ( SELECT 1 AS m UNION ALL SELECT 2 UNION ALL SELECT 3 UNION ALL SELECT 4 UNION ALL SELECT 5 UNION ALL SELECT 6 UNION ALL SELECT 7 UNION ALL SELECT 8 UNION ALL SELECT 9 UNION ALL SELECT 10 ) SELECT m.m AS month, ROUND(AVG(ar.ride_distance), 2) AS average_ride_distance, ROUND(AVG(ar.ride_duration), 2) AS average_ride_duration FROM months m LEFT JOIN Rides r ON YEAR(r.requested_at) = 2020 AND MONTH(r.requested_at) BETWEEN m.m AND m.m + 2 LEFT JOIN AcceptedRides ar ON ar.ride_id = r.ride_id GROUP BY m.m;

Why this is best: The 3-month bucket is implemented as a range filter on the join condition.

Performance: Calendar is tiny; joins filtered.

Medium #1555 Bank Account Summary

▼

Compute running balance per user and flag negatives.

Tables: Users (user_id, user_name, credit), Transactions (trans_id, paid_by, paid_to, amount, transacted_on)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A P2P payment app shows each wallet the final balance; negative balances gate spending.

▶ 1 Signed Per-User Sums Joined to Users
WITH flows AS ( SELECT paid_by AS user_id, -amount AS amt FROM Transactions UNION ALL SELECT paid_to, amount FROM Transactions ) SELECT u.user_id, u.user_name, u.credit + COALESCE(SUM(f.amt), 0) AS credit, IF(u.credit + COALESCE(SUM(f.amt), 0) < 0, 'Yes', 'No') AS credit_limit_breached FROM Users u LEFT JOIN flows f ON f.user_id = u.user_id GROUP BY u.user_id, u.user_name, u.credit;

Why this is best: Normalize debits and credits into one column, sum per user, add initial credit.

Performance: One aggregate + one join.

Medium #2372 Calculate the Influence of Each Salesperson

▼

Return each salesperson with total sales handled by their customers.

Tables: Salesperson (salesperson_id, name), Customer (customer_id, salesperson_id), Sales (sale_id, customer_id, price)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A compensation analyst computes book-of-business sales per rep to inform bonus payouts.

▶ 1 Chain Join + Sum
SELECT sp.salesperson_id, sp.name, COALESCE(SUM(s.price), 0) AS total FROM Salesperson sp LEFT JOIN Customer c ON c.salesperson_id = sp.salesperson_id LEFT JOIN Sales s ON s.customer_id = c.customer_id GROUP BY sp.salesperson_id, sp.name;

Why this is best: Left-join chain keeps reps without customers and customers without sales.

Performance: Two joins + one aggregate.

Easy #2837 Total Traveled Distance

▼

For each user, total kilometers travelled (0 when no rides).

Tables: Users (user_id, user_name), Rides (user_id, distance)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A car-share platform shows total kilometers each member has logged, with zero-travel members still displayed.

▶ 1 LEFT JOIN + COALESCE SUM
SELECT u.user_id, u.user_name, CONCAT(COALESCE(SUM(r.distance), 0), ' km') AS traveled_distance FROM Users u LEFT JOIN Rides r ON r.user_id = u.user_id GROUP BY u.user_id, u.user_name ORDER BY u.user_id;

Why this is best: Standard non-destructive aggregation with zero default.

Performance: One join + one aggregate.

Rate / ratio / percentage 5 problems

▼

Numerator and denominator both come from a join. Build each as a separate CTE (or as SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) in one pass) and divide. Cast at least one side to NUMERIC to avoid integer division; NULLIF the denominator to avoid divide-by-zero.

#1934 Confirmation Rate (Medium)

▼

User onboarding tracks how many signups complete email/SMS confirmation. High confirmation rates indicate a smooth signup flow; low rates indicate friction or user churn.

Schema: Signups(user_id, time_stamp), Confirmations(user_id, time_stamp, action='confirmed'|'timeout')

For each user, calculate confirmation_rate = COUNT(action='confirmed') / COUNT(*). If no confirmations, return 0.00. Rounded to 2 decimals.

Business Context: Onboarding Funnel Analysis

User onboarding tracks how many signups complete email/SMS confirmation. High confirmation rates indicate a smooth signup flow; low rates indicate friction or user churn.

▶ Rank 1: LEFT JOIN + Conditional Aggregation Includes users with 0 confirmations
SELECT s.user_id, ROUND( COALESCE( COUNT(CASE WHEN c.action = 'confirmed' THEN 1 END) * 1.0 / NULLIF(COUNT(c.user_id), 0), 0 ), 2 ) AS confirmation_rate FROM Signups s LEFT JOIN Confirmations c ON s.user_id = c.user_id GROUP BY s.user_id ORDER BY s.user_id;

Why this ranks first: LEFT JOIN ensures all signups appear, even those with no confirmations. CASE WHEN counts confirmed only. NULLIF turns 0 into NULL so division yields NULL, then COALESCE converts that NULL to 0. This ensures users with zero confirmations get 0.00 instead of NULL.

▶ Rank 2: Subqueries in SELECT Simpler for small datasets
SELECT s.user_id, ROUND( COALESCE( (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Confirmations c1 WHERE c1.user_id = s.user_id AND c1.action = 'confirmed') * 1.0 / NULLIF( (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Confirmations c2 WHERE c2.user_id = s.user_id), 0 ), 0 ), 2 ) AS confirmation_rate FROM Signups s;

Tradeoff: Two correlated subqueries per user (count confirmed, count total). More readable logic but slower on large Signups tables. Better for <10k users.

▶ Rank 3: RIGHT JOIN with Manual UNION Handles users with 0 confirmations differently
SELECT user_id, 0.00 AS confirmation_rate FROM Signups WHERE user_id NOT IN (SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM Confirmations) UNION ALL SELECT s.user_id, ROUND( COUNT(CASE WHEN c.action = 'confirmed' THEN 1 END) * 1.0 / COUNT(*), 2 ) FROM Signups s INNER JOIN Confirmations c ON s.user_id = c.user_id GROUP BY s.user_id;

Tradeoff: Splits logic into two queries (users with zero confirmations get 0.00, users with confirmations calculated). UNION combines. Verbose but explicit handling of edge case.

LEFT JOIN vs. Correlated Subqueries

LEFT JOIN (Rank 1) scans Signups and Confirmations once each. Correlated subqueries (Rank 2) run the confirmation counts for each signup row. For 100k signups, JOIN wins. The UNION approach (Rank 3) requires two table scans and a NOT IN (slower). Prefer Rank 1.

#550 Game Play Analysis IV (Medium)

▼

Day-1 retention is critical for game/app success. If 30% of new users return the next day, the game has traction. Track this weekly to measure changes in user engagement.

📌
Pattern: Find First Date, Then Check Day+1

Use ROW_NUMBER() or MIN() to find first login date per player, then check if player logged in the next day. Business: Gaming/SaaS measuring Day-1 retention rate.

Business Context
Day-1 retention is critical for game/app success. If 30% of new users return the next day, the game has traction. Track this weekly to measure changes in user engagement.
▶ Rank 1: Window Function (ROW_NUMBER) + Self-Join Most efficient grouping approach
SELECT ROUND( COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN second_login THEN player_id END)::NUMERIC / COUNT(DISTINCT player_id), 2 ) AS fraction FROM ( SELECT player_id, event_date, LEAD(event_date) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY event_date) AS next_event_date, LEAD(event_date) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY event_date) = event_date + INTERVAL '1 day' AS second_login FROM Activity ) t;

Performance Analysis: Window function scans Activity once, O(n). PARTITION BY player_id requires sort: O(n log n). LEAD() looks ahead one row: O(1) per row. Memory: O(n) for sort. Final aggregation: O(unique_players). Can use index on (player_id, event_date) to optimize partition.

Why Rank 1: Single scan with efficient window computation. Avoids self-join overhead.

▶ Rank 2: Subquery with MIN + Self-Join More joins, explicit logic
WITH first_login AS ( SELECT player_id, MIN(event_date) AS first_date FROM Activity GROUP BY player_id ) SELECT ROUND( COUNT(DISTINCT a.player_id)::NUMERIC / COUNT(DISTINCT f.player_id), 2 ) AS fraction FROM first_login f LEFT JOIN Activity a ON f.player_id = a.player_id AND a.event_date = f.first_date + INTERVAL '1 day';

Performance Analysis: GROUP BY for MIN: O(n). JOIN: hash join on player_id. For each player, checks if day+1 exists: O(n) worst case. With index on (player_id, event_date), seeks become O(log n). Total: O(n + unique_players * log n) vs window O(n log n).

Why Rank 2: Slightly cleaner logic for some, but requires JOIN which adds overhead vs window function approach.

Hard #2720 Popularity Percentage

▼

For each user, compute share of users who are friends with them (undirected).

Tables: Friends (user1, user2)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A community analyst publishes a "reach score" per user — what share of the user base is connected to them.

▶ 1 Bidirectional Expansion + Normalized Share
WITH f AS ( SELECT user1 AS u, user2 AS v FROM Friends UNION SELECT user2, user1 FROM Friends ), all_users AS ( SELECT DISTINCT u AS uid FROM f UNION SELECT DISTINCT v FROM f ) SELECT u.uid AS user1, ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT f.v) / NULLIF((SELECT COUNT(*) FROM all_users) - 1, 0), 2) AS percentage_popularity FROM all_users u LEFT JOIN f ON f.u = u.uid GROUP BY u.uid ORDER BY u.uid;

Why this is best: Normalize undirected edges once, then compute reach per user against the total user count.

Performance: Two aggregates + one join.

Medium #2989 Class Performance

▼

Compute per-student best vs worst score difference across three assignments.

Tables: Scores (student_id, student_name, assignment1, assignment2, assignment3)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A teacher evaluates consistency by comparing each student's high and low assignment scores.

▶ 1 GREATEST/LEAST Per Row
SELECT student_id, student_name, (assignment1 + assignment2 + assignment3) AS total_score, GREATEST(assignment1, assignment2, assignment3) - LEAST(assignment1, assignment2, assignment3) AS difference_score FROM Scores ORDER BY total_score DESC;

Why this is best: Row-level GREATEST/LEAST avoid an unpivot.

Performance: One pass.

Hard #262 Trips and Users

▼

Daily cancellation rate on trips involving non-banned users, for Oct 1-3, 2013.

Tables: Trips (id, client_id, driver_id, city_id, status, request_at), Users (users_id, banned, role)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A ride-sharing ops team reports daily cancellation rate, excluding banned rider/driver activity to avoid polluting the KPI.

▶ 1 Filter Unbanned + Conditional AVG
SELECT t.request_at AS Day, ROUND(AVG(t.status <> 'completed'), 2) AS 'Cancellation Rate' FROM Trips t JOIN Users c ON c.users_id = t.client_id AND c.banned = 'No' JOIN Users d ON d.users_id = t.driver_id AND d.banned = 'No' WHERE t.request_at BETWEEN '2013-10-01' AND '2013-10-03' GROUP BY t.request_at;

Why this is best: Join-as-filter removes banned participants; boolean mean gives the cancellation share.

Performance: Two joins + one aggregate.

Aggregate + filter (HAVING / conditional CASE) 13 problems

▼

The aggregate is the filter or the filter sits inside the aggregate. HAVING keeps groups whose totals meet a cutoff (bought all products, friends in common ≥ N); SUM(CASE WHEN ...) conditional aggregation counts only the rows that match a predicate per group.

Medium #1045 Customers Who Bought All Products

▼

Find customer IDs who purchased all products in the catalog. This is a relational division problem: customer_id where COUNT(DISTINCT product_key) = total products.

Tables: Customer (customer_id, product_key) and Product (product_key)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern K: Relational Division

Real-World Example

Loyalty program identifies VIP customers who purchased every product in the catalog (or category). These customers qualify for exclusive rewards or early access to new products.

▶ 1 GROUP BY with HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT product_key)
SELECT customer_id FROM Customer GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT product_key) = ( SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Product );

Why this is best: Relational division classic pattern. GROUP BY customer, count distinct products per customer, filter to those matching the total product count. One subquery for cardinality.

Performance: O(n log n) for GROUP BY + COUNT DISTINCT. Subquery executes once (result cached). Indexes on (customer_id, product_key) critical.

▶ 2 GROUP BY with Join to Product Count
SELECT c.customer_id FROM Customer c CROSS JOIN ( SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_products FROM Product ) p GROUP BY c.customer_id, p.total_products HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c.product_key) = p.total_products;

Why this works: Cross join brings product count into every row. GROUP BY includes both customer_id and total_products (to allow reference in HAVING). Equivalent to approach #1 but more explicit.

Performance: Cross join adds minimal cost (single row). GROUP BY with two columns. Marginally slower than approach #1 but more readable for some teams.

▶ 3 NOT EXISTS (Anti-Pattern, Less Efficient)
SELECT DISTINCT c.customer_id FROM Customer c WHERE NOT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM Product p WHERE NOT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM Customer c2 WHERE c2.customer_id = c.customer_id AND c2.product_key = p.product_key ) );

Why this works: Nested NOT EXISTS: for each customer, check that no product exists without that customer having bought it. Classic division logic, but complex SQL.

Performance: Nested subqueries execute per row (O(n³) worst case). Much slower than approach #1. Use only for demonstration or very small datasets.

Caveat: Hard to read, debug, and optimize. Not recommended for production.

#585 Investments in 2016 (Medium)

▼

Insurers filter policies by risk pool (tiv_2015) and geographic diversity (unique locations) to compute total insurable value for correlated risk exposure.

Schema: Insurance(pid, tiv_2015, tiv_2016, lat, lon)

Sum tiv_2016 for all policies where: (1) tiv_2015 is shared with at least one other policy (HAVING COUNT > 1), AND (2) location (lat, lon) is unique (HAVING COUNT = 1). Round to 2 decimals.

Business Context: Insurance Portfolio Risk Analysis

Insurers filter policies by risk pool (tiv_2015) and geographic diversity (unique locations) to compute total insurable value for correlated risk exposure.

▶ Rank 1: Two Subqueries in WHERE Uncorrelated, clear intent
SELECT ROUND(SUM(tiv_2016), 2) AS tiv_2016 FROM Insurance WHERE tiv_2015 IN ( SELECT tiv_2015 FROM Insurance GROUP BY tiv_2015 HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ) AND (lat, lon) IN ( SELECT lat, lon FROM Insurance GROUP BY lat, lon HAVING COUNT(*) = 1 );

Why this ranks first: Two uncorrelated subqueries clearly separate the two conditions. First finds shared tiv_2015 values. Second finds unique locations. WHERE filters to policies matching both. Single pass through Insurance.

▶ Rank 2: Window Functions with CTE PostgreSQL 12+ alternative
WITH counted AS ( SELECT *, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY tiv_2015) AS tiv_count, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY lat, lon) AS loc_count FROM Insurance ) SELECT ROUND(SUM(tiv_2016), 2) AS tiv_2016 FROM counted WHERE tiv_count > 1 AND loc_count = 1;

Tradeoff: Window functions compute counts in a single pass. More efficient for large tables. Single CTE provides both aggregations without separate table scans. Modern databases optimize window functions well.

▶ Rank 3: Self-Joins with HAVING Traditional approach (no window functions)
SELECT ROUND(SUM(i.tiv_2016), 2) AS tiv_2016 FROM Insurance i WHERE ( SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Insurance i2 WHERE i2.tiv_2015 = i.tiv_2015 ) > 1 AND ( SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Insurance i3 WHERE i3.lat = i.lat AND i3.lon = i.lon ) = 1;

Tradeoff: Two correlated subqueries per row. O(n²) performance. Easier to read logic but slower on large tables. Avoid for 10k+ policies.

Uncorrelated Subqueries vs. Window Functions vs. Correlated

Rank 1 runs two GROUP BY subqueries once each (uncorrelated). Rank 2 scans Insurance once with window aggregations (best for large tables). Rank 3 runs two subqueries per row (slowest). For insurance portfolios with 100k+ policies, Rank 2 window function is typically 10-50x faster.

Medium #1212 Team Scores in Football Tournament

▼

Return each team with total points, sorted descending by points then team_id.

Tables: Teams (team_id, team_name), Matches (match_id, host_team, guest_team, host_goals, guest_goals)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A sports portal renders a live league standings table from match results.

▶ 1 Home/Away Normalization + Score
WITH scored AS ( SELECT host_team AS team_id, CASE WHEN host_goals > guest_goals THEN 3 WHEN host_goals = guest_goals THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS pts FROM Matches UNION ALL SELECT guest_team, CASE WHEN guest_goals > host_goals THEN 3 WHEN guest_goals = host_goals THEN 1 ELSE 0 END FROM Matches ) SELECT t.team_id, t.team_name, COALESCE(SUM(s.pts), 0) AS num_points FROM Teams t LEFT JOIN scored s ON s.team_id = t.team_id GROUP BY t.team_id, t.team_name ORDER BY num_points DESC, t.team_id;

Why this is best: Normalize host/away rows into a common schema for a single aggregate.

Performance: Two passes of Matches.

Medium #1949 Strong Friendship

▼

Pairs of friends with at least three common friends.

Tables: Friendship (user1_id, user2_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A community ops team highlights tightly-clustered friend pairs — often a strong community anchor.

▶ 1 Normalize + Common Friend Count
WITH f AS ( SELECT user1_id AS u, user2_id AS v FROM Friendship UNION ALL SELECT user2_id, user1_id FROM Friendship ) SELECT a.u AS user1_id, a.v AS user2_id, COUNT(*) AS common_friend FROM f a JOIN f b ON b.u = a.v AND b.v <> a.u JOIN f c ON c.u = b.v AND c.v = a.u WHERE a.u < a.v GROUP BY a.u, a.v HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;

Why this is best: Normalize friendship to bidirectional; chain three edges to count common friends per pair.

Performance: Graph walk; fine for thousands of nodes.

Medium #2922 Market Analysis III

▼

Return sellers whose very first sold item brand equals their favorite brand.

Tables: Users (user_id, join_date, favorite_brand), Orders (order_id, order_date, item_id, buyer_id, seller_id), Items (item_id, item_brand)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

An onboarding report surfaces sellers whose first sale matches their stated favorite brand — a sign of fit.

▶ 1 First-Order Rank + Brand Match
WITH ranked AS ( SELECT o.seller_id, o.item_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY o.seller_id ORDER BY o.order_date) AS rn FROM Orders o ) SELECT u.user_id AS seller_id FROM Users u JOIN ranked r ON r.seller_id = u.user_id AND r.rn = 1 JOIN Items i ON i.item_id = r.item_id WHERE i.item_brand = u.favorite_brand;

Why this is best: Standard "first row per group + compare" pattern.

Performance: One window + two joins.

Hard #1917 Leetcodify Friends Recommendations

▼

Recommend users who listened to >=3 songs on the same day, and aren't already friends.

Tables: Listens (user_id, song_id, day), Friendship (user1_id, user2_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A music app recommends friends who share >=3 tracks per day — a soft interest-similarity signal.

▶ 1 Same-Day Co-Listen + Threshold
WITH co AS ( SELECT a.user_id AS u1, b.user_id AS u2, a.day, a.song_id FROM Listens a JOIN Listens b ON a.song_id = b.song_id AND a.day = b.day AND a.user_id < b.user_id ), pairs AS ( SELECT u1, u2, COUNT(DISTINCT song_id) AS shared FROM co GROUP BY u1, u2, day HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT song_id) >= 3 ) SELECT u1 AS user1_id, u2 AS user2_id FROM pairs WHERE NOT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM Friendship f WHERE (f.user1_id = pairs.u1 AND f.user2_id = pairs.u2) OR (f.user1_id = pairs.u2 AND f.user2_id = pairs.u1) );

Why this is best: Self-join on shared song same day; threshold on DISTINCT song count; anti-join to existing friendships.

Performance: Self-join is O(n^2) worst case; filter by day first.

Hard #1919 Leetcodify Similar Friends

▼

Same same-day-3-song pattern as 1917 but restricted to already-friends.

Tables: Listens (user_id, song_id, day), Friendship (user1_id, user2_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A music app flags "similar" friends for collaborative playlists.

▶ 1 Restrict Co-Listens to Existing Friendships
SELECT DISTINCT f.user1_id, f.user2_id FROM Friendship f JOIN Listens a ON a.user_id = f.user1_id JOIN Listens b ON b.user_id = f.user2_id AND a.song_id = b.song_id AND a.day = b.day GROUP BY f.user1_id, f.user2_id, a.day HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT a.song_id) >= 3;

Why this is best: Join both sides of existing friendship to Listens and impose the 3-song threshold.

Performance: Limited by friendship size.

Medium #1501 Countries You Can Safely Invest In

▼

Return countries whose average call duration exceeds the global average.

Tables: Person (id, name, phone_number), Country (name, country_code), Calls (caller_id, callee_id, duration)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A telco rates countries for investment by comparing average call duration (a proxy for engagement) to the global mean.

▶ 1 Country AVG vs Global AVG
WITH lined AS ( SELECT p.id, SUBSTRING(p.phone_number,1,3) AS code FROM Person p ), durations AS ( SELECT lined.code, c.duration FROM Calls c JOIN lined ON lined.id = c.caller_id UNION ALL SELECT lined.code, c.duration FROM Calls c JOIN lined ON lined.id = c.callee_id ) SELECT co.name AS country FROM durations d JOIN Country co ON co.country_code = d.code GROUP BY co.name HAVING AVG(d.duration) > (SELECT AVG(duration) FROM Calls);

Why this is best: Normalize caller/callee, join country, then average-per-country against the global benchmark in HAVING.

Performance: Two aggregates + one join.

Hard #1892 Page Recommendations II

▼

For each user, recommend pages liked by a threshold count of their friends.

Tables: Friendship (user1_id, user2_id), Likes (user_id, page_id)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A social product improves on basic page recommendations by weighting recommendations by number of friends liking the page.

▶ 1 Friends Expansion + Aggregate per Page
WITH friends AS ( SELECT user1_id AS u, user2_id AS f FROM Friendship UNION ALL SELECT user2_id, user1_id FROM Friendship ) SELECT f.u AS user_id, l.page_id, COUNT(DISTINCT f.f) AS friends_likes FROM friends f JOIN Likes l ON l.user_id = f.f WHERE NOT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM Likes lk WHERE lk.user_id = f.u AND lk.page_id = l.page_id ) GROUP BY f.u, l.page_id ORDER BY f.u, friends_likes DESC, l.page_id;

Why this is best: Bidirectional friendship expansion + anti-join to user's own likes + friend count per page.

Performance: One aggregate + two joins.

Hard #2995 Viewers Turned Streamers

▼

Users who first appeared as viewers and later started streaming, with count of streams.

Tables: Sessions (user_id, session_start, session_type)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A video platform studies the viewer-to-creator conversion funnel.

▶ 1 First Session Type + Later Stream Count
WITH firsts AS ( SELECT user_id, session_type AS first_type, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY session_start) AS rn FROM Sessions ) SELECT s.user_id, COUNT(*) AS sessions_count FROM firsts f JOIN Sessions s ON s.user_id = f.user_id AND s.session_type = 'Streamer' WHERE f.rn = 1 AND f.first_type = 'Viewer' GROUP BY s.user_id ORDER BY sessions_count DESC, s.user_id DESC;

Why this is best: Identify users whose very first session was Viewer, then count later Streamer sessions.

Performance: One window + one join + one aggregate.

Hard #1159 Market Analysis II

▼

Flag sellers whose 2nd-ever sale was the user's favorite-brand item.

Tables: Users (user_id, join_date, favorite_brand), Orders (order_id, order_date, item_id, buyer_id, seller_id), Items (item_id, item_brand)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

An onboarding analyst checks whether a seller's second sale involves buyers' favorite brand, which often predicts lifetime engagement.

▶ 1 Rank Seller Orders + Join Brand
WITH ranked AS ( SELECT o.seller_id, o.item_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY o.seller_id ORDER BY o.order_date) AS rn FROM Orders o ) SELECT u.user_id AS seller_id, IF(u.favorite_brand = i.item_brand, 'yes', 'no') AS 2nd_item_fav_brand FROM Users u LEFT JOIN ranked r ON r.seller_id = u.user_id AND r.rn = 2 LEFT JOIN Items i ON i.item_id = r.item_id;

Why this is best: ROW_NUMBER isolates the second order per seller; brand is looked up and compared.

Performance: One window + two joins.

▶ 2 Conditional Aggregation on Ranked Base
WITH base AS ( SELECT u.user_id AS seller_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY u.user_id ORDER BY o.order_date ASC) AS order_rn, o.order_id, o.order_date, o.item_id, u.favorite_brand, i.item_brand, CASE WHEN u.favorite_brand = i.item_brand THEN 'yes' ELSE 'no' END AS item_fav_brand FROM Users AS u LEFT JOIN Orders AS o ON u.user_id = o.seller_id LEFT JOIN Items AS i ON i.item_id = o.item_id ) SELECT seller_id, COALESCE(MAX(CASE WHEN order_rn = 2 THEN item_fav_brand END), 'no') AS "2nd_item_fav_brand" FROM base GROUP BY seller_id ORDER BY seller_id;

Why this works: The base CTE attaches the rn flag and the brand match to every order row. The outer GROUP BY collapses each seller; MAX(CASE WHEN order_rn = 2 THEN item_fav_brand END) picks up the rn=2 row's flag (NULL otherwise) and COALESCE defaults to 'no' for sellers with fewer than two orders.

Pattern to keep: "per group, return the value of column X on the row where condition Y" → MAX(CASE WHEN Y THEN X END) over a partitioned base, with COALESCE for the missing-row default. No second pass, no UNION.

Note on column quoting: identifiers that start with a digit (here 2nd_item_fav_brand) must be wrapped in double quotes or the parser reads them as a numeric literal.

Performance: One window + one GROUP BY. Comparable to Rank 1 in cost; trades two LEFT JOINs for one aggregate scan.

Easy #1294 Weather Type in Each Country

▼

Classify each country's Nov 2019 climate as Cold, Hot, or Warm based on average temperature.

Tables: Countries (country_id, country_name), Weather (country_id, weather_state, day)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A travel portal tags countries with a climate label to power destination filters.

▶ 1 Filtered AVG + CASE
SELECT c.country_name, CASE WHEN AVG(w.weather_state) <= 15 THEN 'Cold' WHEN AVG(w.weather_state) >= 25 THEN 'Hot' ELSE 'Warm' END AS weather_type FROM Countries c JOIN Weather w ON w.country_id = c.country_id WHERE w.day BETWEEN '2019-11-01' AND '2019-11-30' GROUP BY c.country_id, c.country_name;

Why this is best: Filter to November, aggregate per country, label via CASE.

Performance: One join + one aggregate.

Hard #2793 Status of Flight Tickets

▼

Label each passenger as Confirmed or Waitlist based on FIFO within flight capacity.

Tables: Flights (flight_id, capacity), Passengers (passenger_id, flight_id, booking_time)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

An airline issues ticket statuses in order of booking time up to capacity.

▶ 1 ROW_NUMBER vs Capacity
SELECT p.passenger_id, CASE WHEN rn <= f.capacity THEN 'Confirmed' ELSE 'Waitlist' END AS Status FROM ( SELECT passenger_id, flight_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY flight_id ORDER BY booking_time) AS rn FROM Passengers ) p JOIN Flights f ON f.flight_id = p.flight_id ORDER BY p.passenger_id;

Why this is best: Row number per flight combined with capacity cleanly splits Confirmed vs Waitlist.

Performance: One window + one join.

Date-window / cohort aggregate 3 problems

▼

The grouping key is a date bucket (DATE_TRUNC('month', signup_date)) or the data has to be reshaped against a calendar / signup spine before aggregating. Cohort retention and reorder-rate problems all live here. For problems where you must MANUFACTURE missing buckets (e.g. "every week including weeks with zero activity"), see Reshape → Series Generation — that recipe owns the generate_series spine + CROSS JOIN entities + LEFT JOIN actuals pattern.

#1327 — List the Products Ordered in a Period

Easy
▼

Find product names with at least 100 units ordered in February 2020, and show their total units.

Problem: Find product names with at least 100 units ordered in February 2020, and show their total units.

Tables: Products (product_id, product_name, product_category) and Orders (product_id, order_date, unit)

Decision Tree Path

JOIN + WHERE date filter + GROUP BY + HAVING. Classic date-range + aggregation pattern with join.

Real-World Example

Inventory management identifying high-demand products in a specific quarter to optimize stock replenishment and predict seasonal trends.

▶ 1 Most Efficient — INNER JOIN + DATE Filter + GROUP BY + HAVING
SELECT p.product_name, SUM(o.unit) AS unit FROM Products p INNER JOIN Orders o ON p.product_id = o.product_id WHERE o.order_date >= '2020-02-01' AND o.order_date < '2020-03-01' GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name HAVING SUM(o.unit) >= 100;

Why this is best: WHERE filters early (Feb 2020 only). GROUP BY aggregates units per product. HAVING filters groups with SUM >= 100. Minimal data processed.

Performance: O(n + m + k log k). Early WHERE filtering reduces data before join and aggregation. Index on order_date crucial.

▶ 2 Alternative — EXTRACT for Date Matching
SELECT p.product_name, SUM(o.unit) AS unit FROM Products p INNER JOIN Orders o ON p.product_id = o.product_id WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.order_date) = 2020 AND EXTRACT(MONTH FROM o.order_date) = 2 GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name HAVING SUM(o.unit) >= 100;

Why this works: EXTRACT is explicit about date components. Good for readability if checking specific month/year.

Caveat: Slightly slower than range comparison because EXTRACT can't use indexes as efficiently. Solution 1 preferred for performance.

Hard #1097 Game Play Analysis V

▼

For each install date, count day-1 retention: users who played on install date and also the next day.

Tables: Activity (player_id, device_id, event_date, games_played)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern E: Joins + Aggregation

Real-World Example

A growth analyst measures day-1 retention per install cohort — a foundational engagement KPI for LTV modeling.

▶ 1 Install Date CTE + Next-Day Self Join
WITH firsts AS ( SELECT player_id, MIN(event_date) AS install_date FROM Activity GROUP BY player_id ) SELECT f.install_date, COUNT(*) AS installs, ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN a.player_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 2) AS Day1_retention FROM firsts f LEFT JOIN Activity a ON a.player_id = f.player_id AND a.event_date = f.install_date + INTERVAL 1 DAY GROUP BY f.install_date ORDER BY f.install_date;

Why this is best: Install-date cohort + LEFT JOIN to the next day captures who returned; ratio gives D1 retention.

Performance: Two aggregates + one join.

Medium Monthly Ad Revenue by Cohort Month (DATE_TRUNC cohorts + join + aggregate)

▼

Bucket players into signup-month cohorts with DATE_TRUNC, join their sessions, and total ad revenue and distinct players per cohort.

Tables: players (player_id, username, signup_date), player_sessions (session_id, player_id, session_start, ad_impressions)

Real-World Example

A free-to-play game reports ad revenue by signup cohort to see which monthly intake of players monetizes best. Every player who signed up in a month belongs to that cohort, whether or not they have played a session yet.

Prompt: Group players into monthly signup cohorts (the first day of their signup month) and compute, per cohort, the count of distinct players and the total ad revenue from their sessions (each ad impression is worth $0.02). Output cohort_month (DATE), total_players, total_ad_revenue (NUMERIC(10,2)). Order by cohort_month ASC.

▶ 1 DATE_TRUNC cohort → LEFT JOIN sessions → aggregate per cohort
WITH cohort_sessions AS ( -- bucket each player into their signup-month cohort, SELECT -- then attach their sessions (LEFT JOIN keeps players DATE_TRUNC('month', p.signup_date)::date AS cohort_month, -- with no sessions) p.player_id, ps.ad_impressions * 0.02 AS ad_revenue FROM players AS p LEFT JOIN player_sessions AS ps ON ps.player_id = p.player_id ) SELECT cohort_month, COUNT(DISTINCT player_id) AS total_players, COALESCE(SUM(ad_revenue), 0)::numeric(10,2) AS total_ad_revenue FROM cohort_sessions GROUP BY cohort_month ORDER BY cohort_month;

Why this is best: DATE_TRUNC('month', signup_date)::date snaps every signup to the first of its month, which is the cohort key. Aggregating once over the joined rows gives both metrics in a single pass.

LEFT JOIN, not inner: total_players is the count of players who signed up that month, not the count who played. A player with zero sessions still belongs to the cohort, so the LEFT JOIN keeps them: they survive in COUNT(DISTINCT player_id) and their NULL revenue is ignored by SUM (with COALESCE covering an all-NULL cohort).

Two gotchas: COUNT(DISTINCT player_id), not COUNT(*) — a player has many sessions, so a plain count would tally sessions, not players. And the cohort comes from signup_date in players, never from session_start; bucketing the session timestamp would scatter one player across several cohorts.

Bought ALL of X, NONE of Y (set membership filter) 1 problem

▼

Filter entities whose set of related rows satisfies a membership rule: ALL of a required category set AND NONE of a forbidden category set. The technique is CASE inside an aggregate, used as a HAVING gate (existence flag per category), not as a SELECT projection. Sister leaf to filter by aggregate threshold: same CASE-in-aggregate family, but the test is presence/absence per category, not a numeric cutoff.

Easy Customers Who Bought A AND B but NOT C (set membership filter, conditional aggregation as HAVING gate)

▼

Recommend product C to customers who already bought A and B but never bought C. The pattern is the conditional aggregation family (CASE inside an aggregate) used as a HAVING gate with existence flags, NOT an arithmetic SUM across products. Misusing SUM here is the most common bug.

Tables: Customers (customer_id, customer_name), Orders (order_id, customer_id, product_name). A customer can appear in Orders multiple times; the same (customer_id, product_name) pair can repeat if a customer bought the product on different orders.

→

Decision Tree Path

Enrich Aggregate decision tree: Q1 grain = per customer → GROUP BY customer. Q2 NOT a numeric threshold (count / sum ≥ N), but a membership rule → this leaf. Q3 ALL of {A, B} required AND C forbidden → three independent existence flags combined with AND. Cross link: single table Rank & Percentile / Special for the related "set difference" framing via INTERSECT / EXCEPT.

Real World Example

Marketing wants a "next best product" recommendation list. Customers who already bought the entry tier products A and B but haven't yet bought the upsell C are the highest converting target. Sending the offer to a customer who already owns C wastes spend; missing customers who own A and B but not C wastes opportunity.

Build order — one flag per category, then AND them in HAVING:

  1. JOIN Customers to Orders on customer_id; group by customer.
  2. For each category that matters (A, B, C), compute an EXISTENCE FLAG: "did this customer ever buy product X" — a value of 1 if yes, 0 if no, regardless of HOW MANY times they bought it. Two Postgres idioms produce this flag: BOOL_OR(product_name = 'X') (returns true/false) or MAX(CASE WHEN product_name = 'X' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) (returns 1/0).
  3. Combine the flags in HAVING with AND: required categories must equal true / 1, forbidden categories must equal false / 0.
  4. SELECT customer_id and customer_name; ORDER BY customer_id.

Trace — flag values per customer on the example data:

customer orders bought A? bought B? bought C? qualify (A AND B AND NOT C)?
1 DanielA, B, D, C111no (bought C)
2 DianaA100no (missing B)
3 ElizabethA, B, D110yes
4 JhonC001no (missing A and B, has C)

Only Elizabeth meets all three independent conditions; a customer who bought A twice would still have bought A? = 1 because the flag is presence, not count.

▶ 1 BOOL_OR per category in HAVING (Postgres, most readable)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name FROM Customers AS c JOIN Orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.customer_name HAVING BOOL_OR(o.product_name = 'A') AND BOOL_OR(o.product_name = 'B') AND NOT BOOL_OR(o.product_name = 'C') ORDER BY c.customer_id;

Why this is best: BOOL_OR(expr) returns true if the boolean expression is true for ANY row in the group, false otherwise. Three independent checks, combined with AND in HAVING; no arithmetic across categories means no counting trap. INNER JOIN drops customers with no orders at all (correct, since they can't have bought A and B).

▶ 2 MAX(CASE) per category in HAVING (portable: works in any dialect)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name FROM Customers AS c JOIN Orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.customer_name HAVING MAX(CASE WHEN o.product_name = 'A' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 1 AND MAX(CASE WHEN o.product_name = 'B' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 1 AND MAX(CASE WHEN o.product_name = 'C' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 0 ORDER BY c.customer_id;

Why this is also good: Same logic, more verbose. MAX(CASE ...) works in MySQL, Redshift, Snowflake, BigQuery; BOOL_OR is Postgres native. Use this form when you need cross dialect portability.

▶ 3 Set operations: INTERSECT and EXCEPT (the "set algebra" framing)
WITH bought_a AS (SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM Orders WHERE product_name = 'A'), bought_b AS (SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM Orders WHERE product_name = 'B'), bought_c AS (SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM Orders WHERE product_name = 'C'), qualifies AS ( SELECT customer_id FROM bought_a INTERSECT SELECT customer_id FROM bought_b EXCEPT SELECT customer_id FROM bought_c ) SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name FROM Customers AS c JOIN qualifies AS q ON q.customer_id = c.customer_id ORDER BY c.customer_id;

Why this is also good: Same problem, different mental model. INTERSECT keeps only customer_ids present in BOTH bought_a and bought_b (the AND part); EXCEPT removes customer_ids present in bought_c (the NOT part). Reads like set algebra. Slightly more code than the HAVING form but maps 1:1 to the prompt phrasing.

Watch out: use UNION / INTERSECT / EXCEPT (set semantics, dedup automatically) NOT UNION ALL. The DISTINCT inside each CTE is technically redundant since INTERSECT / EXCEPT dedupe anyway; keep for readability.

Watch out — the counting trap that breaks the naive SUM approach:

  • Do NOT use SUM(CASE A→+1, B→+1, C→-1) = 2 as the gate. The arithmetic assumes each customer buys each product AT MOST ONCE. Hidden test data ALWAYS includes repeats. A customer who bought A twice and B once lands at SUM = 3 and is excluded incorrectly; a customer who bought A twice, B once, and C once lands at SUM = 2 (1+1+1-1) and is included incorrectly even though they own C. The fix is existence flags per category, not arithmetic across them.
  • Do NOT use COUNT instead of MAX in the CASE form. COUNT(CASE WHEN product = 'A' THEN 1 END) counts how many times they bought A; COUNT(...) = 1 fails for a customer who bought A twice. Use MAX(CASE ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 1 or wrap with >= 1 if you keep COUNT.
  • Direction of LEFT JOIN matters only if you want customers with no orders. This prompt requires customers who bought A AND B, so they MUST have orders; INNER JOIN is correct. If a future variant says "customers who never bought C, including those with no orders at all," you'd need FROM Customers LEFT JOIN Orders and adjust the HAVING to treat NULL flags correctly.
  • DISTINCT in the SELECT is not a fix. Wrapping the wrong logic in SELECT DISTINCT hides duplicate rows but does not fix the gate — if SUM = 2 includes a customer who shouldn't qualify, DISTINCT doesn't remove them.
  • BOOL_OR is Postgres only. MySQL, Redshift, Snowflake, BigQuery don't have it; use the MAX(CASE) form or their equivalent (Snowflake / BigQuery have BOOLOR_AGG, but it's not universal).

Gated Lookup 4 problems

▼

Two tables share an entity key. A flag, threshold, or status in the FIRST table decides whether to compute a per-entity pick (min / max / earliest / latest / first value) from the SECOND table. Non-qualifying entities still appear in the output, usually with NULL or 0.

Reference Recipe overview & key decision rules

▼

Signal words, the gate vs picked-value distinction, and three ways to express "keep the entity even when the gate fails" vs "drop it."

Signal words: "only if," "for matches above," "if eligible," "earliest / latest where condition," "first message for qualifying users"

Technique: LEFT JOIN entity dim → fact + CASE WHEN gate THEN MIN/MAX(value) ELSE NULL END, or the gate inside the JOIN ON clause, or a WHERE filter (drops non-qualifiers).

Gate vs picked value — the core distinction: the GATE column lives in table A and decides whether to compute (compatibility_score, status flag, threshold value). The PICKED value comes from table B (the earliest message, the latest login). Gate reads A, picked value reads B — never confuse the two. NOT a SUM/AVG recipe.

Move What it does When to reach for it Example
LEFT JOIN A → B Keeps every entity from table A; rows in B attach where keys match, otherwise NULL The prompt says "every X" or "matches with no messages still appear" FROM matches m LEFT JOIN messages msg ON msg.match_id = m.match_id
CASE around aggregate Computes the per-entity pick only when the gate passes; otherwise returns NULL / 0 Non-qualifying entities must appear with NULL or 0 in the picked column CASE WHEN m.score >= 70 THEN MIN(msg.sent_at) ELSE NULL END
Gate in ON clause Keeps every entity but only attaches B rows that pass the gate; non-qualifying entities have all-NULL B columns Same effect as CASE-around-aggregate but the gate filters at JOIN time. Cleaner when the gate also depends on a B column LEFT JOIN messages msg ON msg.match_id = m.match_id AND m.score >= 70
WHERE filter Drops non-qualifying entities from the result entirely The prompt says "only X above threshold" with no requirement that non-qualifiers appear — this is the simpler shape WHERE m.score >= 70
DISTINCT ON (entity) (Postgres) Picks one row per entity directly, without GROUP BY + MIN/MAX You need the whole row at the pick, not just one column; clean for "latest message text per match" SELECT DISTINCT ON (match_id) match_id, sent_at, text FROM messages ORDER BY match_id, sent_at

Trap to watch

WHERE drops; CASE / ON keep. If the prompt says non-qualifying entities should appear with NULL / 0, putting the gate in the WHERE clause silently turns the LEFT JOIN into an effective INNER JOIN and drops them. Either wrap the aggregate in a CASE or put the gate inside the ON clause.

The gate reads A, the picked value reads B. A common mistake is to gate on the value you're picking (e.g. WHERE msg.sent_at > ...) when the prompt wanted the gate on table A's column. The picked-value filter is a separate WHERE inside a subquery, not the gate.

How to pick: decision tree

▼

Four questions route you to the right gated-lookup shape.

Q1. Is the answer one row per entity from table A, with a value picked from table B?

  • Yes → Q2.
  • No (you want SUM/AVG of B per entity) → this is plain Join Then Aggregate, not gated lookup.
  • No (you want top N rows per entity, ranked) → Rank Within Groups.

Q2. Does a column in table A decide whether the pick happens at all?

  • Yes (a threshold, flag, status, date) → this is gated lookup → Q3.
  • No (every entity gets the pick) → plain Look Up Columns.

Q3. Should non-qualifying entities still appear in the output?

  • Yes, with NULL / 0 → pick CASE vs JOIN ON by what the gate has to do (Q3a below).
  • No, drop them → ✓ WHERE filter (simplest).

Q3a. CASE around aggregate, or gate in the JOIN ON clause? The order of operations decides.

  • CASE runs AFTER the aggregate. MIN / MAX / COUNT have already looked at every joined row by the time the CASE sees the result. CASE can only decide whether to SHOW the answer or HIDE it as NULL — it cannot change which rows the aggregate counted. Use ✓ CASE around aggregate when the gate is "show / hide" the WHOLE answer based on table A's column alone, and every joined B row should be in the count.
  • ON runs BEFORE the aggregate. The ON clause decides which rows even attach to the entity. By the time MIN counts, only the approved-and-pending rows are in the room. Use ✓ gate in JOIN ON when you need to FILTER which B rows are aggregated (a status filter on B, a date-range filter on B, AND/OR a gate on A) — you can stack as many conditions as you need; non-matching B rows simply don't attach, and the LEFT JOIN keeps the entity row.
  • Tell-tale signs you need ON, not CASE: the prompt has a status / date / category filter on the JOINED table (not the entity), AND non-qualifying entities must still appear. The CASE form would either (a) aggregate the wrong rows, or (b) need that B-column inside the CASE, which forces it into the GROUP BY, which changes the grain.

Q4. What is the per-entity pick from table B?

  • The MIN or MAX of a value column (the cheapest cost, the highest bid amount) → MIN(picked_col) / MAX(picked_col) with the chosen gate technique. The sort key IS the picked column.
  • A column FROM the row ranked first by ANOTHER column (the bid amount FROM the earliest timestamp, the message text FROM the latest sent_at) → ✓ ROW_NUMBER + rn = 1 template. Here MIN(value_col) is the WRONG move — it returns the smallest value, not the value from the row with the smallest sort key.
  • A count of qualifying B rows → COUNT with the gate.
  • The whole row at the pick (text + timestamp + sender, all columns) → ✓ DISTINCT ON (entity) in Postgres, or the ROW_NUMBER template above in any dialect.

Trap to watch

  • WHERE on a LEFT JOIN's right side silently turns it INNER. If the prompt wants non-qualifiers to appear, the gate must NOT live in WHERE on the right-side table's column.
  • Don't gate on the value you're picking. If the prompt says "match must have score ≥ 70," that's table A; don't filter on the B-side column accidentally.
  • Aggregate of an empty group is NULL. When the LEFT JOIN finds no B rows, MIN(b.col) is NULL automatically — no COALESCE needed unless the prompt wants a different default.

Generic templates per method

▼

Copy-paste skeletons. Swap entity, fact, the gate column, and the picked value; the shape stays the same.

CASE around the aggregate (back to tree)

▼

Use when: non-qualifiers must appear with NULL / 0, the gate reads only table A, and you're aggregating one B column.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. LEFT JOIN entity A to fact B (so every A row survives even with no B match).
  2. Aggregate B's picked column inside the SELECT: MIN/MAX/COUNT(b.col).
  3. Wrap the aggregate in a CASE WHEN a.gate ... THEN agg ELSE NULL END. CASE runs AFTER the aggregate — only show or hide.
  4. GROUP BY entity A's columns.
SELECT
    a.entity_id,
    a.gate_col,
    CASE WHEN a.gate_col >= threshold
         THEN MIN(b.picked_col)
         ELSE NULL END AS picked_value
FROM entity a
LEFT JOIN fact b ON b.entity_id = a.entity_id
GROUP BY a.entity_id, a.gate_col
ORDER BY a.entity_id;

Gate inside the JOIN ON clause (filter BEFORE aggregating)

▼

Use when: non-qualifiers must still appear AND you need to control which B rows are aggregated (a status / date / category filter on B, an entity gate on A, or both). The ON clause runs BEFORE the GROUP BY, so any condition you stack here decides what the aggregate even sees; non-matching B rows simply do not attach, and the LEFT JOIN keeps the entity row with NULL.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. LEFT JOIN A to B.
  2. Stack ALL filtering conditions (A-gate AND B-row filter, in any order) inside the ON clause with AND.
  3. ON runs BEFORE aggregation — non-matching B rows do not attach, A rows still appear (with NULL from the join).
  4. Aggregate normally; the LEFT JOIN preserves the A grain.
-- Single gate on A
SELECT
    a.entity_id,
    a.gate_col,
    MIN(b.picked_col) AS picked_value
FROM entity a
LEFT JOIN fact b
       ON b.entity_id = a.entity_id
      AND a.gate_col >= threshold
GROUP BY a.entity_id, a.gate_col
ORDER BY a.entity_id;

-- Stacked: entity gate on A AND row filter on B
-- (multiple conditions just AND together in ON; the order does not matter)
SELECT
    a.entity_id,
    a.gate_col,
    MIN(b.picked_col) AS picked_value
FROM entity a
LEFT JOIN fact b
       ON b.entity_id = a.entity_id
      AND a.gate_col = 'qualified'
      AND b.row_filter = 'pending'
GROUP BY a.entity_id, a.gate_col
ORDER BY a.entity_id;

WHERE filter (drop non-qualifiers)

▼

Use when: only qualifying entities should appear in the result; the simplest shape.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. JOIN A to B normally (LEFT or INNER, both work since we are about to filter anyway).
  2. WHERE filters out non-qualifying entities — they drop from the result entirely.
  3. GROUP BY the entity columns. This is the simplest shape; use only when the prompt does NOT require non-qualifiers to appear.
SELECT
    a.entity_id,
    a.gate_col,
    MIN(b.picked_col) AS picked_value
FROM entity a
LEFT JOIN fact b ON b.entity_id = a.entity_id
WHERE a.gate_col >= threshold
GROUP BY a.entity_id, a.gate_col;

DISTINCT ON (Postgres only)

▼

Use when: you need the whole row at the pick (text + timestamp + sender), not just an aggregate column. Pair with a WHERE gate when non-qualifiers can drop.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. SELECT DISTINCT ON (entity_id) the columns you want — including the WHOLE row at the pick, not just one aggregated column.
  2. ORDER BY entity_id first, then the pick column (ASC for earliest, DESC for latest).
  3. Returns ONE row per entity. Pair with a WHERE clause for the gate when non-qualifiers can drop.
SELECT DISTINCT ON (b.entity_id)
    b.entity_id, b.picked_col, b.other_col
FROM fact b
JOIN entity a ON a.entity_id = b.entity_id
WHERE a.gate_col >= threshold
ORDER BY b.entity_id, b.picked_col;

ROW_NUMBER + rn = 1 (pick by ORDER, not by VALUE)

▼

Use when: the per-entity pick is determined by SORTING on one column (earliest by timestamp, latest by date, top by a ranking metric) but you need to return a DIFFERENT column from that row. Works in any dialect, not just Postgres. This is the case where MIN(value_col) is the wrong move — that returns the smallest value, not the value FROM the row with the smallest sort key.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. CTE: rank fact rows per entity by the sort column with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY entity_id ORDER BY sort_col).
  2. LEFT JOIN the CTE on entity_id AND rn = 1 (put rn = 1 in the JOIN ON so the LEFT JOIN keeps entities with no fact rows).
  3. Wrap the picked column in a CASE for the gate, returning NULL when the gate fails.
  4. This returns the picked column FROM the row at the chosen sort position — not the smallest value of the picked column.
WITH ranked_fact AS (
    SELECT
        f.*,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY entity_id
                           ORDER BY sort_col ASC) AS rn
    FROM fact f
)
SELECT
    a.entity_id,
    a.gate_col,
    CASE WHEN a.gate_col >= threshold
         THEN rf.picked_col
         ELSE NULL END AS picked_value
FROM entity a
LEFT JOIN ranked_fact rf
       ON rf.entity_id = a.entity_id
      AND rf.rn = 1
ORDER BY a.entity_id;
-- Note: the rn = 1 filter goes in the JOIN ON, not in WHERE, so the LEFT JOIN
-- still keeps entities with no fact rows (they get NULL picked_value).

Earliest / latest pick with threshold gate 3 problems

▼

nb01 qtype: gated_lookup — per-entity MIN / MAX from table B, only when table A's gate passes; non-qualifying entities still appear with NULL. Canonical shape: CASE WHEN A.gate THEN MIN(B.col) ELSE NULL over a LEFT JOIN.

Medium Match Eligibility and Best Message Time

▼

Dating app: for each match, return the earliest message timestamp ONLY when compatibility_score ≥ 70. If the score is below 70 OR there are no messages, return NULL. Every match appears in the output exactly once.

Tables: matches (match_id, user_a_id, user_b_id, compatibility_score, matched_at), messages (message_id, match_id, sender_user_id, message_text, sent_at)

→

Decision Tree Path

Gated Lookup decision tree: Q1 one-row-per-entity yes → Q2 gate column in table A yes (score ≥ 70) → Q3 non-qualifiers must appear → CASE around aggregate template → Q4 pick is a single column (sent_at) so MIN is the right aggregate.

Real-World Example

A dating app product team wants to schedule a promotional push at the typical "first message" time, but only for the matches that are actually likely to engage — the low-compatibility matches stay in the dataset for reference, just with NULL on the timing column so downstream filters can decide what to do with them.

Trace — per-match aggregate after the LEFT JOIN:

match_id compatibility_score gate ≥ 70? message sent_at values MIN(sent_at) CASE result
185yes10:05, 10:0310:0310:03
292yes12:00, 11:3011:3011:30
355no10:0010:00NULL (gate fails)
478yes15:00, 14:30, 16:0014:3014:30
548no(none)NULLNULL (gate fails)
688yes(none)NULLNULL (empty group)

Two paths to NULL: gate fails (matches 3, 5) returns NULL via the CASE; gate passes but no messages (match 6) returns NULL because MIN over an empty group is NULL by definition — no COALESCE needed.

▶ 1 CASE around MIN, gate reads table A
SELECT m.match_id, m.compatibility_score, CASE WHEN m.compatibility_score >= 70 THEN MIN(msg.sent_at) ELSE NULL END AS earliest_message_time FROM matches m LEFT JOIN messages msg ON msg.match_id = m.match_id GROUP BY m.match_id, m.compatibility_score ORDER BY m.match_id;

Why this is best: The LEFT JOIN guarantees every match appears in the output exactly once. The CASE around MIN returns NULL when the gate fails, and MIN naturally returns NULL when the LEFT JOIN finds no messages, so both NULL paths fall out for free without a COALESCE.

Watch out:

  • The gate reads m.compatibility_score, not msg.*. A common bug is to put a WHERE on the messages-side column, which (a) confuses the gate with a value filter and (b) drops the LEFT JOIN's unmatched rows.
  • Don't put WHERE m.compatibility_score >= 70. That would drop matches 3 and 5 entirely; the prompt requires them in the output with NULL.
  • GROUP BY both columns you SELECT. Postgres requires compatibility_score in the GROUP BY because it's not aggregated; otherwise you get a "must appear in GROUP BY" error.
  • No COALESCE on MIN. MIN over an empty group is already NULL. Adding COALESCE(MIN(...), NULL) is a no-op; adding COALESCE(MIN(...), '1970-01-01') would corrupt match 6's expected NULL.
▶ 2 Equivalent: gate inside the JOIN ON clause
SELECT m.match_id, m.compatibility_score, MIN(msg.sent_at) AS earliest_message_time FROM matches m LEFT JOIN messages msg ON msg.match_id = m.match_id AND m.compatibility_score >= 70 GROUP BY m.match_id, m.compatibility_score ORDER BY m.match_id;

Same result, different shape: the gate moves into the ON clause so it filters at JOIN time. For matches 3 and 5 (score < 70) the JOIN attaches no message rows, so MIN is NULL. For match 6 (no messages at all) the LEFT JOIN already attaches no rows. Both NULL paths land on the same NULL.

When to prefer this over Rank 1: when the gate would need to read both A and B columns (e.g. "messages from the higher-compatibility user only") — the ON clause lets you reference both sides without nested subqueries.

▶ 3 CTE staircase — one verifiable step at a time
WITH per_match_messages AS ( -- Step 1: LEFT JOIN matches to messages, KEEP every audit column -- so you can SELECT this CTE alone and see exactly what attached. SELECT m.match_id, m.compatibility_score, msg.message_id, msg.sender_user_id, msg.sent_at FROM matches m LEFT JOIN messages msg ON msg.match_id = m.match_id ), match_earliest AS ( -- Step 2: aggregate to one row per match. compatibility_score stays -- in the GROUP BY (and in the SELECT) so the gate is still visible. SELECT match_id, compatibility_score, MIN(sent_at) AS raw_earliest_time FROM per_match_messages GROUP BY match_id, compatibility_score ), gated AS ( -- Step 3: apply the gate as its own step. Keeping raw_earliest_time -- next to earliest_message_time lets you eyeball "did the CASE flip -- the right rows to NULL?" without rerunning the join. SELECT match_id, compatibility_score, raw_earliest_time, CASE WHEN compatibility_score >= 70 THEN raw_earliest_time ELSE NULL END AS earliest_message_time FROM match_earliest ) SELECT match_id, compatibility_score, earliest_message_time FROM gated ORDER BY match_id;

Why this is best for learning / debugging: each CTE has one job, and each one can be SELECTed on its own to verify the intermediate state. per_match_messages shows the raw join (including the NULL-message rows for matches 5 and 6). match_earliest shows the aggregate plus the gate column side by side. gated shows raw_earliest_time AND the post-gate value in the same row, so you can spot a mis-set CASE without redoing the math.

Watch out:

  • Keep compatibility_score in the GROUP BY. Dropping it forces a subquery later to re-fetch it — the staircase only stays clean if the gate column rides along through every step.
  • Don't apply the CASE in Step 2. Doing the aggregate AND the gate in the same step muddles the trace; if a row comes out wrong you can't tell whether the aggregate or the CASE was responsible.
  • Keep raw_earliest_time in gated's output. Dropping it makes the final SELECT non-debuggable; with it, anyone reviewing the CTE can sanity-check the CASE column by hand.
  • Don't drop the audit columns in Step 1. Even if Step 2 only needs sent_at, keeping message_id / sender_user_id in per_match_messages lets you re-run that CTE alone to confirm which messages attached to which match.

When to prefer this over Ranks 1 and 2: when you're debugging a failed test, walking the problem through with someone, or the gate logic is more complex than a single CASE (e.g. multiple thresholds, multi-column gate). The staircase adds lines but each step is independently verifiable, which is the whole point.

Medium Squad Invite Cost by Match Completion Gate

▼

Battle royale: per player, return the cheapest squad-invite cost ONLY when their completion_rate ≥ 75, otherwise 0. Only players who received at least one invite appear. The ELSE branch returns 0 (an integer), not NULL — the variant of gated_lookup where non-qualifiers get a sentinel value instead of NULL.

Tables: players (player_id, player_name, completion_rate), squad_invites (invite_id, player_id, inviter_id, coin_cost, sent_at)

→

Decision Tree Path

Gated Lookup decision tree: Q1 one-row-per-entity yes → Q2 gate column in table A yes (completion_rate ≥ 75) → Q3 non-qualifiers must appear (with 0 as the sentinel) → CASE around aggregate template → Q4 pick is a single column (coin_cost) so MIN is the right aggregate.

Real-World Example

A live-ops team builds a leaderboard view for the matchmaking service: high-completion players get their best invite price surfaced (so they're nudged to accept), low-completion players show 0 so the UI hides the offer instead of dangling a cheaper invite to someone unlikely to use it.

Trace — per-player aggregate of invite costs, then gate:

player_id completion_rate gate ≥ 75? coin_cost values MIN(coin_cost) CASE result
10182.50yes150, 120120120
10268.00no100, 90900 (gate fails)
10391.25yes200200200
10445.00no80, 70700 (gate fails)
10576.00yes110110110

MIN is computed for every player; the CASE then replaces it with 0 for the two players below threshold (102 and 104). The aggregate runs first, the gate filters its output.

▶ 1 CASE around MIN, sentinel = 0 (not NULL)
SELECT s.player_id, p.completion_rate, CASE WHEN p.completion_rate >= 75 THEN MIN(coin_cost) ELSE 0 END AS best_invite_cost FROM squad_invites AS s LEFT JOIN players AS p ON s.player_id = p.player_id GROUP BY s.player_id, p.completion_rate ORDER BY player_id;

Why this is best: Same CASE-around-aggregate shape as Match Eligibility, with two differences worth knowing. (1) The FROM clause is the FACT table (squad_invites), not the dim (players) — this naturally drops players with no invites, which matches the prompt's "include all players who have at least one invite offer." (2) The non-qualifier ELSE returns 0 instead of NULL because the prompt wants a sentinel value, not a missing value. Two small choices, same recipe.

Watch out:

  • Direction matters. FROM squad_invites LEFT JOIN players excludes players with zero invites — that's what the prompt asks for. If the prompt instead said "every player, including those with no invites," reverse to FROM players LEFT JOIN squad_invites.
  • ELSE 0, not ELSE NULL. Read the prompt for the sentinel value. Returning NULL when 0 was expected (or vice versa) is a silent test failure.
  • GROUP BY both player_id and completion_rate. Postgres requires completion_rate in GROUP BY because it appears in SELECT outside an aggregate.
  • MIN, not earliest by date. The prompt says "cheapest" (lowest coin_cost), not "earliest sent invite." Aggregate the value, not the timestamp.
  • LEFT JOIN doesn't add safety here. Every invite has a valid player_id FK, so this LEFT JOIN behaves like INNER. The LEFT keyword is harmless but doesn't change the result — the implicit FK invariant carries the weight.

Medium Reimbursement Cap by Vendor Status (gate on A + filter on B, both in ON)

▼

Per vendor, return the lowest PENDING receipt amount, but only for actively certified vendors; everyone else still appears with NULL. The twist: the prompt has TWO conditions — a gate on the vendor table (certification_status = 'active') and a row filter on the receipts table (reimbursement_status = 'pending'). Both go in the JOIN ON clause.

Tables: vendors (vendor_id, vendor_name, certification_status), receipts (receipt_id, vendor_id, amount, reimbursement_status)

→

Decision Tree Path

Gated Lookup decision tree: Q1 one-row-per-entity yes → Q2 gate on A yes → Q3 non-qualifiers must appear → Q3a needs to filter which receipts are aggregated (only 'pending' ones), so gate-in-JOIN-ON template not CASE-around-aggregate → Q4 pick is MIN of a value column.

Real-World Example

A finance ops team wants the smallest outstanding reimbursement per vendor to schedule "easy wins" payouts, but only for vendors whose compliance is current; suspended vendors still appear on the queue (so the team can see who is blocked) just without an amount.

Why CASE around MIN fails here

A first attempt: keep the receipt filter in the ON, then wrap MIN in CASE WHEN certification_status = 'active' AND reimbursement_status = 'pending' THEN MIN(amount) ELSE NULL. Postgres rejects it: "column reimbursement_status must appear in the GROUP BY clause or be used in an aggregate function."

The reason in plain words: the ON clause is the doorman — it decides who walks in BEFORE counting. CASE around MIN runs AFTER counting, so MIN has already looked at every joined row by then. reimbursement_status lives on the receipts side (many rows per vendor), so the CASE cannot read it without picking one specific row, which means putting it in the GROUP BY — and that changes the grain to one row per (vendor, status), giving the wrong answer.

The fix: move BOTH conditions into the ON clause. Now only the (active-vendor, pending-receipt) rows attach before MIN runs, and the LEFT JOIN keeps non-qualifying vendors with NULL.

Trace — what attaches to each vendor after the ON-clause filters:

vendor_id certification_status gate active? receipts after ON filter (pending + active) MIN(amount)
1 Office Depotactiveyes45.00, 32.50 (78.00 approved → dropped)32.50
2 Staplesactiveyes120.00120.00
3 Amazon Businesssuspendedno(none attach — gate on A fails)NULL
4 FedExactiveyes(none — vendor 4's only receipt is 'approved')NULL
5 UPSsuspendedno(none — no receipts AND suspended)NULL

Three paths land on NULL, all for free: gate fails (vendor 3, 5), or gate passes but the B-side filter excludes every receipt (vendor 4). MIN over an empty group is NULL by definition — no COALESCE needed.

▶ 1 All conditions stacked in ON (entity gate + B-row filter)
SELECT v.vendor_id, v.vendor_name, MIN(r.amount) AS min_pending_amount FROM vendors AS v LEFT JOIN receipts AS r ON v.vendor_id = r.vendor_id AND r.reimbursement_status = 'pending' AND v.certification_status = 'active' GROUP BY v.vendor_id, v.vendor_name ORDER BY vendor_id;

Why this is best: Stacking both conditions in ON means MIN never sees an approved receipt OR a suspended-vendor row — the doorman turns them away before counting starts. The result reads naturally: "find the cheapest receipt amount, where the receipt is pending AND the vendor is active." The LEFT JOIN preserves every vendor row in the output regardless of whether any receipts attach.

Watch out:

  • Don't put either condition in WHERE. Moving r.reimbursement_status = 'pending' to WHERE drops vendors 4 and 5 (no qualifying receipts, NULL r.* after the LEFT JOIN, the WHERE filter rejects them). Same for the vendor gate — you'd lose vendors 3 and 5.
  • Stacking conditions in ON is just AND. Order doesn't matter; the engine evaluates them all per candidate row before the row attaches.
  • Don't try CASE around MIN here. The B-side condition (reimbursement_status) cannot ride into a CASE without going through GROUP BY — and adding reimbursement_status to GROUP BY changes the grain to one row per (vendor, status), so the answer would no longer be one row per vendor. The "must appear in GROUP BY" error is the engine's way of telling you: "you can't read this column at this step." Move it to ON instead, where it runs before aggregation.
  • No COALESCE on MIN. MIN over an empty group is NULL, which matches the prompt's expected output. Adding COALESCE(MIN(amount), 0) would corrupt vendor 4 (expected NULL) into 0.
  • vendor_name does NOT need to be in GROUP BY in Postgres because vendor_id is the PRIMARY KEY — every vendor_id determines exactly one vendor_name, so the engine knows the column is unambiguous. (DuckDB and stricter engines require it explicitly.)

Pick by ORDER, not by VALUE (ROW_NUMBER + rn = 1) 1 problem

▼

nb01 qtype: gated_lookup — The per-entity pick is decided by SORTING on one column (timestamp, date, rank score) but the output needs a DIFFERENT column from that row. MIN(value_col) here is the wrong tool — it returns the smallest value, not the value from the row at the smallest sort key. Rank a CTE by the sort column, then pull the picked column from the rn = 1 row.

Medium Gig Platform: Approved Worker Earliest Bid

▼

Gig marketplace: per worker, return the bid_amount of their EARLIEST bid by bid_timestamp. Approved workers see the actual amount; pending workers see NULL. All workers who placed at least one bid must appear.

Tables: workers (worker_id, worker_name, approval_status), bids (bid_id, worker_id, job_id, bid_amount, bid_timestamp)

→

Decision Tree Path

Gated Lookup decision tree: Q1 one-row-per-entity yes → Q2 gate in table A yes (approval_status) → Q3 non-qualifiers must appear with NULL → Q4 pick is "amount FROM the row ranked first by timestamp" → ROW_NUMBER + rn = 1 template.

Real-World Example

A gig marketplace surfaces "first-bid pricing" for approved workers (so partners can compare opening rates) while hiding it for pending workers whose accounts haven't cleared review — the data set still shows every worker so the review dashboard can see who has bid activity at all.

Lesson: MIN of the value vs value FROM the MIN-by-ordering row

The prompt says "the bid_amount from their earliest bid by timestamp." Two readings are tempting:

  • Wrong: MIN(bid_amount) — returns the smallest amount the worker ever bid, regardless of when.
  • Right: the bid_amount column from the row where bid_timestamp is smallest — usually a different value.

When the example data happens to have the smallest amount and the earliest timestamp on the SAME row (as the sample does for worker 1: 75.00 at 08:00), both readings produce the same number and the bug stays hidden. The hidden test data has them on DIFFERENT rows, so MIN returns the wrong amount.

Trace — per-worker bids ranked by timestamp ASC:

worker_id approval_status bid_timestamp bid_amount rn (by ts ASC) output bid_amount
1approved2024-01-10 08:0075.00175.00
