Two dimensions (A × B) "every A and B combo", "platform x type", a grid, "show zeros for missing combos" 
SELECT DISTINCT a FROM t1   -- set A
CROSS JOIN
(SELECT DISTINCT b FROM t2) -- set B
-- (or type each set as a CTE of literals)
Date or number range "every day/week", a date window, "including days with zero", "hours 0 to 23" 
SELECT generate_series(
  '2024-01-15'::date,
  '2024-01-21'::date,
  INTERVAL '1 day')::date AS d
-- then CROSS JOIN the entities (wards, users)

Table 2 — The shared tail (LEFT JOIN + zero-fill) and the traps

▼

Once the skeleton exists, every shape finishes the same way. These are the rules and the traps.

Rule Why it matters
LEFT JOIN the actuals, never INNER The skeleton holds the empty slots on purpose. An INNER JOIN throws them right back out, undoing the whole point.
Match on every key column Join on all the skeleton dimensions (for example date and ward), not just one. Matching on one column attaches every actual row to every slot.
Zero-fill: COUNT is free, SUM needs COALESCE COUNT(fact_col) already returns 0 for an all-NULL group. SUM and AVG return NULL on all-NULL groups, so wrap them: COALESCE(SUM(x), 0).
Skeleton first, actuals second Write CROSS JOIN (or the generated range) first, then LEFT JOIN ... ON .... A LEFT JOIN with no ON sitting before a CROSS JOIN is a syntax error.
generate_series stands alone Do not add FROM some_table to the generate_series query. With a FROM it emits the whole series once per row of that table, multiplying your dates.

Fixed labels 1 problem

▼

The complete set is a short list of labels you already know. Hand-build it with a VALUES list or a small CTE, then LEFT JOIN and count.

Easy #1435 Create a Session Bar Chart

▼

Count sessions in four duration buckets, ensuring all buckets appear even when empty.

Tables: Sessions (session_id, duration)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern L: UNION ALL Separate Queries

Real-World Example

A product team renders a session-length histogram with fixed bucket labels that always appear.

▶ 1 UNION Skeleton + Bucketed Count
SELECT bin AS bin, COALESCE(SUM(cnt), 0) AS total FROM ( SELECT '[0-5>' AS bin, 0 AS cnt UNION ALL SELECT '[5-10>', 0 UNION ALL SELECT '[10-15>', 0 UNION ALL SELECT '15 or more', 0 UNION ALL SELECT CASE WHEN duration < 5*60 THEN '[0-5>' WHEN duration < 10*60 THEN '[5-10>' WHEN duration < 15*60 THEN '[10-15>' ELSE '15 or more' END, 1 FROM Sessions ) t GROUP BY bin;

Why this is best: Skeleton rows with count 0 guarantee every bucket exists; data rows add to the counts.

Performance: One pass.

Two dimensions (A × B) 2 problems

▼

The complete set is group A × group B. CROSS JOIN the two sets (typed, or SELECT DISTINCT from the tables), then LEFT JOIN actuals. Sorted easy to hard.

Medium #1990 Count the Number of Experiments

▼

Count experiments per (platform, experiment_name), listing zero where missing.

Tables: Experiments (experiment_id, platform, experiment_name)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern L: UNION ALL Separate Queries

Real-World Example

An experimentation platform publishes a grid showing experiment counts by platform x type, with zeros shown explicitly.

▶ 1 CROSS JOIN Skeleton + LEFT JOIN
WITH platforms AS ( SELECT 'Android' AS platform UNION SELECT 'IOS' UNION SELECT 'Web' ), names AS ( SELECT 'Reading' AS experiment_name UNION SELECT 'Sports' UNION SELECT 'Programming' ) SELECT p.platform, n.experiment_name, COALESCE(COUNT(e.experiment_id), 0) AS num_experiments FROM platforms p CROSS JOIN names n LEFT JOIN Experiments e ON e.platform = p.platform AND e.experiment_name = n.experiment_name GROUP BY p.platform, n.experiment_name;

Why this is best: CROSS JOIN gives every combination; LEFT JOIN counts what exists.

Performance: Tiny skeleton; linear scan of Experiments.

Hard #1127 User Purchase Platform

▼

Per (day, platform), return user and amount totals where platform is Desktop / Mobile / Both.

Tables: Spending (user_id, spend_date, platform, amount)

→

Decision Tree Path

Master Tree: Multi-Table Queries → Pattern L: UNION ALL Separate Queries

Real-World Example

A growth analyst reports daily cross-platform engagement to justify app vs web investment.

▶ 1 Per-User Day Platform Flags + UNION
WITH per_user AS ( SELECT spend_date, user_id, MAX(platform = 'mobile') AS has_mobile, MAX(platform = 'desktop') AS has_desktop, SUM(amount) AS amt FROM Spending GROUP BY spend_date, user_id ), labeled AS ( SELECT spend_date, CASE WHEN has_mobile = 1 AND has_desktop = 1 THEN 'both' WHEN has_mobile = 1 THEN 'mobile' ELSE 'desktop' END AS platform, user_id, amt FROM per_user ), all_combos AS ( SELECT DISTINCT spend_date, 'desktop' AS platform FROM labeled UNION SELECT DISTINCT spend_date, 'mobile' FROM labeled UNION SELECT DISTINCT spend_date, 'both' FROM labeled ) SELECT a.spend_date, a.platform, COALESCE(SUM(l.amt), 0) AS total_amount, COALESCE(COUNT(DISTINCT l.user_id), 0) AS total_users FROM all_combos a LEFT JOIN labeled l ON l.spend_date = a.spend_date AND l.platform = a.platform GROUP BY a.spend_date, a.platform;

Why this is best: Label each user-day as desktop/mobile/both, then ensure every (day, platform) appears via a UNION skeleton.

Performance: Two aggregates + outer join.

Reshape Series Generation (calendar / number spine)

▼

Manufacture a complete set of dates, weeks, months, or integers with generate_series, then CROSS JOIN the entities and LEFT JOIN actuals so every (entity, bucket) cell exists in the output, including buckets with zero activity.

Reference Recipe overview & key decision rules

▼

Signal words, the four shapes of generate_series, and the "stands alone" rule that catches the most common bug.

Signal words: "every day / week / month," "include days with zero X," "show all buckets in the range," "fill missing dates," "rolling N-day window where missing days count as 0"

Technique: generate_series(start, end, step) manufactures the spine; CROSS JOIN entities to fan out every (entity, bucket) combo; LEFT JOIN actuals + COALESCE 0 so missing buckets show as 0 instead of dropping out.

Cross-link: the entity-side CROSS JOIN mechanics live in CROSS JOIN / Calendar Skeleton. For the per-row range expansion shape, see CROSS JOIN LATERAL.

Shape What it produces Example
generate_series(d1, d2, INTERVAL '1 day') A TIMESTAMP per day, inclusive on both ends generate_series('2024-01-01', '2024-01-14', INTERVAL '1 day') → 14 timestamps
generate_series(d1, d2, INTERVAL '7 days') One row per week (Monday spine) generate_series('2024-01-01', '2024-01-29', INTERVAL '7 days') → 5 Mondays
generate_series(1, n) Integers 1..n, inclusive generate_series(1, MAX(month))::int AS month — integer spine for fixed buckets
Bounds derived from data Spine that hugs the data's actual range generate_series( DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(d)), DATE_TRUNC('month', MAX(d)) + INTERVAL '1 month' - INTERVAL '1 day', INTERVAL '7 days' )

Traps to watch

  • generate_series stands alone. Do NOT add FROM some_table to its query. With a FROM, it emits the series once per row of that table and multiplies the spine.
  • INTERVAL returns TIMESTAMP, not DATE. generate_series(..., INTERVAL '1 day') rows are TIMESTAMP. Cast to ::date or your join to a DATE column will not match.
  • Inclusive on both ends. A 7-day series is start + 0 through start + 6, not + 7. The series produces (end - start) / step + 1 rows.
  • Build the spine FIRST, actuals LAST. Always: spine CROSS JOIN entities LEFT JOIN actuals. Reversing the order produces broken joins or mis-attached actuals.
  • COALESCE the aggregate, not the column. COALESCE(SUM(x), 0), not SUM(COALESCE(x, 0)) — the latter does nothing for completely missing rows.

How to pick: decision tree

▼

What kind of spine, how its bounds are set, and what shape the entities take.

Q1. What does the spine span?

  • Daily → INTERVAL '1 day' step.
  • Weekly → INTERVAL '7 days' step (the start date sets which day-of-week the spine lands on).
  • Monthly buckets → INTERVAL '1 month' step, usually anchored at DATE_TRUNC('month', d).
  • Integer buckets (months 1..12, tier 1..5) → generate_series(1, n).

Q2. Where do the bounds come from?

  • A literal date range in the prompt → hardcode the start and end as literals (literal-range template).
  • "Every week of the month the data covers" → derive bounds from MIN / MAX of the data, expanded to the month edges (data-bounds template).
  • A function parameter (p_target_week_start) → use the parameter + start + (N-1); the series is inclusive on both ends.

Q3. What entities fan out across the spine?

  • All entities from a dim table → spine CROSS JOIN entities (all-entities template).
  • Only entities that did SOMETHING in the window → spine CROSS JOIN (filtered subquery) (filtered-entities template).
  • No entity, just dates → spine alone, LEFT JOIN actuals + group.

Q4. How do you join actuals?

  • Per-day attendance → LEFT JOIN actuals ON entity = entity AND actuals.date = spine.date.
  • Per-week aggregate → LEFT JOIN actuals ON entity = entity AND actuals.date >= week_start AND actuals.date < week_start + INTERVAL '7 days'.
  • Per-row expansion (one source row → many spine rows) → CROSS JOIN LATERAL generate_series(...) — the spine reads each source row's columns.

Generic templates per method

▼

Three skeletons covering the common shapes. Swap the table / column names; the spine + CROSS JOIN + LEFT JOIN order stays the same.

Literal date range × all entities (back to tree)

▼

Copy-paste skeleton for this method.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. CTE: generate_series with literal start/end dates and the chosen step (1 day, 7 days, 1 month).
  2. CROSS JOIN the dim entities table so every (entity, date) cell exists.
  3. LEFT JOIN actuals on the entity key AND the date window.
  4. GROUP BY (entity, date) and COALESCE the aggregate to 0.
WITH spine AS (
    SELECT generate_series(DATE '2024-01-01',
                            DATE '2024-01-14',
                            INTERVAL '1 day')::date AS d
)
SELECT
    e.entity_id, e.entity_name, s.d AS day,
    COALESCE(SUM(a.metric), 0) AS daily_metric
FROM spine s
CROSS JOIN entities e
LEFT JOIN actuals a
       ON a.entity_id = e.entity_id
      AND a.event_date = s.d
GROUP BY e.entity_id, e.entity_name, s.d
ORDER BY e.entity_id, s.d;

Bounds derived from data × week spine

▼

Copy-paste skeleton for this method.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. CTE 1: derive bounds from data — usually DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(d)) and DATE_TRUNC('month', MAX(d)) + INTERVAL '1 month' - INTERVAL '1 day'.
  2. CTE 2: generate_series using those bounds and the spine step.
  3. CROSS JOIN entities.
  4. LEFT JOIN actuals with a half-open window condition actuals.date >= spine.d AND actuals.date < spine.d + INTERVAL '7 days'.
  5. GROUP BY (entity, spine.d).
WITH bounds AS (
    SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(session_date))                          AS month_start,
           DATE_TRUNC('month', MAX(session_date)) + INTERVAL '1 month'
                                                 - INTERVAL '1 day'        AS month_end
    FROM sessions
),
spine AS (
    SELECT generate_series(b.month_start, b.month_end, INTERVAL '7 days')::date AS week_start
    FROM bounds b
)
SELECT t.therapist_id, s.week_start, COUNT(act.session_id) AS sessions
FROM spine s
CROSS JOIN therapists t
LEFT JOIN sessions act
       ON act.therapist_id = t.therapist_id
      AND act.session_date >= s.week_start
      AND act.session_date <  s.week_start + INTERVAL '7 days'
GROUP BY t.therapist_id, s.week_start
ORDER BY t.therapist_id, s.week_start;

Spine × filtered entity subquery

▼

Use when only entities that did SOMETHING in the window should appear (e.g. "courses with an enrollment in the window," not every course in the catalog).

What this template does, step by step:

  1. CTE 1: build the date spine with generate_series.
  2. CTE 2: SELECT DISTINCT entity FROM actuals WHERE filter — only entities that did SOMETHING in the window.
  3. CROSS JOIN spine to the filtered entities.
  4. LEFT JOIN actuals + GROUP BY (entity, date).
WITH spine AS (
    SELECT generate_series(DATE '2024-03-01', DATE '2024-03-14', INTERVAL '1 day')::date AS d
),
relevant AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT course_id FROM enrollments
    WHERE enrolled_on BETWEEN DATE '2024-03-01' AND DATE '2024-03-14'
)
SELECT r.course_id, s.d,
       COUNT(c.completion_id) AS completions
FROM spine s
CROSS JOIN relevant r
LEFT JOIN completions c
       ON c.course_id = r.course_id
      AND c.completed_on = s.d
GROUP BY r.course_id, s.d
ORDER BY r.course_id, s.d;

Literal label spine × bucketed CASE (categorical bins)

▼

Use when the spine is a fixed set of categorical LABELS (bin names, severity tiers, plan names, status buckets) rather than dates or integers. Build the spine inline with VALUES, then LEFT JOIN a CASE expression that maps each source row to a label. Carry a sort_order column on the spine so the output order is deterministic regardless of label format.

What this template does, step by step:

  1. Inline spine: (VALUES ('label_a', 1), ('label_b', 2), ...) AS b(bin, sort_order) — one row per categorical bin, with an integer sort key.
  2. LEFT JOIN a subquery (or CTE) that selects source rows and a CASE column mapping each row to one of the bin labels (half open intervals via < comparisons, NOT BETWEEN).
  3. USING (bin) or ON b.bin = s.bin joins on the label string; LEFT JOIN preserves bins with zero source rows.
  4. GROUP BY b.bin, b.sort_order; COUNT a non null column from the source side (COUNT(s.session_id), not COUNT(*)) so empty buckets land at 0.
  5. ORDER BY b.sort_order — locks the natural sequence so '15 or more' doesn't sort before '[0-5>' alphabetically.
SELECT
    b.bin,
    COUNT(s.session_id) AS total
FROM (
    VALUES
        ('[0-5>',      1),
        ('[5-10>',     2),
        ('[10-15>',    3),
        ('15 or more', 4)
) AS b(bin, sort_order)
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT
        session_id,
        CASE
            WHEN duration::numeric / 60 <  5 THEN '[0-5>'
            WHEN duration::numeric / 60 < 10 THEN '[5-10>'
            WHEN duration::numeric / 60 < 15 THEN '[10-15>'
            ELSE '15 or more'
        END AS bin
    FROM sessions
) AS s USING (bin)
GROUP BY b.bin, b.sort_order
ORDER BY b.sort_order;

Easy Daily Ward Admission Gaps Report (date_range CTE + CROSS JOIN + LEFT JOIN actuals)

▼
  • Hardcoded date range built with generate_series, then CROSS JOIN wards to get every (date, ward) combo.
  • LEFT JOIN admissions onto the skeleton matched on BOTH ward_id and admission_date.
  • Demonstrates the join-order rule: skeleton FIRST (CROSS JOIN), actuals LAST (LEFT JOIN with ON).

Tables: wards (ward_id, ward_name), admissions (admission_id, ward_id, patient_id, admission_date)

Real-World Example

A hospital ops dashboard reports daily admissions per ward over a fixed window. Days with zero admissions for a ward must show 0 (not be missing) so the report doesn't hide quiet days.

Prompt: Generate a daily admission count per ward for the date range 2024-01-15 through 2024-01-21 (inclusive). Output ward_name, admission_date, admission_count. Order by ward_name ASC, then admission_date ASC.

▶ 1 Date range CTE → CROSS JOIN wards → LEFT JOIN admissions → COUNT
WITH date_range AS ( SELECT generate_series( '2024-01-15'::DATE, '2024-01-21'::DATE, INTERVAL '1 day' )::DATE AS admission_date ), base AS ( SELECT d.admission_date, w.ward_id, w.ward_name, a.patient_id FROM date_range AS d CROSS JOIN wards AS w LEFT JOIN admissions AS a ON a.ward_id = w.ward_id AND a.admission_date = d.admission_date ) SELECT ward_name, admission_date, COUNT(patient_id) AS admission_count FROM base GROUP BY ward_name, admission_date ORDER BY ward_name, admission_date;

The join order is the key insight:

  • Step 1: skeleton — date_range CROSS JOIN wards produces every (date, ward) pair. With 7 days × 2 wards = 14 rows. None can be missing.
  • Step 2: attach actuals — LEFT JOIN admissions ON ward_id AND admission_date brings in patient_id where there's a match, NULL where there isn't.
  • Step 3: aggregate — COUNT(patient_id) per (ward_name, admission_date). COUNT skips NULLs and returns 0 for groups with no matching admissions.

Why CROSS JOIN can't sit AFTER LEFT JOIN with no ON:

Order Result
FROM date_range LEFT JOIN admissions CROSS JOIN wardsSyntax error — LEFT JOIN requires ON before any other join
FROM date_range CROSS JOIN wards LEFT JOIN admissions ON ...Works — skeleton built first, actuals attached after

Trace through Cardiology:

admission_date Matching admissions (LEFT JOIN) COUNT(patient_id)
2024-01-155001, 50022
2024-01-16(none)0
2024-01-1750031
2024-01-18(none)0
2024-01-19(none)0
2024-01-20(none)0
2024-01-21(none)0

7 rows for Cardiology, 7 for Neurology, 14 rows total — matching the expected output.

Watch out:

  • Don't add FROM sessions (or any table) to the generate_series CTE. The function stands alone; adding FROM emits the series once per row in that table, multiplying the date count.
  • LEFT JOIN must have an ON clause. Putting CROSS JOIN immediately after a LEFT JOIN with no ON is a syntax error. Reorder: build the skeleton with CROSS JOIN first, then LEFT JOIN actuals onto it.
  • The LEFT JOIN must match on BOTH ward_id AND admission_date. Joining only on ward_id would attach every admission to every date for that ward.
  • COUNT(patient_id) already returns 0 for empty groups. COALESCE(COUNT(...), 0) is harmless but redundant. Use COALESCE only with SUM or AVG, which return NULL on all-NULL groups.
  • ORDER BY inside the base CTE has no effect on the outer query. Apply ORDER BY at the final SELECT.

Medium Weekly Session Attendance with Zero-Fill (calendar skeleton derived from data)

▼
  • Three CTE staircase: derive month bounds from sessions → generate_series the Mondays → CROSS JOIN therapists × weeks.
  • LEFT JOIN to sessions matched on therapist_id AND DATE_TRUNC('week', session_date).
  • COUNT(s.session_id) returns 0 for empty (therapist, week) cells — no COALESCE needed because COUNT of all-NULL is 0.

Tables: therapists (therapist_id, therapist_name), sessions (session_id, therapist_id, session_date, duration_minutes)

Real-World Example

A mental-health app's engagement dashboard reports per-therapist weekly session counts for January, including weeks where a therapist had zero sessions so the report covers the full month.

Prompt: Generate a per-therapist weekly count for every week in January, including weeks with zero sessions. Output therapist_id, therapist_name, week_start_date (the Monday of each week), session_count. Order by therapist_id, then week_start_date.

▶ 1 Derive bounds from data → generate_series → CROSS JOIN → LEFT JOIN actuals
WITH week_skeleton AS ( SELECT generate_series( DATE_TRUNC('week', DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(session_date)))::DATE, DATE_TRUNC('week', DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(session_date)) + INTERVAL '1 month' - INTERVAL '1 day')::DATE, INTERVAL '7 days' )::DATE AS week_start_date FROM sessions ), all_combos AS ( SELECT t.therapist_id, t.therapist_name, ws.week_start_date FROM therapists AS t CROSS JOIN week_skeleton AS ws ) SELECT ac.therapist_id, ac.therapist_name, ac.week_start_date, COUNT(s.session_id) AS session_count FROM all_combos AS ac LEFT JOIN sessions AS s ON s.therapist_id = ac.therapist_id AND DATE_TRUNC('week', s.session_date)::DATE = ac.week_start_date GROUP BY ac.therapist_id, ac.therapist_name, ac.week_start_date ORDER BY ac.therapist_id, ac.week_start_date;

Why deriving the skeleton from data needs the month-padding step:

  • The expected output covers EVERY week in January — even weeks with zero sessions for any therapist.
  • Plain MIN-to-MAX of session_date only covers weeks the data touched. The trailing empty week (e.g., 2024-01-29 with no sessions) is missing.
  • Padding to month boundaries: take MIN(session_date)'s month, walk from its first Monday to the Monday of its last day. That's all weeks that touch the month containing the data.

The bounds in plain language

Computation Result on example data
MIN(session_date)2024-01-02
DATE_TRUNC('month', ...)2024-01-01
DATE_TRUNC('week', month_start)2024-01-01 (already Monday)
month_start + 1 month - 1 day2024-01-31
DATE_TRUNC('week', 2024-01-31)2024-01-29 (Monday of week containing 01-31)

generate_series(2024-01-01, 2024-01-29, INTERVAL '7 days') yields all 5 Mondays: 01-01, 01-08, 01-15, 01-22, 01-29. CROSS JOIN with 2 therapists gives 10 (therapist, week) combinations — matching the expected 10-row output.

Why no COALESCE on the COUNT:

  • COUNT(s.session_id) on a LEFT JOINed column counts non-NULL values. When no session matches, every row in the group has session_id IS NULL, so COUNT returns 0 (not NULL).
  • If you switched to SUM(s.duration_minutes), you'd need COALESCE(SUM(...), 0) because SUM over an all-NULL group returns NULL.

Watch out:

  • Don't use plain MIN/MAX of session_date for the bounds. If sessions don't span the full month, the output drops the trailing/leading empty weeks.
  • The LEFT JOIN must match on BOTH therapist_id AND the week_start_date. Joining only on therapist_id would attach every session to every week.
  • DATE_TRUNC('week', session_date)::DATE on the join condition. Without the cast, the comparison is timestamp vs date and may not match.
  • GROUP BY all three skeleton columns. Forgetting therapist_name or week_start_date in the GROUP BY raises an error in strict mode (Postgres).
  • The CROSS JOIN is intentional, not a bug. It builds the every-(therapist, week) skeleton; INNER JOIN would lose weeks where a therapist had zero sessions.

Medium Daily Match Activity Report with Zero-Fill (active users × date range)

▼
  • Skeleton = active users CROSS JOIN a hardcoded generate_series date range, so every (user, date) cell exists.
  • LEFT JOIN deliveries matched on BOTH user_id AND date; COUNT the matched column to zero-fill.
  • Filter to is_active = true so inactive users never appear.

Tables: users (user_id, username, is_active), match_deliveries (delivery_id, user_id, delivered_at, match_user_id)

Real-World Example

A dating app's daily engagement dashboard shows matches delivered per user. Quiet days must read 0, not vanish, or the chart implies the user left the app.

Prompt: One row per (user_id, report_date) for every active user across 2024-01-01 through 2024-01-07 inclusive, showing match_count (deliveries that day, or 0). Active users have is_active = true. Order by user_id, then report_date. Use 0 for empty days, not NULL.

▶ 1 Date range CTE → CROSS JOIN active users → LEFT JOIN deliveries → COUNT
WITH date_range AS ( SELECT generate_series( '2024-01-01'::DATE, '2024-01-07'::DATE, INTERVAL '1 day' )::DATE AS report_date ) SELECT u.user_id, d.report_date, COUNT(md.match_user_id) AS match_count FROM users AS u CROSS JOIN date_range AS d LEFT JOIN match_deliveries AS md ON md.user_id = u.user_id AND md.delivered_at = d.report_date WHERE u.is_active = true GROUP BY u.user_id, d.report_date ORDER BY u.user_id, d.report_date;

How the three steps line up:

  • Skeleton — users CROSS JOIN date_range pairs every active user with all 7 days. 2 active users × 7 days = 14 rows. None can go missing.
  • Attach actuals — LEFT JOIN match_deliveries ON user_id AND delivered_at brings in a row per delivery, NULL where a user had none that day.
  • Zero-fill — COUNT(md.match_user_id) per (user, date). COUNT ignores NULLs and returns 0 for empty cells, so no COALESCE is needed.

Trace through Alice (101):

report_date Matched deliveries (LEFT JOIN) match_count
2024-01-01201, 2022
2024-01-02(none)0
2024-01-032031
2024-01-04 .. 01-07(none)0

7 rows for Alice, 7 for Bob, 14 total. Charlie (103) is dropped by is_active = true, matching the expected output.

Watch out:

  • COUNT needs no COALESCE; SUM does. Counting the matched column auto-zeros empty groups. If you instead pre-aggregate into a per-day match_count CTE and then SUM it (a valid approach), SUM over an all-NULL group returns NULL, so you must wrap it: COALESCE(SUM(match_count), 0).
  • Filter active users with WHERE is_active = true. Charlie must not appear at all. Filtering the cross-joined users works; pre-filtering active users in their own CTE before the CROSS JOIN reads a touch cleaner.
  • The LEFT JOIN must match on BOTH user_id AND the date. Joining on user_id alone attaches every one of a user's deliveries to every date.
  • generate_series stands alone. Do not add FROM some_table to it, or it emits the series once per row of that table.
  • ORDER BY belongs on the final SELECT, not inside a CTE, where it has no effect on the outer result.

Medium Daily Video Engagement Report with Zero-Fill (date spine × all courses)

▼
  • generate_series builds the date spine over a literal range; CROSS JOIN the full course list so every (course, day) cell exists.
  • Pre-aggregate watch minutes per (course, day), then LEFT JOIN and COALESCE(..., 0) the empty days.
  • Pull courses from the courses table, not from the watch data, so a course with zero activity still appears.

Tables: courses (course_id, course_name), video_watches (watch_id, course_id, watch_date, minutes_watched)

Real-World Example

A course platform's engagement dashboard needs every day in March per course, so a quiet day reads 0 rather than dropping out and implying the course was removed.

Prompt: One row per (course_id, watch_date) for every day from 2024-03-01 through 2024-03-14, for every course. Report total_minutes_watched (summed minutes that day, or 0). Order by course_id, then watch_date.

▶ 1 Date spine → CROSS JOIN all courses → LEFT JOIN pre-aggregated minutes
WITH date_spine AS ( SELECT generate_series( '2024-03-01'::date, '2024-03-14'::date, INTERVAL '1 day' )::timestamptz AS watch_date ), daily_minutes AS ( SELECT course_id, watch_date, SUM(minutes_watched) AS total_minutes_watched FROM video_watches GROUP BY course_id, watch_date ) SELECT c.course_id, d.watch_date, COALESCE(dm.total_minutes_watched, 0) AS total_minutes_watched FROM courses AS c CROSS JOIN date_spine AS d LEFT JOIN daily_minutes AS dm ON dm.course_id = c.course_id AND dm.watch_date::timestamptz = d.watch_date ORDER BY c.course_id, d.watch_date;

How the three steps line up:

  • Spine — generate_series over a literal 14-day range. Casting to ::timestamptz makes each day print as 2024-03-14 00:00:00+00:00; use ::date instead if you just want a plain date.
  • Pre-aggregate — daily_minutes sums minutes per (course, day) first, so a day with two watch rows (e.g., 45 + 30 = 75) becomes one number before the join.
  • Complete grid — courses CROSS JOIN date_spine gives every (course, day) pair; the LEFT JOIN attaches minutes where they exist, and COALESCE(..., 0) fills the rest.

Cleaner than the common first attempt:

  • Cross join the courses table, not the aggregated watches. Building the course list from the watch data drops any course with zero activity in the window. The full set of courses lives in courses.
  • No DISTINCT needed. Cross joining one row per course (from courses) against the spine already yields unique pairs. DISTINCT is only a band-aid when the course source has duplicate rows (which the aggregated CTE does, one per day).
  • Fold the grid into the final SELECT. A separate "base" CTE just to hold the cross join adds a layer without adding clarity here.

Watch out:

  • Match the join key types. The spine is timestamptz, so cast dm.watch_date::timestamptz on the join (or make both ::date). Comparing a bare date to a timestamptz can mis-match across time zones.
  • SUM needs COALESCE; COUNT would not. SUM over an all-NULL group returns NULL, so the empty days need COALESCE(SUM(...), 0). If you were counting watch rows instead, COUNT already returns 0.
  • generate_series stands alone. Do not append FROM some_table to it, or it emits the series once per row of that table.

Medium Weekly Reorder Rate by Customer Segment (grid + two-level aggregate + zero-fill)

▼
  • generate_series weekly spine CROSS JOIN the distinct segments builds the full (segment, week) grid.
  • DATE_TRUNC('week', order_date) buckets each order; two grouping levels turn raw orders into a count of reordering customers.
  • LEFT JOIN the counts onto the grid and COALESCE to 0, so empty segment weeks show 0 instead of dropping out.

Tables: customers (customer_id, segment, signup_date), orders (order_id, customer_id, order_date, basket_value)

Real-World Example

An online grocery wants weekly reorder rates per customer segment. Every segment must appear for every week of the window, even quiet weeks, so the report does not hide gaps. A reorder is a customer placing two or more orders in the same week.

Prompt: For every combination of customer segment and week in January 2024, count the customers who placed repeat orders that week (two or more orders in the same week). Show all segments for all weeks, with 0 where no reorders occurred. Output segment, week_start, reorder_count. Order by segment ASC, then week_start ASC.

▶ 1 Grid → per-customer flag → sum per segment week → zero-fill
WITH week_spine AS ( -- 1) the five week-start Mondays in January SELECT generate_series( '2024-01-01'::date, '2024-01-31'::date, INTERVAL '1 week' )::date AS week_start ), grid AS ( -- 2) every segment x week combination SELECT s.segment, w.week_start FROM week_spine AS w CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT segment FROM customers) AS s ), orders_tagged AS ( -- 3) tag each order with its week + the customer's segment SELECT DATE_TRUNC('week', o.order_date)::date AS week_start, c.segment, o.customer_id, o.order_id FROM orders AS o JOIN customers AS c USING (customer_id) ), customer_flags AS ( -- 4) per customer per week: reorder = 2+ orders SELECT week_start, segment, customer_id, CASE WHEN COUNT(order_id) >= 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_reorder FROM orders_tagged GROUP BY week_start, segment, customer_id ), reorders AS ( -- 5) count reordering customers per segment + week SELECT week_start, segment, SUM(is_reorder) AS reorder_count FROM customer_flags GROUP BY week_start, segment ) SELECT -- 6) hang counts on the full grid, zero-fill the gaps g.segment, g.week_start, COALESCE(r.reorder_count, 0) AS reorder_count FROM grid AS g LEFT JOIN reorders AS r ON r.segment = g.segment AND r.week_start = g.week_start ORDER BY g.segment, g.week_start;

Why two grouping levels: the metric counts customers, not orders. Step 4 groups by (week_start, segment, customer_id) so each customer gets one 0 or 1 flag for the week (1 when they placed 2+ orders). Step 5 then sums those flags per (week_start, segment), which is the count of customers who reordered. Trying to do it in one GROUP BY on (segment, week) would count orders, not reordering customers.

Why the grid is the left side: the prompt wants every segment for every week, including the empty ones. Driving the final SELECT off grid with a LEFT JOIN to reorders keeps those combinations, and COALESCE(..., 0) turns the misses into 0. Driving off the orders instead would silently drop quiet segment weeks (Budget, every week here).

Why DATE_TRUNC('week', ...) lines up: it snaps each order date to the Monday of its week, and the spine's starts (Jan 1, 8, 15, 22, 29) are those same Mondays, so the bucket and the grid agree. This holds because Jan 1, 2024 is a Monday; DATE_TRUNC('week') is always Monday based in PostgreSQL.

Medium Daily Course Activity Report with Zero-Fill (filtered CROSS JOIN set)

▼
  • generate_series date spine CROSS JOIN only the courses with an enrollment in the window (a filtered subquery, not every course).
  • LEFT JOIN daily completion counts (completions joined to enrollments for the course), then COALESCE to 0.
  • The subtle part is which courses populate the grid: "has an enrollment in the range," which is not the same as "has completions."

Tables: courses (course_id, course_name), enrollments (enrollment_id, course_id, student_id, enrolled_date), lesson_completions (completion_id, enrollment_id, lesson_id, completed_date)

Real-World Example

A learning platform reports daily lessons completed per course for one week. Every day in the window must appear for each active course, with 0 on quiet days, so the engagement chart has no gaps.

Prompt: For every day from 2024-01-15 through 2024-01-21 and every course that has at least one enrollment in that range, count lessons completed that day (0 when none). Output course_id, report_date, completions_count. Order by course_id ASC, then report_date ASC.

▶ 1 Date spine × courses-in-range → LEFT JOIN daily counts → COALESCE
WITH date_spine AS ( -- 1) every day in the window SELECT generate_series( '2024-01-15'::date, '2024-01-21'::date, INTERVAL '1 day' )::date AS report_date ), courses_in_range AS ( -- 2) ONLY courses with an enrollment in the window SELECT DISTINCT course_id FROM enrollments WHERE enrolled_date BETWEEN '2024-01-15' AND '2024-01-21' ), grid AS ( -- 3) every (course, day) combination SELECT c.course_id, d.report_date FROM courses_in_range AS c CROSS JOIN date_spine AS d ), daily_completions AS ( -- 4) completions per course per day SELECT e.course_id, lc.completed_date AS report_date, COUNT(*) AS completions_count FROM lesson_completions AS lc JOIN enrollments AS e USING (enrollment_id) GROUP BY e.course_id, lc.completed_date ) SELECT g.course_id, g.report_date, COALESCE(dc.completions_count, 0) AS completions_count FROM grid AS g LEFT JOIN daily_completions AS dc ON dc.course_id = g.course_id AND dc.report_date = g.report_date ORDER BY g.course_id, g.report_date;

Pick the CROSS JOIN set carefully (the trap): the prompt says the grid covers courses "that have at least one enrollment during that period," so the set is SELECT DISTINCT course_id FROM enrollments WHERE enrolled_date BETWEEN .... It is tempting to derive it from enrollments JOIN lesson_completions instead, which on small sample data gives the same courses and passes, but that is "courses with completions," a different rule. A course that enrolled someone in the window but recorded no completions belongs in the report (seven rows of 0) and the completions based set would silently drop it.

Counts ignore the enrollment date: completions are attributed to a course through its enrollment and counted by completed_date, regardless of when that enrollment happened. That is why course 1 shows 2 completions on Jan 15 even though those came from an enrollment dated Jan 14 (outside the window). Only the course set is filtered by the in-range rule, not the completion counts.

Zero-fill mechanics: grid is the left side, the daily counts are LEFT JOINed on (course_id, report_date), and COALESCE(..., 0) turns the misses into 0. Because the grid only holds in-window dates, completions outside the window never appear.

Medium Weekly Job Completion Report with Zero-Fill

▼

Gig marketplace: report completions per (worker, week) for 4 weeks — weeks with zero completions must appear as 0, not NULL or missing. Hardcoded literal date range, every worker shown for every week.

Tables: workers (worker_id, worker_name), job_completions (completion_id, worker_id, completion_date)

→

Decision Tree Path

Series Generation decision tree: Q1 weekly → INTERVAL '1 week'. Q2 literal bounds → literal-range template. Q3 all workers (every worker every week) → CROSS JOIN workers. Q4 per-week count of B rows → LEFT JOIN job_completions ON worker matches AND completion_date within the week window.

Real-World Example

An ops dashboard surfaces a "completions by worker by week" heatmap; weeks where a worker did nothing must still render as a 0 cell so the empty rectangles are visually obvious — you cannot show a "no activity" pattern if those rows are missing from the result set.

Build order — spine FIRST, entities NEXT, actuals LAST:

  1. Manufacture week_spine: 4 Mondays from generate_series. Stands alone, no FROM.
  2. CROSS JOIN workers: 4 weeks × 3 workers = 12 (week_start, worker) cells, every combination present.
  3. LEFT JOIN job_completions: attach when the completion's date falls within the week's [start, start + 7 days) window AND the worker matches. Misses stay attached as NULL on the completion side.
  4. GROUP BY (week_start, worker) + COUNT(jc.completion_id): COUNT of a column ignores NULLs, so a cell with no attached completion counts to 0 — COALESCE is redundant but kept for clarity.

Trace — what attaches to each (worker, week) cell:

worker week_start window [start, start+7d) attached completions completions_count
101 Alice2024-01-01Jan 01 - Jan 07Jan 02, Jan 032
101 Alice2024-01-08Jan 08 - Jan 14(none)0
101 Alice2024-01-15Jan 15 - Jan 21Jan 161
101 Alice2024-01-22Jan 22 - Jan 28(none)0
102 Bob2024-01-15Jan 15 - Jan 21Jan 151
102 Bob2024-01-22Jan 22 - Jan 28Jan 231
103 Carol2024-01-22Jan 22 - Jan 28Jan 221

Bob's weeks 1 and 2 and Carol's weeks 1, 2, 3 (5 cells total) all attach no completions and the COUNT lands at 0 — exactly the shape the CROSS JOIN guarantees.

▶ 1 Week spine × workers CROSS JOIN × LEFT JOIN completions with date-window ON
WITH week_spine AS ( SELECT generate_series( '2024-01-01'::date, '2024-01-28'::date, INTERVAL '1 week' )::date AS week_start ) SELECT w.worker_id, w.worker_name, ws.week_start, COALESCE(COUNT(jc.completion_id), 0) AS completions_count FROM week_spine AS ws CROSS JOIN workers AS w LEFT JOIN job_completions AS jc ON jc.worker_id = w.worker_id AND jc.completion_date >= ws.week_start AND jc.completion_date < ws.week_start + INTERVAL '7 days' GROUP BY ws.week_start, w.worker_id, w.worker_name ORDER BY w.worker_id ASC, ws.week_start ASC;

Why this is best: The CROSS JOIN between the 4-row spine and the 3-row workers table guarantees the 12 (week, worker) cells you need, before any completions data enters the picture. The LEFT JOIN then attaches completions where they belong; cells with no completions still exist, just with NULL on the jc side. COUNT(jc.completion_id) ignores those NULLs and lands at 0 naturally.

Watch out:

  • The week-range condition belongs in ON, not WHERE. Moving jc.completion_date BETWEEN ws.week_start AND ... to WHERE drops every (worker, week) cell with no completions — the LEFT JOIN's NULL row gets rejected by the WHERE check. ON keeps them.
  • Half-open interval, not BETWEEN. >= week_start AND < week_start + 7 days avoids the off-by-one trap that BETWEEN week_start AND week_start + 7 days creates (BETWEEN is inclusive on the upper bound, so a Sunday completion would also land in the next week's window).
  • COUNT(jc.completion_id), not COUNT(*). COUNT(*) counts the NULL-filled row as 1, so every zero-completion cell would show 1 instead of 0. Always count a column from the right-side table after a LEFT JOIN.
  • worker_name in GROUP BY. Strict engines (DuckDB) and ANSI SQL require any non-aggregated SELECT column in GROUP BY. Postgres lets you drop it because worker_id is the PRIMARY KEY, but keeping it works in any dialect.
  • generate_series stands alone, no FROM. Adding FROM workers to the spine CTE would emit the 4 weeks once per worker (12 rows), and the later CROSS JOIN would multiply that by another 3 → 36 rows in the spine.
  • COALESCE around COUNT is technically redundant — COUNT never returns NULL on an empty group; it returns 0. The COALESCE is harmless but a stricter reviewer would remove it.

Medium Bank Transactions per Visit Histogram (INTEGER spine, bounds derived from data)

▼

Bank visit log: for every possible "transactions in one visit" count from 0 to the busiest visit, return how many visits hit that count. The bucket nobody hit (e.g. 2 transactions) must still appear as 0. This is the INTEGER flavor of the spine pattern — bounds derived from MIN/MAX of a CTE, not literal dates or function parameters.

Tables: Visits (user_id, visit_date) primary key (user_id, visit_date); Transactions (user_id, transaction_date, amount) may contain duplicate rows (multiple transactions per visit). Guarantee: every transaction's (user_id, transaction_date) is present in Visits.

→

Decision Tree Path

Series Generation decision tree: Q1 integer buckets → generate_series(MIN, MAX). Q2 bounds derived from data → subqueries against the per-visit CTE. Q3 no entity fan-out needed (one row per bucket). Q4 attach actuals by joining the per-visit count to the spine bucket.

Real-World Example

A retail bank wants a histogram of "how many transactions does a visit usually involve" to staff teller windows; the chart must include the zero-transaction visits (lobby check-ins) and the empty buckets between common values so the distribution shape is honest.

Why an INTEGER spine, not a date spine

The spine pattern is usually a date series (every week, every day). Here the spine is an INTEGER series — one row per possible transaction count from 0 to MAX(transaction_count). Same shape, same reason: a GROUP BY transaction_count on the per-visit data alone would skip the empty bucket (count = 2), because no row carries that value. The spine manufactures the row so the LEFT JOIN can attach a 0.

Use this shape any time the output is a histogram / distribution over an integer axis (tier 1..5, score 0..10, visit counts).

What this query does, step by step:

  1. Per visit: count transactions — LEFT JOIN Visits to Transactions on (user_id, date); COUNT(t.amount) lands at 0 for visits with no matching transaction because COUNT ignores the NULL from the unmatched LEFT JOIN row.
  2. Integer spine, bounds from data — generate_series((SELECT MIN(transaction_count) FROM base), (SELECT MAX(transaction_count) FROM base)) manufactures every integer from 0 through the busiest visit, including the gap buckets.
  3. Spine LEFT JOIN base on the bucket — for each spine row, attach every visit whose transaction_count equals the spine value. Buckets with no matching visit attach NULL.
  4. GROUP BY spine + COUNT(b.col) — COUNT of the joined column ignores the NULL-filled unmatched rows, so the empty bucket lands at 0 (not 1, which is what COUNT(*) would give).

Trace — spine 0..3 LEFT JOIN per-visit counts:

spine.transactions_count attached (user, visit_date, count) from base COUNT(b.transaction_count)
0(1,'01-01',0), (2,'01-02',0), (12,'01-01',0), (19,'01-03',0)4
1(1,'01-02',1), (1,'01-04',1), (2,'01-03',1), (7,'01-11',1), (8,'01-28',1)5
2(nothing attaches — LEFT JOIN row, NULL on base side)0
3(9,'01-25',3)1

The 2-transactions bucket is the whole point: a naive GROUP BY transaction_count on base alone would not have produced that row. The spine forces it to exist; the LEFT JOIN + COUNT(b.col) fills it with 0.

▶ 1 Integer spine, bounds from MIN/MAX of the per-visit CTE, LEFT JOIN + COUNT(col)
WITH base AS ( -- 1. Per-visit count of transactions; LEFT JOIN puts NULL for no-transaction -- visits, COUNT(t.amount) ignores those NULLs and lands at 0. SELECT v.user_id, v.visit_date, COUNT(t.amount) AS transaction_count FROM Visits AS v LEFT JOIN Transactions AS t ON t.user_id = v.user_id AND t.transaction_date = v.visit_date GROUP BY v.user_id, v.visit_date ), spine AS ( -- 2. Integer spine. LOWER bound is LITERAL 0 because the prompt says -- "transactions_count should take all values from 0 to max." Using -- MIN(transaction_count) FROM base would skip the 0 / 1 buckets on test -- data where every visit had at least one transaction. UPPER bound is -- MAX FROM base so the spine sizes itself to the busiest visit. SELECT generate_series( 0, (SELECT MAX(transaction_count) FROM base) ) AS transactions_count ) -- 3 + 4. Spine LEFT JOIN base on the bucket value, COUNT(b.col) per bucket SELECT s.transactions_count, COUNT(b.transaction_count) AS visits_count FROM spine AS s LEFT JOIN base AS b ON b.transaction_count = s.transactions_count GROUP BY s.transactions_count ORDER BY s.transactions_count;

Why this is best: Three CTEs, each with one job and one grain. base is one row per (user, visit). spine is one row per possible bucket. The final SELECT is one row per bucket with the COUNT of base rows attached. Every empty bucket appears for free, no COALESCE needed.

Watch out:

  • Read the prompt for the LOWER bound — it is rarely MIN of the data. Most histogram prompts hardcode the lower bound (counts start at 0, months at 1, hours at 0). Using (SELECT MIN(transaction_count) FROM base) works on example data where some visit had 0 transactions, then silently breaks on hidden test data where every visit had at least one transaction (the 0 and 1 buckets vanish from the output). LOWER bound = literal from the prompt; UPPER bound = (SELECT MAX(...) FROM base) so the spine right-sizes.
  • COUNT(col), not COUNT(*). In BOTH CTEs (the per-visit count and the final bucket count), COUNT(*) would count the NULL-filled LEFT JOIN row as 1, so every empty bucket would show 1 instead of 0. Always count a column from the right-side table after a LEFT JOIN.
  • The subquery for the UPPER bound needs its own parentheses. generate_series(0, SELECT MAX(...) FROM base) is a parse error; wrap as (SELECT MAX(...) FROM base).
  • No cosmetic ::int or COALESCE needed. The series inherits its type from the integer arguments, and the outer COUNT can never return NULL on a GROUP BY result — it returns 0.
  • Upper bound from data, not hardcoded. Hardcoding the upper bound (e.g. generate_series(0, 10)) breaks the moment a visit has more transactions than the literal. The MAX subquery keeps the spine right-sized to the data.
  • Guarantee from the prompt matters. The prompt says "every transaction's (user_id, transaction_date) is in Visits" — that's why the per-visit COUNT in base is correct. Without that guarantee you'd need an extra check for stray transactions on days the user didn't visit.

Medium Total Sales Amount by Year (per row date range × LATERAL generate_series × year aggregate)

▼

Each Sales row carries its own [period_start, period_end] window. Expand every row into one row per day via CROSS JOIN LATERAL generate_series, extract the year from each day, then aggregate to (product, year). Year boundaries inside a single sales period are handled by the year extraction, not by hardcoded calendars.

Tables: Product (product_id, product_name), Sales (product_id, period_start, period_end, average_daily_sales). average_daily_sales is constant over the whole period; the year report needs the SUM of that rate over all days in each year inside the period.

→

Decision Tree Path

Series Generation decision tree: Q1 daily granularity → INTERVAL '1 day'. Q2 bounds come from each Sales row, not literals → data bounds template with the LATERAL twist (each row's window expands independently). Q3 aggregate to year → GROUP BY product, EXTRACT(YEAR FROM d).

Real World Example

A merchandising team reports annual revenue per SKU but the source table only stores a flat per period daily rate (sales contracts are written that way). A SKU whose period straddles years 2018, 2019, 2020 should appear as three rows; the per year totals are driven by how many days of that period fall in each calendar year, not by any year column in the source.

Build order — per row expansion, then per year aggregate:

  1. CTE 1 base: CROSS JOIN LATERAL generate_series(s.period_start, s.period_end, INTERVAL '1 day') expands each Sales row into one row per day inside that period. LATERAL lets the series read each row's bounds.
  2. For each emitted day, compute EXTRACT(YEAR FROM d)::int AS report_year. Cast to int because EXTRACT returns numeric / double precision.
  3. JOIN Product on product_id to attach product_name.
  4. GROUP BY (product_id, product_name, report_year) + SUM(average_daily_sales). Since the rate is constant per day, summing it across all days in a year for a product equals (days in that year for that product) × rate.
  5. ORDER BY product_id, report_year — sort by the integer year so 2018 / 2019 / 2020 land in numeric order, not in string order (string sort happens to work for 4 digit years but breaks if you ever mix in a 3 digit year or a label).

Trace — product 2 (LC T Shirt) spans 2018-12-01 to 2020-01-01 at rate 10 per day:

product year days emitted by series SUM(average_daily_sales) total_amount
2 LC T Shirt2018Dec 1 - Dec 31 = 3131 × 10310
2 LC T Shirt2019Jan 1 - Dec 31 = 365365 × 103650
2 LC T Shirt2020Jan 1 only = 11 × 1010

The year boundary is handled by EXTRACT splitting the 397 day expansion into three year buckets; no explicit calendar table or year list is needed.

▶ 1 LATERAL generate_series per row → EXTRACT(YEAR) → GROUP BY year
WITH base AS ( -- 1. Expand each Sales row into one row per day in its period. -- LATERAL lets generate_series read s.period_start / s.period_end per row. SELECT s.product_id, EXTRACT(YEAR FROM d)::int AS report_year, s.average_daily_sales FROM Sales AS s CROSS JOIN LATERAL generate_series( s.period_start, s.period_end, INTERVAL '1 day' ) AS d ) -- 2. Attach product_name and aggregate to (product, year). SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name, b.report_year::varchar AS report_year, SUM(b.average_daily_sales) AS total_amount FROM base AS b JOIN Product AS p USING (product_id) GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name, b.report_year ORDER BY p.product_id, b.report_year;

Why this is best: The per row LATERAL expansion is the only step that needs to know about each row's bounds; once base exists, the rest is a plain GROUP BY / SUM. EXTRACT lets the year split fall out of the data instead of a hardcoded (2018, 2019, 2020) list, so a Sales row that lands entirely in 2021 would still report correctly with zero changes.

Watch out:

  • LATERAL is required (or the implicit comma form). CROSS JOIN generate_series(s.period_start, s.period_end, ...) without LATERAL is a syntax error in Postgres because the series can't see s. The shortcut FROM Sales s, generate_series(s.period_start, s.period_end, INTERVAL '1 day') AS d is implicitly LATERAL and works too — pick one for the whole file.
  • EXTRACT returns numeric / double precision. Cast to ::int before any integer comparison and to ::varchar only if the grader literally requires a string column (some LeetCode graders do; the underlying data type is numeric). Mixing 2019 and '2019' in a comparison without a cast will not error but can silently use a slower plan.
  • generate_series with date inputs returns timestamp. If anything downstream expects a true date, cast with d::date; if you only need the year, EXTRACT works on timestamp directly and the cast is optional.
  • SUM, not COUNT. Each emitted day represents average_daily_sales dollars, not 1 unit. A COUNT would return the number of days in the year window; you want days × rate which is the SUM of the constant rate column.
  • GROUP BY needs product_id AND product_name for portability. Postgres lets you drop product_name because product_id is a PRIMARY KEY (functional dependency), but Redshift, Snowflake, and ANSI strict modes require it. Keep it for the same query to run everywhere.
  • ORDER BY the integer year, not the cast string. Sorting by b.report_year::varchar works for 2018 / 2019 / 2020 by accident (lexicographic order happens to match) but is the wrong sort key in general. Cast for output, sort on the int.
  • Inclusive bounds. generate_series is inclusive on both endpoints, which matches the prompt's "both dates are inclusive." For product 2 that's Dec 1 2018 through Jan 1 2020 = 397 days, not 396.

Easy Session Duration Bins by Minute Range (label spine via VALUES × CASE bucketing × zero fill)

▼

Bucket session durations into 4 categorical bins ([0-5>, [5-10>, [10-15>, 15 or more) and count sessions per bin, with empty bins reported as 0. The novel technique is the LABEL spine: manufacturing 4 spine rows from a literal VALUES clause and LEFT JOINing a CASE expression that maps each source row to a bin label.

Tables: Sessions (session_id, duration). duration is in seconds; divide by 60 for the minute bins.

→

Decision Tree Path

Series Generation decision tree: Q1 granularity = categorical bins (not date / number) → LABEL spine via VALUES. Q2 bounds = fixed label set named in the prompt → label spine template. Q3 zero fill required (empty bins must show 0) → LEFT JOIN spine → bucketed CASE, COUNT a non null column.

Real World Example

A product analytics dashboard reports session length distribution. The bins must always render (a "0 sessions" bar is meaningful: nobody used the app for 10 to 15 minutes), so missing bins can't simply be dropped from the query result. The label spine pattern guarantees every bin appears in the output regardless of data presence.

Build order — spine FIRST, bucketing NEXT, LEFT JOIN LAST:

  1. Manufacture the bin spine inline with VALUES: one row per bin label, plus a sort_order column to lock the output order. VALUES ('[0-5>', 1), ('[5-10>', 2), ...) AS b(bin, sort_order) — 4 spine rows regardless of source data.
  2. Bucket source rows with a CASE expression that maps each duration to a bin label using HALF OPEN intervals via < comparisons. CASE evaluates top to bottom, so the first matching branch wins; WHEN duration::numeric / 60 < 5 catches everything below 5 minutes, the next WHEN ... < 10 catches 5 up to 10, and so on. Use < not BETWEEN because BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends and would put a 5 minute session into [0-5>, contradicting the bin's half open semantics.
  3. LEFT JOIN spine to the bucketed source via USING (bin). LEFT JOIN preserves all 4 spine rows even when no source row maps to a bin.
  4. GROUP BY b.bin, b.sort_order + COUNT(s.session_id). COUNT of the source column ignores the NULL filled rows from unmatched spine entries, so empty bins land at 0 naturally. COUNT(*) would count the NULL filled row as 1 and zero bins would show 1.
  5. ORDER BY b.sort_order so the output is [0-5>, [5-10>, [10-15>, 15 or more. Without it, lexicographic sort would put 15 or more first (digits before brackets in ASCII).

Trace — each session's bin assignment on the example data:

session_id duration (sec) duration / 60 (min) CASE picks bin
1300.5[0-5>
21993.32[0-5>
32994.98[0-5>
45809.67[5-10>
5100016.6715 or more

No session falls into [10-15>, so that bin's COUNT is 0 — the LEFT JOIN preserves the spine row and COUNT(s.session_id) on the NULL filled row lands at 0.

▶ 1 VALUES label spine × CASE bucketing × LEFT JOIN with USING (bin)
SELECT b.bin, COUNT(s.session_id) AS total FROM ( VALUES ('[0-5>', 1), ('[5-10>', 2), ('[10-15>', 3), ('15 or more', 4) ) AS b(bin, sort_order) LEFT JOIN ( SELECT session_id, CASE WHEN duration::numeric / 60 < 5 THEN '[0-5>' WHEN duration::numeric / 60 < 10 THEN '[5-10>' WHEN duration::numeric / 60 < 15 THEN '[10-15>' ELSE '15 or more' END AS bin FROM Sessions ) AS s USING (bin) GROUP BY b.bin, b.sort_order ORDER BY b.sort_order;

Why this is best: The spine guarantees all 4 bins exist before any source row is examined. The CASE bucketing produces a label per source row that JOINs cleanly to the spine. The sort_order column locks output order independent of label format. The whole query is a single pass with no subquery correlation.

Watch out:

  • The spine subquery SELECT ('a', 'b', 'c', 'd') AS bin does NOT make 4 rows. Postgres parses the parens as a row constructor and you get ONE row with a record valued column. Use VALUES, UNNEST(ARRAY[...]), or four SELECT ... UNION ALL branches.
  • BETWEEN 0 AND 5 overlaps with BETWEEN 5 AND 10 at the endpoint. BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends. With CASE top to bottom evaluation, a 5 minute session would land in [0-5>, contradicting the bin's half open semantics. Use plain < comparisons.
  • COUNT(s.session_id) not COUNT(*). After a LEFT JOIN, the NULL filled rows for unmatched spine entries would count as 1 in COUNT(*), making zero bins show 1. COUNT(non_null_source_col) ignores NULLs and lands at 0.
  • ORDER BY a numeric sort_order, not the label. ORDER BY b.bin sorts lexicographically — 15 or more would come before [0-5> because digit characters sort below bracket characters in ASCII. The integer sort_order column on the spine makes the output deterministic regardless of label format.
  • duration::numeric / 60 is the safe cast. If duration is INT, integer division by 60 truncates (a 299 second session yields 4, not 4.98), but BOTH map to the [0-5> bin so the answer happens to be right. For a 599 second session, integer 599/60 = 9 (lands in [5-10>) vs numeric 599/60 = 9.98 (also [5-10>). Edge cases where integer truncation crosses a bin boundary (e.g. 600 / 60 = 10 vs 600/60.0 = 10.0) land in the same bin since the comparison is < not <=, but casting to numeric removes the cognitive load entirely.
  • COALESCE(COUNT(...), 0) is redundant. COUNT never returns NULL on an empty group; it returns 0. Harmless to keep but a stricter reviewer would remove it.
Procedures

Non-SELECT problem shapes that some practice platforms include but most analytical SQL drills skip. Five topics live here: Procedural Blocks (anonymous DO $$ ... END $$; blocks that mutate state row by row or via sequential UPDATEs), Functions (CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION wrappers that return a scalar value or a table), Recursive Queries (WITH RECURSIVE for hierarchies, paths, and chains of unknown depth), Updates, Deletes, and Inserts (single-statement DML with conditional logic and confirming SELECTs), and Window Function Edges (frame and ranking nuances that flip answers). Each topic opens with a Reference card covering methods and pitfalls, followed by recipe cards with anchor problems.

Scaffolds Quick Code Scaffolds (paste-ready starters for each method)

▼

Five canonical structures: when you open a problem and recognize the shape, copy the matching scaffold and fill in the named slots. Order is roughly difficulty/frequency: DML → DO sequential → DO row-by-row → RETURNS scalar → RETURNS TABLE.

1. DML (single UPDATE / DELETE / INSERT)

When to use: the prompt says "write a single UPDATE statement" / "write a DELETE that ..." / "INSERT into archive ...". One statement, often with CASE WHEN for tiered logic, followed by a confirming SELECT.

-- UPDATE shape (tiered with CASE)
UPDATE <target_table>
   SET <col> = CASE
                 WHEN <condition_a> THEN <value_a>
                 WHEN <condition_b> THEN <value_b>
                 ELSE <col>
               END
 WHERE <optional_filter_for_rows_to_touch>;

-- DELETE shape (dedup keeping smallest pk per group)
DELETE FROM <target_table>
 WHERE <pk> NOT IN (
   SELECT MIN(<pk>) FROM <target_table> GROUP BY <group_cols>
 );

-- INSERT shape (archive matching rows with derived columns)
INSERT INTO <archive_table> (<col_list>)
SELECT
    <passthrough_cols>,
    <computed_col_1>  AS <name_1>,
    <computed_col_2>  AS <name_2>,
    CURRENT_TIMESTAMP AS archived_at
FROM <source_table>
WHERE <eligibility_filter>;

-- Trailing confirming SELECT
SELECT * FROM <target_table> ORDER BY <pk>;

2. DO block — Simple Sequential UPDATEs (set-based, NO loop)

When to use: the prompt gives 2-4 ordered rules where each rule's condition lives entirely on the row being updated and ordering the UPDATEs is enough. Self-test: "Could I rewrite this as a single UPDATE with CASE WHEN?" If yes, set-based.

DO $$
BEGIN
  UPDATE <target_table>
     SET <col> = <value_a>
   WHERE <condition_a>;

  UPDATE <target_table>
     SET <col> = <value_b>
   WHERE <condition_b>;

  UPDATE <target_table>
     SET <other_col> = <col> * <multiplier>
   WHERE <tier_condition>;
END $$;

SELECT * FROM <target_table> ORDER BY <pk>;

3. DO block — Row-by-Row State Mutation (FOR LOOP, per-iteration state read)

When to use: the prompt hands you a queue/event log AND each event must read the row's CURRENT state because earlier events changed it. Branching on event type AND current state. Self-test: "If I ran rule A and rule B in different orders, would I need to look up the latest value of the row in between?" If yes, FOR LOOP.

DO $$
DECLARE
   r              RECORD;
   current_status INT;
   current_owner  INT;
BEGIN
   FOR r IN
     SELECT * FROM <event_log_table> ORDER BY <sequence_col>
   LOOP
     SELECT <state_col_1>, <state_col_2>
       INTO current_status, current_owner
     FROM <state_table>
     WHERE <state_pk> = r.<event_fk>;

     IF r.<event_type> = <type_a> AND current_status = <precondition_a> THEN
        UPDATE <state_table>
           SET <col> = <new_value>,
               <owner_col> = r.<actor_col>
         WHERE <state_pk> = r.<event_fk>;
     ELSIF r.<event_type> = <type_b> AND current_status IN (<precondition_b1>, <precondition_b2>) THEN
        UPDATE <state_table>
           SET <col> = <reset_value>,
               <owner_col> = NULL
         WHERE <state_pk> = r.<event_fk>;
     END IF;

     -- Optional cleanup: mark this event processed (after END IF, before END LOOP)
     UPDATE <event_log_table>
        SET is_processed = TRUE
      WHERE <event_pk> = r.<event_pk>;
   END LOOP;
END $$;

SELECT * FROM <state_table> ORDER BY <state_pk>;

4. RETURNS scalar function (one value back)

When to use: the prompt names a function that returns one number, boolean, or text value (rate, count, sum, max). Body uses RETURN ( ... ); NOT RETURN QUERY.

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION <fn_name>(p_arg1 <TYPE1>, p_arg2 <TYPE2>)
RETURNS <NUMERIC|INT|BOOLEAN|VARCHAR> AS $$
BEGIN
   RETURN (
     WITH base AS (
       SELECT
         <col_1>,
         <col_2>,
         CASE WHEN <condition> THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END AS flag
       FROM <source_table>
       WHERE <filter_using_p_args>
     )
     SELECT COALESCE(
              ROUND(AVG(flag) * 100, 2),
              0.00
            )
     FROM base
   );
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

SELECT <fn_name>(<arg1>, <arg2>) AS result;

5. RETURNS TABLE function (row set back)

When to use: the prompt names a function that returns multiple rows (and usually multiple columns). Body uses RETURN QUERY ( ... );. Cast every output column to the declared type to dodge "structure of query does not match function result type."

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION <fn_name>(p_arg1 <TYPE1>, p_arg2 <TYPE2>)
RETURNS TABLE (
    <out_col_1>  INT,
    <out_col_2>  VARCHAR(100),
    <out_col_3>  DATE,
    <out_col_4>  NUMERIC(10,2)
) AS $$
BEGIN
   RETURN QUERY (
     WITH base AS (
       SELECT
         t.<col_1>,
         t.<col_2>,
         t.<col_3>,
         <computed_expr> AS <derived_col>
       FROM <source_table> AS t
       WHERE <filter_using_p_args>
     )
     SELECT
       b.<col_1>::INT,
       b.<col_2>::VARCHAR(100),
       b.<col_3>::DATE,
       b.<derived_col>::NUMERIC(10,2)
     FROM base AS b
     WHERE b.<derived_col> >= p_arg1
     ORDER BY b.<col_1> ASC, b.<col_3> ASC
   );
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

SELECT * FROM <fn_name>(<arg1>, <arg2>);

Quick decision guide

Prompt signal Reach for Body keyword
"Write a single UPDATE / DELETE / INSERT statement" DML (#1) N/A — bare statement
"Apply these rules in order; each rule's condition lives on the row itself" DO sequential (#2) DO $$ BEGIN ... END $$;
"Process the events/queue in order; each event reads the row's current state" DO row-by-row (#3) FOR ... LOOP / SELECT INTO
"Function returns a single value (rate, count, max, ...)" RETURNS scalar (#4) RETURN ( ... );
"Function returns multiple rows / a table of results" RETURNS TABLE (#5) RETURN QUERY ( ... );

Index Procedural Problem Types Generated by the Practice Notebook

▼

The seven question types the practice notebook can generate, what each one looks like, and how to spot them in a prompt.

Select Analytical PostgreSQL or MySQL
When you'll see it

Standard analytical question (filter, aggregate, join, window) — baseline shape.

What you write

A SELECT or CTE that returns the requested rows.

SELECT col, AGG(...)
FROM t
WHERE cond
GROUP BY col;
DO Block (sequential UPDATE) PostgreSQL only
When you'll see it

Prompt says "apply these requests in order" or "after the requests have been performed, return the table." Often involves per-row state checks.

What you write

A DO $$ ... $$; block with a FOR loop and conditional UPDATEs, plus a trailing SELECT.

DO $$
DECLARE r RECORD;
BEGIN
  FOR r IN SELECT * FROM requests
           ORDER BY request_id LOOP
    -- conditional UPDATE
  END LOOP;
END $$;
SELECT * FROM target ORDER BY id;
RETURNS TABLE Function PostgreSQL only
When you'll see it

Prompt names a function like getNthHighestSalary(N) and the IDE pre-fills a CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION ... RETURNS TABLE scaffold.

What you write

Fill in the inner SELECT or CTE inside RETURN QUERY ( ... );. Alias the table to avoid column shadowing.

RETURNS TABLE (Salary INT) AS $$
BEGIN
  RETURN QUERY (
    SELECT e.salary FROM Employee e ...
  );
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;
RETURNS Scalar Function PostgreSQL only
When you'll see it

Prompt asks for a single value (count, max, ratio) returned from a named function.

What you write

Use plain RETURN, not RETURN QUERY.

RETURNS INT AS $$
BEGIN
  RETURN ( SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ... );
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;
Recursive CTE PostgreSQL or MySQL 8+
When you'll see it

Hierarchy traversal (employees / managers, parent / child), path enumeration, or running calculations over a chain.

What you write

A self-referencing CTE: anchor query UNION ALL'd with a recursive step.

WITH RECURSIVE cte AS (
  -- anchor
  SELECT ... FROM t WHERE ...
  UNION ALL
  -- recursive step
  SELECT ... FROM t JOIN cte ON ...
)
SELECT * FROM cte;
UPDATE / DELETE / INSERT (mutating the table) PostgreSQL or MySQL
When you'll see it

Prompt mutates a table directly with conditions; final SELECT confirms the result.

What you write

One or more UPDATE, DELETE, or INSERT statements followed by SELECT * FROM target ORDER BY ...;.

UPDATE target SET col = expr WHERE cond;
SELECT * FROM target ORDER BY id;
Window Function Edge Cases PostgreSQL or MySQL 8+
When you'll see it

A normal-looking window problem where the choice between ROWS / RANGE or RANK / DENSE_RANK / ROW_NUMBER materially changes the answer.

What you write

A SELECT with a carefully chosen window frame.

... OVER (
  PARTITION BY group_col
  ORDER BY ts
  ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING
       AND CURRENT ROW
)

Procedural Blocks topic

▼
  • Anonymous DO $$ ... END $$; blocks for procedural logic.
  • Simple Sequential UPDATEs — reach for this when every rule's condition lives entirely on the row being updated and the order of UPDATEs alone keeps things consistent.
  • Row-by-Row State Mutation — reach for this when events arrive in a queue (event log) AND each event has to read the row's CURRENT state because earlier events may have changed it.
  • One-question test: "If I ran rule A and rule B in different orders, would I need to look up the latest value of the row in between?" — yes → loop, no → set-based.

When to reach for a FOR LOOP vs when to skip it

Set-based UPDATEs (no loop) work when every rule's condition can be checked using only columns on the row being updated, and ordering the UPDATEs is enough to keep things consistent. Loyalty points, shipment delays, tiered discounts — all this shape. WHERE priority_level = 'high' AND ... is all the engine needs; it handles "which rows match" in one pass per UPDATE.

Reach for a FOR LOOP when the prompt hands you an event or request log (a queue) AND each event has to read the current state of the target row because an earlier event in the queue may have just changed it. Airline seats, refund queue, cohort enrollment, content watch sessions — two tables (state + queue), and SELECT INTO pulls fresh state into scalars every iteration.

One-question test: "If I ran rule A and rule B in different orders, would I need to look up the latest value of the row in between?" If yes, you need a loop. If no, set-based UPDATEs in the right order are enough.

Reference Methods & Pitfalls

▼

The five building blocks of a DO block: DO $$ wrapper, DECLARE, FOR ... LOOP, SELECT INTO, and IF / ELSIF.

DO $$ ... $$;

What it does
Runs an anonymous PL/pgSQL block: declare variables, run loops, call UPDATE in sequence as one unit.
When to reach for it
The prompt asks for sequential state mutation that can't be expressed as one SELECT (apply rules in order, iterate over requests, sequential UPDATE chains).
DO $$
BEGIN
  UPDATE t SET col = expr1;
  UPDATE t SET col = expr2 WHERE cond;
END $$;

SELECT * FROM t;

DECLARE ... RECORD;

What it does
Declares a variable to hold one row at a time inside a procedural block.
When to reach for it
You need to iterate through rows and reference whole-row attributes, e.g., r.seat_no, r.request_id.
DECLARE
  r RECORD;
  current_status INT;
BEGIN
  -- body
END;

FOR r IN SELECT ... LOOP

What it does
Iterates a result set row by row, binding each row to a record variable.
When to reach for it
The prompt requires processing rows in a specific order (e.g., requests by id) where each iteration's decision depends on prior iterations.
FOR r IN
  SELECT * FROM requests
  ORDER BY request_id
LOOP
  -- handle r
END LOOP;

SELECT col INTO var

What it does
Reads a single value from a SELECT into a variable inside a procedural block.
When to reach for it
You need to capture current state mid-loop before deciding whether to mutate (e.g., is the seat free right now?).
SELECT status INTO current_status
FROM seats
WHERE seat_no = r.seat_no;

IF / ELSIF / END IF

What it does
Procedural conditional branching inside a DO block or function.
When to reach for it
Different rules apply depending on a request type or current row state; the conditions are too complex for a single CASE.
IF cond1 THEN
  -- branch 1
ELSIF cond2 THEN
  -- branch 2
ELSE
  -- fallback
END IF;

Simple Sequential UPDATEs recipe

▼
  • Apply N rules in order to one table.
  • Each rule is a single UPDATE ... WHERE ... inside a DO $$ ... END $$; block.
  • No DECLARE, no FOR LOOP, no IF — the order of the UPDATEs is what makes it sequential.
  • Use this when each rule's condition lives entirely on the row being updated.

Signal words: "apply these adjustments in order," "after step N, ...," "round to two decimals at the end," "for every row in the table, do X then Y then Z."

Technique: DO $$ BEGIN UPDATE ... ; UPDATE ... ; UPDATE ... ; END $$; SELECT * FROM target ORDER BY ...;

Common pitfalls:

Pitfall How to avoid
Re-applying a rule to a row it already changed Add a guard predicate in the WHERE clause (e.g., tier <> 'platinum') so a row that already moved up does not re-match a later rule's filter and get reclassified.
Reading "after step N" as conditional "After step N" means temporally after — later rules still run even if step N did not match. Each rule has its own WHERE; do not nest them.
DECIMAL rounding flips a strict comparison A DECIMAL(10,2) column rounds intermediate UPDATE results, which can flip a strict > or < comparison on borderline values. Test edge data.
Reaching for a FOR LOOP unnecessarily If every rule's condition lives on the same row being updated, the set-based shape works. The loop is for cases where one row's mutation changes whether a different row qualifies, or where order across rows matters (use the row-by-row recipe).
Forgetting the trailing SELECT Without a final SELECT * FROM target ORDER BY ...; the harness sees no output and reports failure even when the mutations are correct. Also remember the ; after END $$.

Skeleton you'll fill in:

DO $$
BEGIN
  UPDATE target_table SET col_a = expr_a WHERE rule_1_predicate;
  UPDATE target_table SET col_b = expr_b WHERE rule_2_predicate AND guard_predicate;
  UPDATE target_table SET col_c = expr_c WHERE rule_3_predicate AND guard_predicate;
END $$;

-- Trailing SELECT so the test scaffold sees output:
SELECT * FROM target_table ORDER BY key;

Anchor problems — tiered discounts (chained percentage UPDATEs), driver shifts (rule chain on independent guard columns), loyalty points (set-based with guard predicates, plus a per-row variant for when guards are not enough).

Easy Sequential Price Updates with Tiered Discounts

▼

A simpler DO block anchor: apply a fixed sequence of UPDATE statements to the same table without any per-row loop. Useful for problems where the rule order matters but each rule is a single set-based UPDATE.

Tables: products (id, category, base_price, final_price)

Prompt: Apply the following rules in sequence, then return the updated table.

  1. Set final_price = base_price for all rows.
  2. Apply a 10% discount (multiply final_price by 0.90) to all Electronics products.
  3. Apply an additional 5% discount (multiply final_price by 0.95) to all products where final_price > 100 after the previous step.
  4. Round all final_price values to 2 decimal places.
▶ 1 DO block with set-based UPDATEs (no per-row loop)
DO $$ BEGIN UPDATE products SET final_price = base_price; UPDATE products SET final_price = final_price * 0.90 WHERE category = 'Electronics'; UPDATE products SET final_price = final_price * 0.95 WHERE final_price > 100; UPDATE products SET final_price = ROUND(final_price, 2); END $$; SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY id;

Why this is best: Each rule is a single set-based UPDATE inside the DO block, applied in the exact order written. Postgres treats the four UPDATEs as one procedural unit, so each rule sees the result of the previous one. The trailing SELECT gives the test harness its output.

Differences from the airline seats pattern:

  • No DECLARE needed — there are no variables.
  • No FOR ... LOOP — every UPDATE is set-based.
  • No IF / ELSIF — conditions live in WHERE clauses on each UPDATE.
  • This is the right shape when the prompt is "apply N rules in order to one table," not "iterate through a list of requests."

Watch out:

  • "Where final_price > 100 after the previous step" means the comparison runs against the value sitting in final_price at that moment, not the original base_price.
  • If the column is DECIMAL(10,2), intermediate rounding can flip strict > comparisons. Test borderline values.
  • Don't forget the trailing ; after END $$.

Easy Apply Driver Shift Performance Adjustments

▼

Same set-based shape as tiered discounts, applied to a ride-share payout table. Three sequential UPDATEs, each one reading the value left behind by the previous rule.

Tables: driver_shifts (shift_id, driver_name, hours_worked, completed_trips, acceptance_rate, base_payout)

Prompt: Apply the following rules to driver_shifts in order, then return the updated table sorted by shift_id.

  1. If completed_trips >= 15, multiply base_payout by 1.20 (a 20% bonus).
  2. After step 1, if acceptance_rate < 0.75, multiply base_payout by 0.85 (a 15% penalty).
  3. After step 2, if hours_worked > 10, add a flat $25 bonus to base_payout.
▶ 1 Three set-based UPDATEs in a DO block
DO $$ BEGIN UPDATE driver_shifts SET base_payout = base_payout * 1.20 WHERE completed_trips >= 15; UPDATE driver_shifts SET base_payout = base_payout * 0.85 WHERE acceptance_rate < 0.75; UPDATE driver_shifts SET base_payout = base_payout + 25 WHERE hours_worked > 10; END $$; SELECT * FROM driver_shifts ORDER BY shift_id;

Why this is best: Every rule is a single set-based UPDATE that filters on a column the prior rule did not change (completed_trips, acceptance_rate, hours_worked). So the order of UPDATEs only affects the cumulative base_payout, not which rows match. No DECLARE, no FOR LOOP, no IF.

Watch out:

  • base_payout is DECIMAL(10,2). Two multiplicative UPDATEs in a row can introduce penny-level rounding. Test borderline values if the prompt depends on a strict > or < comparison against payout.
  • If a future variant adds a rule that filters on base_payout itself, the set-based shape still works — just remember the filter sees the value after prior UPDATEs, not the original.
  • Trailing ; after END $$, and a trailing SELECT so the harness has output.

Medium Loyalty Points Sequential Tier Adjustment

▼

Three rules where each rule's filter depends on a column an earlier rule just changed (tier). Solvable with set-based UPDATEs only if you add a guard so a row that already moved up does not get reclassified.

Tables: member_accounts (member_id, member_name, current_points, tier)

Prompt: Apply the following rules to member_accounts in order, then return the table sorted by member_id.

  1. If current_points >= 5000, set tier = 'platinum' and deduct 500 points.
  2. After step 1, if current_points >= 2000 AND tier <> 'platinum', set tier = 'gold' and deduct 200 points.
  3. After step 2, if current_points < 500 AND tier <> 'bronze', set tier = 'bronze' and add 100 points.
▶ 1 Set-based UPDATEs with guard predicates
DO $$ BEGIN UPDATE member_accounts SET tier = 'platinum', current_points = current_points - 500 WHERE current_points >= 5000; UPDATE member_accounts SET tier = 'gold', current_points = current_points - 200 WHERE current_points >= 2000 AND tier <> 'platinum'; UPDATE member_accounts SET tier = 'bronze', current_points = current_points + 100 WHERE current_points < 500 AND tier <> 'bronze'; END $$; SELECT * FROM member_accounts ORDER BY member_id;

Why the guards matter: The platinum UPDATE drops points by 500. Without tier <> 'platinum' on rule 2, a member that just became platinum at 5300 points would land at 4800 and re-match the gold rule (current_points >= 2000), demoting them. The guard pins each row to the highest tier it qualified for in this pass.

Watch out:

  • Reading "set tier to X if current_points satisfies condition" without a tier guard is the trap. Always ask: could a row that already mutated still match a later rule's WHERE?
  • The bronze rule uses current_points < 500. After the gold UPDATE, a row that started at 2400 now sits at 2200 — it does not match. But a row that started at 600 with no tier change drops nowhere from rule 1 or 2 and stays eligible for rule 3.
  • Trailing SELECT * FROM member_accounts ORDER BY member_id; after END $$; so the harness sees output.
▶ 2 Per-row FOR LOOP with IF blocks (when guards are not enough)
DO $$ DECLARE rec RECORD; curr_points INT; curr_tier VARCHAR(20); BEGIN FOR rec IN SELECT member_id FROM member_accounts ORDER BY member_id LOOP SELECT current_points, tier INTO curr_points, curr_tier FROM member_accounts WHERE member_id = rec.member_id; IF curr_points >= 5000 THEN UPDATE member_accounts SET tier = 'platinum', current_points = current_points - 500 WHERE member_id = rec.member_id; END IF; SELECT current_points, tier INTO curr_points, curr_tier FROM member_accounts WHERE member_id = rec.member_id; IF curr_points >= 2000 AND curr_tier <> 'platinum' THEN UPDATE member_accounts SET tier = 'gold', current_points = current_points - 200 WHERE member_id = rec.member_id; END IF; SELECT current_points, tier INTO curr_points, curr_tier FROM member_accounts WHERE member_id = rec.member_id; IF curr_points < 500 AND curr_tier <> 'bronze' THEN UPDATE member_accounts SET tier = 'bronze', current_points = current_points + 100 WHERE member_id = rec.member_id; END IF; END LOOP; END $$; SELECT * FROM member_accounts ORDER BY member_id;

When you actually need this: If the prompt says "process rows in a specific order and the result for row N depends on what just happened to row M," the loop is required. The set-based version above only works because each row's three rules read and write that row's own columns. A loop is also the right fall back if you cannot construct a clean guard predicate.

How to spot the loop case: The prompt names a specific iteration order ("for each member, in order"), or one row's outcome would change another row's eligibility. If neither holds, prefer the set-based version — it is shorter and ships fewer round trips between the procedural body and the table.

Easy Update Delayed Shipment Priority Levels

▼

Two set-based UPDATEs that promote rows up a priority ladder for delayed shipments. Order of UPDATEs matters — the higher-tier promotion runs first so freshly-promoted rows do not get double-promoted. Includes the current_date reserved-keyword trap.

Tables:

Column Type Notes
shipment_idINTprimary key
tracking_numberVARCHARpassthrough
