scheduled_delivery_dateDATEdelay reference point
actual_delivery_dateDATENULL means undelivered (shipment can be delayed)
priority_levelVARCHAR'standard' | 'high' | 'critical'

Prompt: Assume the current date is '2024-01-15'. A shipment is "delayed" when actual_delivery_date IS NULL AND the current date is more than 2 days past scheduled_delivery_date. For every delayed shipment:

  • If priority is 'high', promote it to 'critical'.
  • If priority is 'standard', promote it to 'high'.
  • 'critical' stays 'critical'.
▶ 1 Two set-based UPDATEs in a DO block, highest tier first
DO $$ DECLARE v_today DATE := '2024-01-15'; BEGIN -- Promote 'high' to 'critical' FIRST. This must run before the standard-to-high -- UPDATE, otherwise rows that just became 'high' would get double-promoted. UPDATE shipments SET priority_level = 'critical' WHERE priority_level = 'high' AND actual_delivery_date IS NULL AND v_today > scheduled_delivery_date + INTERVAL '2 days'; -- Promote 'standard' to 'high' second. The first UPDATE has already finished, -- so the rows that just became 'critical' are NOT in the 'standard' set. UPDATE shipments SET priority_level = 'high' WHERE priority_level = 'standard' AND actual_delivery_date IS NULL AND v_today > scheduled_delivery_date + INTERVAL '2 days'; END $$; SELECT * FROM shipments ORDER BY shipment_id;

Why no FOR LOOP is needed: Both rules check columns that live on the row being updated (priority_level, actual_delivery_date, scheduled_delivery_date). Promoting one row never affects whether a different row qualifies. So set-based UPDATEs in the right order are enough — passes the "one-question test" at the top of this topic.

Why order matters:

  • Run standard → high first and a delayed standard shipment becomes high. Then the second UPDATE (high → critical) sees it and double-promotes it to critical. Wrong.
  • Run high → critical first. The freshly-critical rows are no longer 'high'. The second UPDATE only sees the original standards and promotes them to high. Correct.
  • Same shape as the loyalty points anchor: when a chain of UPDATEs walks rows up a tier ladder, do the topmost promotion first or use a guard predicate.

Two traps that look right but break this problem:

  • Naming a variable current_date. current_date is a reserved keyword in Postgres that returns today's actual date. A local variable with the same name is silently ignored — the engine substitutes the keyword. Comparisons like "today (2026) > scheduled (2024) + 2 days" then evaluate as TRUE for everything, and rows that should not have been delayed get promoted anyway. Rename to something unambiguous like v_today.
  • Reading "more than 2 days past" as >=. "More than" is strict >. A shipment scheduled exactly 2 days ago does NOT qualify. Using >= would silently flip a row that should stay unchanged.

Trace through the example data (today = 2024-01-15):

id priority before delivered? scheduled days late delayed? priority after
1highno2024-01-105yescritical
2standardno2024-01-123yeshigh
3standardyes (2024-01-14)2024-01-14—no (delivered)standard
4criticalno2024-01-114yescritical (no rule)
5highno2024-01-132no (not > 2)high (unchanged)
6standardno2024-01-087yeshigh

Watch out:

  • Use a v_ prefix (or any non-keyword name) for variables. Postgres has many reserved words: current_date, current_time, current_user, session_user, localtime, localtimestamp, etc.
  • Trailing SELECT * FROM shipments ORDER BY shipment_id; after END $$; so the harness has output to compare.
  • Even though the prompt asks for a DO block, no DECLARE-of-record + FOR LOOP is required. Reach for the loop only when the topic-level decision rule says you must.

Row-by-Row State Mutation recipe

▼
  • Iterate a request queue strictly in ID order.
  • Inside the loop, read the target row's current state into scalar variables.
  • Branch on event type and state with IF / ELSIF.
  • Issue a scoped UPDATE based on which branch matched.
  • Use this when the result for one row depends on the latest state of that same row, or when one row's mutation changes whether a later request is valid.

Signal words: "return the table after the requests have been performed," "apply these updates in order," "process each request from lowest id," "if the seat is free / reserved by this person, then..."

Technique: DO $$ DECLARE r RECORD; ... BEGIN FOR r IN SELECT * FROM requests ORDER BY id LOOP ... IF ... THEN UPDATE ... END IF; END LOOP; END $$; SELECT * FROM table ORDER BY ...;

Common pitfalls:

Pitfall How to avoid
Missing trailing SELECT Without a final SELECT * FROM table ORDER BY ...; the test panel's Return Value column is empty and the harness reports "Wrong answer" even when the table is correct.
Variables declared in wrong place All variables go in DECLARE before BEGIN. Use RECORD for loop rows, scalar types (e.g., INT) for captured fields.
Stale state inside loop SELECT col INTO var FROM ... reads the current state into your variable. Re-read inside each iteration if a prior iteration may have updated the same row.
Identifier case mismatch Lowercase function and column names match Postgres defaults. Mixed-case identifiers must be wrapped in double quotes.
Hard to drill on standard platforms Most analytical SQL practice platforms do not cover this shape. Practice on SQL Fiddle or DB Fiddle with custom schemas.

Skeleton you'll fill in:

DO $$
DECLARE
  r RECORD;
  current_state INT;
BEGIN
  FOR r IN SELECT * FROM requests ORDER BY request_id LOOP
    SELECT col INTO current_state
    FROM target_table
    WHERE key = r.key;

    IF some_condition_using_r_and_current_state THEN
      UPDATE target_table
      SET col = new_value
      WHERE key = r.key;
    END IF;
  END LOOP;
END $$;

-- Trailing SELECT so the test scaffold sees output:
SELECT * FROM target_table ORDER BY key;

Anchor problems — airline seats (queue + seat state), refund queue (queue + line state with amount guard), cohort enrollment (queue + two-column state guard), readmission severity (history lookup with self-gating downstream rules), content watch session (four-state FSM with viewer guard and progress cap).

Medium Airline Seats: apply reserve / purchase requests in order

▼

Anchor problem for the DO block recipe. Apply requests from lowest request_id upward. A reserve succeeds only if the seat is free; a purchase succeeds if the seat is free or already reserved by that same person.

Tables:

  • seats(seat_no, status, person_id) — status: 0 free, 1 reserved, 2 purchased.
  • requests(request_id, request, seat_no, person_id) — request: 1 reserve, 2 purchase.
▶ 1 DO block + FOR loop + IF / ELSIF + trailing SELECT
DO $$ DECLARE r RECORD; current_status INT; current_owner INT; BEGIN FOR r IN SELECT * FROM requests ORDER BY request_id LOOP SELECT status, person_id INTO current_status, current_owner FROM seats WHERE seat_no = r.seat_no; IF r.request = 1 AND current_status = 0 THEN UPDATE seats SET status = 1, person_id = r.person_id WHERE seat_no = r.seat_no; ELSIF r.request = 2 AND (current_status = 0 OR (current_status = 1 AND current_owner = r.person_id)) THEN UPDATE seats SET status = 2, person_id = r.person_id WHERE seat_no = r.seat_no; END IF; END LOOP; END $$; SELECT * FROM seats ORDER BY seat_no;

Line-by-line walkthrough:

Line What it does
DO $$ Opens an anonymous procedural block. Postgres treats everything between the dollar quotes as a single PL/pgSQL routine.
DECLARE Starts the variable declaration section. All variables used in the body must be declared here before BEGIN.
r RECORD; Declares r as a generic row type that will hold one request row at a time during the loop.
current_status INT;
current_owner INT;		 Two scalar variables that will hold the seat's current state (read fresh each iteration).
BEGIN Marks the start of the procedural body. Logic runs from here until END.
FOR r IN SELECT * FROM requests ORDER BY request_id LOOP Iterates through every request, one row at a time, in request_id order. The current request is bound to r on each pass.
SELECT status, person_id INTO current_status, current_owner FROM seats WHERE seat_no = r.seat_no; Reads the seat's current status and owner into the scalar variables. Done fresh each iteration so any update from a prior iteration is reflected.
IF r.request = 1 AND current_status = 0 THEN Reserve branch: only fires when the request is "reserve" (1) and the seat is currently free (0).
UPDATE seats SET status = 1, person_id = r.person_id WHERE seat_no = r.seat_no; Marks the seat reserved (status 1) and records the requester as the owner.
ELSIF r.request = 2 AND (current_status = 0 OR (current_status = 1 AND current_owner = r.person_id)) THEN Purchase branch: fires when the request is "purchase" (2) and the seat is either free, or already reserved by the same person making this request.
UPDATE seats SET status = 2, person_id = r.person_id WHERE seat_no = r.seat_no; Marks the seat purchased (status 2) and records the buyer as the owner.
END IF; Closes the IF/ELSIF block. Requests that match neither branch are silently ignored, which is what the prompt requires.
END LOOP; Closes the FOR loop. Returns to the next request until requests are exhausted.
END $$; Closes the procedural body and the DO block. The mutations to seats are now committed.
SELECT * FROM seats ORDER BY seat_no; Trailing SELECT so the test harness has output to compare against the expected table. Without this line the Return Value column is empty and the test fails.

Medium Process Refund Requests in Queue Order

▼

Same shape as airline seats: a state table plus a request queue, processed one request at a time in request_id order. The current row's status is read fresh each iteration so a state change from an earlier request affects whether a later request fires.

Tables:

Table Column Type Notes
refund_stateorder_line_idINTprimary key
statusVARCHAR(20)'none' | 'pending' | 'approved'
refundable_amountDECIMAL(10,2)decreases as approvals consume it
refund_requestsrequest_idINTprimary key, queue order
request_typeINT1 = initiate, 2 = approve, 3 = cancel
order_line_idINTFK into refund_state
customer_idINTpayload
requested_amountDECIMAL(10,2)amount to deduct on approve

Prompt: Iterate refund_requests in request_id order. For each request, read the current state of the referenced line and apply the matching rule.

  • If request_type = 1 AND current status = 'none': set status = 'pending'.
  • If request_type = 2 AND current status = 'pending' AND refundable_amount >= requested_amount: set status = 'approved' and subtract requested_amount from refundable_amount.
  • If request_type = 3 AND current status = 'pending': reset to 'none'.
  • Anything else is a no-op.
▶ 1 FOR loop + SELECT INTO + IF / ELSIF, mirroring airline seats
DO $$ DECLARE rec RECORD; cur_status VARCHAR(20); cur_refundable DECIMAL(10,2); BEGIN FOR rec IN SELECT * FROM refund_requests ORDER BY request_id LOOP SELECT status, refundable_amount INTO cur_status, cur_refundable FROM refund_state WHERE order_line_id = rec.order_line_id; IF rec.request_type = 1 AND cur_status = 'none' THEN UPDATE refund_state SET status = 'pending' WHERE order_line_id = rec.order_line_id; ELSIF rec.request_type = 2 AND cur_status = 'pending' AND cur_refundable >= rec.requested_amount THEN UPDATE refund_state SET status = 'approved', refundable_amount = refundable_amount - rec.requested_amount WHERE order_line_id = rec.order_line_id; ELSIF rec.request_type = 3 AND cur_status = 'pending' THEN UPDATE refund_state SET status = 'none' WHERE order_line_id = rec.order_line_id; END IF; END LOOP; END $$; SELECT * FROM refund_state ORDER BY order_line_id;

Why this is best: The FOR loop walks the queue strictly in request_id order. The SELECT INTO reads the current state freshly each iteration so the prior iteration's UPDATE is visible. Each IF / ELSIF branch checks both the request type and the current state, so a request that does not match any condition is silently a no-op — exactly the behavior the prompt requires.

Why a set-based UPDATE chain fails here:

  • Request 1 marks line 101 'pending'. Request 2 then approves it — this only works if request 1 already ran. A set-based UPDATE refund_state SET status='approved' WHERE ... can't see the intermediate 'pending' state because all UPDATEs would run against the original snapshot.
  • Request 4 (cancel on line 102) only fires if line 102 is currently 'pending', which it became from request 3. The order matters.
  • Request 6 (initiate on line 104) is a no-op because line 104 is already 'approved'. A set-based UPDATE with no state guard would wrongly reset it to 'pending'.

Trace through the example data:

request_id type line state read action resulting state
11 (initiate)101none, $50set 'pending'pending, $50
22 (approve)101pending, $50approve, $50 ≥ $50approved, $0
31 (initiate)102none, $100set 'pending'pending, $100
43 (cancel)102pending, $100reset to 'none'none, $100
52 (approve)103pending, $75approve, $75 ≥ $75approved, $0
61 (initiate)104approved, $0no match (status ≠ 'none')unchanged

Watch out:

  • refundable_amount is DECIMAL(10,2). The strict >= comparison can flip on borderline values if you pre-rounded the input. Trust the column's stored value, not a computed approximation.
  • Re-read state with SELECT INTO at the top of every iteration. Reading once before the loop and reusing the variables would miss the mutations made by earlier requests in the same run.
  • An UPDATE inside an IF branch must filter by WHERE order_line_id = rec.order_line_id; — not a global UPDATE.
  • Trailing ; after END $$, then a trailing SELECT * FROM refund_state ORDER BY order_line_id; so the harness sees output.

Medium Patient Cohort Enrollment DO Block Processor

▼

Same queue + state shape as airline seats and refund queue. The twist: the DISCHARGE rule guards on TWO state columns, so the iteration must read both enrollment_status and program_id fresh each pass.

Tables:

Table Column Type Notes
cohort_enrollmentspatient_idINTprimary key
enrollment_statusVARCHAR(20)'ACTIVE' | 'INACTIVE'
program_idINTNULL when INACTIVE
cohort_enrollment_requestsrequest_idINTprimary key, queue order
patient_idINTFK into cohort_enrollments
request_typeVARCHAR(20)'ENROLL' | 'TRANSFER' | 'DISCHARGE'
program_idINTtarget program for ENROLL/TRANSFER, must-match key for DISCHARGE

Prompt: Iterate cohort_enrollment_requests in request_id order. For each request, read the patient's current enrollment_status and program_id from cohort_enrollments, then apply the matching rule.

  • ENROLL AND current status is 'INACTIVE': set status to 'ACTIVE' and copy program_id from the request.
  • TRANSFER AND current status is 'ACTIVE': overwrite program_id with the request's value (status stays ACTIVE).
  • DISCHARGE AND current status is 'ACTIVE' AND current program_id equals the request's program_id: set status to 'INACTIVE' and clear program_id to NULL.
  • Anything else is a no-op.
▶ 1 FOR loop + per-iteration SELECT INTO + three-branch IF / ELSIF
DO $$ DECLARE r RECORD; current_status VARCHAR(20); current_program INT; BEGIN FOR r IN SELECT * FROM cohort_enrollment_requests ORDER BY request_id LOOP SELECT enrollment_status, program_id INTO current_status, current_program FROM cohort_enrollments WHERE patient_id = r.patient_id; IF r.request_type = 'ENROLL' AND current_status = 'INACTIVE' THEN UPDATE cohort_enrollments SET enrollment_status = 'ACTIVE', program_id = r.program_id WHERE patient_id = r.patient_id; ELSIF r.request_type = 'TRANSFER' AND current_status = 'ACTIVE' THEN UPDATE cohort_enrollments SET program_id = r.program_id WHERE patient_id = r.patient_id; ELSIF r.request_type = 'DISCHARGE' AND current_status = 'ACTIVE' AND current_program = r.program_id THEN UPDATE cohort_enrollments SET enrollment_status = 'INACTIVE', program_id = NULL WHERE patient_id = r.patient_id; END IF; END LOOP; END $$; SELECT * FROM cohort_enrollments ORDER BY patient_id;

Why this is best: Three branches, three guards. The DISCHARGE branch is the load-bearing one — it requires that the request's program_id matches the row's CURRENT program_id, not the original. So if a TRANSFER changed the program earlier in the queue, a later DISCHARGE that names the old program is correctly skipped.

Why a set-based UPDATE chain fails here:

  • A patient can be ENROLLED, then TRANSFERRED, then DISCHARGED in the same run. Each step depends on the prior step's mutation being visible.
  • A second ENROLL on a patient who is already ACTIVE must be a no-op. A set-based UPDATE without the current_status = 'INACTIVE' guard would clobber the existing program.
  • A DISCHARGE that names the wrong program (because a TRANSFER moved them) must be silently skipped. Only a fresh per-iteration read can catch that.

Watch out:

  • Two scalars in DECLARE, not one. Both current_status and current_program need to be re-read every iteration because either can change.
  • SELECT INTO requires the column order in the target list to match the variable order. Mixing them swaps the values silently.
  • The DISCHARGE branch's current_program = r.program_id guard will fail unexpectedly if current_program is NULL (NULL never equals anything). That is fine here because the status guard already excludes INACTIVE rows where program is NULL, but if the prompt allowed ACTIVE-with-NULL-program rows you'd need IS NOT DISTINCT FROM instead.
  • Trailing ; after END $$, then a trailing SELECT * FROM cohort_enrollments ORDER BY patient_id; so the harness sees output.

Medium Sequential Readmission Severity Update via DO Block

▼

One table only, but each iteration must look up the patient's prior discharge before applying the rules. Mixes a guarded UPDATE inside an IF with two self-gating UPDATEs whose WHERE clauses do the conditional work outside the IF.

Tables:

Column Type Notes
admission_idINTprimary key
patient_idINTgroups admissions across time
patient_ageINTused by rule 3
admission_dateDATEFOR loop sort key
discharge_dateDATENULL while still admitted
severity_scoreINTmutated by rules 1 and 3
high_riskBOOLEANflipped by rule 2

Prompt: Iterate patient_admissions in chronological order (admission_date, then admission_id). For each admission, apply these rules in order:

  • If the patient was discharged from a prior admission within 30 days of the current admission_date, increase severity_score by 10.
  • After rule 1, if severity_score > 75, set high_risk = TRUE.
  • After rule 2, if high_risk is TRUE AND patient_age > 65, increase severity_score by an additional 5.
  • "After rule N" means temporally after — rules 2 and 3 still run even if rule 1 did not fire.
▶ 1 FOR loop + history lookup + IF for rule 1, self-gating UPDATEs for rules 2 and 3
DO $$ DECLARE r RECORD; prior_discharge DATE; BEGIN FOR r IN SELECT * FROM patient_admissions ORDER BY admission_date, admission_id LOOP -- History lookup: most recent discharge for this patient before the current admission. SELECT MAX(discharge_date) INTO prior_discharge FROM patient_admissions WHERE patient_id = r.patient_id AND admission_date < r.admission_date; -- Rule 1: guarded by IF because the 30-day window only applies when prior_discharge exists. IF r.admission_date - prior_discharge <= 30 THEN UPDATE patient_admissions SET severity_score = severity_score + 10 WHERE admission_id = r.admission_id; END IF; -- Rule 2: self-gates via WHERE; runs every iteration regardless of rule 1. UPDATE patient_admissions SET high_risk = TRUE WHERE admission_id = r.admission_id AND severity_score > 75; -- Rule 3: self-gates via WHERE; runs every iteration regardless of rules 1 and 2. UPDATE patient_admissions SET severity_score = severity_score + 5 WHERE admission_id = r.admission_id AND high_risk = TRUE AND patient_age > 65; END LOOP; END $$; SELECT * FROM patient_admissions ORDER BY admission_id;

Why two shapes in the same loop body:

  • Rule 1's condition (a 30-day gap from a prior discharge) is data the row itself does not carry — you have to look it up. The result lives in a scalar variable, so the gate is a procedural IF.
  • Rules 2 and 3's conditions (severity_score > 75, high_risk = TRUE AND patient_age > 65) live entirely on the row being updated. The WHERE clause already filters them out when the condition fails, so no IF is needed.
  • Putting rules 2 and 3 inside the IF would silently drop them for any admission with no prior discharge — the test fails on those rows because high_risk never flips.

Trace through admission 5 (patient 101, age 72, severity 68, prior discharge 2024-01-30, current admission 2024-02-10):

Step What runs Row state after
Ahistory lookupprior_discharge = 2024-01-30
BIF gap 11 days ≤ 30 → rule 1 fires (+10)severity 78, high_risk FALSE
Crule 2 UPDATE; WHERE severity > 75 matchesseverity 78, high_risk TRUE
Drule 3 UPDATE; WHERE high_risk AND age > 65 matches (age 72)severity 83, high_risk TRUE

Trace through admission 6 (patient 103, age 58, severity 80, no prior admission):

Step What runs Row state after
Ahistory lookupprior_discharge = NULL
BIF NULL ≤ 30 → NULL, branch skippedseverity 80, high_risk FALSE
Crule 2 UPDATE; WHERE severity > 75 matchesseverity 80, high_risk TRUE
Drule 3 UPDATE; high_risk TRUE but age 58 — no matchseverity 80, high_risk TRUE

Watch out:

  • "After applying rule N" is a temporal phrase, not a conditional one. Rules 2 and 3 still run even when rule 1 did not.
  • A window function like LAG(discharge_date) OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ...) cannot sit inside a procedural IF condition. Use a separate SELECT MAX(discharge_date) INTO prior_discharge ... WHERE admission_date < r.admission_date first.
  • NULL minus a date is NULL, and IF NULL <= 30 evaluates as false, so admissions with no prior discharge correctly skip rule 1 with no extra IS NOT NULL guard.
  • Order the FOR loop by admission_date, admission_id. Sorting by admission_id alone happens to be equivalent for this dataset but the prompt asks for chronological order.
  • Each UPDATE filters by admission_id = r.admission_id to scope to the row currently being processed. Skip that scope and rules 2 and 3 will fire on every row in the table on every loop iteration.

Medium Content Watch Session Queue Processing

▼

Classic finite-state-machine queue: idle → watching → paused → watching → idle. Four event types, each guarded by current state and viewer ownership. The FINISH branch also accumulates a delta with a hard cap.

Tables:

Table Column Type Notes
content_itemsitem_idINTprimary key
viewer_idINTNULL when idle
watch_statusINT0=idle, 1=watching, 2=paused
completion_pctINT0–100, accumulated by FINISH
watch_eventsevent_idSERIALprimary key, queue order
item_idINTFK into content_items
viewer_idINTwho fired the event
event_typeINT1=START, 2=PAUSE, 3=RESUME, 4=FINISH
progress_deltaINTadded to completion_pct on FINISH

Prompt: Iterate watch_events in event_id order. For each event, read the item's current watch_status and viewer_id, then apply the matching transition.

  • START (1) AND status = 0: set status to 1, assign viewer_id from the event.
  • PAUSE (2) AND status = 1 AND current viewer matches event viewer: set status to 2.
  • RESUME (3) AND status = 2 AND current viewer matches: set status to 1.
  • FINISH (4) AND status = 1 AND current viewer matches: add progress_delta to completion_pct (cap at 100), set status to 0, clear viewer_id.
  • Anything else is a no-op.
▶ 1 FOR loop in event_id order + four IF / ELSIF transitions + LEAST cap
DO $$ DECLARE r RECORD; current_status INT; current_viewer INT; current_completion_pct INT; BEGIN FOR r IN SELECT * FROM watch_events ORDER BY event_id LOOP SELECT watch_status, viewer_id, completion_pct INTO current_status, current_viewer, current_completion_pct FROM content_items WHERE item_id = r.item_id; IF r.event_type = 1 AND current_status = 0 THEN UPDATE content_items SET watch_status = 1, viewer_id = r.viewer_id WHERE item_id = r.item_id; ELSIF r.event_type = 2 AND current_status = 1 AND current_viewer = r.viewer_id THEN UPDATE content_items SET watch_status = 2 WHERE item_id = r.item_id; ELSIF r.event_type = 3 AND current_status = 2 AND current_viewer = r.viewer_id THEN UPDATE content_items SET watch_status = 1 WHERE item_id = r.item_id; ELSIF r.event_type = 4 AND current_status = 1 AND current_viewer = r.viewer_id THEN UPDATE content_items SET watch_status = 0, completion_pct = LEAST(completion_pct + r.progress_delta, 100), viewer_id = NULL WHERE item_id = r.item_id; END IF; END LOOP; END $$; SELECT * FROM content_items ORDER BY item_id;

Why this is best: Four state transitions, four guarded branches. The viewer guard (current_viewer = r.viewer_id) prevents user B from pausing or finishing user A's session. The LEAST(completion_pct + r.progress_delta, 100) caps cumulative progress so a delta that overshoots saturates instead of overflowing.

Two traps that look right but break this problem:

  • Wrong sort key in the FOR loop. Ordering by item_id instead of event_id processes events grouped by item, in undefined order within an item. A FINISH that fires before its START in that ordering becomes a no-op (status still 0), then the START runs and leaves the row as "watching" forever. Always order by the queue's monotonic key.
  • Procedural IF inside an UPDATE's SET clause. Trying to write SET completion_pct = IF current_completion_pct < 100 THEN ... END IF raises a syntax error. SET only accepts column = expression pairs — use CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END as the expression, or use LEAST(...) for a cap.

Watch out:

  • The PAUSE, RESUME, and FINISH branches do NOT need to overwrite viewer_id; the current viewer stays the same. Only START assigns it; only FINISH clears it.
  • If the viewer guard is omitted on FINISH, a different viewer's FINISH event would close someone else's session and credit progress to the wrong row. The guard is part of correctness, not just defensiveness.
  • An empty UPDATE ... SET watch_status = 1 with no other columns is fine. PostgreSQL does not require you to list every changing column.
  • Reading three scalars in one SELECT INTO is one round trip per iteration; the column order in the SELECT list must match the variable order or values get swapped silently.
  • Trailing ; after END $$, then a trailing SELECT * FROM content_items ORDER BY item_id; so the harness sees output.

Medium Sequential Medication Dose Adjustments

▼

Priority-ordered queue with three operation types — increase and decrease compose multiplicatively, while set overrides whatever the prior operations produced. Adjustments are flagged processed inside the loop. No SELECT INTO needed because each branch is a plain UPDATE that re-reads the row's current value.

Tables:

Table Column Type Notes
medication_ordersorder_idINTprimary key, target of adjustments
patient_idINTunused by mutation
medication_nameVARCHAR(100)unused by mutation
current_daily_doseDECIMAL(10,2)value mutated each iteration
dose_unitVARCHAR(20)passthrough
pending_adjustmentsadjustment_idINTprimary key
order_idINTFK into medication_orders
operation_typeVARCHAR(20)'increase' / 'decrease' / 'set'
adjustment_factorDECIMAL(10,2)multiplier, divisor, or replacement value
adjustment_priorityINTloop ORDER BY column — lowest first
is_processedBOOLEANflipped to TRUE inside the loop

Prompt: Iterate pending_adjustments in adjustment_priority order (lowest first). For each row, apply the operation to the matching medication_orders.current_daily_dose:

  • 'increase': multiply current_daily_dose by adjustment_factor.
  • 'decrease': divide current_daily_dose by adjustment_factor.
  • 'set': replace current_daily_dose with adjustment_factor.

After applying the operation, mark that adjustment is_processed = TRUE. Trailing SELECT * FROM medication_orders ORDER BY order_id;.

▶ 1 FOR LOOP ordered by priority + branchy UPDATE + mark-processed inside loop
DO $$ DECLARE r RECORD; BEGIN FOR r IN SELECT * FROM pending_adjustments ORDER BY adjustment_priority LOOP IF r.operation_type = 'increase' THEN UPDATE medication_orders SET current_daily_dose = current_daily_dose * r.adjustment_factor WHERE order_id = r.order_id; ELSIF r.operation_type = 'decrease' THEN UPDATE medication_orders SET current_daily_dose = current_daily_dose / r.adjustment_factor WHERE order_id = r.order_id; ELSIF r.operation_type = 'set' THEN UPDATE medication_orders SET current_daily_dose = r.adjustment_factor WHERE order_id = r.order_id; END IF; UPDATE pending_adjustments SET is_processed = TRUE WHERE adjustment_id = r.adjustment_id; END LOOP; END $$; SELECT * FROM medication_orders ORDER BY order_id;

Three patterns this anchor adds to the Row-by-Row State Mutation recipe:

  • ORDER BY the priority column, not the surrogate id. The prompt explicitly orders by adjustment_priority, not adjustment_id. On example data the two columns happen to be aligned, so iterating by adjustment_id still passes — but on test data with reshuffled priorities, a 'set' ordered last by priority but middle by id would land in the wrong slot and the final dose would be wrong. Always order by the column the prompt names.
  • FOR LOOP without SELECT INTO. Earlier anchors (airline seats, content watch) capture state into scalar variables because each branch GUARDS on the row's current state. Here every branch is a plain UPDATE with no state guard — the only thing that varies per branch is which arithmetic to apply. UPDATE implicitly re-reads the row each time, so the prior iteration's effect is already visible without a manual SELECT col INTO var step.
  • Mark-processed UPDATE belongs after END IF, not inside a branch. Putting the cleanup UPDATE inside the 'set' branch only marks 'set' rows; putting it before END LOOP; but after END IF; marks every row regardless of which branch fired. The WHERE adjustment_id = r.adjustment_id filter targets only the current iteration's row — without it, every iteration would mark every adjustment, which works on the final state but is wasteful and obscures intent.

Trace through the example data (4 orders, 4 adjustments):

priority order_id op factor dose before dose after
11 (Metformin)increase1.501000.001500.00
22 (Lisinopril)decrease2.0010.005.00
31 (Metformin)set2000.001500.002000.00 (override)
43 (Atorvastatin)increase2.0020.0040.00

Final doses: Metformin 2000.00, Lisinopril 5.00, Atorvastatin 40.00, Levothyroxine 50.00 (no adjustment).

Watch out:

  • 'set' must come AFTER 'increase' and 'decrease' to override. The priority field encodes the intended order. If priority 3 is a 'set' and priority 1–2 are 'increase'/'decrease', the multiplicative ops fire first and the 'set' overwrites them. Reordering would silently change the answer.
  • The mark-processed UPDATE without WHERE is the easy bug. UPDATE pending_adjustments SET is_processed = TRUE with no WHERE sets every row in the table to TRUE on every iteration — the final state is correct, but if the harness checks pending_adjustments per iteration (or if a future requirement adds a partial-failure rollback), the bug surfaces. Always anchor the cleanup UPDATE to WHERE adjustment_id = r.adjustment_id.
  • DECIMAL(10,2) rounds intermediate values. Each UPDATE's result is stored back into a DECIMAL(10,2) column, so values are rounded to 2 decimals between iterations. A sequence like increase * 1.333 then decrease / 1.333 won't return to the original because the intermediate is rounded; the prompt should be designed so this rounding doesn't matter.
  • No-op when order_id doesn't match. If a pending_adjustments.order_id points to a non-existent order, the UPDATE ... WHERE order_id = r.order_id updates zero rows and silently moves on. That's correct behavior here, but worth noting if the prompt expects an error in that case.
  • Trailing ; after END $$, then SELECT * FROM medication_orders ORDER BY order_id; so the harness sees the post-mutation snapshot.

Medium Apply Sequential No-Show Penalties (compounding state mutation)

▼
  • FOR LOOP iterating an event log (appointments) to mutate state in a parent table (patients).
  • Each iteration's contribution depends on the patient's CURRENT penalty_points value, so the increment compounds (doubles plus 1) instead of staying linear.
  • Demonstrates the linear vs compounding distinction: same surface prompt language, very different math.

Tables:

Table Column Type Notes
patientspatient_idINTprimary key, target of mutation
patient_nameVARCHAR(100)passthrough
penalty_pointsINT DEFAULT 0value mutated on each no-show; pre-existing values count as the patient's "starting state"
appointmentsappointment_idINTprimary key
patient_idINTFK into patients
scheduled_atTIMESTAMPloop ORDER BY column — chronological
statusVARCHAR(20)'completed' / 'no_show' / etc.; only 'no_show' triggers mutation

Prompt: Iterate appointments in scheduled_at order. For each row where status = 'no_show', increment that patient's penalty_points using the rule that each no-show contributes (prior penalty + 1) — meaning the patient's current penalty_points value is treated as the running prior count. Trailing SELECT * FROM patients ORDER BY patient_id;.

▶ 1 FOR LOOP + IF status filter + compounding UPDATE (2x+1)
DO $$ DECLARE r RECORD; BEGIN FOR r IN SELECT * FROM appointments ORDER BY scheduled_at LOOP IF r.status = 'no_show' THEN UPDATE patients SET penalty_points = 2 * penalty_points + 1 WHERE patient_id = r.patient_id; END IF; END LOOP; END $$; SELECT * FROM patients ORDER BY patient_id;

Why 2 * penalty_points + 1 matches the expected output:

  • The rule says "increment by (prior count + 1)." If you treat the patient's current penalty_points as the prior count: new = old + (old + 1) = 2 * old + 1.
  • Algebraically equivalent forms: penalty_points + (penalty_points + 1), 2 * penalty_points + 1, (2 * penalty_points) + 1. All three give the same answer.
  • Since the rule reads the column as part of the increment, you don't need a SELECT INTO variable — the UPDATE itself reads the current value and writes the new one in one statement.

Linear vs compounding (the trap):

Approach Formula Bob's path (start 1, 2 no-shows) Final
Linear (external counter)new = old + counter (counter starts at 0, increments by 1)1 → 1+1=2 → 2+2=44 (wrong)
Linear (counter from existing penalty)new = old + counter (counter starts at existing penalty)1 → 1+2=3 → 3+3=66 (still wrong)
Compounding (current value as count)new = 2 * old + 11 → 2(1)+1=3 → 2(3)+1=77 (correct)

Trace through the example data (scheduled_at order):

appointment_id patient_id status patient before UPDATE fires? patient after
1011 AlicecompletedAlice 0noAlice 0
1022 Bobno_showBob 1yesBob 2(1)+1 = 3
1031 Aliceno_showAlice 0yesAlice 2(0)+1 = 1
1043 CarolcompletedCarol 0noCarol 0
1051 Aliceno_showAlice 1yesAlice 2(1)+1 = 3
1062 Bobno_showBob 3yesBob 2(3)+1 = 7

Final: Alice 3, Bob 7, Carol 0.

Linear vs compounding cheatsheet:

  • Linear formula: new = old + k. Add a fixed amount each step. After n steps: start + n*k.
  • Compounding formula (pure): new = old * r. Multiply by a fixed ratio each step. After n steps: start * r^n.
  • Compounding with offset: new = old * r + k. The no-show formula uses r=2, k=1 → new = 2 * old + 1.
  • Spotting compounding in a prompt: if the rule's contribution refers to the CURRENT value of the column you're updating (not a fixed amount, not an external counter), it compounds. Words like "double," "based on current," "depends on existing value" — compounding signal. Words like "add 1 each time," "add a fixed bonus" — linear signal.
  • Snowball memory device: linear adds the same scoop of snow each step; compounding rolls a snowball downhill that picks up more snow because it's already bigger.

Watch out:

  • Status string typo silently no-ops everything. IF r.status = 'now_show' (with a stray 'w') never matches, so no UPDATE fires and the patients table comes back unchanged. Match the literal in the data exactly: 'no_show'.
  • The UPDATE doesn't need SELECT INTO here. Because the new value is a function of the column itself (2 * penalty_points + 1), Postgres reads the current row value as part of the UPDATE expression. Capturing into a variable first is harmless but unnecessary; the FOR LOOP exists only to enforce chronological order on the appointments side.
  • Existing penalty_points values matter. A patient who starts at 0 follows 0 → 1 → 3 → 7 → 15. A patient who starts at 1 (like Bob, who already had 1 prior no-show before the example data) follows 1 → 3 → 7. The compounding rule means starting state heavily affects the final result, unlike linear addition.
  • Pre-filtering the FOR LOOP to only no-show rows is also valid. FOR r IN SELECT * FROM appointments WHERE status = 'no_show' ORDER BY scheduled_at LOOP avoids the IF check inside. Either form works; the IF version is closer to the prompt's "iterate all appointments" wording.
  • Trailing ; after END $$, then SELECT * FROM patients ORDER BY patient_id; so the harness sees the post-mutation snapshot.

Editorial note — why the prompt language was confusing: the prompt phrasing "first no-show adds 1, second adds 2, third adds 3" sounds linear (counter-based), but the answer key uses a compounding rule that treats the patient's current penalty_points as the running "prior count." Those two interpretations only match for a patient starting at 0 — for any non-zero starting value, they diverge. When a problem mixes "increment by N" framing with a column whose value compounds, the math depends on which interpretation the answer key picked, and the prompt has to be explicit about that.

Functions topic

▼
  • CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION wrappers around a SELECT.
  • RETURNS TABLE — the function returns a row set (multiple rows, multiple columns). Body uses RETURN QUERY ( ... ); to stream rows back. Call with SELECT * FROM fn(args);.
  • RETURNS scalar — the function returns one value (number, boolean, text). Body uses RETURN ( ... ); to evaluate a scalar subquery. Call with SELECT fn(args) AS alias;.
  • The body keywords are NOT interchangeable. RETURN QUERY in a scalar function raises "cannot use RETURN QUERY in a non-SETOF function." RETURN ( ... ) in a table-returning function won't stream multiple rows — it tries to coerce the inner query into one composite value.
  • End every script with the trailing call — CREATE FUNCTION alone produces no rows, so the harness sees nothing.

Reference Method Scaffolds & Pitfalls

▼

RETURNS TABLE, scalar RETURNS, and the NULL-safe wrapper. Open each method below for the full scaffold.

Signal words: "find the Nth ...," "write a function," prompt names a function like getNthHighestSalary(N), IDE shows a CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION scaffold.

Technique: drop a normal SELECT or CTE inside RETURN QUERY ( ... );. Use a subquery wrapper to return NULL when no rows match.

Common pitfalls:

Pitfall How to avoid
Output slot shadows column name RETURNS TABLE (Salary INT) declares a salary output. Alias the source table (FROM Employee e) and qualify every reference (e.salary) to avoid "column reference is ambiguous".
Empty result instead of NULL When no rows match, an unwrapped query returns 0 rows. Wrap with SELECT (SELECT salary FROM nth_salary) to force one NULL row.
Missing function body markers Function bodies need BEGIN ... END; inside $$ ... $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;. The IDE pre-fills these — edit only inside RETURN QUERY ( ... );.
RANK vs DENSE_RANK For "Nth distinct" prompts use DENSE_RANK so rank values are 1, 2, 3 even with ties. RANK skips numbers after ties (1, 1, 3) and gives wrong answers.
SELECT expression type doesn't match declared RETURNS TABLE column type RETURNS TABLE is strict about types — Postgres won't auto-widen, auto-narrow, or coerce TEXT to VARCHAR for you. Common offenders: TO_CHAR(...) returns TEXT, not VARCHAR(N); COUNT(...) returns BIGINT, not INT; AVG(...) returns NUMERIC with no precision, not NUMERIC(p,s); VARCHAR (unbounded) doesn't match VARCHAR(N). Error: "structure of query does not match function result type." Fix: cast every SELECT expression to the exact declared type — TO_CHAR(...)::VARCHAR(7), COUNT(...)::INT, ROUND(AVG(...), 2), col::VARCHAR(100).

Methods:

RETURNS TABLE ( ... )

▼

Function returns a result set with named columns.

What it does

Defines a function whose output is a row set. The IDE scaffolds CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION ... RETURNS TABLE (...) and you fill in the inner RETURN QUERY ( ... );.

When to reach for it

"Find the Nth highest ...," "list the top K ...," or any prompt that names a function and expects a row set as the answer.

Full scaffold:

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION getNthHighestSalary(N INT)
RETURNS TABLE (Salary INT) AS $$
BEGIN
  RETURN QUERY (
    -- inner SELECT or CTE goes here
    -- alias the source table (e.g., FROM Employee e)
    -- qualify every reference (e.g., e.salary) to avoid column shadowing
    -- wrap with SELECT ( ... ) if NULL on empty result is required
    SELECT e.salary
    FROM Employee e
    -- ...
  );
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

RETURNS <type> + RETURN ( ... );

▼

Function returns a single scalar value of a fixed type.

What it does

Defines a function whose output is one value (e.g., INT, NUMERIC, BOOLEAN).

When to reach for it

The function returns a single number (count, ratio, max) rather than a row set; use plain RETURN, not RETURN QUERY.

Full scaffold:

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION getUserIDs(startDate DATE, endDate DATE, minAmount INT)
RETURNS INT AS $$
BEGIN
  RETURN (
    -- inner SELECT goes here
    -- this scalar subquery must return exactly one value
    SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)
    FROM Purchases
    WHERE time_stamp >= startDate
      AND time_stamp <= endDate
      AND amount >= minAmount
  );
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

NULL-safe wrapper SELECT (SELECT ... )

▼

Forces an empty inner result to surface as one NULL row.

What it does

Wraps an inner query in SELECT ( ... ) so an empty result set returns one row of NULLs instead of zero rows.

When to reach for it

A function spec says "return null when no rows match" (e.g., Nth highest salary when fewer than N distinct values exist).

Full scaffold:

-- Inner CTE may return zero rows. The outer scalar subquery
-- always returns exactly one row, NULL-filled when the inner is empty.
WITH nth_salary AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT s.salary
  FROM salary_rankings s
  WHERE s.rank = N
)
SELECT (SELECT n.salary FROM nth_salary AS n)

RETURNS scalar recipe

▼
  • Wrap a single-value computation in a function that returns one number, boolean, or text.
  • Body uses RETURN ( ... ); — NOT RETURN QUERY — with a single-value subquery inside.
  • Common shape for rates, ratios, counts, and lookup helpers called from other queries.
  • Use COALESCE(..., 0.00) for the empty-input default, and NULLIF on the denominator to dodge divide-by-zero.

Signal words: "write a function that returns the percentage / count / total / ratio for a given X," prompt names a function like calculate_xxx_rate(args) with a numeric or boolean return type, the call site is SELECT fn(args) AS result;.

Technique: CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION fn(args) RETURNS <type> AS $$ BEGIN RETURN ( /* scalar subquery */ ); END; $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql; followed by a trailing SELECT fn(args); call so the harness sees output.

Common pitfalls:

Pitfall How to avoid
Using RETURN QUERY instead of RETURN RETURN QUERY is for RETURNS TABLE functions. A scalar function uses plain RETURN ( ... ); with a single-value subquery inside the parens.
Integer division silently zeroing out a ratio 3 / 4 returns 0 in integer arithmetic. Cast the numerator with ::NUMERIC or multiply by 100.0 (a numeric literal) before dividing.
Divide-by-zero when the input range is empty Wrap the denominator with NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0) so the division returns NULL rather than throwing, then COALESCE(..., 0) for the empty-range default.
Forgetting ROUND Prompts that say "rounded to N decimals" mean the function returns the rounded value. Apply ROUND(value, N) before RETURN; do not rely on display formatting.
Missing trailing function call CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION ... alone produces no rows. End the script with SELECT fn(args); so the harness has output to compare against.

Skeleton you'll fill in:

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION fn_name(p_arg1 TYPE1, p_arg2 TYPE2)
RETURNS NUMERIC AS $$
BEGIN
  RETURN (
    SELECT COALESCE(
      ROUND( /* numeric expression */ , 2),
      0
    )
    FROM source_table
    WHERE col_a = p_arg1
      AND col_b >= p_arg2
  );
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

-- Trailing call so the harness sees output:
SELECT fn_name(arg1_value, arg2_value);

Anchor problems — SLA breach rate (conditional aggregation inside a scalar function with empty-range guard).

Medium Calculate SLA Breach Rate for Agent

▼

A scalar function that returns one rate. Combines conditional aggregation (SUM over CASE) with empty-range guards (NULLIF + COALESCE) inside a single subquery, so the entire computation is one pass over the filtered rows.

Tables:

Column Type Notes
ticket_idINTprimary key
agent_idINTfilter argument
assigned_dateDATEfilter cutoff (on or after start_date)
sla_target_minutesINTSLA threshold
resolution_time_minutesINTbreach when this exceeds the target
statusVARCHAR(20)unused by the rate calculation

Prompt: Write a function calculate_agent_breach_rate(p_agent_id INTEGER, p_start_date DATE) RETURNS NUMERIC that returns the percentage of tickets assigned to that agent on or after the start date that breached SLA, where breach means resolution_time_minutes > sla_target_minutes.

  • Return the rate as a percentage from 0 to 100.
  • Round to 2 decimals.
  • If the agent has no tickets in range, return 0.00 (not NULL, not an error).
▶ 1 Single-pass conditional aggregation with NULLIF + COALESCE
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION calculate_agent_breach_rate( p_agent_id INTEGER, p_start_date DATE ) RETURNS NUMERIC AS $$ BEGIN RETURN ( SELECT COALESCE( ROUND( 100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN resolution_time_minutes > sla_target_minutes THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)::NUMERIC / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0), 2 ), 0.00 ) FROM support_tickets WHERE agent_id = p_agent_id AND assigned_date >= p_start_date ); END; $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql; SELECT calculate_agent_breach_rate(102, '2024-01-15') AS breach_rate;

Why this is best: One subquery does all four jobs — filter to the agent's tickets in range, count breaches via SUM(CASE WHEN ...), divide by total with NULLIF guarding zero, and COALESCE the NULL back to 0.00 for the empty-range case. Single pass over the table, no IF blocks, no DECLARE.

Trace through the example data (agent 102, start 2024-01-15):

ticket_id assigned_date target / actual in range? CASE WHEN value
12024-01-1060 / 45no (before 2024-01-15)excluded
22024-01-16120 / 150yes1 (breach)
32024-01-1860 / 90yes1 (breach)
42024-01-20180 / 120yes0 (within SLA)
52024-01-1660 / 80no (different agent)excluded
62024-01-2290 / 95yes1 (breach)

SUM = 3, COUNT = 4, ratio = 0.75, × 100 = 75.00. Rounded: 75.00.

Watch out:

  • The ::NUMERIC cast on the SUM (or the 100.0 literal) prevents integer division. Without it, 3 / 4 evaluates to 0 and the function returns 0.00 regardless of how many breaches there were.
  • NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0) is the standard divide-by-zero guard. Postgres throws on x / 0 but quietly returns NULL for x / NULL, which COALESCE then converts to the requested default.
  • The empty-range default has to be 0.00 (NUMERIC), not 0 (INTEGER) — matching the function's declared return type avoids subtle implicit-cast surprises.
  • Use RETURN ( ... ) with parentheses around a single-value subquery. RETURN QUERY is for RETURNS TABLE functions and will fail to compile here.
  • End the script with SELECT calculate_agent_breach_rate(102, '2024-01-15'); — without the trailing call the function definition succeeds but the harness sees no rows and reports failure.

Easy Calculate Denial Rate by Reviewer

▼

Same scalar-function shape as the SLA breach rate, but slimmer: only one parameter and the breach predicate is a simple equality. Demonstrates the AVG(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) shortcut for ratios.

Tables:

Column Type Notes
review_idINTprimary key
reviewer_idINTfilter argument
patient_idINTunused by the rate
diagnosis_codeVARCHAR(20)unused by the rate
review_dateDATEunused by the rate
denial_statusVARCHAR(20)denied when value is 'DENIED'

Prompt: Write a function calculate_reviewer_denial_rate(p_reviewer_id INTEGER) RETURNS NUMERIC that returns the percentage of that reviewer's reviews where denial_status = 'DENIED'.

  • Return as a percentage 0–100 rounded to 2 decimals.
  • If the reviewer has no reviews, return 0.00.
▶ 1 AVG(CASE WHEN ...) shortcut for the ratio
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION calculate_reviewer_denial_rate(p_reviewer_id INTEGER) RETURNS NUMERIC AS $$ BEGIN RETURN ( SELECT COALESCE( ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN denial_status = 'DENIED' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 100, 2), 0.00 ) FROM diagnosis_reviews WHERE reviewer_id = p_reviewer_id ); END; $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql; SELECT calculate_reviewer_denial_rate(1) AS denial_rate;

Why this is best: AVG(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) is the one-liner equivalent of SUM(CASE) / COUNT(*). AVG handles the empty-set case by returning NULL (no divide-by-zero throw), and COALESCE turns that NULL into the required 0.00 default. Multiply by 100 to get a percentage, round to 2 decimals.

Trace through reviewer 1's rows in the example data:

review_id denial_status CASE WHEN value
101APPROVED0
102DENIED1
103APPROVED0
104DENIED1

AVG = 2/4 = 0.50, × 100 = 50.00. Rounded: 50.00.

Watch out:

  • AVG over a CASE expression of 0/1 IS the ratio — no SUM/COUNT/NULLIF needed. Postgres returns NUMERIC from AVG over INTEGER inputs, so no integer-division trap either.
  • The COALESCE(..., 0.00) handles the no-reviews case. Without it, AVG over an empty set returns NULL and the function would propagate that instead of 0.00.
  • String comparison is case-sensitive in Postgres — denial_status = 'DENIED' will not match 'denied' or 'Denied'. Use UPPER(denial_status) = 'DENIED' if the input casing varies.
  • The trailing SELECT calculate_reviewer_denial_rate(1); is required for the harness. CREATE FUNCTION alone does not produce a row.

Medium Calculate Average Session Engagement Score (rolling 90 days)

▼

Scalar function with a rolling-window date filter. Demonstrates the "scalar aggregate always returns one row" rule that lets a single-table function still emit 0.00 for clients with no rows in range — no LEFT JOIN clients scaffold needed.

Tables:

Column Type Notes
session_idINTprimary key
client_idINTfilter argument
session_dateDATErolling-window cutoff lives here
engagement_scoreNUMERIC(5,2)value being averaged
duration_minutesINTunused
therapist_idINTunused

Prompt: Write calculate_avg_engagement(p_client_id INTEGER) RETURNS NUMERIC that returns the average engagement_score across all of that client's sessions in the past 90 days, or 0.00 if the client has no sessions in that window.

▶ 1 Scalar aggregate over a rolling-window WHERE, with COALESCE for the empty case
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION calculate_avg_engagement(p_client_id INTEGER) RETURNS NUMERIC AS $$ BEGIN RETURN ( SELECT COALESCE(AVG(engagement_score), 0.00) FROM therapy_sessions WHERE client_id = p_client_id AND session_date > CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '90 days' ); END; $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql; SELECT calculate_avg_engagement(1) AS avg_score;

Why no LEFT JOIN clients is needed:

  • A SELECT AVG(...) with no GROUP BY is a "scalar aggregate." Postgres always emits exactly one output row, even when the WHERE matches nothing.
  • If the WHERE filters out every row for this client, AVG aggregates an empty set and returns NULL. The output is still one row containing NULL.
  • COALESCE(NULL, 0.00) turns that NULL into 0.00. RETURN reads the single scalar.
  • Compare with a SELECT that has GROUP BY client_id: an empty WHERE truly yields zero rows, and you'd need a LEFT JOIN clients scaffold to keep the client visible. Without GROUP BY, that scaffold is unnecessary.

Three traps that look right but break this function:

  • Comparing date to interval. WHERE session_date > INTERVAL '90 days' raises "operator does not exist: date > interval" because INTERVAL '90 days' is a duration, not a date. Subtract the interval from a date first: session_date > CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '90 days'.
  • Joining clients to keep "every client visible." Adding FROM clients LEFT JOIN base ... in a scalar function returns one row per client — then RETURN errors with "more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression." Drop the join; the function only ever asks about one client.
  • Over-rounding. If the answer key returns the AVG without ROUND, applying ROUND(..., 2) in your version produces 85.72 when the harness expects 85.7187500000000000. Read the expected value carefully; some prompts mention NUMERIC(5,2) but the validator uses unrounded precision.

Watch out:

  • CURRENT_DATE (no parens) returns today as a DATE. now()::date is equivalent. NOW() alone returns a TIMESTAMP — subtracting an interval from a TIMESTAMP returns a TIMESTAMP and the comparison still works, but mixing types invites surprises.
  • If the example data is rooted in a fixed past year (e.g., all sessions in 2024) and "today" is later, every WHERE returns empty and the example output is uniformly 0.00 — that test only exercises the COALESCE path, not the AVG.
  • The trailing SELECT calculate_avg_engagement(1) AS avg_score; is what the harness reads. CREATE FUNCTION alone produces no rows.

Medium Calculate Weekly Sleep Goal Adherence Rate (denominator = N exactly)

▼
  • Scalar function that returns a single percentage over a fixed-length window.
  • The denominator must be exactly N (here, 7 nights), even when some nights have no log entry.
  • Demonstrates the generate_series skeleton + LEFT JOIN pattern that forces the denominator regardless of which rows exist in the source.

Tables:

Table Column Type Notes
membersmember_idINTprimary key
member_nameVARCHARpassthrough
target_hours_per_nightNUMERIC(4,2)per-member sleep goal
sleep_logslog_idSERIALprimary key
member_idINTFK into members
log_dateDATEmay be missing for some nights
actual_hours_sleptNUMERIC(4,2)compared against the member's target

Prompt: Write calculate_sleep_adherence(p_member_id INTEGER, p_target_week_start DATE) RETURNS NUMERIC that returns the percentage of the 7 consecutive nights starting at p_target_week_start where the member's actual_hours_slept ≥ target_hours_per_night, rounded to 2 decimals (0.00–100.00). Nights with no log count as failures.

▶ 1 generate_series skeleton + LEFT JOIN sleep_logs + scalar aggregate
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION calculate_sleep_adherence( p_member_id INTEGER, p_target_week_start DATE ) RETURNS NUMERIC AS $$ BEGIN RETURN ( WITH dates AS ( SELECT generate_series( p_target_week_start, p_target_week_start + 6, INTERVAL '1 day' )::date AS log_date ), member_target AS ( SELECT target_hours_per_night FROM members WHERE member_id = p_member_id ) SELECT ROUND( AVG( CASE WHEN sl.actual_hours_slept >= mt.target_hours_per_night THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END ) * 100, 2 ) FROM dates AS d LEFT JOIN sleep_logs AS sl ON sl.log_date = d.log_date AND sl.member_id = p_member_id CROSS JOIN member_target AS mt ); END; $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql; SELECT calculate_sleep_adherence(1, '2024-01-15') AS result;

Why the dates CTE goes FROM the date skeleton, not from sleep_logs:

  • The FROM dates AS d guarantees 7 rows — one per night in the target week — no matter what's in sleep_logs.
  • LEFT JOIN sleep_logs ON sl.log_date = d.log_date AND sl.member_id = p_member_id attaches a log if one exists for that night, else NULL. Both join conditions live in ON so missing nights stay as NULL on the left.
  • CASE WHEN actual_hours_slept >= target THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END evaluates a NULL actual_hours_slept as the ELSE branch (since NULL >= anything is NULL, which is not TRUE), counting it as 0 — a failure.
  • AVG over 7 numeric values (some 0, some 1) gives the success rate; multiply by 100 and round.

The trap to avoid (FROM members LEFT JOIN sleep_logs JOIN dates):

  • Starting from members and INNER joining to dates only gives you rows where a sleep_log already matches a date. Missing nights vanish before CASE can convert them.
  • For a member with all 7 nights logged, that bug is invisible — they have 7 rows either way. For a member with partial logs, the denominator drops below 7 and the function over-reports adherence.
  • The fix is structural: the FROM clause has to be the table whose row count you want to preserve. Date skeleton FIRST, source LEFT JOINed to it.

Trace through member 1 (Alice, target 8.00, week 2024-01-15):

log_date actual target CASE WHEN value
2024-01-158.508.001
2024-01-167.008.000
2024-01-178.208.001
2024-01-188.008.001
2024-01-199.008.001
2024-01-207.508.000
2024-01-218.108.001

AVG = 5/7 = 0.7142..., × 100 = 71.4285..., rounded to 71.43.

Trace through member 2 (Bob, target 7.50, week 2024-01-15) — only 2 logs exist, the other 5 nights are missing:

log_date actual target CASE WHEN value
2024-01-158.007.501
2024-01-167.507.501
2024-01-17NULL7.500 (NULL falls to ELSE)
2024-01-18NULL7.500
2024-01-19NULL7.500
2024-01-20NULL7.500
2024-01-21NULL7.500

AVG = 2/7 = 0.2857..., × 100 = 28.5714..., rounded to 28.57. The buggy "FROM members" version would have computed 2/2 = 100.00 instead.

Watch out:

  • generate_series with an INTERVAL '1 day' argument returns TIMESTAMPs. Cast with ::date or the join to sleep_logs.log_date (DATE type) won't match.
  • The end of the series is p_target_week_start + 6, not + 7. generate_series is inclusive on both ends, so seven days = start + 0 through start + 6.
  • Both join predicates (sl.log_date = d.log_date AND sl.member_id = p_member_id) belong in the LEFT JOIN's ON clause, not in a trailing WHERE. A right-side filter in WHERE drops missing-night rows and converts the LEFT JOIN to an INNER — same overcounting bug.
  • Parameter names use p_ prefix to avoid colliding with column names like member_id. Skip the prefix and the function silently uses the column instead, which can match every row.
  • The trailing SELECT calculate_sleep_adherence(1, '2024-01-15') AS result; is what the harness reads.

Medium 30-Day Readmission Rate (LAG previous discharge + scalar rate)

▼
  • RETURNS scalar function that uses a window function (LAG) to compare each row against the previous event in the same partition.
  • Demonstrates the "within N days of previous event" shape with admission_date <= prev_discharge_date + INTERVAL '30 days'.
  • Computes a percentage by averaging a 1.0/0 flag, with COALESCE guarding the empty-result case.

Tables:

Table Column Type Notes
patientspatient_idINTprimary key
patient_nameVARCHAR(100)unused
date_of_birthDATEunused
admissionsadmission_idINTprimary key
patient_idINTpartition key
department_nameVARCHAR(100)filter argument and partition key
admission_dateDATEreadmission test column
discharge_dateDATEprior-event reference column

Prompt: Write calculate_readmission_rate(p_department_name VARCHAR) RETURNS NUMERIC(5,2). A readmission is an admission to the same department within 30 days of that patient's previous discharge from the same department. Return (readmissions / total_admissions) * 100, rounded to 2 decimals. Return 0.00 if there are no admissions for the department.

▶ 1 CTE staircase: LAG previous discharge, flag readmissions, AVG the flag
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION calculate_readmission_rate(p_department_name VARCHAR) RETURNS NUMERIC(5,2) AS $$ BEGIN RETURN ( WITH base AS ( SELECT a.admission_id, a.patient_id, a.department_name, a.admission_date, a.discharge_date, LAG(a.discharge_date) OVER ( PARTITION BY a.patient_id, a.department_name ORDER BY a.discharge_date ) AS prev_discharge_date FROM admissions AS a WHERE a.department_name = p_department_name ), check_readmission AS ( SELECT b.admission_id, b.patient_id, b.department_name, b.admission_date, b.discharge_date, b.prev_discharge_date, CASE WHEN b.admission_date <= b.prev_discharge_date + INTERVAL '30 days' THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END AS readmitted FROM base AS b ) SELECT COALESCE( ROUND(AVG(readmitted) * 100, 2), 0.00 ) AS readmission_rate FROM check_readmission ); END; $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql; SELECT calculate_readmission_rate('Cardiology') AS readmission_rate;

Three patterns this anchor adds to the RETURNS scalar recipe:

  • LAG for "previous event in the same partition." LAG(a.discharge_date) OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id, department_name ORDER BY discharge_date) attaches each admission's prior discharge to the row, so the comparison can be a single boolean expression in the next CTE. The first admission per partition gets NULL, which makes the CASE fall to ELSE 0 and counts the row as "not a readmission" — correct because it has no prior discharge.
  • Within-N-days date comparison with INTERVAL. admission_date <= prev_discharge_date + INTERVAL '30 days' tests whether the gap is at most 30 days. Adding INTERVAL to a DATE returns a TIMESTAMP, so the LHS gets implicitly promoted; both directions of comparison work without explicit casts.
  • AVG of a 1.0/0 flag = rate. AVG(readmitted) * 100 turns the 0/1 indicator into a percentage in one aggregation. Wrapping in COALESCE(..., 0.00) handles the empty-result case the prompt specifies — AVG over zero rows returns NULL, not 0.

Trace through Cardiology in the example data (5 admissions, 3 patients):

admission_id patient_id admission_date prev_discharge_date prev + 30 days readmitted
10112024-01-10NULLNULL0 (NULL falls to ELSE)
10212024-01-252024-01-152024-02-141 (Jan 25 ≤ Feb 14)
10322024-02-01NULLNULL0
10422024-02-202024-02-052024-03-061 (Feb 20 ≤ Mar 6)
10532024-03-01NULLNULL0

AVG = 2/5 = 0.40, × 100 = 40.00. Returns 40.00.

Watch out:

  • LAG the right column. LAG(a.admission_date) aliased as prev_discharge_date compiles fine but compares against the previous ADMISSION date, which is "30 days from previous admission" not "30 days from previous discharge." Different rule, often passes by accident on data where length-of-stay is consistent. LAG the column you actually want.
  • ORDER BY inside the window matters. ORDER BY a.discharge_date sequences admissions chronologically by exit. Ordering by admission_id works only if IDs are issued in admission-date order; safer to order by the date column you're comparing against.
  • NULL prev_discharge falls to ELSE 0. First admission per partition has no prior, so NULL + INTERVAL '30 days' is NULL, and admission_date <= NULL is NULL. CASE treats NULL conditions as "not true" and falls through to ELSE — that's the correct behavior here, but it's worth knowing it's NULL semantics doing the work, not an explicit guard.
  • COALESCE around the aggregate, not inside. AVG(readmitted) over zero rows returns NULL; multiplying by 100 keeps NULL; ROUND keeps NULL; the outer COALESCE turns the final NULL into 0.00. Putting COALESCE inside AVG(COALESCE(readmitted, 0)) would change every NULL flag to 0 instead of handling the empty-result case — semantically different.
  • RETURNS NUMERIC(5,2) caps at 999.99. Since the rate is bounded at 100.00, this is fine; for unbounded outputs use bare NUMERIC to avoid overflow errors.
  • Call with SELECT calculate_readmission_rate('Cardiology') AS readmission_rate; — scalar functions use SELECT fn(args), not SELECT * FROM fn(args).

Medium Trial Conversion Rate by Cohort (CTE staircase + cohort filter + denominator gotcha)

▼
  • RETURNS scalar function with two parameters: a cohort_month DATE and a days_window INT.
  • Two-CTE staircase: base tags every row with cohort membership and a per-row deadline; cohort filters to in-cohort rows before averaging.
  • Demonstrates the denominator gotcha: averaging over the WHOLE table dilutes the rate; you must filter to cohort rows BEFORE the aggregate.

Tables:

Column Type Notes
signup_idINTprimary key
company_nameVARCHAR(100)passthrough
trial_start_dateDATEcohort anchor; deadline base
converted_atDATENULL when not yet converted

Prompt: Write calculate_conversion_rate(cohort_month DATE, days_window INT) RETURNS NUMERIC(5,2). Return the percentage of trial signups in the given cohort month that converted within days_window days after their trial_start_date. Cohort = month of trial_start_date. Only count conversions where converted_at is not NULL and is on or before trial_start_date + days_window. Return 0.00 if no signups exist in the cohort. Test with SELECT calculate_conversion_rate('2024-01-01', 14) AS result;.

▶ 1 CTE staircase: tag cohort membership + deadline, filter, then average
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION calculate_conversion_rate(cohort_month DATE, days_window INT) RETURNS NUMERIC(5, 2) AS $$ BEGIN RETURN ( WITH base AS ( SELECT TO_CHAR(ts.trial_start_date, 'YYYY-MM') AS trial_month, TO_CHAR(cohort_month::date, 'YYYY-MM') AS cohort_month, CASE WHEN TO_CHAR(ts.trial_start_date, 'YYYY-MM') = TO_CHAR(cohort_month::date, 'YYYY-MM') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS in_cohort, ts.trial_start_date, ts.signup_id, ts.company_name, ts.converted_at, ts.trial_start_date::date + days_window AS conversation_deadline FROM trial_signups AS ts ), cohort AS ( SELECT b.trial_month, b.cohort_month, b.in_cohort, b.trial_start_date, b.signup_id, b.company_name, b.converted_at, b.conversation_deadline, CASE WHEN b.converted_at <= b.conversation_deadline THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END AS converted FROM base AS b WHERE b.in_cohort = 1 ) SELECT COALESCE( ROUND(AVG(converted) * 100, 2), 0.00 ) FROM cohort ); END; $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql; SELECT calculate_conversion_rate('2024-01-01', 14) AS result;

Three patterns this anchor adds to the RETURNS scalar recipe:

  • CTE staircase for verifiability. base keeps every audit column visible (signup_id, company_name, trial_start_date, converted_at, computed deadline, cohort flag) so each step is independently inspectable. cohort filters to in-cohort rows and adds the converted flag. The outer SELECT just averages. If the rate is wrong, you can SELECT * from each CTE in isolation to find which step diverged.
  • Cohort match via TO_CHAR(date, 'YYYY-MM') equality. Both sides are formatted to the same 'YYYY-MM' string, so February signups don't match a January cohort regardless of day-of-month. Equivalent to DATE_TRUNC('month', trial_start_date) = DATE_TRUNC('month', cohort_month); pick whichever reads cleaner for your team.
  • Filter BEFORE aggregating to avoid the denominator gotcha. If WHERE in_cohort = 1 is missing, AVG runs over ALL signups (including non-cohort months), diluting the rate. For example, with 3 conversions in a 5-row January cohort + 1 February row, AVG over the full table gives 3/6 = 50% instead of the correct 3/5 = 60%. Always filter to the cohort first, then aggregate.

Trace through January 2024 cohort with days_window = 14:

signup_id trial_start_date in_cohort deadline (start + 14) converted_at converted flag
12024-01-0512024-01-192024-01-121 (within window)
22024-01-1012024-01-242024-01-250 (one day late)
32024-01-1512024-01-292024-01-201
42024-01-2212024-02-05NULL0 (NULL falls to ELSE)
52024-02-030——excluded (not in cohort)
62024-01-2812024-02-112024-02-051

Cohort = 5 rows (signup_id 1-4 and 6). Converted = 3 (signups 1, 3, 6). Rate = 3/5 = 0.60 × 100 = 60.00.

Watch out:

  • The denominator gotcha is the easy mistake. Skipping the WHERE in_cohort = 1 in the second CTE (or doing the cohort filter only inside the CASE) makes AVG run over every signup. The CASE-only filter would give converted=0 for non-cohort rows but they'd still count toward the denominator, dragging the rate down.
  • Don't shadow the parameter name. The CTE column alias cohort_month shadows the function parameter cohort_month. In this code it works because the CTE only uses the alias as a passthrough, but inside the CASE the unqualified cohort_month reference would resolve to the column, not the parameter. Safer to rename the column (e.g., signup_cohort_label) or qualify the parameter as $1 in any deeper subquery.
  • NULL converted_at falls to ELSE 0. NULL <= deadline is NULL, which CASE treats as "not true" and routes to ELSE — correct here because non-converted signups should count as "did not convert," not be excluded.
  • Use <= not < on the deadline comparison. "Converted within 14 days" inclusive means a conversion exactly 14 days after the trial start counts; < would silently drop boundary cases.
  • Date plus int returns DATE in Postgres. trial_start_date::date + days_window works because DATE + INTEGER adds days. If days_window were NUMERIC, you'd need to cast or build an INTERVAL: trial_start_date + (days_window || ' days')::INTERVAL.
  • Call with SELECT calculate_conversion_rate('2024-01-01', 14) AS result;. Match the exact arguments the prompt's expected output assumes — different arguments produce different rows even when the function logic is correct.

Hard Average Retry Delay (per-day session detect + last-status filter + LEAD within session)

▼
  • RETURNS scalar function that averages minute-delays between consecutive retry attempts, but ONLY for days that ended in failure with at least 2 attempts.
  • Three-CTE staircase: tag each row with a session number, filter the qualifying days, compute deltas via LEAD inside each session.
  • New technique: detect retry sessions with a running SUM of "is this the first attempt?" markers — produces a session id that partitions the LEAD window.

Tables:

Column Type Notes
attempt_idINTprimary key
job_nameTEXTfilter parameter
attempted_atTIMESTAMPretry attempt time
attempt_numberINTresets to 1 on each new session
statusTEXT'failed' or 'success'

Prompt: Return the average delay in minutes between consecutive retry attempts for runs that ultimately failed. A "run" = all attempts for a job on the same calendar date. Only count runs where the LAST attempt of the day was 'failed' AND there were at least 2 attempts that day. Return 0.00 if no qualifying retries.

▶ 1 Three-CTE staircase with running-SUM session detection
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION calculate_avg_retry_delay(p_job_name TEXT) RETURNS NUMERIC AS $$ BEGIN RETURN ( WITH base AS ( SELECT j.attempt_id, j.job_name, j.attempted_at, j.attempted_at::DATE AS attempted_date, j.attempt_number, j.status, SUM(CASE WHEN j.attempt_number = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) OVER (PARTITION BY j.job_name ORDER BY j.attempted_at) - 1 AS grp FROM job_attempts AS j WHERE j.job_name = p_job_name ), qualifying_days AS ( SELECT job_name, attempted_date FROM base GROUP BY job_name, attempted_date HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 AND MAX(status) <> 'success' ), deltas AS ( SELECT b.attempt_id, b.attempted_at, b.grp, ROUND( EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM LEAD(b.attempted_at) OVER ( PARTITION BY b.job_name, b.grp ORDER BY b.attempted_at ) - b.attempted_at ) / 60, 2) AS min_diff FROM base AS b JOIN qualifying_days AS q ON b.job_name = q.job_name AND b.attempted_date = q.attempted_date ) SELECT COALESCE(ROUND(AVG(min_diff), 2), 0.00) FROM deltas ); END; $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql; SELECT calculate_avg_retry_delay('data_sync') AS result;

The running-SUM session trick (the new pattern this anchor introduces):

  • A new retry session starts whenever attempt_number = 1.
  • Wrap that in a CASE expression that returns 1 at session boundaries and 0 otherwise.
  • Take a running SUM of that CASE inside an OVER window ordered by time — the SUM increments by 1 at each new session.
  • Subtract 1 to make the first session = 0, the second = 1, etc.

Trace through data_sync:

attempted_at attempt_number status is new session? running SUM grp
2024-01-15 08:001failed110
2024-01-15 08:052failed010
2024-01-15 08:123failed010
2024-01-16 09:001failed121
2024-01-16 09:102success021

The per-day filter (qualifying_days):

attempted_date COUNT(*) MAX(status) Qualifies?
2024-01-153failedyes
2024-01-162successno (last status = success)

Only 2024-01-15 survives, so deltas use just the first three rows: 5 min, 7 min, then NULL at the end of the session. AVG = (5 + 7) / 2 = 6.00.

LEAD must partition by session, not just by job:

PARTITION BY Result on last row of session 0
job_name onlyLEAD jumps to next day's 09:00 — a 24-hour gap that pollutes the average
job_name AND grpLEAD returns NULL at the end of each session, so cross-session jumps don't appear in the delta

Watch out:

  • The MAX(status) trick works because of an implicit invariant. Alphabetically 'failed' < 'success', AND once a day's run hits 'success' the retries stop. So if 'success' appears anywhere in the day, it must be at the end. If the schema introduced more statuses ('pending', 'cancelled') or allowed retries after success, you'd need LAST_VALUE(status) OVER (PARTITION BY job_name, attempted_date ORDER BY attempted_at ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) or a separate "row_number = max(row_number) per day" filter.
  • The running SUM creates the session id; without it, LEAD spans across sessions. This is the same pattern as the consecutive-id gaps-and-islands trick, but here you can't use attempted_at - rn because timestamps aren't evenly spaced. The CASE-WHEN running SUM is the right tool when the "new session" signal comes from a column reset rather than a calendar gap.
  • Subtract 1 from the SUM so the first session = 0. Purely cosmetic, but matches the convention in the rest of the playbook's gaps-and-islands anchors.
  • COALESCE the final AVG. If no day qualifies, AVG over zero rows is NULL; the prompt asks for 0.00.
  • Call with SELECT calculate_avg_retry_delay('data_sync') AS result; — the trailing call must use the literal argument that produces the expected output.

Medium Calculate User Match Success Rate (bidirectional message exchange)

▼

A scalar function whose subquery is a CTE staircase across the matches and messages tables. Counts messages in each direction per match, flags a match successful only when both directions exist, then averages the flags into a percentage.

Tables: matches (match_id, user1_id, user2_id, match_date), messages (message_id, sender_id, recipient_id, match_id, sent_at), and users for reference.

Prompt: Write calculate_match_success_rate(user_id_param INT, min_date DATE) RETURNS NUMERIC returning the percentage of a user's matches (on or after min_date) that resulted in at least one message in both directions after the match was created. Round to 2 decimals; return 0.00 if the user has no matches in range.

Test call: SELECT calculate_match_success_rate(101, '2024-01-01') AS result; → expected 66.67.

▶ 1 CTE staircase: count both directions, flag, then average
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION calculate_match_success_rate(user_id_param INT, min_date DATE) RETURNS NUMERIC AS $$ BEGIN RETURN ( WITH user_matches AS ( -- step 1: this user's matches on or after min_date SELECT match_id, user1_id, user2_id, match_date FROM matches WHERE (user1_id = user_id_param OR user2_id = user_id_param) AND match_date >= min_date ), direction_counts AS ( -- step 2: count messages each way, sent after the match SELECT um.match_id, um.user1_id, um.user2_id, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE msg.sender_id = um.user1_id AND msg.recipient_id = um.user2_id) AS msgs_u1_to_u2, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE msg.sender_id = um.user2_id AND msg.recipient_id = um.user1_id) AS msgs_u2_to_u1 FROM user_matches um LEFT JOIN messages msg ON msg.match_id = um.match_id AND msg.sent_at > um.match_date GROUP BY um.match_id, um.user1_id, um.user2_id ), success_flag AS ( -- step 3: success = at least one message BOTH ways SELECT match_id, msgs_u1_to_u2, msgs_u2_to_u1, CASE WHEN msgs_u1_to_u2 > 0 AND msgs_u2_to_u1 > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_success FROM direction_counts ) SELECT COALESCE(ROUND(AVG(is_success) * 100, 2), 0.00) -- step 4: rate, 0.00 if none FROM success_flag ); END; $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql; SELECT calculate_match_success_rate(101, '2024-01-01') AS result;

Why a CTE staircase: each step is independently checkable. Step 1 narrows to the right matches, step 2 keeps the raw per-direction counts as columns you can eyeball, step 3 derives the flag from those counts, and step 4 collapses to one number. The whole stack is the single-value subquery inside RETURN ( ... ), so it is still a scalar function.

Trace through the example (user 101, min_date 2024-01-01). Step 1 drops match 1 (2023-12-20, too early) and match 5 (does not involve 101), leaving matches 2, 3, and 4. Step 2 counts each direction:

match_id pair (u1, u2) msgs_u1_to_u2 msgs_u2_to_u1 is_success
2(101, 103)111
3(101, 104)100
4(101, 105)111

Match 3 fails because 104 never replied to 101. Step 4 averages the flags: AVG(1, 0, 1) = 0.6667, × 100 = 66.6667, rounded to 66.67.

Watch out:

  • Use LEFT JOIN, not INNER. A match where nobody messaged still has to count toward the denominator as a failure. An INNER JOIN would silently drop those dead matches, shrinking the denominator and inflating the rate.
  • COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE ...) tallies both directions in one pass instead of two correlated subqueries. Each filter only counts the messages going that one way, so the two columns are the per-direction tallies side by side.
  • sent_at > match_date enforces "after the match was created." Because match_date is a DATE, it compares against midnight of that day, so a message sent later the same day still counts; only one timed exactly at 00:00:00 would be excluded.
  • AVG(is_success) is shorthand for SUM(is_success) / COUNT(*). When step 1 returns nothing, AVG over zero rows is NULL, and COALESCE(..., 0.00) converts that to the required default. Use 0.00 (NUMERIC), not 0 (INTEGER), to match the declared return type.
  • End the script with the trailing SELECT ...; — the function definition alone produces no rows, so the harness needs the call to see output.

Medium Count Invites from Top Squad Leaders (RETURNS scalar + DENSE_RANK gate)

▼

For a given player, return how many squad invites they have sent — but ONLY if they rank among the top 3 by total match wins. Below the cutoff, return 0. Ties at the third place rank are all included (DENSE_RANK semantics).

Tables: players (player_id, ...), match_results (player_id, placement, ...), squad_invites (inviter_player_id, ...)

Real-World Example

A battle-royale platform surfaces a "top squad leaders" leaderboard for in-game discovery; the count of invites each top-tier leader has sent gauges how recruiting-active the elite players are, while non-elite players are silently hidden by returning 0.

Why the rank is computed over EVERY player, not just the input player

The naive temptation is to filter WHERE player_id = p_player_id early. That kills the rank: a window function over a single row is always 1, so every input player would falsely qualify. The fix: rank ALL players first, THEN filter to the input. Window functions need the full population in context.

What this query does, step by step:

  1. Per-player win count — in player_rankings, GROUP BY player_id and SUM(CASE WHEN placement = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END). Equivalent shorthand: COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE placement = 1).
  2. DENSE_RANK across all players — same CTE, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total_wins DESC). DENSE_RANK (not RANK) so ties at rank 3 all keep rank 3, matching the prompt's "include all tied players."
  3. Per-player invites sent — in total_sent, GROUP BY inviter_player_id and COUNT(*).
  4. LEFT JOIN rankings + sent — in base, on player_id. LEFT (not INNER) so a top-3 player who has sent zero invites still appears, with NULL for invites_sent → COALESCE to 0.
  5. Cast to INT — COUNT returns BIGINT; the function returns INT, so cast invites_sent down.
  6. Gate + filter to the input player — final SELECT applies CASE WHEN rnk ≤ 3 THEN invites_sent ELSE 0 END and filters WHERE player_id = p_player_id. The WHERE goes LAST, after the rank is computed over everyone.

Trace — player rankings on the example data:

player_id wins (placement = 1) DENSE_RANK invites_sent result for that player
1013133 (top 3, returns invites)
1022222
1031311
1040410 (gate fails)
1050400
106(no match rows)—0NULL ← edge case, see watch-out
